docs.text:
find_max_rho_f_scaling(
    network: Network,
    bus_names: List[str],
    u_limit: float,
    k_ref: KVector,
    *,
    c_bounds: Tuple[float, float] = (0.001, 1000.0),
    tol_rel: float = 0.001,
    max_iter: int = 60,
    fault_scalings: Optional[Dict[float, float]] = None,
    run_fault_kwargs: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None,
    progress: Optional[
        Callable[[int, int, str], None]
    ] = None,
    should_cancel: Optional[Callable[[], bool]] = None,
) -> Dict[str, Any]

Find the largest scaling factor c of a reference k-vector.

Performs a log-scale bisection on c so that k = c * k_ref yields a maximum RMS EPR (across all buses swept as faults) that is at or below u_limit. k_ref is typically obtained by fitting the rho-f model above to measured impedance points; this function answers how much head-room the network has around that characteristic.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default network Network

The simulation network. Buses, branches, sources and paths must already be configured.

required bus_names list of str

Buses whose impedance is parameterised by k and which are swept as fault locations.

required u_limit float

Upper bound on the RMS EPR (in volts) at any swept bus. Must be finite and strictly positive.

required k_ref tuple of (float, float, float, float, float)

Reference 5-tuple (k1_ref, ..., k5_ref). Must have length 5 and not be the zero vector.

required c_bounds tuple of (float, float)

Search interval for c. Finite, strictly positive, c_bounds[0] < c_bounds[1]. Defaults to (1e-3, 1e3).

(0.001, 1000.0) tol_rel float

Bisection tolerance on the relative bracket width (c_hi - c_lo) / c_lo. Must be finite and strictly positive. Defaults to 1e-3.

0.001 max_iter int

Hard cap on bisection steps. Must be an int of at least 1. Defaults to 60.

60 fault_scalings dict of float to float

See :func:evaluate_max_epr_under_k.

None run_fault_kwargs dict

Forwarded to :func:run_fault.

None progress callable

progress(done, total, label), called after every bus solve of every trial factor (label "c = <factor>, bus <name>"). total is len(bus_names) times the trial factors the bracket and tolerance require; see :mod:groundinsight.progress.

None should_cancel callable

Asked before every bus solve; a true answer raises :class:~groundinsight.progress.StudyCancelled, also in the middle of a bus sweep.

None

Returns:

Type Description dict

Mapping with keys

  • "c_max" (float): a scaling factor whose swept maximum EPR was evaluated and found compatible with u_limit. It is the largest such factor only when "converged" is True.
  • "k_max" (tuple of float): c_max * k_ref.
  • "max_epr_rms_at_c_max" (float): maximum RMS EPR across all swept buses at c_max, in volts.
  • "epr_rms_per_bus_at_c_max" (dict of str to float): RMS EPR per swept bus at c_max.
  • "iterations" (int): number of bisection steps taken.
  • "converged" (bool): True iff the bracket was closed to within tol_rel. Check this before using c_max or k_max as a design value.
  • "status" (str): "converged", "bracket_within_tol_on_entry", "max_iter_reached" or "bracket_fully_admissible".
  • "c_bracket" (tuple of float): the interval provably containing the true maximum; (c_hi, inf) when the whole bracket was admissible.
  • "bracket_rel_width" (float): (c_hi - c_lo) / c_lo of that interval, comparable against tol_rel.

As in :func:~groundinsight.analysis.find_max_rho_scaling, iterations == 0 does not identify a case on its own; read "status".

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

For invalid input -- u_limit, tol_rel, max_iter and c_bounds are checked for finiteness as well as range -- or if c = c_bounds[0] already violates the EPR limit, or if the model returns a non-finite EPR at some trial factor.

TypeError

If progress or should_cancel is not callable.

StudyCancelled

If should_cancel() returned true; the network is as found.

Notes

The monotonicity assumption. The bisection finds the crossing of max EPR(c) with u_limit and therefore presumes there is only one. Unlike :func:~groundinsight.analysis.find_max_rho_scaling, this search scales all five k and with them every term of the impedance, so at a single bus the whole impedance scales with c and monotonicity follows. In a coupled multi-bus network it does not follow: the swept maximum is a maximum over buses, each of which sees the others through the shields, and a chain resonance can in principle make it turn. That case has not been constructed, so treat it as unproven rather than as excluded -- if c_max looks implausible, sweep c explicitly with :func:evaluate_max_epr_under_k and look at the curve. The rho-only search has a pre-scan for exactly this (monotonicity_grid); here the same scan would cost a full bus sweep per point and is left to the caller.

Examples:

>>> import groundinsight as gi
>>> from groundinsight.api.examples import build_minimal
>>> report = gi.find_max_rho_f_scaling(build_minimal(), ["bus3"], u_limit=10.0,
...                                    k_ref=(0.01, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0))
>>> report["status"], report["max_epr_rms_at_c_max"] <= 10.0
('converged', True)

def find_max_rho_f_scaling(
    network: Network,
    bus_names: List[str],
    u_limit: float,
    k_ref: KVector,
    *,
    c_bounds: Tuple[float, float] = (1e-3, 1e3),
    tol_rel: float = 1e-3,
    max_iter: int = 60,
    fault_scalings: Optional[Dict[float, float]] = None,
    run_fault_kwargs: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None,
    progress: Optional[Callable[[int, int, str], None]] = None,
    should_cancel: Optional[Callable[[], bool]] = None,
) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """Find the largest scaling factor ``c`` of a reference k-vector.

    Performs a log-scale bisection on ``c`` so that ``k = c * k_ref``
    yields a maximum RMS EPR (across all buses swept as faults) that is
    at or below ``u_limit``. ``k_ref`` is typically obtained by fitting
    the rho-f model above to measured impedance points; this function
    answers *how much head-room the network has around that
    characteristic*.

    Parameters
    ----------
    network : Network
        The simulation network. Buses, branches, sources and paths must
        already be configured.
    bus_names : list of str
        Buses whose impedance is parameterised by ``k`` *and* which are
        swept as fault locations.
    u_limit : float
        Upper bound on the RMS EPR (in volts) at any swept bus. Must be
        finite and strictly positive.
    k_ref : tuple of (float, float, float, float, float)
        Reference 5-tuple ``(k1_ref, ..., k5_ref)``. Must have length 5
        and not be the zero vector.
    c_bounds : tuple of (float, float), optional
        Search interval for ``c``. Finite, strictly positive,
        ``c_bounds[0] < c_bounds[1]``. Defaults to ``(1e-3, 1e3)``.
    tol_rel : float, optional
        Bisection tolerance on the relative bracket width
        ``(c_hi - c_lo) / c_lo``. Must be finite and strictly positive.
        Defaults to ``1e-3``.
    max_iter : int, optional
        Hard cap on bisection steps. Must be an ``int`` of at least 1.
        Defaults to ``60``.
    fault_scalings : dict of float to float, optional
        See :func:`evaluate_max_epr_under_k`.
    run_fault_kwargs : dict, optional
        Forwarded to :func:`run_fault`.
    progress : callable, optional
        ``progress(done, total, label)``, called after every bus solve of
        every trial factor (label ``"c = <factor>, bus <name>"``). ``total``
        is ``len(bus_names)`` times the trial factors the bracket and
        tolerance require; see :mod:`groundinsight.progress`.
    should_cancel : callable, optional
        Asked before every bus solve; a true answer raises
        :class:`~groundinsight.progress.StudyCancelled`, also in the middle
        of a bus sweep.

    Returns
    -------
    dict
        Mapping with keys

        - ``"c_max"`` (float): a scaling factor whose swept maximum EPR
          was evaluated and found compatible with ``u_limit``. It is the
          *largest* such factor only when ``"converged"`` is ``True``.
        - ``"k_max"`` (tuple of float): ``c_max * k_ref``.
        - ``"max_epr_rms_at_c_max"`` (float): maximum RMS EPR across all
          swept buses at ``c_max``, in volts.
        - ``"epr_rms_per_bus_at_c_max"`` (dict of str to float): RMS EPR
          per swept bus at ``c_max``.
        - ``"iterations"`` (int): number of bisection steps taken.
        - ``"converged"`` (bool): ``True`` iff the bracket was closed to
          within ``tol_rel``. Check this before using ``c_max`` or
          ``k_max`` as a design value.
        - ``"status"`` (str): ``"converged"``,
          ``"bracket_within_tol_on_entry"``, ``"max_iter_reached"`` or
          ``"bracket_fully_admissible"``.
        - ``"c_bracket"`` (tuple of float): the interval provably
          containing the true maximum; ``(c_hi, inf)`` when the whole
          bracket was admissible.
        - ``"bracket_rel_width"`` (float): ``(c_hi - c_lo) / c_lo`` of
          that interval, comparable against ``tol_rel``.

        As in :func:`~groundinsight.analysis.find_max_rho_scaling`,
        ``iterations == 0`` does not identify a case on its own; read
        ``"status"``.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        For invalid input -- ``u_limit``, ``tol_rel``, ``max_iter`` and
        ``c_bounds`` are checked for finiteness as well as range -- or if
        ``c = c_bounds[0]`` already violates the EPR limit, or if the
        model returns a non-finite EPR at some trial factor.
    TypeError
        If ``progress`` or ``should_cancel`` is not callable.
    StudyCancelled
        If ``should_cancel()`` returned true; the network is as found.

    Notes
    -----
    **The monotonicity assumption.** The bisection finds *the* crossing of
    ``max EPR(c)`` with ``u_limit`` and therefore presumes there is only one.
    Unlike :func:`~groundinsight.analysis.find_max_rho_scaling`, this search
    scales all five ``k`` and with them every term of the impedance, so at a
    single bus the whole impedance scales with ``c`` and monotonicity follows.
    In a coupled multi-bus network it does **not** follow: the swept maximum
    is a maximum over buses, each of which sees the others through the
    shields, and a chain resonance can in principle make it turn. That case
    has not been constructed, so treat it as unproven rather than as excluded
    -- if ``c_max`` looks implausible, sweep ``c`` explicitly with
    :func:`evaluate_max_epr_under_k` and look at the curve. The rho-only
    search has a pre-scan for exactly this (``monotonicity_grid``); here the
    same scan would cost a full bus sweep per point and is left to the caller.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import groundinsight as gi
    >>> from groundinsight.api.examples import build_minimal
    >>> report = gi.find_max_rho_f_scaling(build_minimal(), ["bus3"], u_limit=10.0,
    ...                                    k_ref=(0.01, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0))
    >>> report["status"], report["max_epr_rms_at_c_max"] <= 10.0
    ('converged', True)
    """
    validate_limit(u_limit, "u_limit")
    validate_tol_rel(tol_rel)
    validate_max_iter(max_iter)
    if not bus_names:
        raise ValueError("bus_names must not be empty.")
    if len(k_ref) != 5:
        raise ValueError(f"k_ref must be a 5-tuple, got length {len(k_ref)}.")
    if all(x == 0 for x in k_ref):
        raise ValueError("k_ref must not be the zero vector.")
    c_lo_init, c_hi_init = validate_c_bounds(c_bounds)
    # Both bracket ends, then the halvings that close the bracket: a fixed
    # count (see planned_steps), times one solve per swept bus.
    hooks = StudyHooks(
        "find_max_rho_f_scaling",
        len(bus_names) * (2 + planned_steps(c_lo_init, c_hi_init, tol_rel, max_iter)),
        progress,
        should_cancel,
    )

    last_epr_per_bus: Dict[str, Dict[str, float]] = {"value": {}}
    # A trial factor changes the grounding impedances of the swept buses and
    # nothing else; every fault location keeps its injection vectors and its
    # stamp pattern from the first full sweep. Later trials are re-solved on
    # those (P4, see analysis._session) -- bit for bit the EPRs a full sweep
    # computes. A bus whose session cannot answer a trial is solved in full.
    sessions: Dict[str, Optional[BusImpedanceSession]] = {}
    # Per swept bus: does its session share the nodal matrix of the first
    # one? Decided once per set of sessions.
    sharing: Dict[str, bool] = {}

    def _session_eprs(k: KVector, label: str) -> Optional[Dict[str, float]]:
        """The EPR per swept bus from the sessions, or ``None`` for a full sweep."""
        if not sessions or any(sessions.get(b) is None for b in bus_names):
            return None
        frequencies = [float(f) for f in network.frequencies]
        impedances: Dict[str, np.ndarray] = {}
        for b in bus_names:
            rho = float(network.buses[b].specific_earth_resistance)
            impedances[b] = np.array(
                [complex(z.real, z.imag)
                 for z in (_z_rho_f(k, rho, f) for f in frequencies)],
                dtype=complex,
            )
        # Fault locations without a voltage-source loop share their nodal
        # matrix, so one factorisation per trial serves all of them.
        anchor = sessions[bus_names[0]]
        if not sharing:
            sharing.update(
                {b: sessions[b].same_matrix_as(anchor) for b in bus_names}
            )
        shared: Dict[int, Optional[list]] = {}

        def factors_for(b: str) -> Optional[list]:
            if not sharing[b]:
                return None
            if 0 not in shared:
                shared[0] = anchor.factorise(impedances)
            return shared[0]

        eprs: Dict[str, float] = {}
        for b in bus_names:
            hooks.checkpoint()
            epr = sessions[b].epr_rms(impedances, factors_for(b))
            if epr is None:
                epr = _evaluate_max_epr_under_k(
                    network, bus_names, k=k,
                    fault_scalings=fault_scalings,
                    run_fault_kwargs=run_fault_kwargs,
                    solve_buses=[b],
                )[b]
            eprs[b] = epr
            hooks.advance(f"{label}bus {b}")
        return eprs

    def _max_epr_at(c: float) -> float:
        k = tuple(c * x for x in k_ref)
        label = f"c = {c:.6g}, "
        eprs = _session_eprs(k, label)
        if eprs is None:
            sessions.clear()
            sharing.clear()
            eprs = _evaluate_max_epr_under_k(
                network, bus_names,
                k=k,
                fault_scalings=fault_scalings,
                run_fault_kwargs=run_fault_kwargs,
                hooks=hooks,
                label=label,
                sessions=sessions,
            )
        last_epr_per_bus["value"] = eprs
        epr = max(eprs.values()) if eprs else 0.0
        if not math.isfinite(epr):
            # Same reasoning as in ``inverse_rho``: a non-finite EPR makes
            # every comparison against u_limit False, so the bisection would
            # take the same turn at every step and reach the lower bracket
            # bound without ever raising.
            raise ValueError(
                f"The swept maximum EPR evaluated to {epr!r} for the scaling "
                f"factor c={c:g} (k = {tuple(c * x for x in k_ref)!r}). A "
                "non-finite EPR cannot be compared against u_limit -- every "
                "comparison would be False and the bisection would walk to "
                "the lower bracket bound without raising. Check the k-vector "
                "at that scale against the buses' specific_earth_resistance."
            )
        return epr

    epr_lo = _max_epr_at(c_lo_init)
    eprs_lo_snapshot: Dict[str, float] = dict(last_epr_per_bus["value"])
    if epr_lo > u_limit:
        raise ValueError(
            f"u_limit={u_limit:g} V is below the maximum EPR at "
            f"c={c_lo_init:g}: max EPR_RMS={epr_lo:g} V — no scaling "
            f"factor in the bracket {c_bounds!r} satisfies the constraint."
        )

    epr_hi = _max_epr_at(c_hi_init)
    iterations = 0
    if epr_hi <= u_limit:
        logger.info(
            "Bracket fully admissible: max EPR_RMS at c=%g is %g V <= "
            "u_limit=%g V. Consider widening c_bounds.",
            c_hi_init, epr_hi, u_limit,
        )
        c_max, epr_at = c_hi_init, epr_hi
        epr_per_bus_at = dict(last_epr_per_bus["value"])
        status = STATUS_BRACKET_FULLY_ADMISSIBLE
        c_lo, c_hi = c_lo_init, c_hi_init
    else:
        c_lo, c_hi = c_lo_init, c_hi_init
        while iterations < max_iter and (c_hi - c_lo) / c_lo > tol_rel:
            c_mid = math.sqrt(c_lo * c_hi)  # geometric mean -> log bisection
            epr_mid = _max_epr_at(c_mid)
            if epr_mid <= u_limit:
                c_lo, epr_lo = c_mid, epr_mid
                eprs_lo_snapshot = dict(last_epr_per_bus["value"])
            else:
                c_hi = c_mid
            iterations += 1
        c_max, epr_at = c_lo, epr_lo
        epr_per_bus_at = eprs_lo_snapshot
        status = classify(iterations, c_lo, c_hi, tol_rel)
        if status == STATUS_MAX_ITER_REACHED:
            logger.warning(
                "Bisection stopped at the step cap max_iter=%d without "
                "closing the bracket: c in [%g, %g], relative width %g > "
                "tol_rel=%g. c_max=%g is admissible but may be well below "
                "the true maximum.",
                max_iter, c_lo, c_hi, (c_hi - c_lo) / c_lo, tol_rel, c_lo,
            )

    # The invariant: the maximum of the per-bus EPRs at c_max is the reported
    # ``max_epr_rms_at_c_max``. It holds without evaluating ``c_max`` once
    # more -- a full bus sweep, ``N`` run_fault calls -- because
    # ``eprs_lo_snapshot`` is the per-bus dict of exactly the evaluation that
    # set ``epr_lo``, at exactly this ``c``. Taking the headline figure *from*
    # the snapshot rather than beside it makes the two agree by construction
    # instead of by repetition, at (iter + 2)*N run_fault calls instead of
    # (iter + 3)*N.
    epr_at = max(epr_per_bus_at.values()) if epr_per_bus_at else epr_at

    return {
        "c_max": c_max,
        "k_max": tuple(c_max * x for x in k_ref),
        "max_epr_rms_at_c_max": epr_at,
        "epr_rms_per_bus_at_c_max": epr_per_bus_at,
        "iterations": iterations,
        **report(status, c_lo, c_hi),
    }

docs.title: find_max_rho_scaling
docs.text:
find_max_rho_scaling(
    network: Network,
    fault: str,
    bus_names: List[str],
    u_limit: float,
    *,
    c_bounds: Tuple[float, float] = (0.001, 1000.0),
    tol_rel: float = 0.001,
    max_iter: int = 60,
    monotonicity_grid: int = 9,
    run_fault_kwargs: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None,
    progress: Optional[
        Callable[[int, int, str], None]
    ] = None,
    should_cancel: Optional[Callable[[], bool]] = None,

Find the largest uniform rho-scaling factor compatible with an EPR limit.

The assumption, and what happens when it does not hold. A bisection finds the crossing of EPR(c) with u_limit, which presumes there is only one -- i.e. that EPR rises monotonically with c. The EPR of a trial is bit for bit the one a full run_fault reports, so the search takes the same steps; it is about seven times faster on a 1000-bus ring with every bus scaled. A trial the re-solve cannot answer (a 0 Hz stand-in, a bus that gains or loses its electrode, a value the model rejects) is a full run_fault again, with its errors.

    -----
    **The assumption, and what happens when it does not hold.** A bisection
    finds *the* crossing of ``EPR(c)`` with ``u_limit``, which presumes there
    is only one -- i.e. that ``EPR`` rises monotonically with ``c``. That is
    the usual case but not a theorem: this function scales the scalar ``rho``,
    and an impedance formula in which only part of the expression carries
    ``rho`` (``"0.02*rho + 0.1*f*j"``, say) leaves the reactance fixed. The
    network admittance ``|Y_net| = |G + 1/(R + jX)|`` then has a *maximum* at
    ``R = (-1 + sqrt(1 + 4 G^2 X^2)) / (2 G)``, so the EPR has a minimum

    the half of the bracket that holds the answer, and it did: the review's
    case reported "no scaling factor satisfies the constraint" while ``c = 1``
    satisfied it.

    ``monotonicity_grid`` scans for exactly that before the bisection starts.
    Where the curve turns, the result comes back with
    ``status = "non_monotone"`` and ``converged = False``: ``c_max`` is then
    the largest *measured* admissible factor, refined inside its grid

    Its resolution is the grid's.

    changes nothing but the grounding impedances of the selected buses, which
    enter the nodal matrix on its diagonal only, so every later trial is
    re-solved on what the first one assembled -- injection vectors, phase
    currents, stamp pattern -- by re-assembling the matrix values and
    factorising them (P4, :mod:`groundinsight.analysis._session`). The EPR of
    a trial is bit for bit the one a full ``run_fault`` reports, so the
    search takes the same steps; it is about seven times faster on a
    1000-bus ring with every bus scaled. A trial the re-solve cannot answer
    (a 0 Hz stand-in, a bus that gains or loses its electrode, a value the
    model rejects) is a full ``run_fault`` again, with its errors.

    Examples
    --------
    Two stations whose electrodes follow the soil (``rho * 0.01``): by which
    factor ``c`` may the resistivity around both change before the EPR at the
    fault exceeds 5 V?

    >>> import groundinsight as gi
    >>> net = gi.create_network(name="station", frequencies=[50.0])
    >>> grid = gi.BusType(name="grid", system_type="Substation", voltage_level=20.0,
    ...                   impedance_formula="rho * 0.01")
    >>> line = gi.BranchType(name="line", grounding_conductor=True,
    ...                      self_impedance_formula="0.25 * l",
    ...                      mutual_impedance_formula="0 * l")
    >>> for name in ("B1", "B2"):
    ...     _ = gi.create_bus(name=name, type=grid, network=net)
    >>> _ = gi.create_branch(name="L1", type=line, from_bus="B1", to_bus="B2",
    ...                      length=1.0, network=net)
    >>> _ = gi.create_source(name="S1", bus="B1", values={50.0: 100.0}, network=net)
    >>> _ = gi.create_fault(name="F1", bus="B2", network=net)
    >>> report = gi.find_max_rho_scaling(net, "F1", ["B1", "B2"], u_limit=5.0)
    >>> report["status"], round(report["c_max"], 3), report["u_epr_rms_at_c_max"] <= 5.0
    ('converged', 0.083, True)
    """
    validate_limit(u_limit, "u_limit")
    validate_tol_rel(tol_rel)
    validate_max_iter(max_iter)
    validate_grid_points(monotonicity_grid)
    if not bus_names:
        raise ValueError("bus_names must not be empty.")
    c_lo_init, c_hi_init = validate_c_bounds(c_bounds)
    missing = [b for b in bus_names if b not in network.buses]
    if missing:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown bus(es) in network: {missing!r}.")
    if fault not in network.faults:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown fault {fault!r} in network.")

    rfk: Dict[str, Any] = dict(run_fault_kwargs) if run_fault_kwargs else {}

    # The evaluation count is known before the first solve: the scan, plus the
    # halvings that close one scan interval (the whole bracket without a scan)
    # to tol_rel -- a log-bisection needs the same number wherever the
    # threshold lies.
    n_scan = len(log_grid(c_lo_init, c_hi_init, monotonicity_grid))
    interval = (c_hi_init / c_lo_init) ** (1.0 / max(n_scan - 1, 1))
    hooks = StudyHooks(
        "find_max_rho_scaling",
        n_scan + planned_steps(1.0, interval, tol_rel, max_iter),
        progress,
        should_cancel,
    )

    fault_bus_name = network.faults[fault].bus

    # Snapshot original rhos so the network can be restored at the end.
    rho_0: Dict[str, float] = {
        b: float(network.buses[b].specific_earth_resistance) for b in bus_names
    }
    # Snapshot the state run_fault will mutate so the search leaves the network
    # exactly as it found it (the returned figures are already final).
    active_fault_backup = network.active_fault
    result_backup = network.results.get(fault)
    had_result = fault in network.results
    # The assembled nodal system is *not* recomputed by anything the caller
    # does afterwards -- ``bus_response`` and ``analyze_cuts`` read it back as
    # it stands. Every ``run_fault`` below replaces it with the matrices of a
    # trial rho, so without this backup the network would be left carrying the
    # Y of the last bisection step next to the restored rho. That combination
    # is not merely stale, it is inconsistent: it gives a *negative*
    # driving-point impedance in the review case. The pre-search object was
    # built from exactly the state restored below, so putting it back is
    # correct rather than merely conservative.
    electrical_backup = network.electrical_network

    # A trial changes nothing but the grounding impedances of the selected
    # buses, i.e. the diagonal of Y. The first trial is a full run_fault; the
    # others are re-solved on what it assembled (P4, see analysis._session):
    # the same matrix values, factorisation and RMS, so the same EPR bit for
    # bit. A trial the session cannot answer is solved in full again, and the
    # session then continues from that solve.
    session_box: Dict[str, Optional[BusImpedanceSession]] = {"session": None}

    def _session_epr(c: float) -> Optional[float]:
        """The EPR of a trial from the session, or ``None`` for a full solve."""
        session = session_box["session"]
        if session is None:
            return None
        try:
            impedances = {
                b: bus_impedance_at(
                    network.buses[b], c * rho_0[b], network.frequencies
                )
                for b in bus_names
            }
        except Exception:  # noqa: BLE001 -- the full solve raises it in its own words
            return None
        return session.epr_rms(impedances)

    def _epr_rms_at(c: float) -> float:
        """Evaluate the RMS EPR at the fault bus for a given scaling factor."""
        hooks.checkpoint()
        epr = _session_epr(c)
        if epr is None:
            for b in bus_names:
                bus = network.buses[b]
                bus.specific_earth_resistance = c * rho_0[b]
                bus.calculate_impedance(network.frequencies)
            run_fault(network, fault=fault, **rfk)
            result_bus = next(
                rb
                for rb in network.results[fault].buses
                if rb.name == fault_bus_name
            )
            epr = float(result_bus.uepr)
            session_box["session"] = BusImpedanceSession.attach(network, fault)
        if not math.isfinite(epr):
            # A non-finite EPR cannot be compared against u_limit: every
            # comparison is False, so the bisection would take the same turn
            # at every step and walk silently to the lower bracket bound.
            # The impedance pipeline raises on NaN before a formula can get
            # this far today, so this is a second lock on the same door --
            # it defends the search below it, not the model above it.
            raise ValueError(
                f"The EPR at bus {fault_bus_name!r} evaluated to {epr!r} for "
                f"the scaling factor c={c:g}. A non-finite EPR cannot be "
                "compared against u_limit -- every comparison would be False "
                "and the bisection would walk to the lower bracket bound "
                "without ever raising. This is a model problem, not a search "
                "problem: check the bus impedance formula at the scaled rho."
            )
        hooks.advance(f"c = {c:.6g}")
        return epr

    # Everything above restores the network field by field; this records the
    # network-level state as a whole, so the restore in ``finally`` is exact
    # -- result order, path set and private state included (GUI5).
    state = NetworkState(network)
    iterations = 0
    try:
        c_lo, c_hi = c_lo_init, c_hi_init
        # Pre-scan. The bisection needs EPR(c) to rise with c, and the rho
        # sweep does not always: only the resistive part of the bus impedance
        # scales, so |Y_net| = |G + 1/(R + jX)| passes through a maximum at
        # R = (-1 + sqrt(1 + 4 G^2 X^2)) / (2G) and the EPR through a minimum
        # there. The scan measures whether that happens inside this bracket
        # instead of assuming it does not.
        grid = log_grid(c_lo, c_hi, monotonicity_grid)
        grid_eprs = tuple(_epr_rms_at(c) for c in grid)
        monotone = monotonicity_grid < 3 or is_monotone(grid_eprs)
        epr_lo, epr_hi = grid_eprs[0], grid_eprs[-1]

        if not monotone:
            return _non_monotone_result(
                grid, grid_eprs, u_limit, tol_rel, max_iter, _epr_rms_at,
                rho_0, bus_names, c_bounds,
            )

        # Monotone: the scan also narrows the bracket to the one grid interval
        # the threshold falls in, which pays back part of its own cost --
        # every interval skipped is a bisection step not taken.
        for value, epr in zip(grid, grid_eprs, strict=True):
            if epr <= u_limit:
                c_lo, epr_lo = value, epr
            else:
                c_hi, epr_hi = value, epr
                break

        if epr_lo > u_limit:
            raise ValueError(
                f"u_limit={u_limit:g} V is below the EPR at c_min={c_lo:g}: "
                f"|u_EPR|_rms(c_min)={epr_lo:g} V — no scaling factor in "
                f"the bracket {c_bounds!r} satisfies the constraint."
            )
        if epr_hi <= u_limit:
            # Whole bracket is admissible. c_hi is a real, measured answer,
            # but it is a lower bound on the true maximum, not the maximum:
            # nothing above c_hi was evaluated. The status says so, and
            # ``c_bracket`` comes back as (c_hi, inf) to make that
            # machine-readable.
            logger.info(
                "Bracket fully admissible: |u_EPR|_rms(c_hi=%g)=%g V <= "
                "u_limit=%g V. Consider widening c_bounds.",
                c_hi, epr_hi, u_limit,
            )
            c_max, epr_at = c_hi, epr_hi
            status = STATUS_BRACKET_FULLY_ADMISSIBLE
        else:
            # From here on epr(c_lo) <= u_limit < epr(c_hi) holds and is
            # preserved by every step, so c_lo is always a *verified*
            # admissible factor and the threshold stays bracketed.
            while iterations < max_iter and (c_hi - c_lo) / c_lo > tol_rel:
                c_mid = math.sqrt(c_lo * c_hi)  # geometric mean -> log bisection
                epr_mid = _epr_rms_at(c_mid)
                if epr_mid <= u_limit:
                    c_lo, epr_lo = c_mid, epr_mid
                else:
                    c_hi, epr_hi = c_mid, epr_mid
                iterations += 1
            c_max, epr_at = c_lo, epr_lo
            status = classify(iterations, c_lo, c_hi, tol_rel)
            # Ask the classifier rather than re-deriving the same condition:
            # two copies of "did it close?" is exactly how a status and its
            # log message drift apart.
            if status == STATUS_MAX_ITER_REACHED:
                logger.warning(
                    "Bisection stopped at the step cap max_iter=%d without "
                    "closing the bracket: c in [%g, %g], relative width %g > "
                    "tol_rel=%g. c_max=%g is admissible but may be well below "
                    "the true maximum.",
                    max_iter, c_lo, c_hi, (c_hi - c_lo) / c_lo, tol_rel, c_lo,
                )
    finally:
        # Restore original rhos and recompute their impedances no matter what.
        for b in bus_names:
            bus = network.buses[b]
            bus.specific_earth_resistance = rho_0[b]
            bus.calculate_impedance(network.frequencies)
        # Restore the result cache and active fault so no trace of the search
        # remains on the network.
        if had_result:
            network.results[fault] = result_backup
        else:
            network.results.pop(fault, None)
        if active_fault_backup is None:
            network.active_fault = None
            for _flt in network.faults.values():
                _flt.mark_active(False)
        elif active_fault_backup in network.faults:
            network.set_active_fault(active_fault_backup, keep_results=True)
        # Restore the assembled system last: it has to agree with the rho,
        # results and active fault put back above. If the network carried none
        # on entry it gets none back -- a stale matrix is worse than no matrix,
        # because the readers above it raise on the second and not on the first.
        network.electrical_network = electrical_backup
        # And the network-level state exactly as recorded before the search.
        state.restore()

    return {
        "c_max": c_max,
        "u_epr_rms_at_c_max": epr_at,
        "rho_max": {b: c_max * rho_0[b] for b in bus_names},
        "iterations": iterations,
        **report(status, c_lo, c_hi),
    }

iec60909_m(
    kappa: float, frequency: float, t_k_s: float

Heat-effect factor m of the aperiodic (DC) short-circuit component.

m = (exp(4*f*Tk*ln(kappa-1)) - 1) / (2*f*Tk*ln(kappa-1)) per IEC 60909-0. The limits are handled explicitly: kappa -> 1 (no DC offset) gives m -> 0; kappa -> 2 (non-decaying DC, X/R -> inf) gives m -> 2.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default kappa float

Peak factor kappa in (1, 2] (see :func:kappa_from_r_to_x).

required frequency float

System frequency f in Hz (50 or 60). The former keyword f is accepted as a deprecated alias.

required t_k_s float

Fault duration T_k in seconds. Must be strictly positive. The former keyword t_k is accepted as a deprecated alias.

required

Returns:

Type Description float

The dimensionless factor m (>= 0).

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If t_k_s or frequency is not strictly positive.

Notes

The kappa -> 2 limit is worth spelling out because it is easy to get backwards. Substituting a = ln(kappa - 1) -> 0 and expanding, (exp(4 f Tk a) - 1) / (2 f Tk a) -> 4 f Tk a / (2 f Tk a) = 2. A vanishing-resistance fault therefore carries the maximum DC heat, not none. pandapower's _calc_ith sets m = 0 for kappa > 1.99, which is why :func:groundinsight.io.pandapower_sc.read_shortcircuit_results recomputes I_th with this function instead of copying pandapower's ith_ka.

>>> iec60909_m(2.0, 50.0, 0.5)
2.0

@renamed_parameters(f="frequency", t_k="t_k_s")
def iec60909_m(kappa: float, frequency: float, t_k_s: float) -> float:
    """
    Heat-effect factor ``m`` of the aperiodic (DC) short-circuit component.

    ``m = (exp(4*f*Tk*ln(kappa-1)) - 1) / (2*f*Tk*ln(kappa-1))`` per
    IEC 60909-0. The limits are handled explicitly: ``kappa -> 1`` (no DC
    offset) gives ``m -> 0``; ``kappa -> 2`` (non-decaying DC, ``X/R -> inf``)
    gives ``m -> 2``.

    Parameters
    ----------
    kappa : float
        Peak factor ``kappa`` in ``(1, 2]`` (see :func:`kappa_from_r_to_x`).
    frequency : float
        System frequency ``f`` in Hz (50 or 60). The former keyword ``f`` is
        accepted as a deprecated alias.
    t_k_s : float
        Fault duration ``T_k`` in seconds. Must be strictly positive. The
        former keyword ``t_k`` is accepted as a deprecated alias.

    Returns
    -------
    float
        The dimensionless factor ``m`` (``>= 0``).

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If ``t_k_s`` or ``frequency`` is not strictly positive.

    Notes
    -----
    The ``kappa -> 2`` limit is worth spelling out because it is easy to get
    backwards. Substituting ``a = ln(kappa - 1) -> 0`` and expanding,
    ``(exp(4 f Tk a) - 1) / (2 f Tk a) -> 4 f Tk a / (2 f Tk a) = 2``. A
    vanishing-resistance fault therefore carries the *maximum* DC heat, not
    none. pandapower's ``_calc_ith`` sets ``m = 0`` for ``kappa > 1.99``,
    which is why :func:`groundinsight.io.pandapower_sc.read_shortcircuit_results`
    recomputes ``I_th`` with this function instead of copying pandapower's
    ``ith_ka``.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> iec60909_m(1.0, 50.0, 0.5)
    0.0
    >>> iec60909_m(2.0, 50.0, 0.5)
    2.0
    """
    if t_k_s <= 0:
        raise ValueError(f"t_k_s must be strictly positive, got {t_k_s!r}.")
    if frequency <= 0:
        raise ValueError(f"frequency must be strictly positive, got {frequency!r}.")
    if kappa <= 1.0:
        return 0.0
    if kappa >= 2.0:
        return 2.0
    a = math.log(kappa - 1.0)  # negative for 1 < kappa < 2
    denom = 2.0 * frequency * t_k_s * a
    if abs(denom) < 1e-12:  # kappa extremely close to 2 -> non-decaying DC
        return 2.0
    return (math.exp(4.0 * frequency * t_k_s * a) - 1.0) / denom

Material constant k of the adiabatic short-circuit equation.

k = K * sqrt(ln((theta_f + beta) / (theta_i + beta))) per IEC 60949 / IEC 60364-5-54, with the base constant K and beta taken from :data:IEC60949_MATERIALS.

Parameters:

20.0 theta_final_C float

Final (maximum permissible) conductor temperature theta_f in °C. Defaults to the material's bare-earthing-conductor value from :data:IEC60949_MATERIALS.

None

Returns:

Type Description float

The material constant k in A·s^0.5/mm².

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If material is unknown or theta_final_C <= theta_initial_C.

>>> round(iec60949_k("Cu", theta_initial_C=90.0, theta_final_C=250.0))
143
Source code in src/groundinsight/analysis/thermal.py 
def iec60949_k(
    material: str,
    theta_initial_C: float = 20.0,
    theta_final_C: Optional[float] = None,
) -> float:
    """
    Material constant ``k`` of the adiabatic short-circuit equation.

    ``k = K * sqrt(ln((theta_f + beta) / (theta_i + beta)))`` per IEC 60949 /
    IEC 60364-5-54, with the base constant ``K`` and ``beta`` taken from
    :data:`IEC60949_MATERIALS`.

    Parameters
    ----------
    material : str
        One of the keys of :data:`IEC60949_MATERIALS` (``"Cu"``, ``"Al"``,
        ``"Steel"``).
    theta_initial_C : float
        Initial conductor temperature ``theta_i`` in °C. Defaults to
        ``20.0`` (ambient). For a conductor that also carries load current
        use its maximum continuous operating temperature.
    theta_final_C : float, optional
        Final (maximum permissible) conductor temperature ``theta_f`` in °C.
        Defaults to the material's bare-earthing-conductor value from
        :data:`IEC60949_MATERIALS`.

    Returns
    -------
    float
        The material constant ``k`` in A·s^0.5/mm².

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If ``material`` is unknown or ``theta_final_C <= theta_initial_C``.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> round(iec60949_k("Cu", theta_initial_C=90.0, theta_final_C=250.0))
    143
    """
    if material not in IEC60949_MATERIALS:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Unknown conductor material {material!r}. Known materials: "
            f"{sorted(IEC60949_MATERIALS)}."
        )
    data = IEC60949_MATERIALS[material]
    theta_f = (
        data["theta_final_default_C"] if theta_final_C is None else float(theta_final_C)
    )
    beta = data["beta"]
    if theta_f <= theta_initial_C:
        raise ValueError(
            f"theta_final_C ({theta_f}) must exceed theta_initial_C "
            f"({theta_initial_C}) for material {material!r}."
        )
    return data["K"] * math.sqrt(
        math.log((theta_f + beta) / (theta_initial_C + beta))
    )

kappa_from_r_to_x(r_to_x: float) -> float

Peak factor kappa from the R/X ratio (IEC 60909-0).

kappa = 1.02 + 0.98 * exp(-3 * R/X).

The range of the expression is [1.02, 2], not the (1, 2] the IEC formula is often quoted with: the constant term is 1.02, so the exponential approaches 1.02 from above as R/X grows and never reaches 1. Consumers that range-check kappa against (1, 2] therefore accept everything this function can return, which is the point of saying so here.

The R/X to insert is the ratio of the fault loop, not of the positive-sequence system alone. For a three-phase fault the two coincide; for the line-to-earth fault that dominates grounding studies the loop impedance is 2*Z1 + Z0, hence R/X = (2*R1 + R0) / (2*X1 + X0) (see :func:groundinsight.io.pandapower_sc.read_shortcircuit_results).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default r_to_x float

The R/X ratio of the fault loop. Must be non-negative.

required

Returns:

Type Description float

The peak factor kappa.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If r_to_x is negative.

Examples:

>>> round(kappa_from_r_to_x(0.0), 3)
2.0
>>> round(kappa_from_r_to_x(0.1), 4)
1.746

def kappa_from_r_to_x(r_to_x: float) -> float:
    """
    Peak factor ``kappa`` from the ``R/X`` ratio (IEC 60909-0).

    ``kappa = 1.02 + 0.98 * exp(-3 * R/X)``.

    The range of the expression is ``[1.02, 2]``, not the ``(1, 2]`` the IEC
    formula is often quoted with: the constant term is 1.02, so the exponential
    approaches 1.02 from above as ``R/X`` grows and never reaches 1. Consumers
    that range-check ``kappa`` against ``(1, 2]`` therefore accept everything
    this function can return, which is the point of saying so here.

    The ``R/X`` to insert is the ratio of the **fault loop**, not of the
    positive-sequence system alone. For a three-phase fault the two
    coincide; for the line-to-earth fault that dominates grounding studies
    the loop impedance is ``2*Z1 + Z0``, hence
    ``R/X = (2*R1 + R0) / (2*X1 + X0)``
    (see :func:`groundinsight.io.pandapower_sc.read_shortcircuit_results`).

    Parameters
    ----------
    r_to_x : float
        The ``R/X`` ratio of the fault loop. Must be non-negative.

    Returns
    -------
    float
        The peak factor ``kappa``.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If ``r_to_x`` is negative.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> round(kappa_from_r_to_x(0.0), 3)
    2.0
    >>> round(kappa_from_r_to_x(0.1), 4)
    1.746
    """
    if r_to_x < 0:
        raise ValueError(f"r_to_x must be non-negative, got {r_to_x!r}.")
    return 1.02 + 0.98 * math.exp(-3.0 * r_to_x)

def peak_short_circuit_current(i_k: float, kappa: float) -> float:
    """
    Peak short-circuit current ``i_p = kappa * sqrt(2) * I_k''`` (IEC 60909-0).

    ``i_p`` drives the *electrodynamic* (mechanical) stress on conductors and
    supports; the thermal counterpart is
    :func:`thermal_equivalent_current`.

    Parameters
    ----------
    i_k : float
        RMS short-circuit current ``I_k''`` in amperes. Must be
        non-negative.
    kappa : float
        Peak factor from :func:`kappa_from_r_to_x`.

    Returns
    -------
    float
        The peak current in amperes.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If ``i_k`` is negative.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> round(peak_short_circuit_current(1000.0, 1.8), 2)
    2545.58
    """
    if i_k < 0:
        raise ValueError(f"i_k must be non-negative, got {i_k!r}.")
    return kappa * math.sqrt(2.0) * i_k

docs.text:
resolve_fault_sc_characteristics(
    network: Network,
    fault: str,
    *,
    frequency: Optional[float] = None,
    aggregation: str = "weighted",
) -> FaultShortCircuitData

Aggregate the IEC 60909 data of a fault and its sources.

The result is one set of characteristics for the fault.

This is the executable form of the project's superposition rule (see the module docstring): the linear RMS currents stay superposed by the solve, and one effective kappa is resolved here so that the non-linear 60909 factors are applied exactly once, to the aggregate.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default network Network

The network holding the fault and its sources.

required fault str

Name of the fault to resolve. The former keyword fault_name is accepted as a deprecated alias.

required frequency float

Frequency in Hz at which the source injections are weighted. Defaults to the lowest positive frequency of network (the power frequency in a harmonic study), or 50.0.

None aggregation (weighted, max)

"weighted" (default) takes the current-weighted mean of the source kappa values, which reproduces the sum of the individual peak currents exactly. "max" takes the largest kappa, a strictly conservative bound.

'weighted'

Returns:

Type Description FaultShortCircuitData

The resolved characteristics. kappa is None when no contributing source carries 60909 data -- callers must then fall back to an explicit argument.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If fault is unknown or aggregation is not one of the supported modes.

Warns:

Type Description ModelAssumptionWarning

Code SC_KAPPA_MIXED (elements: the sources with a kappa and the fault) when the feeding sources have different R/X: the non-linear IEC 60909 factors are applied once, with the aggregated kappa.

InputWarning

Code SC_DATA_INCOMPLETE (elements: the sources without IEC 60909 data and the fault) when part of the current comes from sources that carry no r_to_x or kappa: kappa_eff then describes only the remaining share and i_p applies it to the whole current.

Notes

What the aggregation actually does, stated exactly. The two returned quantities are not taken over the same set of sources, and it matters:

  • kappa is the weighted mean over the sources that carry 60909 data (kappa or r_to_x). Sources without it cannot contribute a value and are left out; they are listed in sources_without_kappa.
  • i_k_a is the sum over all feeding sources, those included.

A consumer that then forms i_p = kappa * sqrt(2) * i_k_a -- which is what :func:~groundinsight.check_conductor_limits and :func:~groundinsight.check_node_limits do -- therefore applies the peak factor of one subset to the current of the whole. Where every source carries data the subsets coincide and the result is exact; where they do not, the answer is an approximation whose quality is the share of the current the data covers. That share is reported in the InputWarning (SC_DATA_INCOMPLETE) this function emits, and above half of the current the message says outright that i_p rests mostly on an assumption. The alternative -- dropping the undocumented sources from i_k_a as well -- would understate the current, which is the unsafe direction.

Examples:

>>> import groundinsight as gi
>>> net = gi.create_network(name="demo", frequencies=[50.0])
>>> bt = gi.BusType(name="b", system_type="s", voltage_level=20.0,
...                 impedance_formula="rho*0 + 1.0")
>>> _ = gi.create_bus(name="B1", type=bt, network=net)
>>> _ = gi.create_source(name="S1", bus="B1", values={50.0: 1000.0},
...                      network=net, r_to_x=0.1)
>>> _ = gi.create_fault(name="F1", bus="B1", scalings={50.0: 1.0},
...                     network=net, t_k_s=0.5)
>>> data = gi.resolve_fault_sc_characteristics(net, "F1")
>>> round(data.kappa, 4)
1.746
Source code in src/groundinsight/analysis/shortcircuit.py 
@renamed_parameters(fault_name="fault")
def resolve_fault_sc_characteristics(
    network: Network,
    fault: str,
    *,
    frequency: Optional[float] = None,
    aggregation: str = "weighted",
) -> FaultShortCircuitData:
    """
    Aggregate the IEC 60909 data of a fault and its sources.

    The result is one set of characteristics for the fault.

    This is the executable form of the project's superposition rule (see the
    module docstring): the *linear* RMS currents stay superposed by the
    solve, and one effective ``kappa`` is resolved here so that the
    *non-linear* 60909 factors are applied exactly once, to the aggregate.

    Parameters
    ----------
    network : Network
        The network holding the fault and its sources.
    fault : str
        Name of the fault to resolve. The former keyword ``fault_name`` is
        accepted as a deprecated alias.
    frequency : float, optional
        Frequency in Hz at which the source injections are weighted.
        Defaults to the lowest positive frequency of ``network`` (the power
        frequency in a harmonic study), or ``50.0``.
    aggregation : {'weighted', 'max'}
        ``"weighted"`` (default) takes the current-weighted mean of the
        source ``kappa`` values, which reproduces the sum of the individual
        peak currents exactly. ``"max"`` takes the largest ``kappa``, a
        strictly conservative bound.

    Returns
    -------
    FaultShortCircuitData
        The resolved characteristics. ``kappa`` is ``None`` when no
        contributing source carries 60909 data -- callers must then fall
        back to an explicit argument.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If ``fault`` is unknown or ``aggregation`` is not one of the
        supported modes.

    Warns
    -----
    ModelAssumptionWarning
        Code ``SC_KAPPA_MIXED`` (elements: the sources with a ``kappa`` and the
        fault) when the feeding sources have different R/X: the non-linear
        IEC 60909 factors are applied once, with the aggregated ``kappa``.
    InputWarning
        Code ``SC_DATA_INCOMPLETE`` (elements: the sources without IEC 60909
        data and the fault) when part of the current comes from sources that
        carry no ``r_to_x`` or ``kappa``: ``kappa_eff`` then describes only
        the remaining share and ``i_p`` applies it to the whole current.

    Notes
    -----
    **What the aggregation actually does, stated exactly.** The two returned
    quantities are not taken over the same set of sources, and it matters:

    * ``kappa`` is the weighted mean over the sources that **carry** 60909
      data (``kappa`` or ``r_to_x``). Sources without it cannot contribute a
      value and are left out; they are listed in ``sources_without_kappa``.
    * ``i_k_a`` is the sum over **all** feeding sources, those included.

    A consumer that then forms ``i_p = kappa * sqrt(2) * i_k_a`` -- which is
    what :func:`~groundinsight.check_conductor_limits` and
    :func:`~groundinsight.check_node_limits` do -- therefore applies the peak
    factor of one subset to the current of the whole. Where every source
    carries data the subsets coincide and the result is exact; where they do
    not, the answer is an approximation whose quality is the share of the
    current the data covers. That share is reported in the ``InputWarning``
    (``SC_DATA_INCOMPLETE``) this function emits, and above half of the
    current the message says outright that ``i_p`` rests mostly on an
    assumption. The alternative -- dropping the undocumented sources from
    ``i_k_a`` as well -- would understate the current, which is the unsafe
    direction.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import groundinsight as gi
    >>> net = gi.create_network(name="demo", frequencies=[50.0])
    >>> bt = gi.BusType(name="b", system_type="s", voltage_level=20.0,
    ...                 impedance_formula="rho*0 + 1.0")
    >>> _ = gi.create_bus(name="B1", type=bt, network=net)
    >>> _ = gi.create_source(name="S1", bus="B1", values={50.0: 1000.0},
    ...                      network=net, r_to_x=0.1)
    >>> _ = gi.create_fault(name="F1", bus="B1", scalings={50.0: 1.0},
    ...                     network=net, t_k_s=0.5)
    >>> data = gi.resolve_fault_sc_characteristics(net, "F1")
    >>> round(data.kappa, 4)
    1.746
    """
    if aggregation not in ("weighted", "max"):
        raise ValueError(
            f"aggregation must be 'weighted' or 'max', got {aggregation!r}."
        )
    fault_obj = network.faults.get(fault)
    if fault_obj is None:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Unknown fault {fault!r}. Known faults: "
            f"{sorted(network.faults)}."
        )

    if frequency is None:
        frequency = next((float(x) for x in network.frequencies if x > 0), 50.0)
    frequency = float(frequency)
    scaling = fault_obj.scaling_at(frequency)

    weights: Dict[str, float] = {}
    kappas: Dict[str, float] = {}
    r_values: List[float] = []
    without_kappa: List[str] = []
    i_k_total = 0.0
    weight_without_kappa = 0.0

    for source_name in sources_feeding(network, fault):
        source = network.sources[source_name]
        weight = _source_injection_magnitude(source, frequency, scaling)
        kappa_i = _source_kappa(source)
        if kappa_i is None:
            if weight > 0:
                without_kappa.append(source_name)
                weight_without_kappa += weight
            i_k_total += weight
            continue
        # A source that carries 60909 data but injects nothing at this
        # frequency would silently vanish from a purely current-weighted
        # mean; give it a nominal weight so its kappa still counts.
        if weight <= 0:
            weight = float(getattr(source, "i_k_a", None) or 0.0)
        weights[source_name] = weight
        kappas[source_name] = kappa_i
        r_to_x_i = getattr(source, "r_to_x", None)
        if r_to_x_i is not None:
            r_values.append(float(r_to_x_i))
        i_k_total += weight

    n_factor = float(getattr(fault_obj, "n_factor", 1.0) or 1.0)
    t_k_s = getattr(fault_obj, "t_k_s", None)
    t_k_s = None if t_k_s is None else float(t_k_s)

    if not kappas:
        if without_kappa:
            logger.debug(
                "Fault %r: none of the feeding sources (%s) carries IEC 60909 "
                "data; kappa stays unresolved.",
                fault,
                ", ".join(without_kappa),
            )
        return FaultShortCircuitData(
            fault_name=fault,
            frequency=frequency,
            t_k_s=t_k_s,
            n_factor=n_factor,
            i_k_a=i_k_total,
            aggregation=aggregation,
            sources_without_kappa=without_kappa,
        )

    kappa_list = list(kappas.values())
    homogeneous = (max(kappa_list) - min(kappa_list)) <= 1e-9

    if aggregation == "max" or homogeneous:
        kappa_eff = max(kappa_list)
    else:
        weight_sum = sum(weights.values())
        if weight_sum > 0:
            kappa_eff = (
                sum(kappas[name] * weights[name] for name in kappas) / weight_sum
            )
        else:  # no current information at all -> plain mean
            kappa_eff = sum(kappa_list) / len(kappa_list)

    if not homogeneous:
        emit(
            ModelAssumptionWarning,
            f"Fault {fault!r} is fed by sources with different R/X (kappa "
            f"between {min(kappa_list):.4f} and {max(kappa_list):.4f}). The "
            f"non-linear IEC 60909 factors are applied once, with the "
            f"{aggregation} kappa = {kappa_eff:.4f}. Use the transient solver "
            f"for an exact mixed-R/X result.",
            code="SC_KAPPA_MIXED",
            elements=[("source", name) for name in kappas] + [("fault", fault)],
            stacklevel=2,
        )
    if without_kappa:
        share = weight_without_kappa / i_k_total if i_k_total > 0 else 0.0
        majority = (
            " That is the majority of the current, so i_p and I_th rest "
            "mostly on an assumption: give those sources an r_to_x or a "
            "kappa, or pass kappa explicitly."
            if share > 0.5
            else ""
        )
        emit(
            InputWarning,
            f"Fault {fault!r}: source(s) {', '.join(without_kappa)} inject "
            f"{100.0 * share:.0f} % of the current at {frequency:.1f} Hz but "
            f"carry no IEC 60909 data. They are excluded from the kappa "
            f"aggregation and included in i_k_a, so kappa_eff = {kappa_eff:.4f} "
            f"is the figure of the remaining {100.0 * (1.0 - share):.0f} % and "
            f"i_p applies it to the whole current.{majority}",
            code="SC_DATA_INCOMPLETE",
            elements=[("source", name) for name in without_kappa] + [("fault", fault)],
            stacklevel=2,
        )

    r_to_x_eff = None
    if r_values and (max(r_values) - min(r_values)) <= 1e-12:
        r_to_x_eff = r_values[0]

    m = None
    if t_k_s is not None and t_k_s > 0:
        m = iec60909_m(kappa_eff, frequency, t_k_s)

    return FaultShortCircuitData(
        fault_name=fault,
        frequency=frequency,
        kappa=kappa_eff,
        r_to_x=r_to_x_eff,
        t_k_s=t_k_s,
        n_factor=n_factor,
        m=m,
        i_k_a=i_k_total,
        i_p_a=peak_short_circuit_current(i_k_total, kappa_eff),
        aggregation=aggregation,
        homogeneous=homogeneous,
        sources=sorted(kappas),
        sources_without_kappa=without_kappa,
    )

def run_reference_cases(
    cases: Optional[List[ReferenceCase]] = None,
) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """
    Run the closed-form reference cases and report the comparison.

    Parameters
    ----------
    cases : list of ReferenceCase, optional
        Defaults to :data:`REFERENCE_CASES`.

    Returns
    -------
    pl.DataFrame
        One row per case: ``case``, ``quantity``, ``conditions``,
        ``closed_form``, ``model``, ``rel_deviation``, ``tolerance``,
        ``agrees``.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import groundinsight as gi
    >>> table = gi.run_reference_cases()
    >>> table.height == len(gi.REFERENCE_CASES), table["agrees"].all()
    (True, True)
    """
    rows = [case.evaluate() for case in (cases or REFERENCE_CASES)]
    frame = pl.DataFrame(rows)
    failed = frame.filter(~pl.col("agrees"))
    if failed.height:
        logger.warning(
            "%d reference case(s) missed their closed form: %s. Either the model "
            "is wrong or a stated boundary condition was not met -- the second "
            "is the more common finding, so read the 'conditions' column first.",
            failed.height,
            ", ".join(failed["case"].to_list()),
        )
    return frame

    network: Network,
    bus_names: List[str],
    u_limit: float,

Pick admissible rho-f characteristics from a user-provided catalog.

Evaluates every candidate k in the catalog with :func:evaluate_max_epr_under_k and reports, per candidate, the maximum RMS EPR observed across the bus sweep, the per-bus EPRs and whether the candidate satisfies the limit u_limit. The catalog is typically a hand-curated list of soil scenarios (e.g. dry sand, wet clay, permafrost) or rho-f fits from previous measurements.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default network Network

The simulation network. Sources, branches and the buses to be swept must already be configured.

required bus_names list of str

required u_limit float

Upper bound on the RMS EPR (in volts) at any swept bus. Must be strictly positive.

required candidates dict of str to tuple of float

Mapping {name: (k1, k2, k3, k4, k5)} of the candidate rho-f characteristics. Names must be unique (Python dict guarantees that), tuples must each have length 5. May be empty -- the result is then an empty DataFrame with the documented schema.

None run_fault_kwargs dict

Forwarded to :func:run_fault.

None sort_by (max_epr_asc, max_epr_desc, name)

How to sort the result rows.

  • "max_epr_asc" (default): admissible candidates first, tightest-EPR-margin candidates at the top.
  • "max_epr_desc": largest EPR first; useful to inspect the worst-case candidates.
  • "name": lexicographic by candidate name.
"max_epr_asc"

Returns:

Type Description DataFrame

One row per candidate, with the columns

  • "name" (str);
  • "k1" ... "k5" (float);
  • "max_epr_rms_V" (float): the maximum RMS EPR across the bus sweep, in volts;
  • "admissible" (bool): True iff max_epr_rms_V <= u_limit;
  • one "epr_<bus>_V" column per swept bus: the RMS EPR at that bus when it is the active fault, in volts.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If u_limit is not finite and strictly positive, bus_names is empty, or any candidate has a wrong-length k or refers to an unknown bus (the underlying helper validates this). A NaN u_limit is rejected explicitly: it would otherwise pass a plain positivity check and mark the whole catalog inadmissible.

Examples:

>>> import groundinsight as gi
>>> from groundinsight.models.core_models import BusType, BranchType
>>> from groundinsight.analysis import select_rho_f_from_catalog
>>> bt = BusType(name="BT", system_type="Grounded",
...              voltage_level=20.0,
...              impedance_formula="rho * 0.01 + 0*f")
>>> brt = BranchType(name="BRT", grounding_conductor=True,
...                  self_impedance_formula="(0.25 + I*0.6)*l",

>>> _ = gi.create_bus(name="b0", type=bt, network=net)
>>> _ = gi.create_bus(name="b1", type=bt, network=net)
>>> _ = gi.create_branch(name="br", type=brt, from_bus="b0",
...                      to_bus="b1", length=1.0, network=net)
>>> _ = gi.create_source(name="src", bus="b0",
...                      values={50: 100.0}, network=net)
>>> catalog = {
...     "low":   (0.005, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0),
...     "med":   (0.01,  0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0),
...     "high":  (0.05,  0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0),
... }
>>> df = select_rho_f_from_catalog(
...     net, ["b0", "b1"], u_limit=20.0, candidates=catalog,
... )
>>> set(df.columns) >= {"name", "k1", "max_epr_rms_V", "admissible"}

def select_rho_f_from_catalog(
    network: Network,
    bus_names: List[str],
    u_limit: float,
    candidates: Dict[str, KVector],
    *,
    fault_scalings: Optional[Dict[float, float]] = None,
    run_fault_kwargs: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None,
    sort_by: Literal["max_epr_asc", "max_epr_desc", "name"] = "max_epr_asc",
) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """Pick admissible rho-f characteristics from a user-provided catalog.

    Evaluates every candidate ``k`` in the catalog with
    :func:`evaluate_max_epr_under_k` and reports, per candidate, the
    maximum RMS EPR observed across the bus sweep, the per-bus EPRs and
    whether the candidate satisfies the limit ``u_limit``. The catalog is
    typically a hand-curated list of soil scenarios (e.g. dry sand, wet
    clay, permafrost) or rho-f fits from previous measurements.

    Parameters
    ----------
    network : Network
        The simulation network. Sources, branches and the buses
        to be swept must already be configured.
    bus_names : list of str
        Buses whose impedance is parameterised by every
        candidate ``k`` and which are swept as fault locations.
    u_limit : float
        Upper bound on the RMS EPR (in volts) at any swept bus.
        Must be strictly positive.
    candidates : dict of str to tuple of float
        Mapping ``{name: (k1, k2, k3, k4, k5)}`` of the
        candidate rho-f characteristics. Names must be unique
        (Python dict guarantees that), tuples must each have length
        5. May be empty -- the result is then an empty DataFrame
        with the documented schema.
    fault_scalings : dict of float to float, optional
        Frequency-resolved scalings for any fault that
        has to be created on the fly. See
        :func:`evaluate_max_epr_under_k`.
    run_fault_kwargs : dict, optional
        Forwarded to :func:`run_fault`.
    sort_by : {"max_epr_asc", "max_epr_desc", "name"}, optional
        How to sort the result rows.

        - ``"max_epr_asc"`` (default): admissible candidates first,
          tightest-EPR-margin candidates at the top.
        - ``"max_epr_desc"``: largest EPR first; useful to inspect
          the worst-case candidates.
        - ``"name"``: lexicographic by candidate name.

    Returns
    -------
    pl.DataFrame
        One row per candidate, with the columns

        - ``"name"`` (str);
        - ``"k1"`` ... ``"k5"`` (float);
        - ``"max_epr_rms_V"`` (float): the maximum RMS EPR across the bus
          sweep, in volts;
        - ``"admissible"`` (bool): ``True`` iff ``max_epr_rms_V <= u_limit``;
        - one ``"epr_<bus>_V"`` column per swept bus: the RMS EPR at that
          bus when it is the active fault, in volts.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If ``u_limit`` is not finite and strictly positive,
        ``bus_names`` is empty, or any candidate has a wrong-length
        ``k`` or refers to an unknown bus (the underlying helper
        validates this). A NaN ``u_limit`` is rejected explicitly:
        it would otherwise pass a plain positivity check and mark
        the whole catalog inadmissible.

    Examples
    --------
        >>> import groundinsight as gi
        >>> from groundinsight.models.core_models import BusType, BranchType
        >>> from groundinsight.analysis import select_rho_f_from_catalog
        >>> bt = BusType(name="BT", system_type="Grounded",
        ...              voltage_level=20.0,
        ...              impedance_formula="rho * 0.01 + 0*f")
        >>> brt = BranchType(name="BRT", grounding_conductor=True,
        ...                  self_impedance_formula="(0.25 + I*0.6)*l",
        ...                  mutual_impedance_formula="(0.0 + I*0.6)*l")
        >>> net = gi.create_network(name="N", frequencies=[50])
        >>> _ = gi.create_bus(name="b0", type=bt, network=net)
        >>> _ = gi.create_bus(name="b1", type=bt, network=net)
        >>> _ = gi.create_branch(name="br", type=brt, from_bus="b0",
        ...                      to_bus="b1", length=1.0, network=net)
        >>> _ = gi.create_source(name="src", bus="b0",
        ...                      values={50: 100.0}, network=net)
        >>> catalog = {
        ...     "low":   (0.005, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0),
        ...     "med":   (0.01,  0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0),
        ...     "high":  (0.05,  0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0),
        ... }
        >>> df = select_rho_f_from_catalog(
        ...     net, ["b0", "b1"], u_limit=20.0, candidates=catalog,
        ... )
        >>> set(df.columns) >= {"name", "k1", "max_epr_rms_V", "admissible"}
        True
    """
    # Same check as in the two searches, and for the same reason -- but the
    # consequence here is worse. This function does not return a scalar a
    # reader might sanity-check, it returns a table with an ``admissible``
    # column, and every entry in it is ``max_epr <= u_limit``. Against NaN
    # every one of those comparisons is False, so the table would report
    # that *no* soil model in the catalog is usable, next to an EPR column
    # that is correct and finite. Nothing in the output would point at the
    # limit as the broken part.
    validate_limit(u_limit, "u_limit")
    if not bus_names:
        raise ValueError("bus_names must not be empty.")

    # Empty catalog -> return an empty DataFrame with the documented schema.
    if not candidates:
        schema = {
            "name": pl.Utf8,
            "k1": pl.Float64, "k2": pl.Float64, "k3": pl.Float64,
            "k4": pl.Float64, "k5": pl.Float64,
            "max_epr_rms_V": pl.Float64,
            "admissible": pl.Boolean,
        }
        for b in bus_names:
            schema[f"epr_{b}_V"] = pl.Float64
        return pl.DataFrame(schema=schema)

    rows: List[Dict[str, Any]] = []
    for name, k in candidates.items():
        if len(k) != 5:
            raise ValueError(
                f"Candidate {name!r}: k must be a 5-tuple, got length {len(k)}."
            )
        eprs = evaluate_max_epr_under_k(
            network, bus_names, k=tuple(k),
            fault_scalings=fault_scalings,
            run_fault_kwargs=run_fault_kwargs,
        )
        max_epr = max(eprs.values()) if eprs else 0.0
        row: Dict[str, Any] = {
            "name": name,
            "k1": float(k[0]),
            "k2": float(k[1]),
            "k3": float(k[2]),
            "k4": float(k[3]),
            "k5": float(k[4]),
            "max_epr_rms_V": float(max_epr),
            "admissible": bool(max_epr <= u_limit),
        }
        for b in bus_names:
            row[f"epr_{b}_V"] = float(eprs[b])
        rows.append(row)

    df = pl.DataFrame(rows)

    if sort_by == "max_epr_asc":
        # Admissible first (True -> 1 sorts after False -> 0 by default,
        # so descending on ``admissible`` puts True on top), then
        # ascending EPR within each block.
        df = df.sort(
            by=["admissible", "max_epr_rms_V"], descending=[True, False]
        )
    elif sort_by == "max_epr_desc":
        df = df.sort(by="max_epr_rms_V", descending=True)
    elif sort_by == "name":
        df = df.sort(by="name")
    else:  # pragma: no cover -- guarded by Literal type, defensive
        raise ValueError(
            f"sort_by must be one of "
            f"'max_epr_asc' | 'max_epr_desc' | 'name', got {sort_by!r}."
        )

    return df

summarize(
    frame: DataFrame,
    value: str,
    *,
    by: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None,
    quantiles: Sequence[float] = DEFAULT_QUANTILES,
) -> pl.DataFrame

Reduce one column to count, spread, quantiles and extremes.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default frame DataFrame

Long-format results, e.g. from :meth:~groundinsight.simulation.sweep.SweepResult.buses.

required value str

Numeric column to summarise.

required by sequence of str

Grouping columns. Without them the whole frame is one group.

None quantiles sequence of float

Quantiles in [0, 1]. Each becomes a column p05, p50, ...

DEFAULT_QUANTILES

Returns:

Type Description DataFrame

One row per group: the grouping columns, then n, n_null, n_nan, mean, std, min, the quantiles, and max. Sorted by the grouping columns so repeated runs produce identical output.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If a named column is missing, if the value column is not numeric, or if a quantile lies outside [0, 1].

Notes

Read n_nan before the statistics. Polars counts a NaN as a value, not as a null: it lands in n, not in n_null, it propagates through mean, std and every quantile, and min / max skip it -- so a single NaN leaves a summary in which the extremes look sound and the mean is NaN, with nothing in the row saying why. That is a realistic input here rather than a hypothetical: a sweep point that failed under on_error="record" writes NaN into the value column. n_nan is the column that says how many, and it is 0 for an integer column, which cannot carry one.

Examples:

>>> import polars as pl
>>> from groundinsight.analysis import summarize
>>> frame = pl.DataFrame({"bus_name": ["A", "A", "B"], "EPR_V": [10.0, 30.0, 5.0]})
>>> summary = summarize(frame, "EPR_V", by=["bus_name"])
>>> summary.select("bus_name", "n", "mean", "max").rows()
[('A', 2, 20.0, 30.0), ('B', 1, 5.0, 5.0)]

def summarize(
    frame: pl.DataFrame,
    value: str,
    *,
    by: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None,
    quantiles: Sequence[float] = DEFAULT_QUANTILES,
) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """
    Reduce one column to count, spread, quantiles and extremes.

    Parameters
    ----------
    frame : pl.DataFrame
        Long-format results, e.g. from
        :meth:`~groundinsight.simulation.sweep.SweepResult.buses`.
    value : str
        Numeric column to summarise.
    by : sequence of str, optional
        Grouping columns. Without them the whole frame is one group.
    quantiles : sequence of float, optional
        Quantiles in ``[0, 1]``. Each becomes a column ``p05``, ``p50``, ...

    Returns
    -------
    pl.DataFrame
        One row per group: the grouping columns, then ``n``, ``n_null``,
        ``n_nan``, ``mean``, ``std``, ``min``, the quantiles, and ``max``.
        Sorted by the grouping columns so repeated runs produce identical
        output.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If a named column is missing, if the value column is not numeric, or if
        a quantile lies outside ``[0, 1]``.

    Notes
    -----
    **Read ``n_nan`` before the statistics.** Polars counts a NaN as a
    *value*, not as a null: it lands in ``n``, not in ``n_null``, it
    propagates through ``mean``, ``std`` and every quantile, and ``min`` /
    ``max`` skip it -- so a single NaN leaves a summary in which the extremes
    look sound and the mean is NaN, with nothing in the row saying why. That
    is a realistic input here rather than a hypothetical: a sweep point that
    failed under ``on_error="record"`` writes NaN into the value column.
    ``n_nan`` is the column that says how many, and it is ``0`` for an integer
    column, which cannot carry one.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import polars as pl
    >>> from groundinsight.analysis import summarize
    >>> frame = pl.DataFrame({"bus_name": ["A", "A", "B"], "EPR_V": [10.0, 30.0, 5.0]})
    >>> summary = summarize(frame, "EPR_V", by=["bus_name"])
    >>> summary.select("bus_name", "n", "mean", "max").rows()
    [('A', 2, 20.0, 30.0), ('B', 1, 5.0, 5.0)]
    """
    missing = [c for c in [value, *(by or [])] if c not in frame.columns]
    if missing:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Column(s) {missing} are not in the frame. Available: "
            f"{frame.columns}."
        )
    if not frame.schema[value].is_numeric():
        raise ValueError(
            f"Column '{value}' has dtype {frame.schema[value]}, which cannot be "
            f"summarised numerically. Cast it, or group on it with `by=` "
            f"instead of summarising it."
        )
    bad = [q for q in quantiles if not 0.0 <= q <= 1.0]
    if bad:
        raise ValueError(f"Quantile(s) {bad} lie outside [0, 1].")

    # ``is_nan`` is only defined on the float dtypes; an integer column cannot
    # carry a NaN, so the count is a constant zero there rather than an error.
    n_nan = (
        pl.col(value).is_nan().sum().alias("n_nan")
        if frame.schema[value].is_float()
        else pl.lit(0, dtype=pl.UInt32).alias("n_nan")
    )
    aggregations = [
        pl.col(value).count().alias("n"),
        pl.col(value).null_count().alias("n_null"),
        n_nan,
        pl.col(value).mean().alias("mean"),
        pl.col(value).std().alias("std"),
        pl.col(value).min().alias("min"),
    ]
    aggregations += [
        pl.col(value).quantile(q, interpolation="linear").alias(_quantile_name(q))
        for q in quantiles
    ]
    aggregations.append(pl.col(value).max().alias("max"))

    if by:
        return frame.group_by(list(by)).agg(aggregations).sort(list(by))
    return frame.select(aggregations)

thermal_equivalent_current(
    i_k: float, m: float, n_factor: float = 1.0

Thermally equivalent short-time current I_th = I_k'' * sqrt(m + n).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default i_k float

RMS short-circuit current I_k'' in amperes. Must be non-negative.

required m float

DC heat-effect factor from :func:iec60909_m. Must be non-negative.

required n_factor float

AC-decay heat factor n in (0, 1]. 1.0 for the far-from-generator faults typical of distribution grounding studies. The former keyword n is accepted as a deprecated alias.

1.0

Returns:

Type Description float

The thermally equivalent current in amperes.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If i_k or m is negative, or n_factor is not in (0, 1].

Notes

The bounds are enforced rather than clipped because violating them fails silently downwards: a negative m, or an n above one supplied in place of a correct smaller value, changes sqrt(m + n) without any visible symptom, and a too-small result under-estimates the thermal stress -- the unsafe direction for a limit check. A caller that hands in such a value has a bug upstream and should hear about it.

>>> round(thermal_equivalent_current(1000.0, 0.0, 1.0), 6)
1000.0

@renamed_parameters(n="n_factor")
def thermal_equivalent_current(
    i_k: float, m: float, n_factor: float = 1.0
) -> float:
    """
    Thermally equivalent short-time current ``I_th = I_k'' * sqrt(m + n)``.

    Parameters
    ----------
    i_k : float
        RMS short-circuit current ``I_k''`` in amperes. Must be
        non-negative.
    m : float
        DC heat-effect factor from :func:`iec60909_m`. Must be
        non-negative.
    n_factor : float
        AC-decay heat factor ``n`` in ``(0, 1]``. ``1.0`` for the
        far-from-generator faults typical of distribution grounding
        studies. The former keyword ``n`` is accepted as a deprecated
        alias.

    Returns
    -------
    float
        The thermally equivalent current in amperes.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If ``i_k`` or ``m`` is negative, or ``n_factor`` is not in ``(0, 1]``.

    Notes
    -----
    The bounds are enforced rather than clipped because violating them
    fails *silently downwards*: a negative ``m``, or an ``n`` above one
    supplied in place of a correct smaller value, changes ``sqrt(m + n)``
    without any visible symptom, and a too-small result under-estimates the
    thermal stress -- the unsafe direction for a limit check. A caller that
    hands in such a value has a bug upstream and should hear about it.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> round(thermal_equivalent_current(1000.0, 0.0, 1.0), 6)
    1000.0
    """
    if i_k < 0:
        raise ValueError(f"i_k must be non-negative, got {i_k!r}.")
    if m < 0:
        raise ValueError(f"m must be non-negative, got {m!r}.")
    if not 0.0 < n_factor <= 1.0:
        raise ValueError(f"n_factor must lie in (0, 1], got {n_factor!r}.")
    return i_k * math.sqrt(m + n_factor)
