Enable console logging for the groundinsight package.

Convenience helper for interactive use (notebooks, scripts). Attaches a single :class:logging.StreamHandler with a simple formatter to the groundinsight package logger and sets the requested level. Subsequent calls only adjust the level on the same handler instance, so it is safe to call this helper repeatedly without accumulating duplicate console handlers — even across mixed set_log_level("DEBUG") -> set_log_level("INFO") toggles, and even when logging.basicConfig(...) has been called at the root logger.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default level int or str

Log level either as a numeric constant (e.g. logging.INFO) or as a string name ("DEBUG", "INFO", "WARNING", "ERROR", "CRITICAL"). Defaults to "INFO".

'INFO'

Returns:

Type Description Logger

The configured groundinsight package logger, for further adjustments by the caller if desired.

Notes

If you have also called :func:logging.basicConfig at the root logger level, every record will be emitted twice: once through the package handler installed here and once through the root handler installed by basicConfig. To suppress the duplicate either call logging.getLogger("groundinsight").propagate = False explicitly, or rely solely on basicConfig and do not call :func:set_log_level.

Examples:

>>> import groundinsight as gi
>>> gi.set_log_level("INFO")
<Logger groundinsight (INFO)>

def set_log_level(level: Union[int, str] = "INFO") -> logging.Logger:
    """
    Enable console logging for the ``groundinsight`` package.

    Convenience helper for interactive use (notebooks, scripts). Attaches a
    single :class:`logging.StreamHandler` with a simple formatter to the
    ``groundinsight`` package logger and sets the requested level.
    Subsequent calls only adjust the level on the *same* handler instance,
    so it is safe to call this helper repeatedly without accumulating
    duplicate console handlers — even across mixed
    ``set_log_level("DEBUG") -> set_log_level("INFO")`` toggles, and even
    when ``logging.basicConfig(...)`` has been called at the root logger.

    Parameters
    ----------
    level : int or str, optional
        Log level either as a numeric constant (e.g. ``logging.INFO``) or
        as a string name (``"DEBUG"``, ``"INFO"``, ``"WARNING"``,
        ``"ERROR"``, ``"CRITICAL"``). Defaults to ``"INFO"``.

    Returns
    -------
    logging.Logger
        The configured ``groundinsight`` package logger, for further
        adjustments by the caller if desired.

    Notes
    -----
    If you have also called :func:`logging.basicConfig` at the root logger
    level, every record will be emitted twice: once through the package
    handler installed here and once through the root handler installed by
    ``basicConfig``. To suppress the duplicate either call
    ``logging.getLogger("groundinsight").propagate = False`` explicitly,
    or rely solely on ``basicConfig`` and do not call
    :func:`set_log_level`.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import groundinsight as gi
    >>> gi.set_log_level("INFO")  # doctest: +ELLIPSIS
    <Logger groundinsight (INFO)>
    """
    pkg_logger = logging.getLogger(PACKAGE_LOGGER)
    pkg_logger.setLevel(level)

    # Keep the marked handler of an earlier call and remove every other
    # StreamHandler of the package logger (one attached by user code, for
    # instance), so that a record is not printed twice.
    marked = [
        h for h in pkg_logger.handlers if getattr(h, _GI_HANDLER_MARK, False)
    ]
    for h in list(pkg_logger.handlers):
        if (
            isinstance(h, logging.StreamHandler)
            and not isinstance(h, logging.NullHandler)
            and not getattr(h, _GI_HANDLER_MARK, False)
        ):
            pkg_logger.removeHandler(h)

    if marked:
        # Re-use the existing marked handler — just align its level so
        # filtering happens at both the logger and the handler level.
        handler = marked[0]
        # Defensive: if more than one marked handler is attached, keep only
        # the first.
        for extra in marked[1:]:
            pkg_logger.removeHandler(extra)
        handler.setLevel(level)
    else:
        handler = logging.StreamHandler()
        handler.setFormatter(
            logging.Formatter("%(levelname)s [%(name)s] %(message)s")
        )
        handler.setLevel(level)
        setattr(handler, _GI_HANDLER_MARK, True)
        pkg_logger.addHandler(handler)

    return pkg_logger

def show_versions() -> Dict[str, str]:
    """Return version information for ``groundinsight`` and its peers.

    Cross-repo convention helper introduced for the *seventh
    2026-05-18 review pass* roadmap entry "ADR-0013 — Cross-repo
    `show_versions` convention". The returned mapping always contains
    a ``"groundinsight"`` key with the value of :data:`__version__`;
    optional peers ``"groundfield"`` and ``"groundmeas"`` are added
    when the respective package is installed in the active
    interpreter. Python and platform information are reported under
    the ``"python"`` and ``"platform"`` keys so a bug report can
    include the full earthing-platform stack in a single call.

    Returns
    -------
    dict of str to str
        A mapping ``{"groundinsight": <__version__>, "python": "3.14.6",
        "platform": "Linux-...", ...}``. The first value is always
        :data:`__version__`; no version literal is repeated here so the
        docstring cannot drift away from the release. The dict is freshly
        built on every call and safe to mutate.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import groundinsight as gi
    >>> info = gi.show_versions()
    >>> info["groundinsight"] == gi.__version__
    True
    """
    import platform
    import sys

    # The package ``__init__`` imports this module before it defines
    # ``__version__``; read it at call time.
    from . import __version__

    info: Dict[str, str] = {
        "groundinsight": __version__,
        "python": sys.version.split()[0],
        "platform": platform.platform(),
    }
    for peer in ("groundfield", "groundmeas"):
        try:
            mod = __import__(peer)
        except ImportError:
            continue
        peer_version = getattr(mod, "__version__", None)
        if peer_version is not None:
            info[peer] = str(peer_version)
    return info

docs.title: Transient simulations
docs.text: The groundinsight.simulation.transient module extends the package beyond the steady-state phasor solve into the time domain. A TransientStudy binds a network, an active fault and one or more user-defined source waveforms together and produces a ResultTransient with EPR and shield-current time series at the declared observation points.

docs.title: Physical / modelling context
docs.text:
The frequency-domain solver answers "given a sinusoidal injection at frequency \(f\), what is the EPR?". Real fault currents are non-sinusoidal: they switch on at fault inception, may carry an exponentially decaying DC offset, and switch off again at clearing. Two complementary solver paths are implemented to capture that behaviour:

  • FFT solver (solver="fft") — samples the user waveform on a regular time grid, transforms to the frequency domain via NumPy's real-valued FFT, evaluates the existing nodal-admittance solve at every FFT bin, and transforms the bus voltages back via IFFT. It reuses BusType.impedance_formula and BranchType.self_impedance_formula and is therefore consistent with the stationary results bin-by-bin. Only current sources are accepted, and only those with a galvanic connection to the fault bus inject — the same rule the stationary solver applies through its source-to-fault paths. Mutual coupling is not evaluated by this path; a network that carries it raises a TransientModelWarning, and the state-space solver is the one that models it. The DFT's periodicity is checked at the end of the window and solve(..., zero_pad=True) solves on a doubled window when the response has not decayed.
  • State-space solver (solver="state_space") — assembles a modified-nodal-analysis ODE system \(\dot x = A x + B u\), \(y = C x + D u\) from the lumped RLC fields on BusType and BranchType (R_formula, L_formula, C_formula, R_self_formula, L_self_formula, C_self_formula, R_mutual_formula, M_mutual_formula) and integrates with scipy.signal.lsim. Voltage sources, Carson-style mutual coupling and pi-section branch capacitance are supported.

Source waveforms are produced by the small library in groundinsight.simulation.waveforms: step, sinusoidal_with_dc_offset (the textbook single-line-to-ground fault current with DC asymmetry) and damped_oscillation. Custom waveforms are any vectorised callable f(t) -> values. A waveform gives instantaneous values, so its amplitude is a peak value, while Source.values holds RMS phasors: a fault current of 1000 A RMS has the amplitude \(\sqrt 2 \cdot 1000\) A.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
# fragment: assumes a network `net` with the current source "infeed", the fault "fault1", the bus "bus_fault" and the branch "cable_1"
import math

import groundinsight as gi
from groundinsight import waveforms

# Assume `net` is a built network with one current source 'infeed'
# and a fault 'fault1'.

study = gi.TransientStudy(network=net, fault="fault1")
study.set_source_waveform(
    "infeed",
    waveforms.sinusoidal_with_dc_offset(
        amplitude=math.sqrt(2) * 1e3,   # peak value: a fault current of 1000 A RMS
        frequency_hz=50.0,
        t_on=0.02, t_off=0.12,
        dc_amplitude=500.0,             # initial value of the DC offset, in A
        dc_decay_tau=0.05,
    ),
)
study.set_observation(buses=["bus_fault"], branches=["cable_1"])

result = study.solve(t_end=0.2, dt=1e-4, solver="fft")

# Plot the time series
gi.plot_epr_transient(result=result, title="EPR transient")
gi.plot_branch_current_transient(result=result, title="Shield current")

# Long-format DataFrame for further post-processing
df = result.to_polars()

Switching to the state-space solver only requires changing the solver argument and ensuring the network's bus and branch types carry the lumped RLC formulas required by the ODE form. That path reads those values at one frequency — the smallest strictly positive entry of network.frequencies unless solve(..., f_eval=...) names another one — and rejects a negative R, L or C instead of dropping the element.

Both solvers ignore Fault.scalings (the source waveform is the literal injection) and both warn when the active fault carries any. See Transient simulation for the derivations, the limitations of each path and the measured cross-checks.

docs.title: Memory of the FFT solver
docs.text:
The FFT solver assembles the dense \(n \times n\) admittance matrices of up to 512 frequency bins at a time and hands them to LAPACK as one stacked array — \(16\,n^2\) bytes per bin for \(n\) active buses. Since audit pass 19 the batch also stays within a byte budget, solve(..., fft_block_bytes=...), 256 MiB by default, which binds from 182 buses on. The fixed 512-bin batch needed 1.3 GB at 400 buses and 8.2 GB at 1000, and the previous batch was still alive while the next one was assembled; with the default budget a 400-bus solve over 1001 bins peaks at about 0.3 GB. The budget changes the memory, not the result: every bin is an independent solve, and the spectra are bit-identical to the old batching. A very small budget does cost time on mid-size networks, because each batch is one assembly pass over all elements — 150 buses and 1001 bins take 0.7 s at the default and 4.5 s at 1 MiB (two bins per batch). A single matrix larger than the budget is solved one bin at a time, with a log message.

# fragment: continues the study above
result = study.solve(t_end=0.2, dt=1e-4, solver="fft",
                     fft_block_bytes=64 * 2**20)   # 64 MiB per batch

docs.title: transient
docs.text:
Transient Simulation Layer.

This module hosts the high-level :class:TransientStudy workflow and the matching :class:ResultTransient Pydantic model. One study object and one observation contract serve two solvers:

  • solver="fft" samples a user-defined source waveform on a regular time grid, transforms it to a frequency spectrum via NumPy's real-valued FFT, feeds it into the per-frequency network solve and transforms the result back via IFFT.
  • solver="state_space" integrates one linear ODE built from the lumped R / L / C fields of the bus and branch types.

Design choices:

  • The FFT solver takes current sources only (Source.source_type='current'). A current source's frequency-dependent values are replaced by the FFT spectrum of the user-supplied waveform; the rest of the network remains untouched. A Thevenin (voltage) source needs the state-space solver, where the loop closure is naturally part of the ODE system.
  • Observation points (buses for EPR, branches for shield current) are passed explicitly to set_observation -- there is no "all" default, to keep memory and post-processing tractable on large networks.
  • The FFT solver does not evaluate mutual coupling: the phase current along each path would itself be time-dependent and is more natural to handle in the state-space formulation. It ignores mutual impedance and says so: meeting a coupled branch it raises a :class:~groundinsight.models.core_models.TransientModelWarning, because the same network solved stationarily or with the state-space solver returns a lower EPR at the fault (49.2 V against 77.6 V on a coupled two-bus cable link) and a silent difference of that size is indistinguishable from a modelling result. The FFT answer is the conservative one at the fault bus.
  • Only sources that can actually reach the fault inject. The stationary solver filters its sources through the source-to-fault paths; the FFT solver reproduces that with a breadth-first reachability search over the active branches, so a galvanically isolated source contributes 0 V in both solvers instead of its full spectrum in one of them.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseModel

Container for the time-domain results of a transient simulation.

Attributes:

Name Type Description time_s list of float

Time samples in seconds, equally spaced.

epr_t dict of str to list of float

Mapping of observed bus name to its EPR time series in volts.

i_branch_t dict of str to list of float

Mapping of observed branch name to its branch current time series in amperes.

source_t dict of str to list of float

The sampled source waveforms keyed by source name, in the natural unit of the source (amperes for current sources, volts for voltage sources).

fault str

Name of the fault that was active during the simulation.

solver str

Identifier of the solver that produced this result ("fft" or "state_space").

Notes

The list-typed fields use plain Python lists for JSON serialisability. Convert to numpy.ndarray at the call site if you need vectorised post-processing.

Examples:

>>> import groundinsight as gi
>>> net = gi.create_network(name="station", frequencies=[50.0])
>>> grid = gi.BusType(name="grid", system_type="Substation", voltage_level=20.0,
...                   impedance_formula="rho * 0.01")
>>> line = gi.BranchType(name="line", grounding_conductor=True,
...                      self_impedance_formula="0.25 * l",
...                      mutual_impedance_formula="0 * l")
>>> for name in ("B1", "B2"):
...     _ = gi.create_bus(name=name, type=grid, network=net)
>>> _ = gi.create_branch(name="L1", type=line, from_bus="B1", to_bus="B2",
...                      length=1.0, network=net)
>>> _ = gi.create_source(name="S1", bus="B1", values={50.0: 100.0}, network=net)
>>> _ = gi.create_fault(name="F1", bus="B2", network=net)
>>> from groundinsight.simulation import waveforms
>>> study = gi.TransientStudy(net, fault="F1")
>>> study.set_source_waveform("S1", waveforms.step(100.0, t_on=0.01, t_off=0.03))
>>> result = study.solve(t_end=0.05, dt=1e-3)
>>> result.solver, result.fault, len(result.time_s)
('fft', 'F1', 50)
>>> sorted(result.epr_t)
[]

docs.title: to_polars
docs.text:
to_polars() -> pl.DataFrame

Convert the result to a Polars DataFrame in long form.

Returns:

Type Description DataFrame

A DataFrame with columns time_s, signal_kind ("epr" / "i_branch" / "source"), name and value. Rows are grouped by signal kind and then by name, in the insertion order of the result dictionaries, with the time axis running inside each group.

Notes

Assembled one series at a time -- the time axis and the values as NumPy columns, the two label columns as Polars literals -- and stacked with pl.concat. A transient of 20 000 samples over 25 buses and 24 branches is a million rows, and materialising a million single-row Python dictionaries to hand them to Polars took 1.0 s and several hundred MB of temporary objects. Expanding the labels inside Polars instead keeps the whole conversion in Arrow: the same million-row frame is built in ~0.02 s.

Source code in src/groundinsight/simulation/transient.py 
def to_polars(self) -> "pl.DataFrame":  # noqa: F821 -- forward ref
    """
    Convert the result to a Polars DataFrame in long form.

    Returns
    -------
    polars.DataFrame
        A DataFrame with columns ``time_s``, ``signal_kind``
        (``"epr"`` / ``"i_branch"`` / ``"source"``), ``name`` and
        ``value``. Rows are grouped by signal kind and then by name,
        in the insertion order of the result dictionaries, with the
        time axis running inside each group.

    Notes
    -----
    Assembled one *series* at a time -- the time axis and the values as
    NumPy columns, the two label columns as Polars literals -- and
    stacked with ``pl.concat``. A transient of 20 000 samples over
    25 buses and 24 branches is a million rows, and materialising a
    million single-row Python dictionaries to hand them to Polars took
    1.0 s and several hundred MB of temporary objects. Expanding the
    labels inside Polars instead keeps the whole conversion in Arrow:
    the same million-row frame is built in ~0.02 s.
    """
    import polars as pl

    schema = {
        "time_s": pl.Float64,
        "signal_kind": pl.Utf8,
        "name": pl.Utf8,
        "value": pl.Float64,
    }
    time = np.asarray(self.time_s, dtype=float)

    frames: List[pl.DataFrame] = []
    for kind, table in (
        ("epr", self.epr_t),
        ("i_branch", self.i_branch_t),
        ("source", self.source_t),
    ):
        for name, series in table.items():
            frames.append(
                pl.DataFrame(
                    {
                        "time_s": time,
                        "value": np.asarray(series, dtype=float),
                    }
                )
                .with_columns(
                    pl.lit(kind, dtype=pl.Utf8).alias("signal_kind"),
                    pl.lit(name, dtype=pl.Utf8).alias("name"),
                )
                .select(list(schema))
            )

    if not frames:
        return pl.DataFrame(schema=schema)
    return pl.concat(frames)

docs.title: TransientStudy
docs.text:
TransientStudy(network: Network, fault: str)

High-level entry point for transient simulations.

A study binds together a :class:Network, the active fault to study, a set of source waveforms (one per source contributing to the fault), and the list of observation points (buses and branches) that should be returned as time series. Calling :meth:solve produces a :class:ResultTransient.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default network Network

The network model. Buses, branches, sources and faults are taken from this object. Nothing is written back -- no impedance, no active flag, no stored result, no network.paths and not network.active_fault. The state-space solver takes the phase split for its mutual coupling from the stationary phase-network solve, which needs no path set.

required fault str

Name of the fault this study simulates. It does not have to be the network's active fault. It is kept as the attribute fault_name. The former keyword fault_name is accepted as a deprecated alias.

required

Examples:

A 100 A pulse into a resistive two-station network:

>>> import groundinsight as gi
>>> net = gi.create_network(name="station", frequencies=[50.0])
>>> grid = gi.BusType(name="grid", system_type="Substation", voltage_level=20.0,
...                   impedance_formula="rho * 0.01")
>>> line = gi.BranchType(name="line", grounding_conductor=True,
...                      self_impedance_formula="0.25 * l",
...                      mutual_impedance_formula="0 * l")
>>> for name in ("B1", "B2"):
...     _ = gi.create_bus(name=name, type=grid, network=net)
>>> _ = gi.create_branch(name="L1", type=line, from_bus="B1", to_bus="B2",
...                      length=1.0, network=net)
>>> _ = gi.create_source(name="S1", bus="B1", values={50.0: 100.0}, network=net)
>>> _ = gi.create_fault(name="F1", bus="B2", network=net)
>>> from groundinsight.simulation import waveforms
>>> study = gi.TransientStudy(net, fault="F1")
>>> study.set_source_waveform("S1", waveforms.step(100.0, t_on=0.01, t_off=0.03))
>>> study.set_observation(buses=["B2"], branches=["L1"])
>>> result = study.solve(t_end=0.05, dt=1e-3)
>>> round(max(abs(v) for v in result.epr_t["B2"]), 2)

@renamed_parameters(fault_name="fault")
def __init__(self, network: Network, fault: str):
    if fault not in network.faults:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Fault '{fault}' does not exist in the network."
        )
    self.network = network
    self.fault_name = fault
    self._source_waveforms: Dict[str, WaveformFunc] = {}
    self._obs_buses: List[str] = []
    self._obs_branches: List[str] = []
    # Stand-in impedance for elements that are an ideal short circuit at
    # the 0 Hz bin, and the index of that bin. Both stay ``None`` unless
    # the FFT solver actually meets such an element. See
    # :meth:`_dc_substitute_for` and :meth:`_resolved_z_stack`.
    self._dc_substitute: Optional[float] = None
    self._dc_bin: Optional[int] = None

def set_observation(
    self,
    *,
    buses: Optional[List[str]] = None,
    branches: Optional[List[str]] = None,
):
    """
    Declare which buses and branches should be returned as time series.

    Parameters
    ----------
    buses : list of str, optional
        Names of buses whose EPR ``u(t)`` should be returned. Defaults
        to no buses.
    branches : list of str, optional
        Names of branches whose shield current ``i(t)`` should be
        returned. Defaults to no branches.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If a name is not present in the network.
    """
    for name in buses or []:
        if name not in self.network.buses:
            raise ValueError(f"Bus '{name}' not in network.")
    for name in branches or []:
        if name not in self.network.branches:
            raise ValueError(f"Branch '{name}' not in network.")
    self._obs_buses = list(buses or [])
    self._obs_branches = list(branches or [])

def set_source_waveform(self, source_name: str, waveform: WaveformFunc):
    """
    Bind a time-domain waveform to a network source.

    For ``source_type='current'`` the waveform is the injected current
    in amperes. For ``source_type='voltage'`` the waveform is the
    Thevenin EMF in volts (the ``source_impedance`` is taken from the
    :class:`Source` definition). Voltage sources are accepted by the
    state-space solver but rejected by the FFT solver, which still
    only supports current sources — the relevant solver checks the
    type at ``solve()`` time.

    Parameters
    ----------
    source_name : str
        Name of a source defined on the network.
    waveform : callable
        Vectorised function ``f(t) -> values`` mapping a 1-D time
        array to source values of the same shape.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If the source does not exist on the network.
    """
    src = self.network.sources.get(source_name)
    if src is None:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Source '{source_name}' does not exist in the network."
        )
    if src.source_type not in ("current", "voltage"):
        raise ValueError(
            f"Source '{source_name}' has unknown source_type "
            f"'{src.source_type}'."
        )
    self._source_waveforms[source_name] = waveform

solve(
    *,
    t_end: float,
    dt: float,
    solver: str = "fft",
    f_eval: Optional[float] = None,
    zero_pad: bool = False,
    fft_block_bytes: Optional[int] = None,
    progress: Optional[
        Callable[[int, int, str], None]
    ] = None,
    should_cancel: Optional[Callable[[], bool]] = None,
) -> ResultTransient

Run the transient solve and return the resulting time series.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default t_end float

End time of the simulation in seconds. t=0 is always the start. Both solvers use the same grid (see :func:_time_grid), which may extend by one sample so the sample count is even.

required dt float

Time-step in seconds. For the FFT solver this determines the Nyquist frequency f_max = 1/(2*dt) and therefore the highest harmonic resolved. For the state-space solver dt is the integration time-step (first-order hold on the source signal between samples).

required solver (fft, state_space)

Solver to use. "fft" uses BusType.impedance_formula and BranchType.self_impedance_formula (frequency-domain impedances); "state_space" uses the lumped RLC fields on BusType / BranchType and integrates with :func:scipy.signal.lsim. Defaults to "fft".

'fft' f_eval float

State-space solver only. The frequency in Hz at which the lumped R / L / C values and the Thevenin source impedance are read. The state-space model treats them as frequency-independent, so this picks the operating point. Must be one of network.frequencies. Defaults to the smallest strictly positive entry of network.frequencies rather than to its first element: with [0, 50] the first element is 0 Hz, where L_src = Im(Z_src)/omega is not defined -- reading it there as zero changes the EPR of the reference case by a factor of 680, decided by nothing but the order of the frequency list.

None zero_pad bool

FFT solver only. Solve on a window twice as long and return only its first half. The DFT is periodic, so a response that has not decayed by t_end wraps around into the start of the trace; doubling the window pushes the wrap out of the reported interval. Costs twice the solve time. Defaults to False.

False fft_block_bytes int

FFT solver only. Upper bound in bytes for one batch of dense complex admittance matrices (16 * n**2 bytes per frequency bin for n active buses). The solver assembles and solves at most 512 bins per batch; above about 181 buses this budget decides instead, so memory stays bounded for any network size -- a fixed 512-bin batch would take 1.3 GB at 400 buses and 8.2 GB at 1000. The result does not depend on it (every bin is solved on its own). A very small budget costs time on mid-size networks, because every batch is one pass of the element-wise assembly: 150 buses and 1001 bins took 4.5 s at 1 MiB (two bins per batch) against 0.7 s at the default. A single matrix larger than the budget is solved one bin at a time and logged. Defaults to 256 MiB.

None progress callable

progress(done, total, label). The FFT solver reports one unit per batch of frequency bins solved together (see fft_block_bytes), the state-space solver the two stages "assembled" and "integrated". See :mod:groundinsight.progress.

None should_cancel callable

Asked before the solve and before every unit; a true answer raises :class:~groundinsight.progress.StudyCancelled. The integration of the state-space solver is a single library call and cannot be interrupted once it runs.

None

Returns:

Type Description ResultTransient

Time-domain results at the observation points.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If no source waveform is set, if the time parameters are invalid, if f_eval is not one of network.frequencies, if fft_block_bytes is not positive, or if the network is missing the lumped RLC fields required by the state-space solver.

TypeError

If fft_block_bytes is not an integer, or if progress or should_cancel is not callable.

NotImplementedError

If solver is not one of the supported identifiers.

StudyCancelled

If should_cancel() returned true; the network is as found.

Warns:

Type Description TransientModelWarning

If the network carries mutual coupling the FFT solver cannot evaluate, if the active fault carries per-frequency scalings other than 1 (both solvers apply the source waveform as given and ignore them), or if the FFT window ends while the response is still ringing.

ModelAssumptionWarning

Code TRANSIENT_PHASE_SPLIT, state-space solver only: the phase current of a meshed network divides between routes of different R/L ratio, so the split the coupling uses -- exact at f_eval -- differs at the other frequencies in the waveform.

def solve(
    self,
    *,
    t_end: float,
    dt: float,
    solver: str = "fft",
    f_eval: Optional[float] = None,
    zero_pad: bool = False,
    fft_block_bytes: Optional[int] = None,
    progress: Optional[Callable[[int, int, str], None]] = None,
    should_cancel: Optional[Callable[[], bool]] = None,
) -> ResultTransient:
    """
    Run the transient solve and return the resulting time series.

    Parameters
    ----------
    t_end : float
        End time of the simulation in seconds. ``t=0`` is always the
        start. Both solvers use the same grid (see
        :func:`_time_grid`), which may extend by one sample so the
        sample count is even.
    dt : float
        Time-step in seconds. For the FFT solver this determines the
        Nyquist frequency ``f_max = 1/(2*dt)`` and therefore the
        highest harmonic resolved. For the state-space solver ``dt``
        is the integration time-step (first-order hold on the source
        signal between samples).
    solver : {'fft', 'state_space'}, optional
        Solver to use. ``"fft"`` uses ``BusType.impedance_formula``
        and ``BranchType.self_impedance_formula`` (frequency-domain
        impedances); ``"state_space"`` uses the lumped RLC fields on
        ``BusType`` / ``BranchType`` and integrates with
        :func:`scipy.signal.lsim`. Defaults to ``"fft"``.
    f_eval : float, optional
        *State-space solver only.* The frequency in Hz at which the
        lumped ``R`` / ``L`` / ``C`` values and the Thevenin source
        impedance are read. The state-space model treats them as
        frequency-independent, so this picks the operating point.
        Must be one of ``network.frequencies``. Defaults to the
        **smallest strictly positive** entry of ``network.frequencies``
        rather than to its first element: with ``[0, 50]`` the first
        element is 0 Hz, where ``L_src = Im(Z_src)/omega`` is not
        defined -- reading it there as zero changes the EPR of the
        reference case by a factor of 680, decided by nothing but the
        order of the frequency list.
    zero_pad : bool, optional
        *FFT solver only.* Solve on a window twice as long and return
        only its first half. The DFT is periodic, so a response that
        has not decayed by ``t_end`` wraps around into the start of
        the trace; doubling the window pushes the wrap out of the
        reported interval. Costs twice the solve time. Defaults to
        ``False``.
    fft_block_bytes : int, optional
        *FFT solver only.* Upper bound in bytes for one batch of dense
        complex admittance matrices (``16 * n**2`` bytes per frequency
        bin for ``n`` active buses). The solver assembles and solves at
        most 512 bins per batch; above about 181 buses this budget
        decides instead, so memory stays bounded for any network size --
        a fixed 512-bin batch would take 1.3 GB at 400 buses and 8.2 GB
        at 1000. The result does not depend on it (every bin is solved on
        its own). A very small budget costs time on mid-size networks,
        because every batch is one pass of the element-wise assembly:
        150 buses and 1001 bins took 4.5 s at 1 MiB (two bins per batch)
        against 0.7 s at the default. A single matrix larger than the
        budget is solved one bin at a time and logged. Defaults to
        256 MiB.
    progress : callable, optional
        ``progress(done, total, label)``. The FFT solver reports one unit
        per batch of frequency bins solved together (see
        ``fft_block_bytes``), the state-space solver the two stages
        ``"assembled"`` and ``"integrated"``. See
        :mod:`groundinsight.progress`.
    should_cancel : callable, optional
        Asked before the solve and before every unit; a true answer
        raises :class:`~groundinsight.progress.StudyCancelled`. The
        integration of the state-space solver is a single library call
        and cannot be interrupted once it runs.

    Returns
    -------
    ResultTransient
        Time-domain results at the observation points.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If no source waveform is set, if the time parameters are
        invalid, if ``f_eval`` is not one of ``network.frequencies``,
        if ``fft_block_bytes`` is not positive, or if the network is
        missing the lumped RLC fields required by the state-space
        solver.
    TypeError
        If ``fft_block_bytes`` is not an integer, or if ``progress`` or
        ``should_cancel`` is not callable.
    NotImplementedError
        If ``solver`` is not one of the supported identifiers.
    StudyCancelled
        If ``should_cancel()`` returned true; the network is as found.

    Warns
    -----
    TransientModelWarning
        If the network carries mutual coupling the FFT solver cannot
        evaluate, if the active fault carries per-frequency
        ``scalings`` other than 1 (both solvers apply the source
        waveform as given and ignore them), or if the FFT window ends
        while the response is still ringing.
    ModelAssumptionWarning
        Code ``TRANSIENT_PHASE_SPLIT``, state-space solver only: the
        phase current of a meshed network divides between routes of
        different R/L ratio, so the split the coupling uses -- exact at
        ``f_eval`` -- differs at the other frequencies in the waveform.
    """
    block_bytes = _validated_block_bytes(fft_block_bytes)
    if solver not in ("fft", "state_space"):
        raise NotImplementedError(
            f"Unknown transient solver: '{solver}'. "
            "Supported: 'fft', 'state_space'."
        )
    self._hooks = StudyHooks(
        "TransientStudy.solve", 0, progress, should_cancel
    )
    try:
        with restore_on_cancel(self.network):
            self._hooks.checkpoint()
            if solver == "fft":
                return self._solve_fft(
                    t_end=t_end, dt=dt, zero_pad=zero_pad, block_bytes=block_bytes
                )
            return self._solve_state_space(t_end=t_end, dt=dt, f_eval=f_eval)
    finally:
        self._hooks = StudyHooks("TransientStudy.solve", 0)

docs.title: waveforms
docs.text:
Waveform Library for Transient Simulations.

This module provides a small library of factory functions that return Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray] waveforms suitable for the :class:groundinsight.simulation.transient.TransientStudy solver. Each factory captures its own parameters and returns a vectorised function f(t) -> values that can be called with an array of time samples.

The included waveforms cover the typical fault-current scenarios for low- and medium-voltage grounding studies:

  • :func:step -- a Heaviside-style on/off pulse, the simplest fault model (the source comes on at t_on and off again at t_off).
  • :func:sinusoidal_with_dc_offset -- a power-frequency current with an exponentially decaying DC component, the textbook representation of a single-line-to-ground fault current including the asymmetry caused by the inductive loop.
  • :func:damped_oscillation -- a damped sinusoid useful for switching transients and ringing studies.

Custom waveforms can be defined as any user function that accepts a 1-D np.ndarray of time samples and returns an array of the same shape.

Examples:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from groundinsight.simulation import waveforms
>>> pulse = waveforms.step(100.0, t_on=0.01, t_off=0.03)
>>> pulse(np.array([0.0, 0.02, 0.04])).tolist()
[0.0, 100.0, 0.0]

def damped_oscillation(
    amplitude: float,
    frequency_hz: float,
    decay_tau: float,
    *,
    phase_rad: float = 0.0,
    t_on: float = 0.0,
    t_off: Optional[float] = None,
) -> Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray]:
    """
    Construct a damped sinusoid, useful for switching-transient studies.

    The waveform is::

        x(t) = A * exp(-(t - t_on)/tau) * sin(omega*(t - t_on) + phi)

    inside the on-window ``[t_on, t_off)``, and zero outside.

    Parameters
    ----------
    amplitude : float
        Initial peak amplitude.
    frequency_hz : float
        Oscillation frequency in Hz.
    decay_tau : float
        Decay time constant in seconds.
    phase_rad : float, optional
        Phase offset of the sinusoid, in radians. Defaults to ``0.0``.
    t_on : float, optional
        Onset time, in seconds. Defaults to ``0.0``.
    t_off : float, optional
        Cut-off time, in seconds. ``None`` lets the oscillation decay
        naturally to the end of the time grid.

    Returns
    -------
    callable
        A vectorised waveform.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> w = damped_oscillation(
    ...     amplitude=1e3, frequency_hz=500.0, decay_tau=2e-3,
    ...     t_on=0.01,
    ... )
    """
    if not np.isfinite(frequency_hz) or frequency_hz <= 0:
        raise ValueError(
            "damped_oscillation: frequency_hz must be a finite positive "
            f"number (got {frequency_hz!r})."
        )
    if not np.isfinite(decay_tau) or decay_tau <= 0:
        raise ValueError(
            "damped_oscillation: decay_tau must be a finite positive "
            f"number (got {decay_tau!r}). decay_tau == 0 divides by zero "
            "and decay_tau < 0 produces an exponentially growing "
            "waveform — almost certainly not what was intended."
        )
    _validate_window(t_on, t_off, "damped_oscillation")
    omega = 2.0 * np.pi * frequency_hz

    def _wave(t: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        t = np.asarray(t, dtype=float)
        on = t >= t_on
        if t_off is not None:
            on = on & (t < t_off)
        tau_local = np.maximum(t - t_on, 0.0)
        envelope = amplitude * np.exp(-tau_local / decay_tau)
        signal = envelope * np.sin(omega * tau_local + phase_rad)
        return np.where(on, signal, 0.0)

    return _wave

def sinusoidal_with_dc_offset(
    amplitude: float,
    frequency_hz: float,
    *,
    phase_rad: float = 0.0,
    t_on: float = 0.0,
    t_off: Optional[float] = None,
    dc_amplitude: float = 0.0,
    dc_decay_tau: Optional[float] = None,
) -> Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray]:
    """
    Construct a windowed sinusoid with optional exponentially decaying DC.

    Models the typical single-line-to-ground fault current::

        i(t) = A * sin(omega*(t - t_on) + phi) + I_dc * exp(-(t - t_on)/tau)

    multiplied by a rectangular window between ``t_on`` and ``t_off``.
    The DC component captures the asymmetric peak that arises when the
    fault occurs at a non-zero-crossing instant of the source voltage
    and the loop has finite inductance.

    Parameters
    ----------
    amplitude : float
        Peak value of the AC component.
    frequency_hz : float
        Power frequency in Hz (e.g. 50 or 60).
    phase_rad : float, optional
        Initial phase of the AC component, in radians. Defaults to ``0.0``.
    t_on : float, optional
        Fault initiation time, in seconds. Defaults to ``0.0``.
    t_off : float, optional
        Fault clearing time, in seconds. ``None`` keeps the fault on
        until the end of the time grid.
    dc_amplitude : float, optional
        Initial value of the DC component. Defaults to ``0.0`` (no DC
        offset).
    dc_decay_tau : float, optional
        Time constant ``L/R`` of the loop governing the DC decay, in
        seconds. ``None`` disables the decay (DC stays constant during
        the on-window). Required when ``dc_amplitude != 0`` and a finite
        decay is desired.

    Returns
    -------
    callable
        A vectorised waveform ``f(t) -> values``.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> w = sinusoidal_with_dc_offset(
    ...     amplitude=20e3, frequency_hz=50.0,
    ...     t_on=0.02, t_off=0.12,
    ...     dc_amplitude=10e3, dc_decay_tau=0.05,
    ... )
    """
    if not np.isfinite(frequency_hz) or frequency_hz <= 0:
        raise ValueError(
            "sinusoidal_with_dc_offset: frequency_hz must be a finite "
            f"positive number (got {frequency_hz!r}). Negative frequency "
            "is silently equivalent to flipping the phase and "
            "frequency_hz == 0 collapses to a constant offset that "
            "masks user confusion with the dc_amplitude term."
        )
    if dc_decay_tau is not None and (
        not np.isfinite(dc_decay_tau) or dc_decay_tau <= 0
    ):
        raise ValueError(
            "sinusoidal_with_dc_offset: dc_decay_tau must be a finite "
            f"positive number when set (got {dc_decay_tau!r}). Pass "
            "dc_decay_tau=None to disable the decay altogether."
        )
    _validate_window(t_on, t_off, "sinusoidal_with_dc_offset")
    omega = 2.0 * np.pi * frequency_hz

    def _wave(t: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        t = np.asarray(t, dtype=float)
        on = t >= t_on
        if t_off is not None:
            on = on & (t < t_off)

        tau_local = t - t_on
        ac = amplitude * np.sin(omega * tau_local + phase_rad)
        if dc_amplitude == 0.0:
            dc = np.zeros_like(t)
        elif dc_decay_tau is None:
            dc = np.full_like(t, dc_amplitude)
        else:
            # Exponential decay starting at t_on, only meaningful in the
            # on-window. Outside the window the rectangular factor below
            # forces it to zero anyway.
            dc = dc_amplitude * np.exp(
                -np.maximum(tau_local, 0.0) / dc_decay_tau
            )

        return np.where(on, ac + dc, 0.0)

    return _wave

def step(
    amplitude: float,
    *,
    t_on: float = 0.0,
    t_off: Optional[float] = None,
) -> Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray]:
    """
    Construct a rectangular pulse waveform.

    The output is zero before ``t_on``, equals ``amplitude`` between
    ``t_on`` and ``t_off`` and is zero again after ``t_off``. With
    ``t_off=None`` the pulse extends to the end of the time grid
    (a classic Heaviside step).

    Parameters
    ----------
    amplitude : float
        Plateau value of the pulse.
    t_on : float, optional
        Time at which the pulse switches on, in seconds. Defaults to
        ``0.0``.
    t_off : float, optional
        Time at which the pulse switches off, in seconds. ``None`` means
        "stays on indefinitely". Defaults to ``None``.

    Returns
    -------
    callable
        A vectorised waveform function ``f(t) -> values``.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import numpy as np
    >>> w = step(amplitude=100.0, t_on=0.02, t_off=0.12)
    >>> y = w(np.linspace(0.0, 0.2, 5))
    """
    _validate_window(t_on, t_off, "step")

    def _wave(t: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        t = np.asarray(t, dtype=float)
        on = t >= t_on
        if t_off is not None:
            on = on & (t < t_off)
        return np.where(on, amplitude, 0.0)

    return _wave

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: The examples are Jupyter notebooks. They are stored without outputs and executed when this site is built, so every table and figure on these pages is the output of the code next to it, run against the documented release — a notebook that fails stops the build. Each one states the numbers it expects and checks them a second way: against a closed form, a nodal solve written in NumPy, or a second solver.

docs.title: First steps with the model
docs.text:
• Minimal example — three stations on a cable line, one source, one fault: build, solve, read the results as tables, and check four of them against Kirchhoff's laws and the closed forms of a line. The tutorial Your first fault calculation takes the same steps more slowly.
  • MV ring (stationary) — a 20 kV ring with 20 substations in the frequency domain: earth potential rise per bus, both reduction factors and the earthing impedance at the fault.
  • MV ring (transient) — the same ring in the time domain: the FFT and the state-space solver, each against the stationary solve it must reproduce, a fault current with DC offset, and a Thévenin source switched onto the ring.
  • Pandapower import — preview and convert a pandapower network with preview_pandapower_import and from_pandapower, add a fault, solve, and run an outage study on the result.
  • Fault sweep — the fault moved over every bus of a 10-bus cable line at five frequencies: earthing impedance and both reduction factors per fault location, with Network.res_all_impedances().

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
• Fault decomposition — the analysis layer on top of a solve: the two reduction factors, analyze_cuts, bus_response, run_sweep with summarize and classify, and the closed-form reference cases.
  • Electrode at the fault location — which electrode does the faulted station need? The network split at the fault into what belongs to the network and what to the electrode, a catalogue of electrodes in the \(\rho\)–\(f\) form through run_sweep, statistics and classes on the stacked results.
  • Location response bracket — a station characterised without knowing its electrode: the response to every electrode from two solves, the bracket of no electrode, an ideal one and the passive worst case, and what that bracket does not cover.
  • Phase currents in meshes — how the fault current divides in rings, meshes and parallel cables, what the legacy paths mode makes of it, and what phase_impedance_formula changes — checked against a fully coupled multi-conductor solve.
  • Direct-current studies — f = 0 as an ordinary frequency: removable singularities, dropped reactances, ideal bonds and true poles, each against a reference that does not come from groundinsight.
  • Thermal limits — whether an earthing conductor survives the fault current, after IEC 60949 and IEC 60909-0.

docs.title: Run them yourself
docs.text:
The button at the top of each notebook page downloads the notebook, without outputs. To run it, install the package with the pandapower extra and JupyterLab into a virtual environment (Installation):

pip install "groundinsight[pandapower]" jupyterlab
jupyter lab

To run all of them from a clone of the repository instead:

git clone https://github.com/Ce1ectric/groundinsight.git
cd groundinsight
pip install -e ".[pandapower]" jupyterlab
jupyter lab docs/examples/

FREQUENCIES = [50.0, 250.0]
SOURCE = {50.0: 1000.0, 250.0: 200.0}   # A
Z_STATION = 10.0                        # Ohm
BUSES = ["S0", "S1", "site", "S3"]
SECTIONS = [("C1", "S0", "S1"), ("C2", "S1", "site"), ("C3", "site", "S3")]


def zs(f):
    "Shield-earth loop of one 1 km section in Ohm."
    return 0.1 + 0.2j * f / 50


def zm(f):
    "Coupling of one 1 km section in Ohm."
    return 0.05 + 0.1j * f / 50


CABLE = gi.BranchType(name="cable", grounding_conductor=True,
                      self_impedance_formula="(0.1 + 0.2*j*f/50)*l",
                      mutual_impedance_formula="(0.05 + 0.1*j*f/50)*l",
                      phase_impedance_formula="(0.06 + 0.11*j*f/50)*l")


def network(site_electrode=repr(Z_STATION)):
    "The feeder; ``site_electrode`` is the impedance formula at the site."
    net = gi.create_network(name="feeder", frequencies=FREQUENCIES)
    for bus in BUSES:
        formula = site_electrode if bus == "site" else repr(Z_STATION)
        bus_type = gi.BusType(name=f"electrode_{bus}", system_type="MV", voltage_level=20.0,
                              impedance_formula=formula)
        gi.create_bus(name=bus, type=bus_type, network=net)
    for name, a, b in SECTIONS:
        gi.create_branch(name=name, type=CABLE, from_bus=a, to_bus=b, length=1.0, network=net)
    gi.create_source(name="infeed", bus="S0", values=SOURCE, network=net)
    gi.create_fault(name="earth_fault", bus="site", network=net)
    return net

def by_hand(f, z_site):
    "Earth potentials of all buses for a site electrode z_site (None: open, 0: ideal)."
    index = {bus: i for i, bus in enumerate(BUSES)}
    Y = np.zeros((4, 4), dtype=complex)
    for bus in BUSES:
        if bus != "site":
            Y[index[bus], index[bus]] += 1 / Z_STATION
        elif z_site is not None and z_site != 0:
            Y[index[bus], index[bus]] += 1 / z_site
    for _, a, b in SECTIONS:
        y = 1 / zs(f)
        i, j = index[a], index[b]
        Y[i, i] += y
        Y[j, j] += y
        Y[i, j] -= y
        Y[j, i] -= y
    current = (1 - zm(f) / zs(f)) * SOURCE[f]
    rhs = np.zeros(4, dtype=complex)
    rhs[index["S0"]], rhs[index["site"]] = current, -current
    if z_site == 0:                     # ideal: the site is remote earth
        keep = [index[bus] for bus in BUSES if bus != "site"]
        u = np.zeros(4, dtype=complex)
        u[keep] = np.linalg.solve(Y[np.ix_(keep, keep)], rhs[keep])
    else:
        u = np.linalg.solve(Y, rhs)
    return {bus: u[index[bus]] for bus in BUSES}


def ladder_z_net(f):
    "Closed form: towards the infeed (S1 behind S0) in parallel with towards S3."
    def par(a, b):
        return a * b / (a + b)
    return par(zs(f) + par(Z_STATION, zs(f) + Z_STATION), zs(f) + Z_STATION)


for f in FREQUENCIES:
    print(f"{f:5.1f} Hz  Z_net closed form {ladder_z_net(f):.6f} Ohm,"
          f" deviation {abs(response.z_network[f] - ladder_z_net(f)) / abs(ladder_z_net(f)):.1e}")

What the bracket says:

  • $Z_\text{driving point}$ runs from $Z_\text{net}$ (no electrode) to zero (ideal electrode). The passive worst case lies 0.08 % above $Z_\text{net}$ at 50 Hz and 1.8 % at 250 Hz, where the network is more inductive — small in a cable network, but it is the true bound rather than an assumed one.
  • r_epr does not move. The closed form says why: the potential of the bus is $u_b = u_{0,b}/(1 + Y_B Z_\text{net})$, with and without the coupling alike, so the factor cancels in the quotient. The invariance is algebra, not an observation.
  • EPR_S0_V: an ideal electrode at the site almost doubles the earth potential rise at the infeed station. Earthing the site better pushes potential onto its neighbours.

The capacitive electrode cancels the reactance of $Z_\text{net}$, a series resonance: the electrode current is $u_{0,b}/(Z_\text{net} + Z_B)$, and with $Z_B = -j\operatorname{Im} Z_\text{net}$ it exceeds the current into an ideal electrode. The local earth potential rise stays inside its bracket; the potential at the infeed and r_current leave theirs — only slightly here, but a bound that a passive electrode can cross is no bound. Read the extremes as bounds for the local quantities only.

docs.title: Characterising a location without knowing its electrode¶
docs.text:
The question: what does the network do at one particular station, whatever electrode is or will be installed there?

The obvious approach is to bracket it: compute once with no electrode at all and once with an ideal one. That is right, and it goes further. Adding an electrode at bus $b$ is a rank-one change of the nodal admittance matrix, so by the Sherman–Morrison formula every nodal voltage is a Möbius function of the electrode admittance $Y_B$:

$$ \underline{u}(Y_B) = \underline{u}_0 - \frac{Y_B\,\underline{z}\,u_{0,b}}{1 + Y_B Z_\text{net}} . $$

Three quantities that do not depend on the electrode determine the response to every electrode, and two solves give them:

quantity meaning $\underline{u}_0$ the potentials with the electrode at $b$ removed — the open-circuit response of the location $\underline{z}$ the potential everywhere per ampere injected at $b$, source-free $Z_\text{net} = z_b$ the driving-point impedance of everything except the local electrode

The two extremes are then not two isolated samples but the end points of a curve that is known in closed form. bus_response computes it; this notebook checks it against solved networks and against a nodal solve written here in NumPy. Background: Characterising a location without its electrode.

docs.title: The network¶
docs.text: Four stations on a radial 20 kV cable, 1 km per section: the infeed at S0, then S1, the location under study site with the earth fault, and S3 behind it. Every station has a $10\ \Omega$ electrode; the cable is that of Which electrode does the faulted station need?, with $k = Z_m/Z_s = 0.5$. The source current has a fifth harmonic.

docs.title: The second method: a nodal solve by hand¶
docs.text: The earthing network of a radial feeder is a ladder, and with the same $k$ on every section it is driven by $(1-k)\,I$, entering at the infeed and leaving at the fault (in the sign frame of groundinsight). The site electrode is a parameter: None for none at all, 0 for an ideal one, which pins the site to remote earth.

docs.title: 1  The bracket¶
docs.text: extremes() evaluates three electrodes: open (none at all), ideal ($Z_B = 0$) and worst_passive, the electrode that maximises the driving-point impedance among all passive ones. The last one is not the open end: a purely reactive electrode that cancels the susceptance of the network, $Y_B = -j\,\operatorname{Im}(1/Z_\text{net})$, lies slightly above it.

docs.title: 2  The closed form against solved networks¶
docs.text: Two solves, any number of electrodes: here the closed form is checked against networks that were actually built with that electrode and solved, and against the nodal solve by hand.

docs.title: 3  The whole curve, without another solve¶
docs.text: sweep evaluates the closed form for a list of electrodes — a hundred points cost as much as one. For a real electrode resistance the driving-point impedance falls monotonically from $Z_\text{net}$ to zero.

docs.title: 4  What the bracket covers — and what it does not¶
docs.text: open, ideal and worst_passive bracket the quantities of the location itself: its earth potential rise and its driving-point impedance. They do not bracket the transfer quantities in the same table — the potential at a neighbouring station or r_current. A purely capacitive electrode is passive and therefore inside the same class, yet it can drive the potential at the infeed above the value of the ideal electrode:

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
1. $Z_\text{net}$ is the number that describes the location without knowing anything about its electrode: what the rest of the earthing system contributes in parallel to it.
  2. The extremes bracket the local quantities. Every passive electrode gives an earth potential rise and a driving-point impedance between ideal and worst_passive; if even the worst passive case keeps the limits, the location needs no further field computation for that question.
  3. The curve in between is known in closed form. A sensitivity study over electrode characteristics needs no further solve — only evaluate or sweep.
  4. Two reduction factors, two statements. r_epr characterises the cable run and does not respond to the electrode at the location; r_current describes how the fault current divides there.

Which electrode does the faulted station need? splits $Z_\text{net}$ further into its directions with analyze_cuts. The API: Location response.

Z_STATION = 10.0                                                  # Ohm
SECTION_KM = 0.8
BUSES = ["S0", "S1", "S2", "S3", "S4", "S5"]

            ("C34", "S3", "S4"), ("C45", "S4", "S5")]
FAULT_BUS = "S3"


def zs(f):
    "Shield-earth loop in Ohm/km."
    return 0.1 + 0.2j * f / 50


def zm(f):
    "Coupling phase conductor <-> shield loop in Ohm/km."
    return 0.05 + 0.1j * f / 50


STATION = gi.BusType(name="station", system_type="MV", voltage_level=20.0,
                     impedance_formula=repr(Z_STATION))
CABLE = gi.BranchType(name="cable", grounding_conductor=True,
                      self_impedance_formula="(0.1 + 0.2*j*f/50)*l",
                      mutual_impedance_formula="(0.05 + 0.1*j*f/50)*l",
                      phase_impedance_formula="(0.06 + 0.11*j*f/50)*l")


def feeder(sections=SECTIONS):
    net = gi.create_network(name="feeder", frequencies=FREQUENCIES)
    for bus in BUSES:
        gi.create_bus(name=bus, type=STATION, network=net)
    for name, a, b in sections:
        gi.create_branch(name=name, type=CABLE, from_bus=a, to_bus=b, length=SECTION_KM,
                         network=net)
    gi.create_source(name="infeed", bus="S0", values=SOURCE, network=net)
    gi.create_fault(name="earth_fault", bus=FAULT_BUS, network=net)
    return net

def impedance_matrix(f, electrode_at_fault=Z_STATION, sections=SECTIONS):
    "Inverse of the nodal admittance matrix of the earthing network at f."
    index = {bus: i for i, bus in enumerate(BUSES)}
    Y = np.zeros((len(BUSES), len(BUSES)), dtype=complex)
    for bus in BUSES:
        Y[index[bus], index[bus]] += 1 / (electrode_at_fault if bus == FAULT_BUS else Z_STATION)
    for _, a, b in sections:
        y = 1 / (zs(f) * SECTION_KM)
        i, j = index[a], index[b]
        Y[i, i] += y
        Y[j, j] += y
        Y[i, j] -= y
        Y[j, i] -= y
    return np.linalg.inv(Y), index


def u_e_by_hand(f, electrode_at_fault=Z_STATION, sections=SECTIONS):
    "EPR at the fault bus: (1 - k) I in at S0, out at S3."
    Z, index = impedance_matrix(f, electrode_at_fault, sections)
    k = zm(f) / zs(f)
    current = (1 - k) * SOURCE[f]
    return Z[index[FAULT_BUS], index["S0"]] * current - Z[index[FAULT_BUS], index[FAULT_BUS]] * current

On a radial feeder each side is a ladder, so $Z_\text{side}$ has a closed form: the section, then the station electrode in parallel with the rest of the ladder.

def parallel(*impedances):
    return 1 / sum(1 / z for z in impedances)


def ladder(f, n_sections):
    "Seen from the fault bus through n sections, each ending at a 10 Ohm station."
    z = Z_STATION
    for _ in range(n_sections - 1):
        z = parallel(Z_STATION, zs(f) * SECTION_KM + z)
    return zs(f) * SECTION_KM + z


worst = 0.0
for f in FREQUENCIES:
    by_hand = {"towards_infeed": ladder(f, 3), "towards_end": ladder(f, 2)}
    z_par = parallel(Z_STATION, *by_hand.values())
    for name, z in by_hand.items():
        worst = max(worst, abs(cuts.z_side[name][f] - z) / abs(z))
    worst = max(worst, abs(cuts.z_parallel[f] - z_par) / abs(z_par))
    worst = max(worst, abs(cuts.z_driving_point[f] - z_par) / abs(z_par))
    print(f"{f:5.0f} Hz  Z_infeed = {by_hand['towards_infeed']:.5f}  Z_end = {by_hand['towards_end']:.5f}"
          f"  Z_parallel = {z_par:.5f} Ohm")
print(f"\nlargest relative deviation of groundinsight from the closed forms: {worst:.1e}")

Three kinds of quantity, three behaviours:

  • Z_side does not move. It belongs to the network, not to the electrode.
  • $Z_E$ (grounding_impedance_Ohm), $U_E$ and the reduction factor on a current basis, reduction_factor_current, follow the electrode.
  • The EPR ratio, reduction_factor, stays at $0.5 = \lvert 1 - k\rvert$ over two and a half decades of $Z_B$. It is computed from two solves that share the same nodal matrix, so a change at the fault bus cancels in the quotient — which is why the EN 50522 reduction factor of Reduction factors and earthing impedance is the current-based one.

docs.title: Which electrode does the faulted station need?¶
docs.text:
A 20 kV cable feeder, an earth fault at a station in the middle, a fault current with harmonics — and the question an earthing study often ends with: which electrode does the faulted station need? This notebook

  1. splits the network at the fault with analyze_cuts and separates what belongs to the network from what belongs to the electrode,
  2. varies the electrode at the fault and watches both reduction factors,
  3. runs a catalogue of electrode characteristics in the $\rho$–$f$ form through run_sweep, and
  4. summarises and classifies the stacked results.

Every number is checked a second way: against the closed form of the ladder network the feeder is, or against a nodal solve written here in NumPy. The basics of cuts and reduction factors are in Decomposing a fault; the background in Splitting the network, location response.

docs.title: The feeder¶
docs.text:
Six stations S0 … S5 on a radial cable, 0.8 km per section, the infeed at S0 and the earth fault at S3. The source current carries the 50 Hz fundamental and three harmonics. All values are illustrative:

value station electrode $10\ \Omega$, every station shield–earth loop $Z_s'$ $0.1 + 0.2j\,f/50\ \Omega$/km coupling $Z_m'$ $0.05 + 0.1j\,f/50\ \Omega$/km phase–earth loop, shield bonded, $Z_\text{red}'$ $0.06 + 0.11j\,f/50\ \Omega$/km source current 1000 A at 50 Hz, 120 A at 150 Hz, 60 A at 250 Hz, 30 A at 350 Hz

The ratio $k = Z_m/Z_s = 0.5$ is the same on every section and at every frequency.

docs.title: The second method: a nodal solve by hand¶
docs.text: The earthing network is a ladder: electrodes to remote earth at every station, the shields between them. Its nodal matrix takes ten lines. With the same $k$ on every section, the phase current enters it only through $k$: the earthing network is driven by $(1-k)\,I$, entering at the infeed and leaving at the fault, in the sign frame of groundinsight.

docs.title: 1  The cuts: network and electrode apart¶
docs.text: A Cut is a named set of branches at the fault bus. Here one points towards the infeed and one towards the end of the feeder. Z_side is what the network offers in that direction, Z_local is the electrode of the faulted station itself, and Z_parallel combines them: $1/Z_\text{parallel} = 1/Z_\text{local} + \sum 1/Z_\text{side}$.

docs.title: 2  The electrode at the fault, varied¶
docs.text: The same feeder with five electrodes at S3, from $0.5$ to $200\ \Omega$. Each one is a SweepPoint that overrides the impedance table of the bus; run_sweep restores the network afterwards.

docs.title: 3  A catalogue of electrodes in the $\rho$–$f$ form¶
docs.text:
A field computation or a measurement campaign can hand an electrode over as five numbers $k_1 \dots k_5$ of the form

$$ Z(\rho, f) = k_1\,\rho + (k_2 + j\,k_3)\,f + (k_4 + j\,k_5)\,\rho\,f . $$

rho_f_points turns a catalogue of such vectors into sweep points for one bus, evaluated at the network frequencies and a soil resistivity, and copies $k_1 \dots k_5$ and $\rho$ into the result frames as ordinary columns.

docs.title: 4  Statistics and classification¶
docs.text: The sweep frames are long-format tables, one row per point, bus and frequency plus an RMS row, so the usual Polars tools apply. summarize reduces a column to count, spread, quantiles and extremes, classify bins it into bands that you supply — there is deliberately no built-in table of admissible values. The edges below are illustrative, not limits of a standard.

docs.title: 5  When the feeder is closed into a ring¶
docs.text: A sixth section S5 – S0 closes the feeder into a ring. The two cuts no longer lead to separate parts of the network: both directions end up at the infeed. The decomposition stays exact — Z_side is defined by how a test current injected at the fault bus divides, and the identity holds whatever the topology — but the two sides share their stations, sides_are_disjoint is False, and r_side, which needs a side of its own, is left empty.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
quantity what it describes moves with the electrode at the fault Z_side_Ohm per cut what the network offers in that direction no — a property of the network Z_local_Ohm the electrode of the faulted station it is the electrode Z_parallel_Ohm both in parallel, equal to $Z_E$ yes reduction_factor (EPR ratio) EPR with coupling over EPR without no reduction_factor_current share of the fault current returning through the soil yes current_share per cut share of the fault current leaving through that cut yes r_side earth share over that cut yes, and only for disjoint sides with a source

The API used here: Fault-location decomposition, Parameter sweeps, Statistics and classification.

Z_A, Z_B, Z_C = 0.8, 12.0, 3.5   # Ohm    earthing impedance of the three buses
RHO = 100.0                      # Ohm m  soil resistivity
I_DC = 1000.0                    # A      direct current entering at A

# Two spellings of the same 0.25 Ohm/km earthing conductor. The first lets the
# reactance vanish at DC by itself, the second does not.
CARSON = "(0.25 + I*2*pi*f*2e-7*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.01)) * l"
CONSTANT_X = "(0.25 + I*0.6) * l"
NO_COUPLING = "(rho*0 + 0.0 + I*f*0) * l"


def build(name, ab_formula, bc_formula, *, frequencies=(0.0,),
          ab_length=10.0, bc_length=10.0, voltage_source=False):
    "Chain A -- B -- C with ``I_DC`` entering at A and the fault at C."
    freqs = sorted(float(f) for f in frequencies)
    bus_types = {
        label: gi.BusType(
            name=f"{name}_bt_{label}",
            description=f"Earthing system at {label}",
            system_type="Substation",
            voltage_level=110.0,
            impedance_formula=f"rho*0 + {z!r} + I*f*0",
        )
        for label, z in (("A", Z_A), ("B", Z_B), ("C", Z_C))
    }
    ab_type = gi.BranchType(name=f"{name}_ab", grounding_conductor=True,
                            self_impedance_formula=ab_formula,
                            mutual_impedance_formula=NO_COUPLING)
    bc_type = gi.BranchType(name=f"{name}_bc", grounding_conductor=True,
                            self_impedance_formula=bc_formula,
                            mutual_impedance_formula=NO_COUPLING)
    net = gi.create_network(name=name, frequencies=freqs, description="DC earth-current study")
    for label in ("A", "B", "C"):
        gi.create_bus(name=label, type=bus_types[label], specific_earth_resistance=RHO, network=net)
    gi.create_branch(name="A-B", type=ab_type, from_bus="A", to_bus="B", length=ab_length, network=net)
    gi.create_branch(name="B-C", type=bc_type, from_bus="B", to_bus="C", length=bc_length, network=net)
    if voltage_source:
        gi.create_voltage_source(
            name="dc", bus="A",
            voltage={f: I_DC + 0.0j for f in freqs},
            source_impedance={f: 0.5 + 0.0j for f in freqs},
            network=net,
        )
    else:
        gi.create_source(name="dc", bus="A", values={f: I_DC + 0.0j for f in freqs}, network=net)
    gi.create_fault(name="F", bus="C", network=net)
    return net


def epr(net, freq=0.0, fault="F"):
    "Earth potential rise per bus as complex phasors; at DC they are real."
    return {b.name: complex(b.uepr_freq[freq].real, b.uepr_freq[freq].imag)
            for b in net.results[fault].buses}


def evaluate(formula, frequencies, length=10.0):
    "The self impedance of one branch with this formula, per frequency."
    probe_net = gi.create_network(name="probe", frequencies=sorted(frequencies))
    station = gi.BusType(name="probe_station", system_type="Substation", voltage_level=110.0,
                         impedance_formula="1.0")
    for bus in ("P", "Q"):
        gi.create_bus(name=bus, type=station, specific_earth_resistance=RHO, network=probe_net)
    probe = gi.BranchType(name="probe", grounding_conductor=True, self_impedance_formula=formula,
                          mutual_impedance_formula=NO_COUPLING)
    branch = gi.create_branch(name="P-Q", type=probe, from_bus="P", to_bus="Q", length=length,

DCLimitWarning (DC_LIMIT):
  Impedance formula '(0.25 + I*0.6) * l' carries a finite reactance at 0 Hz (X/R = 2.4). At DC a reactance either vanishes (j*omega*L -> 0) or is infinite (1/(j*omega*C) -> inf); a finite non-zero one has no physical reading, so the 0 Hz bin falls back to the real part and the reactance is dropped. This is usually a constant term such as '+ j*X' that was meant to apply at power frequency; writing the reactance as 'j*2*pi*f*L' makes it vanish at DC by itself. All other frequencies are unaffected.

Only the constant-reactance formula warns. Two things about that warning are deliberate:

  • it quotes the ratio $X/R$ rather than the two values, because the ratio is length-invariant and therefore identical for every branch sharing a BranchType — which lets Python's default warning filter collapse a hundred-branch network into a single line instead of a hundred;
  • it names the remedy: write the reactance as I*2*pi*f*L and it vanishes at DC by itself, with nothing dropped and nothing warned about.

The reactance falls by one decade per decade of frequency and is exactly zero at 0 Hz, where the real part is the DC resistance $0.25\ \Omega/\text{km} \times 10\ \text{km} = 2.5\ \Omega$. The limit is found numerically, by approaching zero on the decade sequence 1e-6, 1e-7, 1e-8 Hz and comparing two consecutive absolute differences: shrinking means a removable singularity, growing means a true pole. The criterion has to be absolute — a relative one cannot classify a formula whose limit is zero, because there the relative change per decade stays at 90 % forever.

The tie-break is biased towards convergent on purpose. Mistaking a pole for a limit yields a very large finite impedance, which behaves almost like the open circuit it should have been; the opposite mistake would silently disconnect a real earthing conductor. A formula that is NaN on the approach as well is a genuine failure and raises, with a message that names the formula, the frequency and the parameters.

NaN is not a valid impedance -- it propagates into the admittance matrix and surfaces much later as a singular-matrix error. def merged_reference():
    "DC solution with the ideal bond merged into a single node {A, B}."
    g = 1.0 / R_BC
    Y = np.array([[1 / Z_A + 1 / Z_B + g, -g], [-g, 1 / Z_C + g]])
    u = np.linalg.solve(Y, np.array([I_DC, -I_DC]))
    return {"A": u[0], "B": u[0], "C": u[1]}


def open_reference():
    "DC solution with the bond dropped from the matrix (a short modelled as open)."
    g = 1.0 / R_BC
    Y = np.array([
        [1 / Z_A, 0.0, 0.0],
        [0.0, 1 / Z_B + g, -g],
        [0.0, -g, 1 / Z_C + g],
    ])
    u = np.linalg.solve(Y, np.array([I_DC, 0.0, -I_DC]))
    return {"A": u[0], "B": u[1], "C": u[2]}

DCLimitWarning (DC_LIMIT):
  Zero impedance at 0 Hz in the steady-state solve: branch 'A-B'. At DC a purely inductive element is an ideal short circuit, which is the correct limit but has no reciprocal, so the nodal system cannot use it directly. The affected elements are modelled with 5.21541e-09 Ohm instead (sqrt(machine epsilon) times the smallest other impedance in the network (0.35 Ohm)). That reproduces the ideal short to roughly five significant digits and is far better than dropping the element, which would model a short as an open circuit. Only the 0 Hz bin is affected. For an exact result, model the two buses of an ideal bond as a single bus.

The substitution agrees with the merged reference to better than $10^{-7}$ relative at every bus. Dropping the element instead would be wrong by an order of magnitude at every bus and would reverse the sign at bus B: bus A would be cut off from the network and report its own electrode ($1000\ \text{A} \times 0.8\ \Omega = 800\ \text{V}$) instead of the parallel combination.

The stand-in is $\sqrt{\varepsilon_\text{mach}}\,Z_\text{min} = 1.4901\cdot 10^{-8}\,Z_\text{min}$, with $Z_\text{min}$ the smallest finite non-zero impedance magnitude in the network at that frequency, and it is applied at the 0 Hz bin only. Nothing else in the study is touched.

Giving the bond a small but honest resistance converges to the same answer from the other side: the deviation shrinks in proportion to the resistance, about $3.5\,R_\text{bond}/\Omega$ relative in this network.

When to merge the two buses instead. The exact model of an ideal bond is one node, not two, and the stand-in is an approximation of that merge. Prefer the merge — a single bus whose impedance is the parallel combination of the two electrodes — whenever the difference in earth potential rise across the bond is part of what you report (across an ideal bond it is zero, and whatever the stand-in produces there is numerical residue), or when the bonded buses carry impedances many orders of magnitude away from $Z_\text{min}$. For the usual question — the earth potential rise of the bonded group and the current leaving it — the substitution needs no change to the model.

The transient run applies the same stand-in in its own 0 Hz bin and lands on the stationary answer. The TRANSIENT_MODEL warning is expected for this input: it is meant for a response that should have died away by the end of the window, and a step that stays on never does. For the FFT solver a constant is exactly periodic, so the result is not affected. The DC components of the branch currents are physical currents from from_bus to to_bus: $923.9\ \text{A}$ in B-C is $(u_B - u_C)/0.35\ \Omega$ of the merged reference, and A-B carries $4.8\ \text{A}$ more: the current that enters the soil through the electrode at B, $u_B / 12\ \Omega$.

The state-space solver is the independent cross-check of this path. It integrates the lumped fields R_self_formula and L_self_formula in time, keeps the bond as the inductance it is and never inverts an impedance, so it needs no stand-in. Its settled DC state:

def lumped_bond_network():
    "The bond configuration with the lumped fields the state-space solver integrates."
    lumped = gi.create_network(name="bond_state_space", frequencies=[50.0])
    for label, z in (("A", Z_A), ("B", Z_B), ("C", Z_C)):
        bus_type = gi.BusType(name=f"ss_{label}", system_type="Substation", voltage_level=110.0,
                              impedance_formula=f"rho*0 + {z!r} + I*f*0", R_formula=f"rho*0 + {z!r}")
        gi.create_bus(name=label, type=bus_type, specific_earth_resistance=RHO, network=lumped)
    bond = gi.BranchType(name="ss_bond", grounding_conductor=True, self_impedance_formula=BOND,
                         mutual_impedance_formula=NO_COUPLING,
                         R_self_formula="0.0*l", L_self_formula=f"{L_BOND!r}*l")
    ordinary = gi.BranchType(name="ss_ordinary", grounding_conductor=True,
                             self_impedance_formula=ORDINARY, mutual_impedance_formula=NO_COUPLING,
                             R_self_formula=f"{R_BC!r}*l", L_self_formula="4e-4*l")
    gi.create_branch(name="A-B", type=bond, from_bus="A", to_bus="B", length=1.0, network=lumped)
    gi.create_branch(name="B-C", type=ordinary, from_bus="B", to_bus="C", length=1.0, network=lumped)
    gi.create_source(name="dc", bus="A", values={50.0: I_DC}, network=lumped)

A voltage source is the second way to drive the study, and at DC it is worth seeing what it does. groundinsight closes the Thévenin loop between the source bus and the fault bus, so the current that ends up flowing is

$$ I = \frac{U}{Z_{\text{source}} + Z_{\text{loop}}}, \qquad Z_{\text{loop}} = \frac{u_A - u_C}{I_{\text{DC}}} $$

with $u_A$, $u_C$ taken from the current-source study above. Since the system is linear, every bus potential of the voltage-source study must then be the corresponding current-source potential scaled by $I / I_{\text{DC}}$ — a cheap, exact check that the DC path is doing arithmetic and not something else. source_impedance needs a real part for this: a purely inductive internal impedance is zero at DC and the division above would not exist.
