docs.title: Direct-current studies¶
docs.text:
f = 0 is an ordinary entry in Network.frequencies, and a direct-current study needs nothing beyond it. What needs care at zero frequency is not the solver — $Y(f)\,\underline u(f) = \underline i(f)$ has no frequency dependence of its own and is exact at zero — but what an impedance formula means there:

what example what groundinsight does at 0 Hz a removable singularity Carson's earth-return term 2*pi*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/GMR) evaluates the limit, the DC resistance a finite reactance (0.25 + I*0.6)*l drops the reactance and warns an impedance of exactly zero a purely inductive bond, I*2*pi*f*L*l a finite stand-in, announced by a warning a real part of minus infinity log(f) without a factor f refuses the formula

This notebook measures each case against references that do not come from groundinsight — a node-merged $2\times2$ system and an open-circuit $3\times3$ system solved with NumPy, the closed-form limit of Carson's term and the linearity of the network — and it puts a number on what the old workaround, entering f = 0.1 Hz instead of zero, costs.

Background: Direct current (f = 0).

docs.title: The reference network¶
docs.text:
Three buses in a chain, $A - B - C$:

bus what it is $Z_B$ A earthing grid of a 110 kV substation $0.8\ \Omega$ B tower footing / joint bay half way along the line $12\ \Omega$ C earthing grid of the remote station $3.5\ \Omega$

A direct current of 1 kA is driven through the earthing system between A and C — stray direct current from a nearby DC traction return, the electrode line of an HVDC link, a cathodic-protection installation, or the quasi-DC neutral current of a geomagnetic disturbance. The question is the usual one: how much of it takes the earthing conductor and how much takes the soil, and what earth potential rise is left at each station.

The same chain is used in two configurations:

  • a line configuration for sections 1 to 3, where both spans are 10 km of the earthing conductor under test;
  • a bond configuration for sections 4 to 6, where A-B is a short bonding conductor with no resistance at all and B-C is an ordinary $0.35\ \Omega$ conductor.

Two buses are not enough for the second one: an ideal bond between the source bus and the fault bus merges them into a single node at which the injection +I and -I cancels, so every potential is zero and the treatment of the bond is invisible.

In the sign frame of groundinsight the source current enters the earthing network at the source bus A and leaves it at the fault bus C, so the potentials come out positive at A and negative at C; the physical fault picture, with the earth current entering the soil at the fault, is the reverse (Signs and phase angles). Every magnitude below is independent of that choice.

docs.title: 1 What the f = 0.1 Hz workaround costs¶
docs.text: The same study four times: two spellings of the conductor, each at 0.1 Hz and at 0 Hz. $Z_E$ is the earthing impedance at the fault bus C.

docs.title: 2  A finite reactance has no reading at DC¶
docs.text: At zero frequency a reactance can only vanish ($j\omega L \to 0$) or be infinite ($1/(j\omega C) \to \infty$). A finite non-zero one is a statement about nothing, so the 0 Hz bin takes the real part, drops the reactance and says so. Every other frequency is untouched.

docs.title: 3  Carson's earth-return term at zero frequency¶
docs.text:
$$ \underline Z(f) = \Big(R' + j\,\omega\,2\cdot10^{-7} \ln\frac{658\sqrt{\rho/f}}{\text{GMR}}\Big)\, l , \qquad \omega = 2\pi f . $$

At $f = 0$ this is $0\cdot\infty$: $\omega$ vanishes linearly while the logarithm diverges only logarithmically, so the limit exists and is $0$ — the conductor tends to its DC resistance, which is the one number a DC study is about. Floating point renders the limit as NaN; the evaluator finds the limit instead of reporting a formula error.

docs.title: 4  An ideal bond is a short circuit, and a short circuit has no admittance¶
docs.text:
Now the bond configuration: A-B is a 1 km bonding conductor written as pure inductance, with no resistance at all, and B-C is an ordinary $0.35\ \Omega$ conductor. At DC the bond is an exact zero — correct physics, and a number the nodal formulation cannot invert.

The reference is not groundinsight: an ideal bond means the two buses are one node, so the correct DC answer comes from a hand-solved $2\times2$ system in which $A$ and $B$ are merged and their electrodes are in parallel. The second reference is what dropping the element would give — modelling the short circuit as a disconnection.

docs.title: 5  Every transient run contains DC¶
docs.text: An rfft frequency grid always contains a 0 Hz bin, so every transient run evaluates every formula at zero frequency, whether or not the study is about DC. The DC component of the time-domain answer is the mean of $u(t)$ over a full FFT window, which is exactly the 0 Hz bin — so the stationary reference above applies unchanged.

docs.title: 6  A true pole is still an open circuit¶
docs.text: The substitution must not touch a capacitance. A series capacitance really is an open circuit at DC, $1/(j\omega C) \to \infty$ says so, and the solver already reads infinity as an open circuit. The expected answer is therefore the open-circuit reference, not the merged one — bus A reduced to its own electrode.

docs.title: 7  What a source and a fault need at DC¶
docs.text:
• Current source — values needs a 0.0 key. Without it the source contributes nothing at DC, announced once per run (InputWarning, code SOURCE_FREQUENCY_GAP). Give it a real number: at zero frequency the imaginary part is not a phase shift.
  • Voltage source — voltage and source_impedance both need a 0.0 entry; a network solved at 0 Hz without one is rejected at the solve. The 0.0 entry of source_impedance is the DC resistance of the source: the values are numbers, not formulas, so nothing drops a reactance there for you, and zero is rejected when the source is built.
  • Fault — scalings does not need a 0.0 key: a frequency without a key is scaled with 1.0, so the sources contribute in full at DC. Give 0.0: 0.0 to keep the DC bin out of a fault. A mapping that names some network frequencies but not others is announced once per run (InputWarning, code SCALINGS_INCOMPLETE).
  • IEC 60909 characteristics — i_k_a, r_to_x and kappa of create_source describe the DC offset and the thermal equivalent of an alternating short-circuit current. They are metadata that the solve does not use, and they have no meaning in a pure DC study; leave them unset there.
  • Mixed studies — frequencies=[0.0, 50.0] is legal, and the two do not interact: the DC handling is confined to the 0 Hz bin.

The three cases are the extremes of the local quantities: open (no electrode at all), ideal ($Z_B = 0$) and worst_passive, which maximises $|Z_{dp}|$ at the reactive resonance $Y_B = -j\,\mathrm{Im}(1/Z_{net})$. Both endpoints are exact limits rather than numerical stand-ins — the ideal electrode in particular, which the solver rejects outright because a zero impedance is not invertible.

Read them as a bracket for EPR_V and Z_driving_point_Ohm, and not for the transfer quantities in the same table. EPR_S0_V and r_current are not bounded by these three cases: a purely capacitive electrode at S3 — passive, so inside the same class — drives the EPR at S0 above the ideal value. If a study needs the worst case of a transfer quantity, sweep for it with .sweep([...]), which costs no solve, rather than reading it off extremes().

What the three cases do surface is the direction of the effect, which is easy to get backwards. An ideal electrode at the faulted station drives the potential rise at the infeed station up, not down: grounding the fault location harder pulls more current through the shields towards it. Over $|Z_B|$ from $10^{-3}$ to $10^{4}\,\Omega$ the EPR at S0 falls monotonically, so the plot below is the whole story for that pair.

reduction_factor does not move at all — not approximately, but to six decimals, sitting exactly on $|1 - Z_m/Z_s| = 0.310003$. Two separate reasons coincide here, and they are worth keeping apart:

  1. It is structurally blind to the electrode at the fault bus. Both solves behind it share the same $Y$, so changing the fault-bus admittance is a rank-1 update that cancels in the quotient. That holds in any network.
  2. This particular sweep changes $\rho$ at all six stations, and the invariance across all of them is a property of this network rather than a general one: every branch has the same $Z_m/Z_s$, so the mutual Norton vector telescopes along the path to $i_{mut} = -(Z_m/Z_s)\,i_{src}$ and $u_{with} = (1 - Z_m/Z_s)\,u_{without}$ at every bus, independent of $Y$. Mix cable and overhead-line branches and the same sweep does move value.

Either way, a $\rho$ sensitivity study plotted against value would be a horizontal line while the earthing impedance grows by a factor of 66 (0.154 to 10.2 ohm). reduction_factor_current responds, because it is a current share rather than a voltage ratio.

docs.title: Decomposing a fault: cuts, both reduction factors and a location without its electrode¶
docs.text:
A 20 kV cable feeder with six substations, faulted in the middle. The point of this example is not the fault solve itself — that is the minimal example — but the analysis layer on top of it:

  1. the two reduction factors and why they answer different questions,
  2. analyze_cuts — what each direction away from the fault contributes,
  3. bus_response — the whole network response to any electrode at the faulted station, from two solves,
  4. run_sweep + summarize/classify — the same study across a range of soil resistivities,
  5. run_reference_cases — the closed-form checks the package runs against itself.

docs.title: 1. The network¶
docs.text:
Six substations S0 … S5, connected by 1.2 km sections of a 20 kV cable whose shield-earth loop carries 0.25 Ω/km and 1.9 mH/km, with 0.05 Ω/km and 1.85 mH/km of Carson earth-return mutual coupling to the phase conductor.

phase_impedance_formula describes the phase conductor — the faulted one whose current induces the longitudinal EMF on the shield. It never enters the nodal admittance matrix; it is what the automatic phase-current distribution solves on. On a radial feeder like this one the phase current is unambiguous either way, but declaring it costs nothing and makes the model honest if a ring is closed later.

docs.title: 2. Two reduction factors, two questions¶
docs.text:
reduction_factor is the EPR-based one: the same system is solved twice, once with the mutual Norton sources and once without, and the quotient is taken at the fault bus. It keeps the meaning of the closed form $r = |1 - Z_m/Z_s|$.

reduction_factor_current is the share of the fault current that returned through earth rather than through the shields — $|I_E| / |3 I_0|$, the quantity EN 50522 means.

The result also carries the split itself, so it can be inspected rather than trusted: earth_buses names the group whose electrode currents were summed, anchored on the fault bus.

The earthing voltage and the earthing impedance of the norm are taken at the fault bus: $U_E$ is u_earthing, the EPR of the fault bus itself, and $Z_E$ is z_earthing, the driving-point impedance of the earthing network there — the reported grounding impedance. The norm's chain $U_E = r \cdot 3 I_0 \cdot Z_E$ is a physical statement that holds in its ideal case (a fault far from the infeed on a long bonded run); a six-station feeder faulted three stations from the infeed is not that case, and the cell prints how far apart the two sides are. The earth group's own mean potential and its quotient by $I_E$ are kept as u_earthing_group / z_earthing_group. The mean lies far below the EPR of the faulted station, which is why it is no longer reported as $U_E$.

docs.title: 3. Splitting the network at the fault¶
docs.text:
A Cut is a named set of branches, all incident to the fault bus. The analysis reports what each direction contributes:

parallel impedance left --- fault location --- parallel impedance right

Z_side comes from source-free current division: one ampere is injected at the fault bus with all sources and mutual injections removed, and the share leaving through each cut gives $Z_{side} = u_{fault} / i_{cut}$. The decomposition closes by construction — $1/Z_{dp} = 1/Z_{local} + \sum 1/Z_{side}$: the side admittances and the local one add up to the driving-point admittance of the whole network.

Note sides_are_disjoint: only when the directions do not reach around into one another do the per-side current quantities have an unambiguous meaning.

docs.title: 4. Characterising the location, not the electrode¶
docs.text:
Adding an electrode is a rank-one change to the nodal matrix, so by Sherman–Morrison every nodal voltage is a Möbius function of its admittance. Two solves with the electrode removed therefore determine the response for every electrode. BusResponse.evaluate(z) and .sweep([...]) then cost no solve at all.

z_network is the site-independent number the analysis is built around: the driving-point impedance of everything except the local electrode. It is a property of the location, not of what happens to be installed there.

docs.title: 5. The same study across soil resistivities¶
docs.text:
run_sweep solves the fault once per parameter point and stacks the results into long-format frames that carry the parameters as ordinary columns. Anything a point overrides is undone in a finally block, so a failing point leaves neither the network nor the remaining points contaminated.

This is where the difference between the two reduction factors stops being a subtlety and becomes the whole answer.

docs.title: 6. The closed-form reference cases¶
docs.text: Six configurations whose answer is known in closed form, run through the ordinary public API and compared. Each case states the boundary conditions its closed form needs — a deviation more often means a condition was not met than that the model is wrong. These also run as tests, so a change that quietly breaks agreement cannot reach a release.

docs.title: Where to go next¶
docs.text:
• Reduction factors and earthing impedance and Splitting the network, location response carry the derivations: the reduction factor on a current basis, the cuts, and characterising a location without its electrode.
  • Fault-location decomposition, Location response, Parameter sweeps, Statistics and classification, Reference cases — the API surface used above.
  • Electrode at the fault location and Location response bracket take the cuts and the location response further, with every number checked against a nodal solve.

docs.title: Fault sweep — earthing impedance and reduction factors per bus¶
docs.text:
When the fault location is not known a priori, a common analysis is to sweep the fault across every candidate bus and read off the earthing impedance $Z_E$ and the reduction factors at each fault site. This notebook demonstrates that workflow on a 10-bus MV cable line and visualises the results with Network.res_all_impedances().

Steps:

  1. Build a 10-bus MV cable line at five frequencies (50, 250, 350, 450, 550 Hz).
  2. Create one fault per bus, plus a single source at bus01.
  3. Loop gi.run_fault over every fault.
  4. Read the long-format DataFrame returned by res_all_impedances().
  5. Plot $|Z_E|$ and both reduction factors per fault bus and frequency.

docs.title: 1. Bus and branch types¶
docs.text: Illustrative MV cable values: a shield-earth loop of $0.25 + j0.6\ \Omega$/km at 50 Hz whose reactance and the mutual reactance both grow with frequency. The cable has full mutual coupling ($\mathrm{Im}\,Z_\text{self} = \mathrm{Im}\,Z_\text{mutual}$), so its reduction factor at 50 Hz is $|1 - Z_\text{mutual}/Z_\text{self}| = 0.25/|0.25 + j0.6| = 0.384615$. Every station has an electrode of 1 Ω.

docs.title: 2. Build a 10-bus line¶
docs.text: Source at bus01, one fault definition at every bus. Each fault re-uses the same source; run_fault solves one fault at a time.

docs.title: 3. Run the sweep¶
docs.text:
One gi.run_fault call per fault location. The fault at bus01 sits on the source bus itself: the source current enters and leaves the earthing system at the same bus, no current flows through the network, and both reduction factors are undefined there — res_all_impedances emits null for them. The earthing impedance is a property of the network at the fault bus and is defined there as well.

Seven of the ten fault locations add EARTH_GROUP_SPREAD to their diagnostics: the electrode currents of the stations point in clearly different directions, so the earth current $I_E$ and the reduction factor on a current basis describe the dominant direction only (Reduction factor on a current basis).

docs.title: 4. Slice and pivot¶
docs.text: res_all_impedances() returns one row per (fault, frequency). To plot the sweep we pivot it to one row per fault bus and one column per frequency.

docs.title: 5. A second way to $Z_E$¶
docs.text: $Z_E$ is the driving-point impedance of the earthing network at the fault bus. gi.bus_response computes, from two solves, the impedance $Z_\text{net}$ that the rest of the network offers at a bus; in parallel with the bus's own electrode (1 Ω) it must give $Z_E$.

docs.title: 6. Visualisation¶
docs.text: Grouped bar plots: one bar per frequency at each fault bus.

docs.title: 7. Profile interpretation¶
docs.text:
• $|Z_E|$ is symmetric about the middle of the line. It is the impedance of the earthing network seen from the fault bus — all electrodes in parallel through the shields — and does not depend on where the source is. The two end stations have bonded neighbours on one side only and show the highest value; inside the line it is nearly constant.
  • The EPR ratio is the same at every fault location at a given frequency: every section is the same cable, so it is $|1 - Z_m/Z_s|$ of the cable, 0.384615 at 50 Hz. It falls with frequency, because the shield reactance grows while its resistance stays — to below 0.05 at 550 Hz.
  • The reduction factor of EN 50522 depends on the position. Close to the infeed the shield back to it is short and carries almost all of the return current; the farther away the fault, the longer that path and the more current takes the soil. At 50 Hz it grows from 0.079 at bus02 to 0.389 at bus10; at the harmonics, where the shield reactance dominates, it levels off after a few stations close to the EPR ratio of that frequency. It is the factor that responds to the electrodes and the position; the EPR ratio describes the cable.

The wide DataFrames can be exported to CSV or Excel directly via polars.DataFrame.write_csv / write_excel for downstream reporting. Reduction factors and earthing impedance explains the two factors.

FREQUENCY = 50.0
I_SOURCE = 1000.0          # A
Z_ELECTRODE = 10.0         # Ohm, every station

ZS = 0.1 + 0.2j            # Ohm/km  shield - earth loop
ZM = 0.05 + 0.1j           # Ohm/km  phase conductor <-> shield loop
ZPP = 0.2 + 0.7j           # Ohm/km  phase conductor - earth loop on its own
Z_RED = ZPP - ZM**2 / ZS   # Ohm/km  phase - earth loop, shield bonded at both ends

print(f"k = Z_m/Z_s = {ZM / ZS}")
print(f"Z_red'      = {Z_RED:.4f} Ohm/km")


def per_km(z):
    "A constant per-km impedance as a formula in the length l."
    return f"({z.real!r} + {z.imag!r}*j)*l"


STATION = gi.BusType(name="station", system_type="MV", voltage_level=20.0,
                     impedance_formula=repr(Z_ELECTRODE))


def cable(name="cable", z_red=Z_RED):
    "The cable type; ``z_red=None`` leaves the phase impedance undeclared."
    return gi.BranchType(
        name=name, grounding_conductor=True,
        self_impedance_formula=per_km(ZS),
        mutual_impedance_formula=per_km(ZM),
        phase_impedance_formula=None if z_red is None else per_km(z_red),
    )


def build(branches, *, types=None, parallel_coefficient=1.0, default=None):
    "A network of 1 km branches ``(name, from_bus, to_bus)``, source at S, fault at F."
    default = default or cable()
    net = gi.create_network(name="mesh", frequencies=[FREQUENCY])
    for bus in sorted({bus for _, a, b in branches for bus in (a, b)}):
        gi.create_bus(name=bus, type=STATION, network=net)
    for name, a, b in branches:
        gi.create_branch(name=name, type=(types or {}).get(name, default), from_bus=a,
                         to_bus=b, length=1.0, parallel_coefficient=parallel_coefficient,
                         network=net)
    gi.create_source(name="infeed", bus="S", values={FREQUENCY: I_SOURCE}, network=net)
    gi.create_fault(name="F", bus="F", network=net)
    return net


def solve(net, mode="auto"):
    "Run the fault; the 50 Hz row of res_fault and the diagnostic codes of the run."
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        warnings.simplefilter("ignore")   # every warning is kept in result.diagnostics
        result = gi.run_fault(net, fault="F", phase_current_mode=mode)
    return net.res_fault("F").row(0, named=True), sorted({d.code for d in result.diagnostics})

def coupled_reference(branches, zpp=None):
    '''Phase conductors, shields and electrodes in one linear system.

    ``branches`` as for ``build``; ``zpp`` maps a branch name to its Z_pp'
    (default ``ZPP``). Returns earth potentials (physical frame), phase
    currents and shield currents.
    '''
    zpp = zpp or {}
    buses = sorted({bus for _, a, b in branches for bus in (a, b)})
    n, m = len(buses), len(branches)
    ue = {bus: i for i, bus in enumerate(buses)}          # unknown index of u_e
    up = {bus: n + i for i, bus in enumerate(buses)}      # ... of u_p
    ip = {name: 2 * n + k for k, (name, _, _) in enumerate(branches)}
    is_ = {name: 2 * n + m + k for k, (name, _, _) in enumerate(branches)}

    A = np.zeros((2 * n + 2 * m, 2 * n + 2 * m), dtype=complex)
    rhs = np.zeros(2 * n + 2 * m, dtype=complex)
    row = 0
    for name, a, b in branches:                           # two loop laws per branch
        A[row, [up[a], up[b], ip[name], is_[name]]] = 1, -1, -zpp.get(name, ZPP), -ZM
        A[row + 1, [ue[a], ue[b], ip[name], is_[name]]] = 1, -1, -ZM, -ZS
        row += 2
    for bus in buses:                                     # Kirchhoff's current law
        if bus == "F":
            continue
        for name, a, b in branches:
            sign = 1 if a == bus else -1 if b == bus else 0
            A[row, is_[name]] += sign
            A[row + 1, ip[name]] += sign
        A[row, ue[bus]] += 1 / Z_ELECTRODE
        rhs[row], rhs[row + 1] = (-I_SOURCE, I_SOURCE) if bus == "S" else (0, 0)
        row += 2
    A[row, [up["F"], ue["F"]]] = 1, -1                    # the fault: u_p(F) = u_e(F)
    for name, a, b in branches:                           # one node at F
        sign = 1 if a == "F" else -1 if b == "F" else 0
        A[row + 1, [ip[name], is_[name]]] += sign
    A[row + 1, ue["F"]] += 1 / Z_ELECTRODE

    x = np.linalg.solve(A, rhs)
    return ({bus: x[i] for bus, i in ue.items()},
            {name: x[i] for name, i in ip.items()},
            {name: x[i] for name, i in is_.items()})


def phasors(net):
    "Earth potentials and shield currents of a solved network as complex numbers."
    buses = net.res_buses("F").filter(~pl.col("is_rms"))
    branches = net.res_branches("F").filter(~pl.col("is_rms"))
    u = {r["bus_name"]: r["EPR_V"] * np.exp(1j * np.radians(r["EPR_degree"]))
         for r in buses.iter_rows(named=True)}
    i = {r["branch_name"]: r["I_branch_A"] * np.exp(1j * np.radians(r["I_branch_degree"]))
         for r in branches.iter_rows(named=True)}
    return u, i


def deviation(net, reference):
    '''Largest deviation of the earth potentials and of the shield currents from
    the reference, each relative to the largest value of the reference.'''
    u_ref, _, i_ref = reference
    u, i = phasors(net)
    du = max(abs(u[bus] + u_ref[bus]) for bus in u) / max(abs(v) for v in u_ref.values())
    di = max(abs(i[name] - i_ref[name]) for name in i) / max(abs(v) for v in i_ref.values())
    return max(du, di)

auto divides the 1000 A into 500 A per route, as the reference does, and agrees with it to rounding. The legacy mode with the default coefficient 1.0 gives both routes the full 1000 A, so the coupling is counted twice: the earthing network sees $(1 - 2k)\,I$ instead of $(1 - k)\,I$, and with $k = 0.5$ that is zero — every potential in the network vanishes. The run warns with PARALLEL_COEFFICIENT_DEFAULT: several paths, default coefficients. A coefficient of 0.5, set by hand, repairs this ring; auto needs nothing and ignores the coefficient.

For other cables the same mistake does not vanish but distorts: the EPR is scaled by $\lvert 1-2k\rvert / \lvert 1-k\rvert$, which can be larger or smaller than one (Enumerated paths and the legacy mode).

The fully coupled solve divides the phase current exactly as the current divider does — the one-way coupling is exact here because $k = Z_m/Z_s$ is the same on every branch of the ring — and groundinsight reproduces all potentials and shield currents of the reference.

The earth potential rise has not moved: 55.6208 V, as in section 2. That is no accident. A phase current $I_p$ drives the shield of its branch like a current source $k\,I_p$ between the two ends, and when $k$ is the same on every branch these sources add up, station by station, to $k$ times what the phase conductors take in and give off — $kI$ at S, $-kI$ at F, nothing in between — however the current divides on the way. With a uniform $k$ the split moves the shield currents and leaves every earth potential where it is. Without phase_impedance_formula the split is a guess: the proxy is the shield impedance, the same on both routes, so it divides 500 : 500:

docs.title: Phase currents in rings, meshes and parallel cables¶
docs.text:
In a line every branch between the infeed and the fault carries the full fault current. As soon as the network has a second route — a ring, a mesh, or simply a second cable between the same two stations — the current divides, and how it divides decides how hard each cable shield is driven.

groundinsight finds the split by solving a reduced network of the phase conductors alone, with the fault bus as reference (phase_current_mode="auto", the default). The legacy mode phase_current_mode="paths" gives every branch on any source-to-fault path the full source current, scaled by its parallel_coefficient; it is kept to reproduce older studies and for a split known from measurement. This notebook

  1. compares both modes on a line, a ring, two parallel cables and a mesh,
  2. shows that BranchType.phase_impedance_formula decides the split, and
  3. checks every result against a fully coupled multi-conductor solve written here in NumPy: phase conductors, shields and electrodes in one system, without the one-way coupling that groundinsight uses.

Background: Phase currents in rings and meshes.

docs.title: The cable and the stations¶
docs.text:
One illustrative cable for every branch, 1 km per branch, at 50 Hz:

per km value loop $Z_s'$ $0.1 + 0.2j\ \Omega$ shield with earth return $Z_m'$ $0.05 + 0.1j\ \Omega$ coupling between the phase conductor and that loop $Z_{pp}'$ $0.2 + 0.7j\ \Omega$ phase conductor with earth return, on its own

The ratio $k = Z_m/Z_s$ is exactly $0.5$, which makes the difference between the two modes as plain as it gets. phase_impedance_formula takes the phase–earth loop with the shield bonded at both ends, $Z_\text{red} = Z_{pp} - Z_m^2/Z_s$. Every station has a $10\ \Omega$ electrode; the source feeds 1000 A at S, the fault is at F.

docs.title: The reference: everything coupled, solved at once¶
docs.text:
The reference does not split the phase current first. Every branch carries two unknown currents, $I_p$ in the phase conductor and $I_s$ in the shield (both from from_bus to to_bus), and obeys the two loop equations with earth return

$$ u_p(a) - u_p(b) = Z_{pp}\,I_p + Z_m\,I_s, \qquad u_e(a) - u_e(b) = Z_m\,I_p + Z_s\,I_s , $$

where $u_p$ is the potential of the phase conductor and $u_e$ that of the earthing system at a bus. The source drives $I$ into the phase conductor at S and draws it from the earthing system at S; the fault ties the phase conductor to the earthing system at F. That is the physical sign frame, in which the earth potentials of groundinsight carry the opposite sign (Signs and phase angles); its shield currents are physical from from_bus to to_bus in both.

docs.title: 1  The line: nothing to divide¶
docs.text: S - A - F, two cable sections. There is one route, it carries everything, and both modes must agree.

docs.title: 2  The ring: the current divides¶
docs.text: S - A - F and S - B - F, two routes of two sections each.

docs.title: 3  Two cables between the same stations¶
docs.text: The same mechanism without a visible ring: a second cable laid next to the first, the most common mesh in practice.

docs.title: 4  A mesh, built in two orders¶
docs.text: Five branches between four stations: S - A, A - B, B - F, S - B, A - F. The answer must not depend on the order in which the branches were added to the network.

docs.title: 5  The phase impedance decides the split¶
docs.text: So far every branch was the same cable, and any impedance proportional to the length would have divided the current correctly. Now route 2 (S - B - F) gets a phase conductor whose $Z_\text{red}$ is ten times that of route 1, at the same angle; the shields stay the same. The current divider expects $10/11$ of the current on route 1 and $1/11$ on route 2.

docs.title: 6  The proxy is announced only where it matters¶
docs.text: In a line the proxy cannot change anything — there is one route. The warning PHASE_PROXY therefore stays silent there and appears once per run, naming the branches, as soon as the phase conductors form a loop around the fault.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
network paths, coefficient 1.0 auto fully coupled reference line the same as auto exact agrees to rounding ring every potential zero 500 A per route agrees to rounding two parallel cables every potential zero 500 A per cable agrees to rounding mesh 27.88 V at stations that stay at zero, depends on the order the same in either order agrees to rounding ring with two phase conductors — 909 A : 91 A, as the phase impedances; without the formula 499 A in every shield instead of 703 A and 294 A agrees to rounding

docs.title: Minimal example¶
docs.text:
The smallest useful network: three stations on a medium-voltage cable line, a current source at one end and an earth fault at the other. The notebook builds it, solves it, reads the results as tables, and checks four of them against what Kirchhoff's laws and the closed forms of a cable line demand.

For a step-by-step introduction in which every number is also computed by hand, see the tutorial Your first fault calculation.

docs.title: 1. The network¶
docs.text: Three stations bus1, bus2, bus3 in a line, joined by two 1 km sections of a cable whose shield is earthed at every station. Each station has an electrode of 1 Ω. 100 A at 50 Hz enter at bus1, the fault is at bus3. The values are illustrative round numbers, chosen so that the closed forms below stay short.

docs.title: 2. Solve and read the results¶
docs.text: run_fault returns the result and keeps it on the network. The res_* methods turn it into Polars tables: res_buses per bus and frequency (plus an RMS row, marked by is_rms), res_branches per branch, and res_fault the key figures of the fault.

docs.title: 3. Four checks¶
docs.text:
(a) Kirchhoff over the whole network. Whatever enters the soil at one electrode leaves it at another, so the electrode currents of all buses add up to zero — as complex numbers, not as magnitudes.

(b) Symmetry. The line is uniform and the electrodes are equal. The coupling of the phase current adds up to a current $(1 - k)\,I$ that enters the earthing network at bus1 and leaves it at bus3, so the potentials are antisymmetric: bus2 stays at 0 V, and bus1 and bus3 rise to the same magnitude with opposite sign.

(c) The EPR ratio of a line with one cable type is $r = |1 - Z_m/Z_s|$, whatever the electrodes.

(d) The reduction factor of EN 50522, $|I_E|/|I|$: with bus2 at 0 V the fault bus sees its own electrode in parallel with one section, and $|I_E|/|I| = |Z_s - Z_m| / |Z_B + Z_s|$ for one section.

docs.title: What the model assumes¶
docs.text:
• One linear solve per frequency in the phasor domain; the potentials are earth potential rises against remote earth.
  • Every station is a lumped electrode; the soil between the stations does not couple them.
  • The fault current returns through the soil and through the cable shields. The phase current induces a voltage along each shield, which enters the solve as a Norton current; on a line the phase current is the source current itself.
  • No fault resistance: the fault bonds the phase conductor to the earthing system of bus3.

Model and assumptions lists the assumptions in full, and Conventions and units explains the angles in the tables above.

docs.title: 20 kV MV ring — stationary fault analysis¶
docs.text:
Classical frequency-domain analysis of a 20 kV medium-voltage ring with 20 substations, each connected by 0.5 km of NA2XS(F)2Y 1x300 RM/25 cable. The shield-earth loop of this cable type carries the per-length values:

quantity value symbol shield-earth resistance 0.25 Ohm/km R' shield-earth inductance 1.9 mH/km L' shield-earth capacitance 300 nF/km C' Carson earth-return resistance 0.05 Ohm/km R'_mutual phase-shield mutual inductance 1.85 mH/km M'

Each substation is grounded with R_g = 5 Ohm. We inject a 1 kA fault current at b01, place a single-phase fault at b10, and solve in the frequency domain to obtain the earth potential rise (EPR), both reduction factors and the earthing impedance at the fault bus.

The values are representative, not taken from one data sheet; Bus and branch types from data sheets derives such values for a real cable. The same network is used in the companion notebook MV ring (transient) to study the time-domain response.

docs.title: 1. Cable + bus parameters¶
docs.text: Per-length values of the shield-earth loop, plus the lumped totals at the chosen 0.5 km section length.

docs.title: 2. Build the network¶
docs.text:
• bus_type carries the frequency-domain impedance_formula — the parallel combination R || 1/(jwC_BUS_LUMPED) — and, for the transient notebook, R_formula.
  • branch_type carries the shield self impedance R + jwL and the mutual impedance R_mutual + jwM, plus the lumped R_self_formula, L_self_formula, C_self_formula, R_mutual_formula and M_mutual_formula that the state-space solver of the transient notebook reads.

docs.title: 3. Stationary fault analysis¶
docs.text: 1 kA at b01, fault at b10. The fault current divides between the two directions around the ring; run_fault finds the split by solving the phase-conductor network. The branch type declares no phase_impedance_formula, so the solver uses the shield impedance as a proxy for the phase conductor and says so with a ModelAssumptionWarning (PHASE_PROXY). In this ring every section is the same cable, so any impedance proportional to length gives the exact split and the warning has no consequence here; in a ring that mixes cable and overhead line it would (Phase currents in rings and meshes).

docs.title: 4. Both reduction factors and the earthing impedance¶
docs.text:
• The EPR ratio (value, column reduction_factor) compares the EPR at the fault bus with and without the coupling between phase conductor and shields. Every section is the same cable, so it equals the closed form $|1 - Z_m/Z_s|$ of one section — the tabulated reduction factor of the cable.
  • The reduction factor of EN 50522 (value_current, column reduction_factor_current) is the share of the fault current that returns through the soil, $|I_E|/|3I_0|$.
  • $Z_E$ is the earthing impedance at the fault bus: the driving-point impedance of all electrodes and shields seen from b10.

Reduction factors and earthing impedance explains why the two factors differ.

def ring(mutual=True, source="current"):
    bus_type = gi.BusType(
        name="MV_substation", system_type="Substation", voltage_level=20.0,
        impedance_formula=f"((rho * 0 + {R_BUS}) / (1 + I * 2 * pi * f * {R_BUS} * {C_BUS_LUMPED}))",
        R_formula=f"rho * 0 + {R_BUS}",
    )
    coupling = {
        "mutual_impedance_formula": f"((rho * 0 + {R_MUT_PER_KM}) + I * 2 * pi * f * {M_PER_KM}) * l",
        "R_mutual_formula": f"({R_MUT_PER_KM}) * l",
        "M_mutual_formula": f"({M_PER_KM}) * l",
    } if mutual else {"mutual_impedance_formula": "(rho * 0 + 0.0) * l"}
    branch_type = gi.BranchType(
        name="NA2XS_300_25", grounding_conductor=True,
        self_impedance_formula=f"((rho * 0 + {R_PER_KM}) + I * 2 * pi * f * {L_PER_KM}) * l",
        R_self_formula=f"({R_PER_KM}) * l",
        L_self_formula=f"({L_PER_KM}) * l",
        C_self_formula=f"({C_PER_KM}) * l",
        **coupling,
    )
    net = gi.create_network(name="mv_ring_20", frequencies=[50.0])
    for k in range(1, N_BUSES + 1):
        gi.create_bus(name=f"b{k:02d}", type=bus_type, network=net)
    for k in range(1, N_BUSES + 1):
        nxt = (k % N_BUSES) + 1
        gi.create_branch(name=f"L_{k:02d}_{nxt:02d}", type=branch_type,
                         from_bus=f"b{k:02d}", to_bus=f"b{nxt:02d}",
                         length=SECTION_LENGTH_KM, network=net)
    if source == "current":
        gi.create_source(name="src", bus="b01", values={50.0: 1000.0 + 0.0j}, network=net)
    else:
        u_phase = 20e3 / math.sqrt(3)
        gi.create_voltage_source(
            name="vsrc", bus="b01", voltage={50.0: u_phase + 0.0j},
            source_impedance={50.0: 12.0 + 1j * 2 * math.pi * 50.0 * 3e-3}, network=net,
        )
    gi.create_fault(name="F1", bus="b10", network=net)
    return net


def stationary_epr(net, bus="b10"):
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        # PHASE_PROXY: the ring has no phase_impedance_formula; every section is
        # the same cable, so the proxy gives the exact split (stationary notebook).
        warnings.simplefilter("ignore", gi.ModelAssumptionWarning)
        result = gi.run_fault(net, fault="F1")
    return abs(complex(next(b.uepr_freq[50.0] for b in result.buses if b.name == bus)))


def rms_of_last_period(result, bus="b10"):
    t = np.asarray(result.time_s)
    u = np.asarray(result.epr_t[bus])
    last = t >= t[-1] - 0.02 + 1e-12
    return math.sqrt(np.mean(u[last] ** 2))


net = ring(mutual=True)
net_no_mut = ring(mutual=False)

sine = waveforms.sinusoidal_with_dc_offset(amplitude=math.sqrt(2) * 1000.0, frequency_hz=50.0)


def steady_state(network, solver, dt):
    study = gi.TransientStudy(network, fault="F1")
    study.set_source_waveform("src", sine)
    study.set_observation(buses=["b10"])
    with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
        warnings.simplefilter("always")
        result = study.solve(t_end=0.2, dt=dt, solver=solver)
    codes = sorted({getattr(w.message, "code", "") for w in caught})
    return rms_of_last_period(result), codes

The FFT solver reproduces the stationary result without the coupling, as its warning says; the state-space solver reproduces the stationary result with it. The PHASE_PROXY notice of the state-space solver is the one of the stationary notebook: the phase current divides between the two directions of the ring, and in a ring of one cable type the proxy gives the exact split. For a study with coupling — every cable network — use the state-space solver.

The phase current induces a voltage along every shield, which drives most of the fault current back through the shields instead of the soil: the coupling lowers the peak EPR at the fault by roughly a factor of eight here, the same order as the ratio of the two stationary results above. During the DC offset the coupling helps less — at DC the shields carry no induced current — which is why the EPR with coupling is lopsided at the start.

docs.title: 20 kV MV ring — transient analysis¶
docs.text:
Time-domain analysis of the same 20 kV medium-voltage ring as in the companion notebook MV ring (stationary): 20 substations linked by 0.5 km sections of NA2XS(F)2Y 1x300 RM/25 cable, R_g = 5 Ohm per substation, 1 kA fed at b01, fault at b10.

groundinsight has two transient solvers, and they model different things:

  • the FFT solver evaluates the frequency-domain impedance formulas per frequency bin. It does not evaluate the inductive coupling between the phase conductor and the shields, and warns when a network has some (TransientModelWarning, code TRANSIENT_MODEL);
  • the state-space solver integrates the lumped R/L/C fields in time. It includes the coupling (R_mutual_formula, M_mutual_formula) for current sources, with the phase current divided between the two directions of the ring as in the stationary solve, and it lumps the branch shunt capacitance onto the adjacent buses (pi-section).

The notebook checks both against the stationary solve in steady state, shows the effect of the coupling on a fault current with a DC offset, and switches a Thévenin source onto the ring. Transient simulation derives both solvers.

docs.title: 1. Cable and bus parameters¶
docs.text: The per-length values of the stationary notebook.

docs.title: 2. Build the network — with and without the coupling¶
docs.text: ring(mutual=...) builds the ring once with the phase-shield coupling and once without it, for comparison. Both carry the frequency-domain formulas (for the FFT solver and the stationary solve) and the lumped fields (for the state-space solver).

docs.title: 3. Steady state: each solver against the stationary solve¶
docs.text: A pure 50 Hz sine of 1000 A RMS — the waveform functions take the peak value, $\sqrt{2}\cdot 1000$ A — drives both solvers for ten periods. The RMS of the EPR at b10 over the last period is compared with the stationary solve of the ring with and without the coupling.

docs.title: 4. A fault current with DC offset: the effect of the coupling¶
docs.text: An asymmetrical fault current — 1000 A peak, switched on at 20 ms with a DC offset of 600 A decaying with 40 ms, cleared at 120 ms — drives the state-space solver on the ring with and without the coupling.

docs.title: 5. A Thévenin source switched onto the ring¶
docs.text: A 20 kV phase voltage behind 12 Ω + 3 mH switched on at 20 ms. The state-space solver models the coupling for current sources only; for a voltage source it skips it and says so (TRANSIENT_COUPLING_SKIPPED), so this run shows the ring without the shield coupling — the switching transient and the ringing of the cable capacitance, not the coupled earthing response. Its steady state is checked against the stationary solve of the uncoupled ring with the same source.

docs.title: Take-aways¶
docs.text:
• C_self_formula on the cable type is enough — the state-space solver lumps it onto the adjacent buses (pi-section); the bus impedance of the frequency-domain formulas carries the same capacitance.
  • The state-space solver includes the phase-shield coupling for current sources and reproduces the stationary solve in steady state. The FFT solver does not include it and reproduces the stationary solve of the network without coupling; for a cable network that overestimates the EPR, here by a factor of three in steady state.
  • The coupling lowers the EPR most for the alternating part of a fault current; a decaying DC offset is not reduced by it.
  • For voltage sources the state-space solver does not model the coupling yet and warns; use a current source carrying the prospective fault current when the coupled response matters.

docs.title: groundinsight — pandapower import walkthrough¶
docs.text:
End-to-end demonstration of the pandapower importer groundinsight.io.pandapower_import:

  1. Build a small pandapower MV network with one out-of-service branch and a low-voltage stub (so we can exercise the voltage-level filter).
  2. Inspect the planned mapping with preview_pandapower_import.
  3. Convert the network with from_pandapower.
  4. Add a project-specific source and fault, solve.
  5. Run an outage study on top of the imported network.

Prerequisite. The pandapower extra:

pip install "groundinsight[pandapower]"

docs.title: 1. Build a small pandapower network¶
docs.text: Five MV buses (20 kV) in a line, plus one LV stub bus (0.4 kV) connected through a non-physical line so we can exercise the voltage-level filter. One MV branch is set to in_service=False to demonstrate that the flag propagates to Branch.active = False on the groundinsight side.

docs.title: 2. Preview the import¶
docs.text: preview_pandapower_import is a pure inspection: it does not build a groundinsight Network. The returned DataFrame lists every pandapower bus and line with status="keep" or status="skip" plus a reason, so the mapping can be confirmed before committing to it.

docs.title: 3. Convert with from_pandapower¶
docs.text: Project-level defaults travel via ImportDefaults. The importer applies default_bus_type to every imported bus and default_branch_type to every imported line; soil resistivity rho and the frequency list are the same for the whole import. The two types below are illustrative.

docs.title: 4. Add a fault and solve¶
docs.text: The importer never invents sources or fault locations — those are project-specific. Here we inject 1 kA at bus_mv_1 and place a single-phase fault at bus_mv_5. The out-of-service line_mv_34_oos would interrupt the feeder, so we re-activate it for this baseline solve; the outage study below takes it out again as a scenario of its own.

docs.title: 5. Outage study on the imported network¶
docs.text:
Take the imported network as it is and compare two what-if scenarios against the base case in a single call. OutageStudyResult.compare_buses returns a long-format DataFrame with absolute and relative deltas against the chosen reference scenario (the base case by default).

The comparison frames join the scenarios on the frequency, and their frequency_Hz column is text, with "RMS" marking the RMS rows — unlike res_buses(), where frequency_Hz is a number and is_rms marks them.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
• preview_pandapower_import validates the mapping before any Network is built. Use it as the first step on real, larger pandapower networks.
  • from_pandapower returns a Network with the imported buses and branches; in_service=False on the pandapower side becomes active=False on the groundinsight side, so outage scenarios start from the real grid state.
  • The result plugs straight into run_fault and into run_outage_study.

Next steps for a real import:

  • Replace the illustrative ImportDefaults with the cable and overhead-line types of the actual assets (Bus and branch types from data sheets).
  • Load an existing case with pp.from_json / pp.from_pickle before calling preview_pandapower_import and from_pandapower.
  • Transformers are not modelled: import one voltage level at a time.
  • A solved pandapower short-circuit case can be read as IEC 60909 quantities with gi.read_shortcircuit_results and applied with gi.apply_shortcircuit_characteristics (I/O — network importers).

docs.title: Thermal limits of earthing conductors (IEC 60949 / IEC 60909-0)¶
docs.text:
Does an earthing conductor survive the fault current thermally? This is the equipment-integrity counterpart to the touch-voltage (person-safety) assessment.

  • IEC 60909-0: thermally equivalent short-time current $I_{th} = I_{s,\mathrm{RMS}} \cdot \sqrt{m + n}$, with the heat factor $m$ of the decaying DC component and $n$ of the AC component.
  • IEC 60949: admissible adiabatic current $I_{adm} = k \cdot S / \sqrt{t_k}$, with the material constant $k$ from the initial and final temperature.

The linear AC RMS shield currents are superposed by the solve as usual; the non-linear IEC 60909 factor is applied to that aggregate ($I_{th}$ is never superposed directly).

docs.title: A small network with a copper earthing conductor¶
docs.text: Two 20 kV buses, a 5000 A earth fault, and a BranchType that carries the conductor material, its cross-section and the initial and final temperatures of the thermal check. The impedances are illustrative.

docs.title: Check a 16 mm² conductor, fault duration 1 s, R/X = 0.1¶
docs.text: t_k_s is the short-circuit duration in seconds; r_to_x the R/X ratio of the source, from which the peak factor $\kappa$ and the DC heat factor $m$ follow.

docs.title: Fault duration matters (adiabatic ∝ 1/√t_k)¶
docs.text: A longer clearing time lowers the admissible current, so the same conductor may fail; the DC heat factor $m$ falls at the same time, because the DC offset has decayed for a larger part of the fault:

docs.title: Notes¶
docs.text:
• kappa (peak factor) comes from r_to_x via $1.02 + 0.98\,e^{-3R/X}$, or is passed directly.
  • n = 1 is the far-from-generator default (distribution earthing); pass n_factor otherwise.
  • gi.check_node_limits checks the earthing conductor and the electrode of every bus in the same way, and gi.read_shortcircuit_results takes $\kappa$ and the short-circuit current from a pandapower calc_sc run (Analysis, I/O).
  • The check is adiabatic: the heat given off during the fault is neglected, which underestimates the admissible current and is on the safe side (Standards and scope).

References: IEC 60909-0:2016, IEC 60949:1988, IEC 60364-5-54, EN 50522.

docs.title: Direct current (f = 0)
docs.text:
f = 0 is an ordinary entry in Network.frequencies and in Fault.scalings, and a direct-current study needs nothing beyond it. The reference chain of this page (dc_chain.py): three earthing systems A – B – C (0.8, 12 and 3.5 Ω) joined by two 10 km spans of an earthing conductor of 0.25 Ω/km, with 1 kA of direct current entering at A and leaving at C:

def build(conductor_formula, frequency):
    """The chain A - B - C with 1 kA DC entering at A and leaving at C."""
    net = gi.create_network(name="dc_return", frequencies=[frequency])
    for name, z_electrode in (("A", 0.8), ("B", 12.0), ("C", 3.5)):
        electrode = gi.BusType(name=f"electrode_{name}", system_type="Substation",
                               voltage_level=110.0, impedance_formula=repr(z_electrode))
        gi.create_bus(name=name, type=electrode, specific_earth_resistance=100.0,
                      network=net)
    conductor = gi.BranchType(name="conductor", grounding_conductor=True,
                              self_impedance_formula=conductor_formula,
                              mutual_impedance_formula="0")
    gi.create_branch(name="A-B", type=conductor, from_bus="A", to_bus="B",
                     length=10.0, network=net)
    gi.create_branch(name="B-C", type=conductor, from_bus="B", to_bus="C",
                     length=10.0, network=net)
    gi.create_source(name="dc", bus="A", values={frequency: 1000.0}, network=net)
    gi.create_fault(name="F", bus="C", network=net)
    return net


net = build(CARSON, 0.0)
result = gi.run_fault(net, "F")
epr_a = abs(complex(next(b.uepr_freq[0.0] for b in result.buses if b.name == "A")))
z_e = abs(complex(result.reduction_factor.z_earthing[0.0]))

The earth potential rise at A is 456.621004566 V and the earthing impedance at the fault bus C is 2.073630 Ω; a nodal solve of the three electrodes and two 2.5 Ω conductors by hand gives the same numbers.

DC needs a section of its own not because the solver is special there but because it is not. \(Y(f)\,\underline{u}(f) = \underline{i}(f)\) has no frequency dependence of its own — \(f\) enters only through the impedances — so a DC solve is an ordinary solve and it is exact. What has to be handled at zero frequency is the other half: what an impedance formula means there, and what happens when the number it produces has no reciprocal.

Why f = 0 and not f = 0.1 Hz

Entering a small frequency instead of zero was the established workaround, and for a conductor whose reactance is written as j*2*pi*f*L it was accurate: on the reference chain above 0.1 Hz gives \(456.621004575\ \text{V}\) and 0 Hz gives \(456.621004566\ \text{V}\) — eleven digits. With f = 0 an ordinary frequency, it is not needed.

For the far more common spelling (0.25 + j*0.6)*l the workaround is wrong, and not marginally: 0.1 Hz keeps the \(6\ \Omega\) of reactance that does not exist at DC and reports 718.54 V instead of 456.62 V — 57 % high — with an earthing impedance \(Z_E = 2.90\ \Omega\) instead of \(2.07\ \Omega\). The reactance is constant, so making the frequency smaller does not make the error smaller.

ROWS = []
for spelling, formula in (("j*2*pi*f*L", CARSON), ("constant j*X", CONSTANT_X)):
    for frequency in (0.1, 0.0):
        with warnings.catch_warnings():
            # the constant reactance at 0 Hz is announced by a DCLimitWarning
            warnings.simplefilter("ignore", gi.DCLimitWarning)
            res = gi.run_fault(build(formula, frequency), "F")
        bus_a = next(b for b in res.buses if b.name == "A")
        ROWS.append({
            "spelling": spelling,
            "f_Hz": frequency,
            "EPR_A_V": abs(complex(bus_a.uepr_freq[frequency])),
            "Z_E_Ohm": abs(complex(res.reduction_factor.z_earthing[frequency])),
        })

docs.title: Three singularities, told apart numerically
docs.text:
At \(f = 0\) three quite different things can happen to a formula string, and in floating point all three arrive as NaN or inf:

At f = 0 the formula … Example What groundinsight does has a removable singularity — \(0\cdot\infty\) with a finite limit Carson's earth-return term \(\omega\ln\!\big(658\sqrt{\rho/f}\,/\,\text{GMR}\big)\), whose limit is 0 because \(\omega\) vanishes linearly while the logarithm diverges logarithmically evaluates the limit and returns it, so the conductor tends to its DC resistance has a true pole a series capacitance, \(1/(j\omega C)\to\infty\) returns infinity, which the solver already reads as an open circuit — the correct physics genuinely fails a NaN parameter, \(\sqrt{\rho}\) with \(\rho<0\), \(0/0\) raises ValueError naming the formula, the frequency and the parameters, exactly as at any other frequency

The limit is determined by approaching zero on the decade sequence 1e-6, 1e-7, 1e-8 Hz and comparing two consecutive absolute differences. Measured on the reference cases: an inductance gives \(d_1 = 1.41\cdot10^{-8}\), \(d_2 = 1.41\cdot10^{-9}\) — shrinking, hence convergent — against \(d_1 = 1.43\cdot10^{12}\), \(d_2 = 1.43\cdot10^{13}\) for a capacitance, growing, hence a pole. The criterion is deliberately absolute: a relative one cannot classify a formula whose limit is zero, because there the relative change per decade stays at 90 % forever. The tie-break is biased towards convergent, because mistaking a pole for a limit yields a very large finite impedance that behaves almost like the open circuit it should have been, whereas the opposite mistake would silently disconnect a real earthing conductor.

A limit found this way is also checked for resolution: if the real part still moves over the last decade, the value at \(10^{-8}\) Hz is only an approximation and a DCLimitWarning says so ("converges only slowly"). A move that is small against the value passes, and so does one that shrinks at least five-fold from one decade to the next — the only test that can judge a limit of zero, such as the earth-return resistance \(\pi^2 10^{-4} f\) of a Carson mutual impedance: its change per decade is 90 % of its value, but that change shrinks ten-fold from one decade to the next. sqrt(f) (3.2-fold) and log(f) (not at all) are reported, and since the ratio does not depend on the length, all branches of one type get the same verdict.

A real part that runs to \(-\infty\) — a log(f) term without a factor \(f\) — is none of the three. It is the limit of negative resistances, not the open circuit \(+\infty\) of a pole, and it is refused for every impedance that is inverted, like a negative real part. Accepted, it would read as an open circuit, because \(1/(-\infty) = 0\).

docs.title: A finite reactance has no reading at DC
docs.text:
(0.25 + j*0.6)*l reports the same reactance at every frequency, zero included — and at DC a reactance can only vanish (\(j\omega L \to 0\)) or be infinite (\(1/(j\omega C)\to\infty\)). A finite non-zero one is a statement about nothing. The 0 Hz bin therefore takes the real part, drops the reactance and emits a DCLimitWarning that quotes \(X/R\) and the remedy; all other frequencies are untouched. Write the reactance as j*2*pi*f*L and nothing is dropped and nothing warns. The warning quotes the ratio rather than the two values because the ratio is length-invariant and therefore identical for every branch sharing a BranchType — which lets Python's default warning filter collapse a hundred-branch network into a single line.

The fallback applies to impedance formulas only. The R_formula, L_formula and C_formula fields consumed by the state-space transient solver are real at every frequency by contract, so a complex value there is reported as an error rather than repaired.

docs.title: An ideal bond is a short circuit, and a short circuit has no admittance
docs.text:
A purely inductive element — a short bonding conductor modelled as j*2*pi*f*L*l, with no resistance — is an exact zero at DC. That is correct physics, and it is also a number the nodal formulation cannot invert. Up to v0.4.0 both solvers responded by dropping such an element, i.e. by modelling a short circuit as a disconnection. On the reference chain (\(Z_A = 0.8\ \Omega\), \(Z_B = 12\ \Omega\), \(Z_C = 3.5\ \Omega\), bond A–B purely inductive, \(R_{BC} = 0.35\ \Omega\), 1 kA at A, fault at C) the correct answer is \(u_A = u_B = 57.07\ \text{V}\), \(u_C = -266.30\ \text{V}\); what came back was \(800.00\), \(-2649.84\) and \(-2727.13\ \text{V}\) — wrong by factors of 14.0, 46.4 and 10.2, with the sign of bus B reversed, because bus A had been cut off from the network and reported its own electrode instead of the parallel combination.

Such an element is now given a finite stand-in at the 0 Hz bin only:

\[ Z_{\text{sub}} = \sqrt{\varepsilon_{\text{mach}}}\; Z_{\min} = 1.4901\cdot10^{-8}\; Z_{\min}, \]

where \(Z_{\min}\) is the smallest finite non-zero impedance magnitude the network carries at that frequency. Tying the stand-in to \(Z_{\min}\) was chosen by measurement against analytically node-merged reference networks; it costs a relative error of about \(10^{-5}\) in the worst case observed, \(1.6\cdot10^{-9}\) on the chain above, and \(8.3\cdot10^{-8}\) at the DC bin of the corresponding transient run — better than modelling the bond as an explicit \(10^{-8}\ \Omega\) resistance. Every use is announced by a DCLimitWarning naming the elements, the substitute and the reference it was scaled to.

When to merge two buses instead. The exact model of an ideal bond is one node, not two, and the stand-in is an approximation of that merge. Prefer the merge — one bus whose impedance is the parallel combination of the two electrodes — whenever the difference in earth potential rise across the bond is part of the result you report (across an ideal bond it is zero, and whatever the stand-in produces there is numerical residue), or when the bonded buses carry impedances many orders of magnitude away from \(Z_{\min}\). For the usual question — the earth potential rise of the bonded group and the current leaving it — the substitution is accurate to the digits above and needs no change to the model. Giving the bond a small but honest resistance works equally well and removes the warning.

Phase conductors follow the same rule. A phase_impedance_formula without a resistive part is an ideal short at 0 Hz as well. When the phase network is solved (phase_current_mode="auto"), such a conductor receives the same stand-in, announced by the same DCLimitWarning; \(Z_{\min}\) stays the smallest impedance of the earthing network, so the earthing results of a network with a DC short do not move because its phase conductors are declared. Above 0 Hz a phase impedance that is zero, too small to invert or has a negative real part is refused with a ValueError naming the branch, as for every other element. One consequence is worth knowing: where all parallel routes of the phase network are ideal shorts at DC, the model has no DC split of its own, and every conductor carrying the same stand-in splits the current as if all of them had one and the same impedance, whatever their lengths. Declare the DC resistance in phase_impedance_formula (e.g. R*l + j*2*pi*f*L*l) when the DC split between routes matters.

docs.title: Every transient study contains DC
docs.text: An rfft frequency grid always contains a 0 Hz bin, so every transient run evaluates every formula at zero frequency, whether or not the study is about DC, and there is no f = 0.1 Hz workaround on that path. The FFT solver therefore follows the rules of the stationary solve: a Carson-type conductor takes its DC limit, an ideal bond the stand-in. The state-space solver works from the lumped R/L/C fields and never inverts an impedance, so it needs no stand-in and serves as the independent cross-check: for the bond of the example notebook its settled DC state agrees with the node-merged solution to \(10^{-13}\), and it keeps the two bonded buses at one potential.

docs.title: What a source and a fault need at DC
docs.text:
• Current source. values needs a 0.0 key: values={0.0: 1000.0}. Without it the source contributes nothing at DC, announced once per run (InputWarning, code SOURCE_FREQUENCY_GAP). Give it a real number — at zero frequency the imaginary part is not a phase shift.
  • Voltage source. voltage and source_impedance both need a 0.0 entry; a network solved at 0 Hz without one is rejected at the solve. The 0.0 entry of source_impedance is the DC resistance of the source: the values are numbers, not formulas, so nothing drops a reactance there for you. A zero source_impedance is rejected when the source is constructed.
  • Fault. scalings does not need a 0.0 key: a frequency without a key is scaled with 1.0, i.e. the sources contribute in full at DC. Give 0.0: 0.0 to exclude the DC bin from a fault. A mapping that names some network frequencies but not others is announced once per run (InputWarning, code SCALINGS_INCOMPLETE); scalings may also be left out entirely, which means 1.0 everywhere.
  • IEC 60909 characteristics. i_k_a, r_to_x and kappa describe the DC offset and thermal equivalent of an alternating short-circuit current. They do not enter the solve (see Objects) and have no meaning in a pure DC study; leave them unset there.
  • Mixed studies. frequencies=[0.0, 50.0] is legal and the two are independent: the DC handling is confined to the 0 Hz bin, and a study carrying both returns the same 50 Hz answer, bit for bit, as one carrying 50 Hz alone.

docs.title: Splitting the network, location response
docs.text: Two analyses sit on top of a fault solve and answer questions about one location rather than about one fault: what the rest of the network contributes at the fault bus, direction by direction (gi.analyze_cuts), and how the network responds to any electrode at a bus (gi.bus_response). Both rest on the same nodal model as the solve, described in Model and assumptions.

docs.title: Characterising a location without its electrode
docs.text:
Adding an electrode Y_B at bus b is a rank-one change to the nodal matrix, so by Sherman-Morrison every nodal voltage is a Möbius function of it:

\[ \underline{u}(Y_B) = \underline{u}_0 - \frac{Y_B\, \underline{z}\, u_{0,b}}{1 + Y_B Z_\text{net}} \]

Three objects on the right, none of which needs the electrode to be known: u_0, the fault solve with the electrode removed; z, the voltage everywhere per ampere injected at b; and Z_net = z_b, the driving-point impedance of everything except the local electrode — the parallel impedance the network offers at that point.

gi.bus_response(network, fault=..., bus=...) builds those from two solves. Evaluating it afterwards costs nothing, for any electrode, including the two extremes as exact limits: Z_B → ∞ (none installed) and Z_B → 0 (ideal, which the solver itself will not accept because a zero impedance cannot be inverted). .extremes() returns the bracket, .evaluate(z) a single electrode and .sweep([...]) any number of them.

The driving-point impedance is exactly Z_dp = 1/(Y_B + 1/Z_net). Its magnitude falls monotonically from |Z_net| to zero as the electrode improves only for an electrode whose admittance lies within 90° of 1/Z_net: along Y_B = t·e^{jφ}, |Z_dp| decreases for every t if and only if cos(φ − arg(1/Z_net)) ≥ 0. A resistive electrode (real Y_B ≥ 0) always qualifies, since Re(1/Z_net) ≥ 0 in a passive network. A reactive electrode of the opposite sign to the network's susceptance first raises |Z_dp| above |Z_net|; the largest magnitude over all passive electrodes is reached at Y_B = -j·Im(1/Z_net), which cancels that susceptance and gives |Z_dp| = 1/Re(1/Z_net) = |Z_net|/cos(arg Z_net). That is 0.08 % above |Z_net| where the network seen from the bus is nearly resistive (arg Z_net = 2.2°), but 57 % at the far end of a four-bus cable chain (arg Z_net = 50°). .extremes() therefore reports it as the worst_passive row instead of assuming it away.

The closed form also derives the invariance of the EPR-based reduction factor that the sensitivity work runs into: u_b(Y_B) = u_{0,b}/(1 + Y_B Z_net) holds with and without mutual coupling alike, so the factor cancels out of the quotient exactly. It is algebra, not a numerical accident. The current-based factor has no such cancellation and responds to the electrode — see Reduction factors and earthing impedance.

docs.title: Splitting the network at the fault
docs.text:
A cut is a named set of branches, all incident to the fault bus. Cuts turn the question "how much grounding does each direction contribute" into numbers:

parallel impedance left --- fault location --- parallel impedance right

gi.analyze_cuts(network, fault=..., cuts=[...]) reports two families of quantity per direction.

Impedances — a property of the network, not of the fault. One ampere is injected at the fault bus with all sources and all mutual injections removed; the share leaving through each cut is read off, and Z_side = u_fault / i_cut. Because the shares and the local electrode current add up to the injected ampere, the decomposition closes by construction,

\[ \frac{1}{Z_\text{driving point}} = \frac{1}{Z_\text{local}} + \sum_\text{sides} \frac{1}{Z_\text{side}}, \]

and the residual of that identity is reported next to the values. Being source-free, Z_side does not change when the fault bus's own characteristic is varied — which is the useful statement: the network's parallel contribution is a fixed property, the local electrode is the variable, and the total is their parallel combination.

Isolating each side into its own sub-network would be equivalent wherever the sides are galvanically separate, and wrong in a ring: removing one branch of a ring separates nothing, so the far side comes out empty and the impedance infinite. Current division has no such blind spot.

Currents — how the fault current actually divides. From a solved fault: i_shield per direction, and current_share = |i_shield| / |i_inj|. KCL at the fault bus closes, i_inj = i_local + Σ i_shield, and the residual is reported. Where the directions are disjoint — no ring — the far-side sums also give i_earth, i_total and the side reduction factor r = |i_earth| / |i_total|. Where they overlap, those three are None and current_share carries the meaning; sides_are_disjoint says which case you are in.

Every cut branch has to be incident to the fault bus. A cut placed further out still separates the network, but its far side is no longer a parallel element of the fault location and the impedances would not sum. Incident branches that no cut claims form the implicit side "rest", so the decomposition always covers the whole network.

In a network without voltage sources the driving-point impedance that the cuts decompose is the earthing impedance \(Z_E\) of the fault bus, the number Reduction factors and earthing impedance defines.
