docs.title: Impedance formulas and where they come from
docs.text: Every impedance in a groundinsight network is a formula string on a type: the electrode of a bus (BusType.impedance_formula), the shield–earth loop and the phase–shield coupling of a branch (BranchType.self_impedance_formula, mutual_impedance_formula) and the phase conductor (phase_impedance_formula). This page explains what a formula means to the model, which values it may produce, how it is evaluated and where good formulas come from. The exact syntax — every symbol, function and limit — is in the reference Formula syntax.

docs.title: Impedance formulas
docs.text:
Formula strings may contain the symbols

Symbol Meaning rho specific earth resistance \(\rho_E\) in \(\Omega\,\text{m}\) f frequency \(f\) in Hz l branch length \(l\) in km j imaginary unit (internally 1j)

plus I as a second spelling of the imaginary unit, pi, and a fixed list of mathematical functions (Formula syntax).

Expressions are evaluated symbolically, so any analytic expression supported by SymPy is admissible. The literal string "nan" maps to an effectively infinite impedance and can be used to model open ends (broken shields, isolators etc.).

docs.title: Which values a formula may produce
docs.text:
Every impedance that ends up on the diagonal of \(Y(f)\) is inverted, so not every number a formula can produce is a physically meaningful model. Four results are rejected with a ValueError that names the element, the frequency and the formula:

Result Why it is rejected \(\underline{Z} = 0\) exactly An element with no impedance has no admittance either. It drops out of the nodal system entirely and therefore reports the opposite of the ideal-earth limit: full earth potential rise and no current into the soil, indistinguishable from a bus with no electrode at all. \(0 < \lvert\underline{Z}\rvert \lesssim 5.6\cdot10^{-309}\ \Omega\) Too small to invert in double precision. \(1/\underline{Z}\) overflows, reaches the admittance matrix as infinity, and the bus current comes back as NaN. \(\operatorname{Re}(\underline{Z}) < 0\) An earth electrode, an earthing conductor and a cable screen are passive; a negative resistance generates energy. It also pushes \(Y(f)\) towards singularity, where the earth potential rise grows without bound while every intermediate number still looks plausible. \(\operatorname{Re}(\underline{Z}) = -\infty\) The limit of a negative resistance, typically log(f) at 0 Hz. It is not an open circuit, but \(1/(-\infty) = 0\) would read as one and disconnect the element without a word.

A near-ideal earth is modelled with a small finite value, not with zero. The solution converges smoothly as \(\underline{Z}\to 0\), with a relative error of the order of the ratio between that value and the other impedances in the network: in a network whose impedances are of the order of \(1\ \Omega\), \(10^{-6}\ \Omega\) reproduces the ideal-earth limit to about seven digits, and every further decade buys another digit.

A negative real part is almost always a fitted formula evaluated outside the range it was fitted on. 0.05*rho - 2, a plausible fit for a rod electrode, is negative below \(\rho_E = 40\ \Omega\,\text{m}\) — wet clay, not an exotic soil. Check a new formula at the lowest \(\rho_E\), the lowest frequency and the shortest length that occur in the model.

The rule applies exactly where an impedance is inverted, and nowhere else:

  • Bus grounding impedances and the self impedances of branches with grounding_conductor=True are checked; the self impedance of a branch with grounding_conductor=False is never inverted and is not checked.
  • Mutual impedances are not checked. Z_mutual = 0 is the normal way to express "no coupling" and stays legal.
  • Source impedances of voltage sources are checked. (A zero source impedance was already rejected when the source was constructed; a negative one was not.)
  • Inactive buses and branches, and frequencies outside network.frequencies, are not checked — they never reach the matrix.
  • Positive infinity stays legal everywhere: it is the documented open-end sentinel, and \(1/\infty = 0\) is the right answer. So does a reactance of \(\pm j\infty\), a capacitance at DC. NaN is reported by its own handler.

The check runs both where the impedance is computed (calculate_impedance) and again immediately before the matrix is assembled, because impedances are not recomputed at solve time — a value written directly into bus.impedance[f], or restored from JSON or from the database, would otherwise reach the solver unexamined.

In a transient simulation the same rule is applied to every bin of the FFT frequency grid, the 0 Hz bin included. At 0 Hz the first two rows of the table are inverted: a purely reactive impedance such as j*2*pi*f*L really is a short circuit at DC, so there the value is accepted and replaced by a small finite stand-in instead of being rejected — see Direct current (f = 0). The negative real part stays rejected at 0 Hz as well, and so does a real part of \(-\infty\); a passive element is passive at DC too.

docs.title: How a formula is evaluated
docs.text:
A formula is evaluated when an element joins a network (create_bus, create_branch, Network.add_*) and again whenever an input it depends on changes — the soil resistivity, the type, the length of the element, or the network frequencies. The solve itself reads the stored impedance tables and evaluates nothing. Each evaluation substitutes the element's own rho and, for a branch, its l, and returns one complex value per network frequency.

Before a string reaches SymPy it passes the formula guard (groundinsight.utils.validations.assert_safe_formula). SymPy then parses it and lambdify turns it into a NumPy function, which is evaluated for all frequencies at once. The compiled function is cached under the formula string, so the hundred buses of one BusType pay the SymPy cost once.

Zero frequency needs more than substitution: Carson's earth-return term is \(0\cdot\infty\) there, a constant reactance has no meaning, a pure inductance is a short circuit. How each case is told apart and what the model does with it is the subject of Direct current (f = 0).

docs.title: Where the formulas come from
docs.text:
The formulas are model input, and the package checks them only for syntax, symbols and passivity. A formula that is passive but describes the wrong conductor produces plausible, wrong numbers. Three sources are common:

  • Data sheets and line theory. The shield–earth loop and the coupling of a cable or an overhead line follow from the conductor data and Carson's earth-return term with the equivalent depth \(D_E = 658\sqrt{\rho/f}\) m. Bus and branch types from data sheets derives both for a real 20 kV cable, checks the closed form against the earth-return integral, and shows the phase impedance a ring needs.
  • Measurements. An electrode impedance measured at a station, at one or several frequencies, can be written as a constant or fitted as a function of f — check the fit at the edges of the range it will be evaluated on.
  • Electrode formulas. Rod, ring and mesh electrodes have textbook formulas in rho; the data-sheet how-to lists them with their sources.

The formulas in the tutorials and examples, such as rho * 0.01 + j * f * 1/50 * 0.1 for an electrode or (0.25 + j * f * 0.012) * l for a cable, are round illustrative numbers that keep the examples short; they are marked as such where they appear.

docs.title: Why a formula is checked before it is parsed
docs.text: sympy.sympify evaluates Python, and formula strings travel with the model: in JSON project files and SQLite databases that are exchanged between people. A formula from a file of unknown origin could otherwise run code on the machine that opens it. The guard admits only numbers, the documented symbols, the listed functions and arithmetic, and bounds the size of what it admits; Formula syntax has the details and the limits.

docs.title: Phase currents in rings and meshes
docs.text: The coupling between the faulted phase conductor and the shields is driven by the phase current in every branch. On a radial feeder that current is the source current on every branch between source and fault. In ring or meshed topologies a single source–fault pair yields multiple routes, and the source current has to be divided between them. This page explains how groundinsight divides it, what phase_impedance_formula must describe, when the result is exact, and what the legacy path-based mode does differently.

docs.title: The phase-conductor network
docs.text:
The division is the default and is computed, not declared: run_fault(..., phase_current_mode="auto") solves a reduced phase-conductor network per source — the fault bus as reference node, the source current injected at the source bus — and reads the branch phase currents off that solution. The split then follows the topology and the conductor impedances, is independent of the order the branches were declared in, and needs no user input.

The solve runs on the galvanic component of the phase network that contains the fault bus; inactive branches and a phase conductor declared open (phase_impedance_formula="nan") are not part of it. A source that reaches the fault through the earthing network but has no phase-conductor connection to it cannot feed the fault; run_fault still injects its current into the earthing system — as if it returned entirely through soil and shields, which is conservative for its share — and says so with a ModelAssumptionWarning, code SOURCE_WITHOUT_PHASE_PATH.

docs.title: What phase_impedance_formula describes
docs.text:
The phase impedance used for that solve comes from BranchType.phase_impedance_formula (symbols f, rho, l, same as the other formulas). It is optional, because in a network without cycles the split is fixed by the topology alone and the impedance value cannot change it.

Where it matters, it has to be the impedance the one-way model needs. Per branch, the phase conductor (voltage \(V\)) and the shield (potential \(u\)) obey, both loops with earth return and both currents in the same direction,

\[ \begin{pmatrix} V_a - V_b \\ u_a - u_b \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} Z_{pp} & Z_m \\ Z_m & Z_s \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} I_p \\ I_s \end{pmatrix}. \]

Eliminating the shield current \(I_s\) gives

\[ (V_a - k\,u_a) - (V_b - k\,u_b) = Z_\text{red}\, I_p, \qquad Z_\text{red} = Z_{pp} - \frac{Z_m^2}{Z_s}, \qquad k = \frac{Z_m}{Z_s}. \]

phase_impedance_formula is therefore the phase–earth loop impedance with the shield bonded at both ends, \(Z_\text{red}\), for a branch with a grounding conductor, and the plain phase–earth loop impedance \(Z_{pp}\) for a branch without one. It is neither the positive-sequence impedance \(R_1 + jX_1\) nor the resistance of the conductor alone. Bus and branch types from data sheets computes \(Z_\text{red}\) for a real cable.

docs.title: Without the formula: the proxy
docs.text:
Where cycles exist and the formula is missing, the solve falls back to a proxy — 1/Z_self for a branch with a grounding conductor, 1/length for one without — and says so once per solve with a ModelAssumptionWarning, code PHASE_PROXY, that names the branches. Those two quantities are not comparable, so the split between routes of different construction is then a heuristic. Declare the formula whenever the ring mixes cable and overhead line.

The warning is raised only where it means something: in a network without a cycle around the fault, the proxy cannot change the result, and it stays silent. A branch whose shield is broken (self_impedance_formula="nan") keeps its phase conductor in the phase network with the length proxy — a broken screen does not open the conductor next to it.

docs.title: One-way coupling: when the split is exact
docs.text:
The model determines the phase currents first and lets them drive the shields afterwards; the shield currents do not act back on the split. The elimination above shows when that is exact. If \(k\) has the same value on every branch of a mesh, \(W = V - k\,u\) is a potential on that mesh, the phase network written in \(W\) no longer contains the shields, and the split it gives is the split of the fully coupled system. If \(k\) differs between the routes of a mesh, the term \((k_1 - k_2)(u_S - u_F)\) drives a circulating current that the one-way model does not see.

The example below makes this concrete (phase_split.py). A ring S – A – F – B – S is fed with 1 kA at S and faulted at F; route 1 is a cable (2 × 1.2 km), route 2 the same cable (homogeneous) or an overhead line with an earth wire (mixed, 2 × 1.5 km). The per-km values are illustrative 50 Hz values:

CABLE = {"zs": 0.29 + 0.625j, "zm": 0.049 + 0.625j, "zpp": 0.174 + 0.740j}
OVERHEAD_LINE = {"zs": 0.65 + 0.785j, "zm": 0.049 + 0.372j, "zpp": 0.355 + 0.759j}


def z_red(construction):
    """Phase-earth loop with the shield bonded at both ends: Z_pp - Z_m^2/Z_s."""
    return construction["zpp"] - construction["zm"] ** 2 / construction["zs"]


def per_km(z):
    """A per-km impedance at 50 Hz as a formula (reactance proportional to f)."""
    return f"({z.real!r} + {z.imag!r}*j*f/50)*l"

def ring(route_2, phase):
    """The ring S-A-F-B-S; ``phase`` is "Z_red", "Z_pp" or "proxy"."""
    net = gi.create_network(name=f"ring_{phase}", frequencies=[50.0])
    electrodes = {"S": "0.2", "A": "2.0", "F": "2.0",
                  "B": "15.0" if route_2 is OVERHEAD_LINE else "2.0"}
    for bus, z_b in electrodes.items():
        bus_type = gi.BusType(name=f"electrode_{bus}", system_type="MV",
                              voltage_level=20.0, impedance_formula=z_b)
        gi.create_bus(name=bus, type=bus_type, network=net)

    def branch_type(name, construction):
        phase_formula = {"Z_red": per_km(z_red(construction)),
                         "Z_pp": per_km(construction["zpp"]),
                         "proxy": None}[phase]
        return gi.BranchType(name=name, grounding_conductor=True,
                             self_impedance_formula=per_km(construction["zs"]),
                             mutual_impedance_formula=per_km(construction["zm"]),
                             phase_impedance_formula=phase_formula)

    route_1_type = branch_type("route_1", CABLE)
    route_2_type = branch_type("route_2", route_2)
    for name, a, b, kind, length in (("SA", "S", "A", route_1_type, 1.2),
                                     ("AF", "A", "F", route_1_type, 1.2),
                                     ("SB", "S", "B", route_2_type, 1.5),
                                     ("BF", "B", "F", route_2_type, 1.5)):
        gi.create_branch(name=name, type=kind, from_bus=a, to_bus=b, length=length,
                         network=net)
    gi.create_source(name="infeed", bus="S", values={50.0: 1000.0}, network=net)
    gi.create_fault(name="F1", bus="F", network=net)
    return net


def split(route_2, phase):
    """Phase current on route 1 in A: the current divider of the two routes.

    The proxy of a branch with a grounding conductor is its shield impedance.
    """
    per_km = {"Z_red": z_red, "Z_pp": lambda c: c["zpp"], "proxy": lambda c: c["zs"]}[phase]
    z_route_1 = per_km(CABLE) * 2 * 1.2
    z_route_2 = per_km(route_2) * 2 * 1.5
    return abs(1000.0 * z_route_2 / (z_route_1 + z_route_2))


def epr_at_fault(net):
    """EPR at the fault bus F in V."""
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        # the proxy variant is announced by a ModelAssumptionWarning PHASE_PROXY
        warnings.simplefilter("ignore", gi.ModelAssumptionWarning)
        result = gi.run_fault(net, "F1")
    return abs(complex(next(b.uepr_freq[50.0] for b in result.buses if b.name == "F")))


TABLE = {
    (label, phase): (split(route_2, phase), epr_at_fault(ring(route_2, phase)))
    for label, route_2 in (("homogeneous", CABLE), ("mixed", OVERHEAD_LINE))
    for phase in ("Z_red", "Z_pp", "proxy")
}

The one-way model divides the source current between the two routes like a current divider of their phase impedances; split computes that share for route 1. The results against a fully coupled multi-conductor model — phase conductors, shields and electrodes solved as one system, the test oracle of the suite:

Ring phase_impedance_formula phase current, route 1 |EPR| at F coupled model homogeneous Z_red 555.56 A 205.863 V 555.56 A, 205.863 V homogeneous Z_pp 555.56 A 205.863 V homogeneous proxy 555.56 A 205.863 V mixed Z_red 728.39 A 310.735 V (+7.4 %) 764.90 A, 289.231 V mixed Z_pp 582.47 A 298.635 V (+3.3 %) mixed proxy 653.92 A 278.187 V (−3.8 %)

In the homogeneous ring all three choices give the coupled result — any phase impedance proportional to length divides the current in inverse proportion to the route lengths (3.0 km against 2.4 km: 555.56 A on route 1). In the mixed ring none is exact. Z_red is the quantity the elimination defines and gives the split closest to the coupled one; the smaller EPR error of the other two choices in this ring is a cancellation of a wrong split against the missing circulating current, not a better model. The size and the sign of the error depend on the network; it grows with the difference in \(k\) between the routes and is largest where a route without an earth wire (\(k = 0\)) runs parallel to a cable.

docs.title: One phase conductor
docs.text: The phase network contains the faulted conductor only. In a ring, the two healthy phases form closed loops as well, and the fault currents induce currents in them that couple back to the faulted phase and to the shields. The model does not represent them, and the size of the effect has not been quantified.

docs.title: Enumerated paths and the legacy mode
docs.text:
Mutual-coupling injections require a direction. In the legacy phase_current_mode="paths" groundinsight derives that direction by enumerating every simple path from each source bus to the active fault bus via a depth-first search (PathFinder). Each path is stored as an ordered list of Branch objects; its injection signs follow the traversal order.

The enumeration is exponential in the number of loops

The number of simple paths grows exponentially with the number of independent loops, not with the number of buses: a 500-bus ring has two paths, a 5×5 grid 8 512 and a 6×6 grid 1 262 816 — roughly a minute of enumeration against milliseconds in the solver. The default phase_current_mode="auto" therefore does not enumerate: it only needs to know which sources reach the fault, and Network.sources_reaching(...) answers that with a breadth-first search. network.paths is empty after a default run_fault; call gi.create_paths on the network if you want the paths as data.

phase_current_mode="paths" selects the pre-0.6 behaviour: every branch on every enumerated path receives the full source current, scaled by that branch's parallel_coefficient. This is correct for a radial network — where both modes agree exactly — but in a meshed one it multiplies the current instead of dividing it. In a ring of two routes of the same construction, at the default coefficient of 1.0, the Norton injections add up to \((1-2k)\,I\) instead of \((1-k)\,I\). With \(Z_m = Z_s/2\) (\(k = 0.5\)) the symmetric ring then solves to EPR = 0 V at the fault, an EPR ratio value = 0 and no current-based factor at all (value_current is None: no current reaches the soil), because the doubled mutual injections cancel the source exactly. With the cable of the tutorials, \(\lvert 1-2k\rvert = 1\) and the EPR comes out as if the shields did not couple at all, 2.6 times the correct value (From a line to a ring). The earthing impedance \(Z_E\) is a property of the earthing network alone and does not change with the mode. The mode is kept so studies produced before 0.6.0 stay reproducible, and for networks where the split is known from measurement and set by hand. When a source reaches the fault over more than one path and the coefficients are still at their default, the mode says so (ModelAssumptionWarning, code PARALLEL_COEFFICIENT_DEFAULT).

The deprecated auto_parallel_coefficients argument still works and still wins when passed: True maps to "auto", False to "paths".

docs.title: When there is no path
docs.text: Two different situations both end in "no paths", and groundinsight treats them differently on purpose. No sources or no faults at all is rejected: the enumeration runs over sources × faults, so an empty side means nothing was ever asked, and the all-zero result that follows is an artefact of an incomplete model rather than a statement about the system. No path between an existing source and an existing fault is accepted: that is the signature of an islanded fault bus — the normal outcome of an outage scenario — and 0 V is then the physically correct answer.

docs.text:

  • Phase currents in meshes — the example notebook: a line, a ring, two parallel cables and a mesh in both modes, checked against a fully coupled multi-conductor solve; with the same \(k\) on every branch the split moves the shield currents but no earth potential.

docs.title: Reduction factors and earthing impedance
docs.text:
groundinsight reports two reduction factors for every fault and frequency, together with the quantities of the EN 50522 chain \(U_E = r \cdot 3I_0 \cdot Z_E\) at the fault bus. This page defines each of them, shows when they agree and when they do not, and says which one the standard means. Where each number appears in the results is in the glossary; how they feed the verification of the standard is in Compare results with EN 50522 limits.

Field of ResultReductionFactor Column of res_all_impedances() Meaning value reduction_factor EPR at the fault bus with coupling over EPR without coupling value_current reduction_factor_current \(\lvert I_E\rvert / \lvert 3I_0\rvert\), the reduction factor r of EN 50522 u_earthing — \(U_E\), the EPR of the fault bus z_earthing grounding_impedance_Ohm, grounding_impedance_deg \(Z_E\), the driving-point impedance of the earthing network at the fault bus i_earth, earth_buses — \(I_E\) and the group of buses whose electrode currents it sums i_fault — \(3I_0\), the scaled source currents that reach the fault

docs.title: The EPR ratio
docs.text:
The reduction factor \(r\) at the fault bus is defined as

\[ r(f) = \frac{|u_{\text{fault}}^{\text{(with mutual)}}(f)|} {|u_{\text{fault}}^{\text{(without mutual)}}(f)|}. \]

groundinsight obtains the denominator by re-solving the same network with all mutual-coupling Norton sources removed. For a single shielded line directly between source and fault with identical impedances the expression collapses to the familiar analytical form

\[ r = \left| 1 - \frac{Z_{\text{mutual}}}{Z_{\text{self}}} \right|. \]

The same closed form applies to a fully symmetric ring with the fault diametrically opposite the source — the Norton injections in the two ring halves are then perfectly anti-parallel and superpose to the same expression as the single-line case. More generally it holds in any network whose branches all have the same ratio \(k = Z_m/Z_s\): the Norton injections then telescope along every route to \((1-k)\) times the source injection, and every potential with coupling is \((1-k)\) times the one without.

docs.title: Reduction factor on a current basis
docs.text:
The ratio above is structurally blind to the impedance at the fault bus. Both solves use the same Y, so changing the diagonal entry Y_ff is a rank-1 update whose effect cancels in the quotient. On the six-station feeder of the decomposition example, sweeping the electrode of the faulted station from 0.01 Ω to 100 Ω leaves value at 0.310003, while \(Z_E\) and the potential rise both grow by a factor of 80 (0.0099 → 0.796 Ω, 8.3 → 668 V) and value_current falls from 0.278 to 0.168. That is not a numerical artefact — the closed form in Characterising a location derives it.

ResultReductionFactor.value_current is the measured definition alongside it: the total earth-return current over the total fault current,

\[ r_I(f) = \frac{|\underline{I}_E(f)|}{|\underline{I}_F(f)|}. \]

I_E is the sum of the electrode currents of every bus that feeds the soil — from the fault outwards in every direction, a ring or a mesh having more than one, up to where the potential profile turns — not the electrode current at the faulted station. In a cable network with continuous shields the stations are bonded to one another, so the current spreads along the shields and leaks into the soil at every one of them; the earthing current is distributed over the whole bonded system by construction. Measured on a six-station feeder, counting only the faulted station understates r_I by a factor of 1.8 to 4.7 depending on where the fault sits.

Two things make the sum less obvious than it looks.

Summing over every bus gives exactly zero. Whatever enters the soil somewhere leaves it somewhere else, so Kirchhoff at the whole network forces Σ I_a = 0. A group has to be selected — and "every bus except the faulted one" is not that group: by the same law it collapses back to the electrode current of the faulted station alone.

The group cannot be found from the potential profile. The crossing between the two groups generally falls between two stations rather than on one, and when the fault sits close to the infeed the profile may never come near zero at all — it passes through a shallow minimum and rises again. On the verification feeder with the fault one station from the infeed, |EPR| runs 91.4, 19.6, 18.7, 18.1, 17.7, 17.5 V: there is no crossing to find.

What is unambiguous per bus is the direction of its electrode current, so the split is made in the complex plane: the group is the set of phasors in one half-plane, and the half-plane is the one whose sum has the largest magnitude. That needs no angle nominated and no tolerance tuned, and it reduces to the obvious answer whenever the two groups are cleanly opposed. Both groups carry the same sum with opposite signs, so |I_E| does not depend on which is called which; the fault bus anchors the naming.

ResultReductionFactor reports i_earth (the ampere value) and earth_buses (the group) next to the ratio, because the split is a modelling statement and should be inspectable. The separation of the two groups says how cleanly the phasors separated; below 0.9 the electrode currents are spread in angle and a single scalar earth-return current is a coarser description than it looks, and run_fault says so (ModelAssumptionWarning, code EARTH_GROUP_SPREAD). Where no electrode carries a noticeable share of the fault current — the fault current returns entirely through shields and conductors — there is no group, and \(I_E\) and value_current are None (EARTH_GROUP_UNDEFINED). res_all_impedances() carries both factors.

The denominator is every source that feeds the fault. i_fault is the sum of the scaled currents of all sources that reach the fault, a source on the fault bus itself included. Such a source injects and withdraws its current at the same bus; it adds to \(3I_0\) but not to \(I_E\). With 1000 A from a remote infeed and 500 A from a source on the fault bus, value_current is exactly two thirds of its value without the local source, while i_earth and value do not change. The reduction factor of a line in the sense of the standard counts the remote infeed only; divide i_earth by it where a local source is present.

docs.title: Which one is the EN 50522 reduction factor
docs.text:
value_current, r = |I_E|/|3I_0|. The norm writes the earthing voltage as

\[ U_E = 3 I_0 \cdot Z_E \cdot r, \]

with two quantities that groundinsight reports at the fault bus (ResultReductionFactor):

  • u_earthing is U_E, the EPR at the fault bus — the same complex number as the fault bus's uepr_freq;
  • z_earthing is Z_E, the driving-point impedance of the earthing network at the fault bus: one ampere injected there against remote earth, every electrode and shield in place, no inductive coupling, no Thevenin loop closure. It is what an earthing-impedance measurement at the station sees, the stations bonded through cable shields included, and it is the reported grounding impedance.

The chain is a physical statement about these, not an identity: it holds where the norm's assumptions hold. On a long homogeneous cable run with the fault far from the infeed it closes with r = |1 - Z_m/Z_s| (the factor value) on the ladder limit Z_E = -Z'/2 + sqrt(Z'^2/4 + Z_e Z') to better than 1e-5 (tests/test_audit_pass19_physics.py, 64 sections). Away from that case — a short feeder, the infeed close by, large electrodes — |U_E| and r \cdot 3I_0 \cdot |Z_E| differ, and the difference measures how far the installation is from the norm's lumped picture; nothing raises or warns.

The long run, built and compared with the closed form (reduction_factors.py; 64 sections of 0.5 km, stations 2 Ω, infeed 0.2 Ω, 1 kA, illustrative per-km values):

N_SECTIONS = 64
SECTION_KM = 0.5
Z_STATION = 2.0          # Ohm, electrode of every station
I_FAULT = 1000.0         # A RMS, 3I_0 at 50 Hz

cable = gi.BranchType(
    name="cable", grounding_conductor=True,
    self_impedance_formula="(0.29 + 0.625*j*f/50)*l",     # Z_s' (illustrative)
    mutual_impedance_formula="(0.049 + 0.625*j*f/50)*l",  # Z_m' (illustrative)
)
station = gi.BusType(name="station", system_type="Station", voltage_level=20.0,
                     impedance_formula=repr(Z_STATION))
infeed = gi.BusType(name="infeed", system_type="Substation", voltage_level=110.0,
                    impedance_formula="0.2")

net = gi.create_network(name="long_run", frequencies=[50.0])
gi.create_bus(name="N0", type=infeed, network=net)
for i in range(1, N_SECTIONS + 1):
    gi.create_bus(name=f"N{i}", type=station, network=net)
for i in range(N_SECTIONS):
    gi.create_branch(name=f"L{i + 1}", type=cable, from_bus=f"N{i}",
                     to_bus=f"N{i + 1}", length=SECTION_KM, network=net)
gi.create_source(name="infeed", bus="N0", values={50.0: I_FAULT}, network=net)
gi.create_fault(name="F", bus=f"N{N_SECTIONS}", network=net)

rf = gi.run_fault(net, "F").reduction_factor
u_e = complex(rf.u_earthing[50.0])        # U_E: EPR of the fault bus
z_e = complex(rf.z_earthing[50.0])        # Z_E: driving-point impedance there
r_epr = rf.value[50.0]                    # EPR ratio, |1 - Z_m/Z_s| here
r_current = rf.value_current[50.0]        # |I_E| / |3I_0|

z_series = (0.29 + 0.625j) * SECTION_KM   # Z' of one section
z_mutual = (0.049 + 0.625j) * SECTION_KM
k = z_mutual / z_series
z_inf = -z_series / 2 + cmath.sqrt(z_series ** 2 / 4 + Z_STATION * z_series)
u_closed = abs(1 - k) * I_FAULT * abs(z_inf)
Quantity Model Closed form value 0.349781 \(\lvert 1 - k\rvert\) = 0.349781 value_current 0.359015 — \(Z_E\) 0.6249 + 0.3081j Ω \(Z_\infty\) = 0.6249 + 0.3081j Ω \(\lvert U_E\rvert\) 243.708 V \(\lvert 1-k\rvert \cdot I \cdot \lvert Z_\infty\rvert\) = 243.708 V value · 3I0 · |ZE| 243.708 V value_current · 3I0 · |ZE| 250.142 V

The chain closes with the coupling factor of the cable. value_current lies 2.6 % above it here: along the run the electrode currents decay and rotate with the complex propagation constant of the ladder, the half-plane split leaves out those that point backwards, and the sum of the rest exceeds \(\lvert 1-k\rvert \cdot I\).

The current-weighted mean potential of the earth group and that mean divided by I_E — which release 0.6.0 reported as u_earthing / z_earthing — are kept as u_earthing_group / z_earthing_group. On that pair the chain closes to machine precision, but only because z_earthing_group is defined as u_earthing_group / I_E; it checks nothing. On the long run above they are 138.83 V and 0.3867 Ω, 43 % and 44.5 % below the fault-bus EPR and the driving-point impedance, which is why they are no longer reported as U_E and Z_E: taken into a touch-voltage assessment they are unconservative.

The fault current the factor divides by is stored as i_fault (sum(scaling * I_src) over the sources that reach the fault).

value uses a different reference: the mutual coupling removed, but the cable shield still in place as a metallic return path. Most of the current still comes back through the shield rather than through the soil, so that reference voltage is far below Z_E \cdot 3I_0 (the norm's r = 1, the whole fault current through the earthing impedance). Both factors are correct answers; they answer different questions.

docs.title: The two factors are not two computations of one number
docs.text:
They coincide in exactly one case, and it is worth knowing which. For a route with shield impedance \(Z_s\), mutual impedance \(Z_m\) and station electrodes summing to \(Z_E\) along the earth-return path,

\[ r_\text{coupling} = \frac{Z_s - Z_m}{Z_s}, \qquad r_I = \frac{Z_s - Z_m}{Z_s + Z_E}, \]

so their ratio is the current divider \(Z_s/(Z_s + Z_E)\) and nothing else. The first is the ideally bonded limit — the tabulated property of the cable, \(1 - Z_m/Z_s\), independent of the station earths by construction. The second is what the earthing system of this network actually passes into the soil.

Verified against the closed form to machine precision over five decades of electrode impedance on a two-section line with \(Z_s = 0.2 + 0.4\mathrm{j}\ \Omega\):

electrode per station \(r_\text{coupling}\) \(r_I\) ratio \(Z_s/(Z_s+Z_E)\) 10 Ω 0.500000 0.011067 0.022135 0.022135 1 Ω 0.500000 0.100000 0.200000 0.200000 0.1 Ω 0.500000 0.395285 0.790569 0.790569 0.01 Ω 0.500000 0.489820 0.979639 0.979639 10 µΩ 0.500000 0.499990 0.999980 0.999980

A wide gap is therefore a statement about the network, not a defect: the stations are not bonded well enough for the cable's tabulated reduction factor to describe what the soil sees. groundinsight logs the divider at INFO where it falls below 0.5, rather than as a warning — with ordinary station electrodes it is the normal case, and a log that warns about the normal case stops being read.

docs.title: Frequency dependence of the reduction factor
docs.text:
For a shielded cable the impedances split into a resistive and an inductive part,

\[ Z_{\text{self}}(f) = R + j\,\omega L, \qquad Z_{\text{mutual}}(f) = j\,\omega M, \qquad \omega = 2\pi f. \]

With full coupling between the faulted phase and the grounding conductor (the geometric ideal \(M = L\)) the closed form simplifies to

\[ r(f) \;=\; \left| 1 - \frac{j\,\omega L}{R + j\,\omega L} \right| \;=\; \frac{R}{\sqrt{R^{2} + (\omega L)^{2}}}. \]

Two limits follow directly:

  • \(f \to 0\): \(\omega L \to 0\), so \(Z_{\text{mutual}}/Z_{\text{self}} \to 0\) and \(r \to 1\). At DC the shield carries no induced current, the entire fault current flows through the local earth path and the reduction factor equals 1.
  • \(f \to \infty\): the imaginary parts dominate, so \(Z_{\text{mutual}}/Z_{\text{self}} \to M/L = 1\) and \(r \to 0\). At high frequency the shield short-circuits the inductive coupling, almost the entire fault current returns metallically and the EPR collapses.

In a real cable the resistive part is small compared with \(\omega L\) already at power frequency, which is why MV cables typically reach \(r \approx 0.3 \ldots 0.4\) at 50 Hz and the reduction factor decays quickly above one or two hundred Hz. This convergence is exercised explicitly by tests/test_topology_and_reduction.py::test_reduction_factor_sweep_*, which sweeps a single MV cable section and a 20-bus symmetric ring from 50 Hz to 5 kHz and asserts both the closed form above and the monotonic decay towards zero.

docs.title: Grounding impedance
docs.text:
ResultGroundingImpedance.value is Z_E in the EN 50522 sense: the driving-point impedance of the earthing network at the fault bus, identical to ResultReductionFactor.z_earthing,

\[ Z_G(f) = Z_E(f) = Z_\text{dp}(F, f) = \left(Y_E(f)^{-1}\right)_{FF}, \]

with \(Y_E\) the nodal matrix of electrodes and shields alone — without the inductive coupling and without the Thevenin loop closures of voltage sources, which belong to the fault loop rather than to the earthing system. It is the impedance an earthing-impedance measurement at the station sees, the stations bonded to it through cable shields included; gi.bus_response(...) (Möbius form) and gi.analyze_cuts(...) (without voltage sources) reproduce it. Note that it is not the station electrodes in parallel either — the shield sections between them add to it.

Z_E is None (with a ModelAssumptionWarning EARTHING_IMPEDANCE_UNDEFINED) where the fault side reaches remote earth only through the loop closure of a voltage source: no bus connected to the fault bus through shields carries an electrode. That is decided from the structure of the earthing network, not from the solver — the matrix of such a group of buses is singular only up to rounding and a solve returns a meaningless 1e15 Ω. In bus_response, where the electrode at the studied bus is the fault side's only one, every ampere leaves through it: Z_E = Z_B + BusResponse.z_fault_ideal.

The quotient of the earth group's mean potential by I_E, which release 0.6.0 reported as the grounding impedance, is kept as z_earthing_group; on a long homogeneous run it is 44.5 % below Z_E. The definition before 0.6.0, \(u_{\text{EPR}}/(r \cdot I_{\text{fault}})\), mixed the coupling ratio into an impedance.

It is exposed per frequency through net.res_all_impedances(), which has one row per (fault, frequency) and no RMS row: a grounding impedance is defined for a frequency, and there is no meaningful way to reduce a set of complex impedances at different frequencies to one scalar. The RMS rows live on net.res_buses() and net.res_branches(), where they aggregate quantities (\(\sqrt{\sum_f |x(f)|^2}\)), and are marked there by the is_rms column.

docs.title: Results stored with the earlier definition
docs.text: A result saved by a release that reported the group quantities as \(U_E\) and \(Z_E\) — in a JSON project file or a database — still loads. Its stored values are moved to u_earthing_group / z_earthing_group, u_earthing, z_earthing and the grounding impedance stay empty, and the result carries an info diagnostic, code LEGACY_EARTHING_DEFINITION, that says why. Run the fault again with run_fault to obtain \(U_E\) and \(Z_E\) in the current sense; nothing is recomputed silently on load.

docs.title: Standards and scope
docs.text:
groundinsight computes the quantities that an earthing study according to the standards needs. It does not carry out the assessment a standard prescribes. This page lists, standard by standard, what the package implements and what it leaves to the engineer.

Scope of the results

groundinsight is a research and engineering tool. Its results support, but do not replace, an assessment according to EN 50522 / IEC 61936-1 by a qualified person, including the measurements the standards require. The software is provided under the MIT License, without warranty of any kind.

docs.title: EN 50522:2022 — earthing of installations above 1 kV AC
docs.text:
The European standard for the design and erection of earthing systems of installations above 1 kV with nominal frequencies up to 60 Hz; the current edition carries the amendment A1:2024.

Implemented

  • The quantities of the touch-voltage verification at the fault location: earth-fault current 3I_0, reduction factor r, earth current I_E, earthing impedance Z_E and earth potential rise U_E (how-to).
  • Reduction factors of cable screens and earth wires from their impedances, for any topology — the standard's informative Annex I gives typical values at 50 Hz.
  • Earth potential rise of every bus, for the transfer of potentials between bonded stations.
  • The final temperatures of uninsulated earthing conductors and electrodes used by the thermal checks (FINAL_TEMPERATURES, EN 50522:2022 Table 2).

Not implemented

  • The permissible touch voltage U_Tp(t_F) (5.4.1, Annexes A and B) and the decision of the design procedure (5.4.3) with the measures M (Annex E).
  • Touch and step voltages, surface potentials, additional resistances.
  • Transferred potentials to low-voltage and telecommunication systems (Clause 6), dimensioning for corrosion and mechanical strength (5.2), the construction rules (Clause 7).
  • The measurements (Clause 8, 9.2, Annexes H and L) — the model needs them to be validated, it does not replace them.

docs.title: IEC 61936-1:2021 — power installations above 1 kV AC
docs.text: The international standard for the design and erection of AC power installations; its Clause 10 "Earthing systems" sets the earthing requirements that EN 50522 details for Europe. The same split applies: groundinsight supplies U_E, Z_E, I_E and r, the assessment is the engineer's.

docs.title: IEC 60909-0:2016 — short-circuit currents
docs.text:
Implemented: the factors that turn a symmetrical short-circuit current into the peak and thermal quantities — the peak factor κ from R/X (kappa_from_r_to_x), the peak current, the DC heat factor m (iec60909_m) and the thermally equivalent short-time current I_th = I_k·√(m + n). They are applied to the current that the linear solve superposes, not to the source currents one by one.

Not implemented: the short-circuit calculation of the network itself. The fault current is an input — from the network operator, or from a pandapower calc_sc run imported with read_shortcircuit_results / apply_shortcircuit_characteristics (I/O).

docs.title: IEC 60949:1988 — thermally permissible short-circuit currents
docs.text:
Implemented: the adiabatic rating I_adm = k·S/√t_k of an earthing conductor or electrode, with k = K·√ln((θ_f + β)/(θ_i + β)) and the material constants of the standard (IEC60949_MATERIALS), in check_conductor_limits and check_node_limits (Analysis).

Not implemented: the non-adiabatic factor of IEC 60949 (heat given off during the fault). Leaving it out underestimates the permissible current, which is on the safe side.

docs.title: IEC 60479-1:2018 and IEC 60479-2:2019 — effects of current on the body
docs.text: Not implemented. They are the physiological basis of the permissible touch voltages of EN 50522, and the documentation uses IEC 60479-2 for one argument: its frequency factors describe thresholds that rise with frequency, which is why comparing the total RMS earth potential rise with the 50 Hz curve is conservative for the body current. The impedance of the skin falls with frequency (DIN IEC/TS 60479-1:2007-05, 4.2), so for the touch voltage this is not shown (how-to).

docs.title: Model assumptions behind every result
docs.text: The results rest on the model described in Model and assumptions and Verification: a quasi-stationary phasor solve per frequency (transient solvers aside), lumped electrodes without resistive coupling between them, homogeneous soil per element through rho, the coupling of the faulted phase to the earthing conductors as Norton sources, and the formulas the user supplies. An assessment has to check that these assumptions fit the installation.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. EN 50522:2022, Earthing of power installations exceeding 1 kV a.c., and EN 50522:2022/A1:2024; table of contents of the national edition STN EN 50522:2022: https://normy.normoff.gov.sk/norma/134904/nahlad.
  2. IEC 61936-1:2021, Power installations exceeding 1 kV AC and 1,5 kV DC — Part 1: AC, edition 3.0.
  3. IEC 60909-0:2016, Short-circuit currents in three-phase a.c. systems — Part 0: Calculation of currents.
  4. IEC 60949:1988 + A1:2008, Calculation of thermally permissible short-circuit currents, taking into account non-adiabatic heating effects.
  5. IEC 60479-1:2018, Effects of current on human beings and livestock — Part 1: General aspects.
  6. IEC 60479-2:2019, Effects of current on human beings and livestock — Part 2: Special aspects.
  7. DIN IEC/TS 60479-1 (VDE V 0140-479-1):2007-05, Effects of current on human beings and livestock — Part 1: General aspects (IEC/TS 60479-1:2005
  8. Corrigendum October 2006).

docs.title: Model and assumptions
docs.text: This page explains the physical and numerical model that groundinsight implements. It is aimed at readers who want to understand why the code returns the numbers it returns — for example to validate results against measurements or analytical expressions. The pages next to it go deeper into single parts of the model: impedance formulas, phase currents in rings and meshes, reduction factors and the earthing impedance, splitting the network and the location response and direct current.

docs.title: Problem statement
docs.text:
Consider a power grid composed of substations (buses) and the cables and overhead lines (branches) that connect them. Each bus possesses a grounding grid tying it to remote earth; each branch carries a grounding conductor (cable shield, overhead-line earth wire) that is bonded to the grids of its two terminals. A single-phase-to-ground fault at one bus drives a fault current back towards the source. That current splits into two parallel paths:

  • the local earth path through the grounding grid at the fault bus, and
  • the metallic return path through the grounding conductor(s) of the connecting branches.

The split depends on the impedances of both paths and on the mutual coupling between the faulted phase and the grounding conductor that runs alongside it. The resulting EPR, the reduction factor and the grounding impedance are the quantities of interest.

docs.title: Objects
docs.text:
groundinsight represents the grid with four Pydantic models:

  • Bus — a node. Carries a grounding impedance \(Z_{\text{B}}(\rho_E, f)\) that couples the bus to remote earth.
  • Branch — an edge between two buses with a self impedance \(Z_{\text{self}}(\rho_E, f, l)\) (series impedance of the grounding conductor) and a mutual impedance \(Z_{\text{mutual}}(\rho_E, f, l)\) (coupling between faulted phase and grounding conductor).
  • Source — a current source anchored at a bus. Holds a dictionary that maps each frequency to the injected phasor current.
  • Fault — a marker at a bus. Holds an optional dictionary of frequency-dependent scaling factors applied to the source currents; a frequency without an entry is scaled with 1.0.

Bus and branch properties are derived from reusable types (BusType, BranchType) whose impedances are parameterised by formula strings. The formulas are parsed with SymPy, turned into lambdify callables and evaluated for every network frequency — see Impedance formulas and where they come from.

docs.title: Nodal-admittance formulation
docs.text:
All computations take place per frequency \(f\) in the phasor domain. groundinsight assembles an admittance matrix \(Y(f)\) of size \(N\times N\) (where \(N\) is the number of buses):

\[ Y_{ii} = \frac{1}{Z_{\text{B},i}(\rho_E, f)} + \sum_{k \in \mathcal{E}(i)} \frac{1}{Z_{\text{self},k}(\rho_E, f, l_k)}, \qquad Y_{ij} = -\frac{1}{Z_{\text{self},k}(\rho_E, f, l_k)} \quad (k \text{ connects } i,j). \]

Each entry can be switched off by setting grounding_conductor=False on the corresponding branch, which is useful for modelling insulated shields.

The right-hand-side vector \(\underline{i}(f)\) holds the source injections scaled by the active fault's frequency scaling and — crucially — the mutual-coupling contributions. For every branch that carries phase current a Norton equivalent is added: the phase current \(I_{\text{phase}}\) driving the branch induces a shield current of magnitude \(I_{\text{mut}} = I_{\text{phase}}\,Z_{\text{mutual}}/Z_{\text{self}}\), injected as \(-I_{\text{mut}}\) at the from bus and \(+I_{\text{mut}}\) at the to bus. The phase currents come from a solve on the phase-conductor network, which divides the source current between the routes of a ring or a mesh — see Phase currents in rings and meshes.

The EPR vector is then

\[ \underline{u}(f) = Y(f)^{-1}\,\underline{i}(f). \]

Numerically the system is solved with SciPy's sparse LU decomposition (scipy.sparse.csc_matrix + splu) — this scales well to meshed low-voltage networks with thousands of buses. The path enumeration of the legacy phase-current mode does not; see Path finding and the legacy mode.

The source current enters the earthing network at the source bus and leaves it at the fault bus. That is the reverse of the physical fault current, which flows from the source through the phase conductor to the fault and returns through soil and shields, so the potentials and electrode currents come out with the opposite sign of their physical values; magnitudes, RMS values, reduction factors and impedances are not affected. Conventions and units gives the two frames with a worked two-bus example.

docs.title: Derived quantities
docs.text: Once \(\underline{u}(f)\) is known for every frequency, three result families are computed: the earth potential rise and the branch currents (below), and the reduction factors and the grounding impedance (Reduction factors and earthing impedance).

docs.title: Earth potential rise (EPR)
docs.text:
The per-frequency bus voltages are stored as ComplexNumber entries on ResultBus objects. RMS values across all frequencies are computed via

\[ U_{\text{RMS},i} = \sqrt{\sum_{f} |u_i(f)|^2}. \]

docs.title: Branch currents
docs.text:
For every branch and frequency the current through the grounding conductor is

\[ I_{\text{branch}}(f) = \frac{u_{\text{to}}(f) - u_{\text{from}}(f)} {Z_{\text{self}}(f)} + I_{\text{mut}}(f), \]

where the second term accounts for the Norton source representing the mutual coupling (compute_branch_currents).

Mind the frame: the potentials \(u\) in the numerator are the earth-side potentials of the solve, the negatives of the physical ones, so \(u_{\text{to}} - u_{\text{from}}\) is the physical \(u_{\text{from}} - u_{\text{to}}\). ResultBranch.i_s is therefore the physical shield current, counted positive from from_bus to to_bus — the same direction as the phase current. In the earth-side frame the same number reads as a current from to_bus towards from_bus. A shield that carries the return current of a phase current flowing from from_bus to to_bus shows a negative i_s; Conventions and units works this through on a line.

docs.title: Active flag and outage studies
docs.text:
Both Bus and Branch carry a boolean active field (default True). The flag has a clean physical interpretation:

  • An inactive Bus is removed from the nodal system entirely. Its row and column drop from \(Y(f)\) and the bus contributes nothing to the right-hand-side vector \(\underline{i}(f)\).
  • An inactive Branch behaves as an open circuit: no contribution to the admittance matrix, no Norton-equivalent injection from the mutual coupling, and a zero current in the result.

The phase-conductor network leaves inactive elements out in the same way, and so does PathFinder when it enumerates source-to-fault paths for the legacy mode, so the per-path Norton bookkeeping stays consistent. The flag is round-tripped through SQLite and JSON; existing payloads load with active=True for every element, which keeps backwards compatibility intact.

That makes maintenance scenarios, planned outages, broken shields and N-1 contingencies expressible without rebuilding the network. The groundinsight.simulation.outage sub-package wraps this into two convenience entry points:

  • outage_context(network, outage) — context manager that flips the listed elements to active=False for the duration of a with block and restores the previous state (including the cached path list) afterwards.
  • run_outage_study(network, fault, scenarios=[...]) — executes the base case plus one fault calculation per Outage scenario and returns an OutageStudyResult whose compare_buses(...) / compare_branches(...) accessors yield long-format Polars DataFrames with absolute and relative deltas against a chosen reference scenario.

docs.title: Inverse rho analysis
docs.text:
The forward solve answers "given \(\rho_E\), what is the EPR?" The sister inverse question — "how large can \(\rho_E\) become before the EPR at the fault bus exceeds a limit \(u_{\text{limit}}\)?" — is answered by groundinsight.analysis.find_max_rho_scaling. It log-bisects a uniform scaling factor \(c\) of Bus.specific_earth_resistance on a user-selected bus set, re-evaluates each BusType.impedance_formula through the existing SymPy machinery and triggers run_fault at every trial value. The output is the largest verified admissible \(c\) — a factor for which \(|U_\text{EPR}(f)|_{\text{RMS}} \le u_{\text{limit}}\) was actually measured — together with the EPR at that point and the per-bus \(\rho_{\max} = c\,\rho_0\). The original \(\rho\) values are restored via a finally block, so the network is unchanged after the call. A frequency-dependent variant (find_max_rho_f_scaling) extends the same idea to two-parameter rho-f curves.

The limit is an earth potential rise, not a touch voltage: the EPR is an upper bound of the touch voltage, and how a permissible touch voltage turns into a limit for the EPR is the subject of Compare results with EN 50522 limits.

"Verified admissible" and "maximal" are not the same claim, and the result distinguishes them. A bisection can also end because the entire bracket was admissible (the true maximum lies above c_bounds[1] and was never determined) or because the iteration cap was reached before the bracket closed. In both cases the returned \(c\) is still a factor that satisfies the limit — it is simply not the largest one. The status and converged keys carry that distinction, and c_bracket gives the interval that provably contains the true threshold; an infinite upper bound is the machine-readable form of "widen c_bounds". Only a converged result is a maximum in the sense the question asks for.

The scaling acts on the soil resistivity of the selected buses only. A branch whose formulas contain rho — Carson's earth-return term, for instance — keeps its own Branch.specific_earth_resistance. For a Carson formula that matters: its reactance grows by \(\omega \cdot 2\cdot10^{-4} \ln\sqrt{10} = 0.072\ \Omega/\text{km}\) per decade of \(\rho\) at 50 Hz, about 11 % of the screen-loop reactance of the cable in Bus and branch types from data sheets.

docs.title: Transient simulations
docs.text: The phasor-domain pipeline above answers the stationary question. For non-sinusoidal fault currents (fault inception, DC offset asymmetry, clearing, switching transients) the groundinsight.simulation.transient sub-module adds a time-domain layer on top of the same network model. Two solver paths are available: an FFT-based path that re-uses the existing impedance_formula of BusType and BranchType per FFT bin, and a state-space ODE path that consumes the lumped RLC fields (R_formula, L_formula, C_formula, R_self_formula, L_self_formula, C_self_formula, R_mutual_formula, M_mutual_formula) and integrates with scipy.signal.lsim. Source waveforms come from the groundinsight.simulation.waveforms library (step, sinusoidal_with_dc_offset, damped_oscillation) or from any user-supplied vectorised callable f(t) -> values. See Transient simulation for the derivations and the transient-simulations reference for the full API.

docs.title: Assumptions and limits of the model
docs.text:
Every result rests on the following assumptions. An assessment has to check that they fit the installation; Verification and validation lists what has been checked against what.

  1. Quasi-stationary phasors. One linear solve per frequency with lumped elements: no travelling waves, no soil ionisation, no frequency dependence other than what the formulas contain. The transient solvers drop the phasor assumption, not the lumped one.
  2. Lumped electrodes in homogeneous soil. Every bus is one impedance to remote earth; neighbouring electrodes do not couple resistively; the soil is one rho per bus and per branch. The model gives earth potential rises, not touch or step voltages and not the potential on the surface.
  3. One-way coupling. The phase currents are determined first, on the phase-conductor network, and then drive the shields; the shields do not act back on the split. That is exact when the ratio \(k = Z_m/Z_s\) is the same on every branch of each mesh of the phase network, and an approximation otherwise — see When the split is exact.
  4. One phase conductor. The phase network contains the faulted conductor only. In a ring the healthy phases form closed loops of their own, and the currents the fault induces in them are not modelled. The size of that effect has not been quantified.
  5. Current sources for the stationary solve. A Thévenin source (create_voltage_source) couples to the shields with \(E/Z_\text{src}\) instead of its actual loop current; where branches with mutual coupling carry its phase current, run_fault warns (ModelAssumptionWarning, code THEVENIN_COUPLING), and the EPR at the fault can come out too low. Model the infeed as a current source carrying the prospective fault current for stationary studies.
  6. A source on the fault bus counts as fault current. The current-based reduction factor divides by the sum of all sources that feed the fault, including one that sits on the fault bus itself, whose current never reaches the earthing network. With 1000 A from a remote infeed and 500 A from a source on the fault bus, value_current is two thirds of its value without the local source, while the earth current \(I_E\) is the same. For the reduction factor of the line, divide i_earth by the remote infeed yourself; see Reduction factors.
  7. Bus ρ only in the inverse analysis. find_max_rho_scaling and find_max_rho_f_scaling scale the soil resistivity of buses; branch formulas keep theirs (see Inverse rho analysis).
  8. Signs in the earth-side frame. Potentials and electrode currents are reported as the negatives of their physical values (Conventions and units).
  9. The formulas are the user's. The package checks a formula's syntax, its symbols and that the impedance it gives is passive, not whether it describes the conductor it is attached to (Impedance formulas).

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The full physical model behind the equations above maps onto the Python API in a single block:

Illustrative values

The formulas below are round numbers chosen to make the example short, not the data of a real cable or electrode. Bus and branch types from data sheets derives them for a real cable.

import groundinsight as gi

net = gi.create_network(name="demo", frequencies=[50.0, 250.0])

bus_type = gi.BusType(
    name="SubstationBus", system_type="Substation",
    voltage_level=20.0,
    impedance_formula="rho * 0.01 + j * f * 1/50 * 0.1",
)
cable_type = gi.BranchType(
    name="MSCable", grounding_conductor=True,
    self_impedance_formula="(0.25 + j * f * 0.012) * l",
    mutual_impedance_formula="(0.0  + j * f * 0.012) * l",
)

gi.create_bus(name="b0", type=bus_type, network=net)
gi.create_bus(name="b1", type=bus_type, network=net)
gi.create_branch(name="ln", type=cable_type,
                 from_bus="b0", to_bus="b1", length=5.0, network=net)
gi.create_source(name="src", bus="b0",
                 values={50.0: 1000.0, 250.0: 200.0}, network=net)
gi.create_fault(name="F1", bus="b1",
                scalings={50.0: 1.0, 250.0: 1.0}, network=net)

gi.run_fault(network=net, fault="F1")
print(net.res_all_impedances())   # Z_E and both reduction factors per frequency

The Network API hides every step listed in the next section behind run_fault; the results are exposed as Polars DataFrames via net.res_buses(fault="F1"), net.res_branches(fault="F1") and net.res_all_impedances().

docs.title: Summary of the calculation pipeline
docs.text:
run_fault(network, fault) executes the following steps (see network_operations.run_fault and ElectricalNetwork for details):

  1. set_active_fault — select the target fault.
  2. Find the sources that reach the fault through the active network — a breadth-first search; paths are enumerated only in the legacy phase_current_mode="paths".
  3. build_electrical_network — create an ElectricalNetwork helper that holds the numerical arrays: \(Y(f)\), and \(\underline{i}(f)\) with the source injections and the Norton injections of the coupling. The phase currents behind the latter come from a solve on the phase-conductor network per source and frequency. The input checks of run_fault (source values per frequency, fault scalings) run here.
  4. solve_network — solve the linear system per frequency (sparse LU).
  5. compute_branch_currents — derive branch currents from \(\Delta u\) plus Norton contributions.
  6. compute_reduction_factors — re-solve without mutual Norton sources and take the EPR ratio at the fault bus (value); sum the electrode currents of the earth group for the current-based factor (value_current); record \(U_E\), \(Z_E\) and \(I_E\).
  7. compute_grounding_impedance — the driving-point impedance of the earthing network at the fault bus, per frequency.

The persistent state of the calculation (sparse matrices, vectors) lives on a private ElectricalNetwork attribute of the Network instance, so re-solving after topology changes only requires a fresh run_fault call. Conditions found on the way that change how a result must be read are collected in Result.diagnostics.

docs.title: Verification and validation
docs.text:
Two different questions decide whether a result can be trusted:

  • Verification — does the code solve its model correctly? This page lists the evidence the package carries for that.
  • Validation — does the model describe a real installation? That needs comparisons with measurements or with other programs, and for those the answer is plain: groundinsight is not yet validated against field measurements or other programs.

docs.title: Closed-form reference cases
docs.text:
gi.run_reference_cases() runs six configurations whose answer is known in closed form through the ordinary public API and compares. Each case names the boundary conditions under which its closed form holds, and its docstring derives the closed form, so it can be checked line by line against the literature (see Reference cases). A deviation beyond the tolerance means that either the model is wrong or a condition was not met.

The table below is produced when this site is built, from the cases in REFERENCE_CASES and one run of gi.run_reference_cases():

case quantity condition closed form model rel. deviation tolerance agrees line_ideal_bonding reduction factor r [-] single line, station electrodes negligible against the shield impedance 0.5 0.499999 2.0e-06 1e-03 yes line_finite_earthing reduction factor r [-] single line, both ends earthed with a finite electrode 0.005562082816 0.005562082816 7.8e-16 1e-09 yes en50522_chain earth-return current I_E [A] six-station chain, I_E re-derived from an independently assembled nodal system 32.38457029 32.38457029 6.6e-16 1e-09 yes ladder_input_impedance input impedance Z_in [Ohm] chain long enough to be semi-infinite (80 sections here) 1.403195874 1.403195879 3.1e-09 1e-06 yes ladder_potential_decay potential ratio u_20/u_0 [-] same chain, far enough from either end 0.07852933524 0.07852931427 2.7e-07 1e-06 yes parallel_decomposition driving-point impedance [Ohm] cuts covering every branch at the station 1.724271703 1.724271703 1.2e-15 1e-12 yes

Generated when this site was built, with groundinsight 0.6.0.

The same call is a quick self-test of an installation (about 0.2 s):

import groundinsight as gi

table = gi.run_reference_cases()
print(table.select("case", "rel_deviation", "tolerance", "agrees"))
assert table["agrees"].all()

docs.title: An independent solver in the test suite
docs.text:
The test suite carries a second solver for the stationary model, tests/_reference_mna.py, written from the model description rather than from the package code: modified nodal analysis with the branch currents as unknowns, in the physical sign frame (the package eliminates the shield currents and uses the reversed earth-side frame, see Conventions). Against it, run_fault is checked to 1e-12 on 17 structural networks — chains, rings, meshes, parallel cables, mixed construction, open ends, two sources, a source on the fault bus, 0/50/150/250 Hz, inactive elements.

On seeded random meshes the suite checks properties that any correct solution of the model must have, independent of a second implementation:

  • Kirchhoff's current law at every bus and over the whole network;
  • reciprocity without coupling: the voltage at one pair of buses per ampere injected at another pair equals the reverse;
  • passivity and Tellegen's theorem without coupling: the real power the sources inject is positive and equals the losses in electrodes and shields.

On a long homogeneous cable run (64 sections) the fault-bus earth potential rise and the earthing impedance meet the closed forms of the ladder network, \(\lvert u_F\rvert = \lvert 1 - k\rvert\, I\,\lvert Z_\infty\rvert\) and \(Z_\infty = -Z'/2 + \sqrt{Z'^2/4 + Z_e Z'}\), to 1e-5.

docs.title: Transient solvers
docs.text: The FFT solver evaluates the stationary formulas per frequency bin, the state-space solver integrates lumped R/L/C fields in time; the two are cross-checked with each other and with the stationary solve in steady state. A second transient solver in the test suite, tests/_transient_reference.py (all branch currents as states, trapezoidal integration), checks the dynamics of the state-space solver, including the phase-current split in a ring. The FFT solver does not evaluate the inductive coupling of the branches and warns when that matters (Transient simulation).

docs.title: The examples in this documentation
docs.text: The worked examples of the how-to pages are scripts in docs/snippets/ that the test suite runs. The cable example of Bus and branch types from data sheets is computed three ways — closed form, Pollaczek's integral, run_fault — and the EN 50522 example is checked against an independent nodal solve.

docs.title: What is not validated
docs.text:
No comparison with measured earthing impedances, earth potential rises or shield currents, and no comparison with another earthing program, is part of the package or its documentation. The model assumptions that such a comparison would test — and that bound what to expect from it — are:

  • the coupling acts one way: the phase current is split first, then drives the shields; this is exact when all routes of a mesh have the same construction and an approximation otherwise (Phase currents);
  • only the faulted phase conductor is modelled, not the healthy phases;
  • electrodes are lumped impedances to remote earth, without resistive coupling between neighbouring electrodes;
  • the soil is homogeneous per element (one rho per bus and per branch);
  • the stationary solve is quasi-stationary: no travelling waves, no soil ionisation;
  • the impedances are the formulas the user supplies; the package checks their syntax and passivity, not their physics.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Reference cases: groundinsight.analysis.reference.
  • Test oracles: tests/_reference_mna.py, tests/_transient_reference.py; physics regressions tests/test_audit_pass19_physics.py, tests/test_audit_pass19_transient.py in the repository.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
Three pages take you from an empty Python environment to a solved ring. Each states the numbers you should get, computes them a second way by hand, and the test suite checks both on every change.

  1. Installation — a virtual environment, the package, Jupyter or VS Code, and a self-test that takes a second.
  2. Your first fault calculation — two stations and a cable at 50 Hz: earth potential rise, earthing impedance, both reduction factors.
  3. From a line to a ring — the same cable as a ring: how the fault current divides, the phase impedance, a harmonic.

docs.title: Your first fault calculation
docs.text: This tutorial builds the smallest network that shows what groundinsight is for, solves it, and then computes every number it prints a second time, by hand. It takes about fifteen minutes; you need an installation and a notebook or a Python file.

docs.title: What you will build
docs.text:
Two substations, joined by a 5 km medium-voltage cable whose shield is earthed at both ends. An earth fault at bus_fault draws 1000 A from the infeed at bus_source:

   1000 A infeed                                         earth fault
    bus_source ============ cable_1, 5 km ============ bus_fault
        |            phase conductor + shield              |
       Z_B                                                Z_B
        |                                                  |
      remote earth  - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -  remote earth

The fault current flows from the infeed through the phase conductor to the fault and has two ways back: through the cable shield, and through the soil — into the earth at bus_fault, out again at bus_source. The phase current induces a voltage along the shield, which pulls most of the return current into the shield. The questions are the ones of every earthing study: how much of the fault current flows through the soil, and to what potential the earthing system at the fault rises against remote earth (its earth potential rise, EPR).

Lengths are in km, soil resistivity in Ω·m, currents are RMS values in A, and impedances are in Ω (Conventions and units).

docs.title: Step 1 — A network at 50 Hz
docs.text:
Everything lives in a Network, which fixes the frequencies to solve. One frequency is enough for the first calculation:

import groundinsight as gi

net = gi.create_network(name="first_calculation", frequencies=[50.0])

docs.title: Step 2 — Types
docs.text:
A type describes a kind of station or cable once; buses and branches refer to it. Its impedances are formulas in the frequency f, the soil resistivity rho and, for a cable, the length l:

station = gi.BusType(
    name="SubstationBus",
    system_type="Substation",
    voltage_level=20.0,
    impedance_formula="rho * 0.01 + j * f * 1/50 * 0.1",  # Z_B, Ohm
)
cable = gi.BranchType(
    name="MSCable",
    grounding_conductor=True,
    self_impedance_formula="(0.25 + j * f * 0.012) * l",   # Z_s: shield-earth loop
    mutual_impedance_formula="(0.0 + j * f * 0.012) * l",  # Z_m: phase-shield coupling
)
  • impedance_formula is the electrode of a station against remote earth, \(Z_B\). With \(\rho\) = 100 Ω·m at 50 Hz it is \(Z_B = 1 + 0.1j\ \Omega\).
  • self_impedance_formula is the loop formed by the shield and the earth return, \(Z_s = 0.25 + 0.6j\ \Omega\)/km at 50 Hz.
  • mutual_impedance_formula is the coupling between the phase conductor and that loop, \(Z_m = 0.6j\ \Omega\)/km at 50 Hz.

Illustrative values

These formulas are round numbers that keep the tutorial short, not the data of a real cable or electrode. Bus and branch types from data sheets derives them for a real 20 kV cable; Formula syntax lists what a formula may contain.

docs.title: Step 3 — Buses and the cable
docs.text:
gi.create_bus(name="bus_source", type=station, specific_earth_resistance=100.0,
              network=net)
gi.create_bus(name="bus_fault", type=station, specific_earth_resistance=100.0,
              network=net)
gi.create_branch(name="cable_1", type=cable, from_bus="bus_source",
                 to_bus="bus_fault", length=5.0, network=net)

Each element evaluates the formulas of its type with its own rho and length as soon as it joins the network.

docs.title: Step 4 — The source and the fault
docs.text:
gi.create_source(name="substation_infeed", bus="bus_source",
                 values={50.0: 1000.0}, network=net)          # A, RMS
gi.create_fault(name="fault_at_remote_bus", bus="bus_fault", network=net)

values holds the source current per frequency as an RMS phasor. A fault can scale the sources per frequency with scalings; without it, every frequency counts in full (Conventions and units).

docs.title: Step 5 — Solve
docs.text:
result = gi.run_fault(net, fault="fault_at_remote_bus")
print("diagnostics:", result.diagnostics)

diagnostics: []

run_fault solves the network for the fault and returns a Result; the network keeps it under net.results["fault_at_remote_bus"] as well. When the solver has to make an assumption that changes how a result must be read, it says so with a Python warning and keeps the same message, with a code and the elements it is about, in result.diagnostics. For this network there is nothing to say. The next tutorial shows one.

docs.title: Step 6 — Read the results
docs.text:
net.res_fault(...) returns the key figures of the fault as a Polars DataFrame, one row per frequency and one RMS row; net.res_buses(...) and net.res_branches(...) give the potential and the currents of every bus and branch:

key = net.res_fault("fault_at_remote_bus").row(0, named=True)  # the 50 Hz row
print(f"U_E  = {key['U_E_V']:.2f} V        EPR at the fault bus")
print(f"Z_E  = {key['Z_E_Ohm']:.4f} Ohm at {key['Z_E_degree']:.2f} deg")
print(f"I_E  = {key['I_E_A']:.2f} A        earth current")
print(f"r    = {key['r_current']:.6f}       reduction factor, EN 50522")
print(f"EPR ratio = {key['r_epr']:.6f}  reduction factor of the cable")

for row in net.res_buses(fault="fault_at_remote_bus").iter_rows(named=True):
    if not row["is_rms"]:
        print(f"{row['bus_name']:<10} EPR {row['EPR_V']:.2f} V at {row['EPR_degree']:7.2f} deg,"
              f" electrode {row['I_bus_A']:.2f} A at {row['I_bus_degree']:7.2f} deg")
shield = net.res_branches(fault="fault_at_remote_bus").row(0, named=True)
print(f"cable_1    shield {shield['I_branch_A']:.2f} A at {shield['I_branch_degree']:.2f} deg")

Expected output:

U_E  = 275.43 V        EPR at the fault bus
Z_E  = 0.8440 Ohm at 15.18 deg
I_E  = 274.06 A        earth current
r    = 0.274064       reduction factor, EN 50522
EPR ratio = 0.384615  reduction factor of the cable
bus_source EPR 275.43 V at  -38.85 deg, electrode 274.06 A at  -44.56 deg
bus_fault  EPR 275.43 V at  141.15 deg, electrode 274.06 A at  135.44 deg
cable_1    shield 827.37 A at -166.56 deg
  • \(U_E\) = 275.43 V is the EPR of the station at the fault.
  • \(Z_E\) is the earthing impedance at the fault: the impedance one would measure there against remote earth with everything bonded to the station — its own electrode and, through the cable shield, the electrode at bus_source.
  • \(I_E\) = 274.06 A of the 1000 A return through the soil; the shield carries 827.37 A. The two do not add up to 1000 A because they are phasors with different angles.
  • Two reduction factors describe the split. r = \(|I_E|/|3I_0|\) is the reduction factor of EN 50522, the share of the fault current that returns through the soil. The EPR ratio compares the EPR at the fault with and without the coupling between phase conductor and shield; for one cable it is the tabulated reduction factor of the cable, \(|1 - Z_m/Z_s|\), whatever the electrodes. Reduction factors and earthing impedance explains why there are two.

The angles are relative to the source current. The potentials and electrode currents are reported for a current that enters the earthing system at the infeed and leaves it at the fault — the reverse of the physical direction — so add 180° for the physical angle; the shield current is the physical one, counted from from_bus to to_bus (Signs and phase angles). Both stations rise to the same EPR here because their electrodes are equal; their electrode currents are equal and opposite — whatever enters the soil at one station leaves it at the other.

docs.title: Step 7 — Check it by hand
docs.text:
A single line has closed forms for all of these numbers. Follow the return current around the loop formed by the shield and the earth path: the soil carries \(I_E\) through both electrodes, the shield carries \(I_s = I - I_E\), and the phase current \(I\) induces \(Z_m I\) in the shield. Kirchhoff's voltage law around that loop gives

\[ 2 Z_B\, I_E = Z_s\,(I - I_E) - Z_m\, I \quad\Longrightarrow\quad I_E = I\,\frac{Z_s - Z_m}{Z_s + 2Z_B}, \qquad U_E = Z_B\, I_E . \]

Without the coupling (\(Z_m = 0\)) the same loop gives \(I\,Z_s/(Z_s + 2Z_B)\), so the EPR ratio is \(|Z_s - Z_m|/|Z_s| = |1 - Z_m/Z_s|\). One ampere injected at bus_fault finds its own electrode in parallel with the shield and the other electrode: \(Z_E = Z_B \parallel (Z_s + Z_B)\). With \(Z_B = 1 + 0.1j\ \Omega\), \(Z_s = 1.25 + 3j\ \Omega\) and \(Z_m = 3j\ \Omega\) for the 5 km:

Quantity By hand groundinsight EPR ratio \(1.25 / \lvert 1.25 + 3j\rvert = 1.25/3.25\) = 0.384615 0.384615 r \(1.25 / \lvert 3.25 + 3.2j\rvert = 1.25/4.5610\) = 0.274064 0.274064 \(\lvert U_E\rvert\) \(\lvert 1 + 0.1j\rvert \cdot 274.06\) A = 275.43 V 275.43 V \(Z_E\) \((1+0.1j)(2.25+3.1j)/(3.25+3.2j)\) = 0.8146 + 0.2210j Ω, |ZE| = 0.8440 Ω 0.8440 Ω at 15.18°

The same in code:

z_b = 1.0 + 0.1j                     # electrode, rho = 100 Ohm m, 50 Hz
z_s = (0.25 + 0.6j) * 5.0            # shield-earth loop of 5 km
z_m = 0.6j * 5.0                     # coupling over 5 km
current = 1000.0

ratio = abs(1 - z_m / z_s)                         # EPR ratio
i_earth = current * (z_s - z_m) / (z_s + 2 * z_b)  # current through the soil
u_e = z_b * i_earth                                # EPR at the fault bus
z_e = z_b * (z_s + z_b) / (z_b + z_s + z_b)        # Z_B parallel to (Z_s + Z_B)

print(f"by hand: EPR ratio = {ratio:.6f}, r = {abs(i_earth) / current:.6f}, "
      f"U_E = {abs(u_e):.2f} V, |Z_E| = {abs(z_e):.4f} Ohm")

by hand: EPR ratio = 0.384615, r = 0.274064, U_E = 275.43 V, |Z_E| = 0.8440 Ohm

EN 50522 writes the EPR as the chain \(U_E = r \cdot 3I_0 \cdot Z_E\). On this short line it does not close: \(0.274064 \cdot 1000\ \text{A} \cdot 0.8440\ \Omega\) = 231.3 V, and with the cable's 0.384615 it is 324.6 V, against the 275.43 V both ways of computing gave above. The chain is the standard's picture of a fault far down a long bonded run, where it does hold; on a single line the electrode of the infeed station sits in the return path. Make that electrode ideal and the chain closes exactly with the cable's factor, \(U_E = |1 - Z_m/Z_s|\, I\, |Z_E|\). Reduction factors and earthing impedance shows the long run.

docs.title: Step 8 — Plot and save
docs.text:
figure = gi.plot_bus_voltages(result=result, title="EPR, first calculation")
gi.save_network_to_json(net, "first_calculation.json")
same_network = gi.load_network_from_json("first_calculation.json")
print(sorted(same_network.buses))

plot_bus_voltages draws the EPR of every bus and returns the Matplotlib figure; save_network_to_json writes the network — types, elements, sources and faults — to a project file that load_network_from_json reads back.
