docs.title: Installation
docs.text: groundinsight requires Python 3.12 or newer and runs on Linux, macOS and Windows. It is pure Python; every dependency ships prebuilt wheels, so no compiler is needed. The steps below take you from an empty folder to an installation that has checked itself.

docs.title: Create a virtual environment
docs.text:
A virtual environment keeps the packages of one project apart from those of the system and of other projects. Create one in your project folder and activate it:

Linux and macOSWindows (PowerShell)Windows (cmd) 
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

py -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

py -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate.bat

python --version inside the activated environment has to show 3.12 or newer.

docs.title: Install from PyPI
docs.text:
pipuvPoetry 
pip install groundinsight

uv add groundinsight

poetry add groundinsight

This pulls in the runtime dependencies: pydantic, numpy, scipy, sympy, sqlalchemy, polars, matplotlib and pillow (the image library matplotlib uses; declared directly so that no release with a known security advisory is installed alongside groundinsight).

docs.title: Optional extras
docs.text:
Runtime-optional features are exposed as extras. They keep the core install lean and let you opt into the heavier dependencies on demand:

Extra Purpose Pulls in pandapower gi.from_pandapower / gi.preview_pandapower_import to import existing distribution-network models, and gi.read_shortcircuit_results for their short-circuit results pandapower 
pip install "groundinsight[pandapower]"

docs.title: Work in Jupyter or VS Code
docs.text:
The examples of this documentation are Jupyter notebooks, and a notebook is the most convenient place for a study. groundinsight does not install a notebook front end; add one to the same environment:

JupyterLabVS Code 
pip install jupyterlab
jupyter lab

Install the Python and Jupyter extensions, open the project folder, open or create a .ipynb file and choose the interpreter of .venv with Select Kernel in the top right corner of the notebook. VS Code asks to install ipykernel into the environment the first time; accept.

docs.title: Verify the installation
docs.text:
gi.run_reference_cases() solves six networks whose answers are known in closed form — a cable line with ideal and with finite earthing, the EN 50522 chain, the input impedance and the potential decay of a long ladder of bonded stations, and the parallel decomposition at a fault — and compares. It takes about a second:

import groundinsight as gi

print("groundinsight", gi.__version__)
table = gi.run_reference_cases()
for case, agrees in table.select("case", "agrees").iter_rows():
    print(f"{case:<24} {'agrees' if agrees else 'DOES NOT AGREE'}")
assert table["agrees"].all(), "a reference case does not agree -- see the table"

Expected output (the version is the one you installed):

groundinsight 0.6.0
line_ideal_bonding       agrees
line_finite_earthing     agrees
en50522_chain            agrees
ladder_input_impedance   agrees
ladder_potential_decay   agrees
parallel_decomposition   agrees

If a case does not agree, the installation computes wrong numbers, and table says by how much (rel_deviation against tolerance). Verification and validation explains what each case checks. For a bug report, gi.show_versions() prints the versions of groundinsight, Python and every dependency.

Continue with Your first fault calculation.

docs.title: Install from source
docs.text:
Clone the repository and install it in editable mode with Poetry:

git clone https://github.com/Ce1ectric/groundinsight.git
cd groundinsight
poetry install

The default poetry install picks up the [tool.poetry.dependencies] group plus the dev group (test tools and notebook kernel). The documentation tools live in the optional docs group and have to be enabled explicitly:

poetry install --with docs

docs.title: Optional dependency groups
docs.text:
The project declares the following Poetry groups:

Group Purpose Includes dev Tests and notebook work pytest, pytest-cov, hypothesis, ipykernel, pandapower, ... docs Build the MkDocs site locally mkdocs, mkdocs-material, mkdocstrings, mkdocs-jupyter, mkdocs-redirects, ...

Install a specific group with:

poetry install --with docs,dev

Contributing describes how to run the tests and build this documentation, and the conventions of the code base.

docs.title: The graphical front end
docs.text: groundinsight-gui is a desktop and browser front end on top of the library: network tables, background runs, the key figures of a fault and the diagnostics, in German and English. It is a separate distribution in the gui/ folder of the repository, released together with the library and with the same version. It is at an early stage (no login, a working skeleton of the screens); see its README in the repository for installing and starting it.

docs.title: From a line to a ring
docs.text: Distribution networks are rarely a single line. In a ring the fault current has two routes to the fault, and how it divides between them decides how much current each cable shield is driven with. This tutorial lays the cable of Your first fault calculation as a ring, shows how groundinsight divides the current, adds a harmonic, and checks the numbers by hand again.

docs.title: What you will build
docs.text:
Four stations on a ring of four 2.5 km sections of the same cable. The infeed sits at bus_source, the fault at bus_fault on the opposite side; each of the two routes is 5 km long, like the line of the first tutorial:

                cable_1, 2.5 km         cable_2, 2.5 km
   bus_source ================= bus_a ================= bus_fault
       ||                                                  ||
       ||       cable_3, 2.5 km         cable_4, 2.5 km    ||
       ++====================== bus_b =====================++

Every station has the electrode of the first tutorial, \(Z_B = 1 + 0.1j\ \Omega\) at 50 Hz.

docs.title: Step 1 — Build the ring
docs.text:
The construction goes into a function, because the ring is built again in later steps:

import groundinsight as gi


def build_ring(frequencies, source_values, phase_impedance_formula=None):
    """The ring of the tutorial, ready to solve."""
    net = gi.create_network(name="ring", frequencies=frequencies)
    station = gi.BusType(
        name="SubstationBus", system_type="Substation", voltage_level=20.0,
        impedance_formula="rho * 0.01 + j * f * 1/50 * 0.1",
    )
    cable = gi.BranchType(
        name="MSCable", grounding_conductor=True,
        self_impedance_formula="(0.25 + j * f * 0.012) * l",
        mutual_impedance_formula="(0.0 + j * f * 0.012) * l",
        phase_impedance_formula=phase_impedance_formula,
    )
    for bus in ("bus_source", "bus_a", "bus_fault", "bus_b"):
        gi.create_bus(name=bus, type=station, specific_earth_resistance=100.0,
                      network=net)
    for name, a, b in (("cable_1", "bus_source", "bus_a"),     # route 1
                       ("cable_2", "bus_a", "bus_fault"),
                       ("cable_3", "bus_source", "bus_b"),     # route 2
                       ("cable_4", "bus_b", "bus_fault")):
        gi.create_branch(name=name, type=cable, from_bus=a, to_bus=b,
                         length=2.5, network=net)
    gi.create_source(name="substation_infeed", bus="bus_source",
                     values=source_values, network=net)
    gi.create_fault(name="fault_at_remote_bus", bus="bus_fault", network=net)
    return net

docs.title: Step 2 — Solve: the current divides
docs.text:
net = build_ring([50.0], {50.0: 1000.0})
with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    result = gi.run_fault(net, fault="fault_at_remote_bus")
for warning in caught:
    print(warning.category.__name__, warning.message.code)
print([d.code for d in result.diagnostics])

ModelAssumptionWarning PHASE_PROXY
['PHASE_PROXY']

In a line every branch between infeed and fault carries the full fault current. In a ring the current divides, and groundinsight finds the split by solving a second network made of the phase conductors alone, with the fault as reference. That network needs the impedance of each phase conductor, which the type does not declare yet. The solver therefore falls back to a proxy — the shield impedance — and says so with a ModelAssumptionWarning, code PHASE_PROXY. Here the proxy happens to be harmless: both routes are the same cable over the same length, so any impedance proportional to length divides the current 500 A : 500 A. In a ring that mixes a cable with an overhead line the proxy is a guess (Phase currents in rings and meshes).

docs.title: Step 3 — Declare the phase impedance
docs.text:
What the split needs is the loop of the faulted phase conductor with earth return, with the shield bonded at both ends: \(Z_\text{red} = Z_{pp} - Z_m^2/Z_s\), where \(Z_{pp}\) is the phase–earth loop on its own. With an illustrative \(Z_{pp} = 0.15 + j\,f\,0.015\ \Omega\)/km the formula reads:

Z_RED = "((0.15 + j*f*0.015) - (j*f*0.012)**2 / (0.25 + j*f*0.012)) * l"

net = build_ring([50.0], {50.0: 1000.0}, phase_impedance_formula=Z_RED)
result = gi.run_fault(net, fault="fault_at_remote_bus")
print([d.code for d in result.diagnostics])

key = net.res_fault("fault_at_remote_bus").row(0, named=True)  # the 50 Hz row
print(f"U_E  = {key['U_E_V']:.2f} V")
print(f"Z_E  = {key['Z_E_Ohm']:.4f} Ohm at {key['Z_E_degree']:.2f} deg")
print(f"I_E  = {key['I_E_A']:.2f} A")
print(f"r    = {key['r_current']:.6f}   EPR ratio = {key['r_epr']:.6f}")

[]
U_E  = 200.84 V
Z_E  = 0.5631 Ohm at 27.11 deg
I_E  = 199.85 A
r    = 0.199847   EPR ratio = 0.384615

The warning is gone, and the numbers are those of Step 2: the symmetric split does not depend on the impedance value. Bus and branch types from data sheets computes \(Z_\text{red}\) for a real cable.

docs.title: Step 4 — Where the current goes
docs.text:
buses = net.res_buses(fault="fault_at_remote_bus")
for row in buses.filter(buses["frequency_Hz"] == 50.0).iter_rows(named=True):
    print(f"{row['bus_name']:<11} EPR {row['EPR_V']:8.2f} V   electrode {row['I_bus_A']:8.2f} A")

bus_source  EPR   200.84 V   electrode   199.85 A
bus_a       EPR     0.00 V   electrode     0.00 A
bus_fault   EPR   200.84 V   electrode   199.85 A
bus_b       EPR     0.00 V   electrode     0.00 A

The two stations half way along the routes stay at zero potential and carry no current: the ring is symmetric about them, and the earth current enters the soil at the fault and leaves it at the infeed only.

docs.title: Step 5 — Check it by hand
docs.text:
The symmetry gives the closed forms. Each route carries \(I/2\); because the ratio \(k = Z_m/Z_s\) is the same on every section, the coupling of the phase current shows up as a current \((1-k)\,I\) that enters the earthing network at the infeed and leaves it at the fault. With bus_a and bus_b at zero potential, the earthing network seen from the fault is its own electrode in parallel with the two half-routes, \(Z_s/2\) for one section of 2.5 km (\(Z_s = 0.625 + 1.5j\ \Omega\), \(Z_m = 1.5j\ \Omega\)):

\[ \lvert U_E\rvert = \lvert 1-k\rvert\, I\, \bigl\lvert Z_B \parallel \tfrac{Z_s}{2} \bigr\rvert, \qquad r = \frac{\lvert I_E\rvert}{I} = \frac{\lvert Z_s - Z_m\rvert/2}{\lvert Z_B + Z_s/2\rvert}, \qquad Z_E = Z_B \parallel \Bigl(\tfrac{Z_s}{2} + \tfrac{Z_B}{2} \parallel \bigl(\tfrac{Z_s}{2} + Z_B\bigr)\Bigr). \]

The last one is one ampere injected at bus_fault: its own electrode in parallel with the two half-routes to the electrodes of bus_a and bus_b (in parallel by symmetry, \(Z_B/2\)), and from there the other two half-routes to the electrode of bus_source.

z_b = 1.0 + 0.1j                 # electrode, rho = 100 Ohm m, 50 Hz
z_s = (0.25 + 0.6j) * 2.5        # shield-earth loop of one 2.5 km section
z_m = 0.6j * 2.5                 # coupling of one section
current = 1000.0


def parallel(a, b):
    """The parallel connection of two impedances."""
    return a * b / (a + b)


# By symmetry each route carries current / 2, and bus_a and bus_b stay at
# zero potential: the earthing network is bus_source and bus_fault joined
# by the two half-routes in parallel (z_s / 2 each), with a Norton current
# (1 - k) * current between them.
k = z_m / z_s
u_e = abs(1 - k) * current * abs(parallel(z_b, z_s / 2))
r = abs(z_s / 2 - z_m / 2) / abs(z_b + z_s / 2)
z_e = parallel(z_b, z_s / 2 + parallel(z_b / 2, z_s / 2 + z_b))
print(f"by hand: U_E = {u_e:.2f} V, r = {r:.6f}, EPR ratio = {abs(1 - k):.6f}, "
      f"Z_E = {abs(z_e):.4f} Ohm at {cmath.phase(z_e) * 180 / cmath.pi:.2f} deg")

by hand: U_E = 200.84 V, r = 0.199847, EPR ratio = 0.384615, Z_E = 0.5631 Ohm at 27.11 deg

Compared with the line of the first tutorial, the second route halves the shield impedance between infeed and fault, so more of the return current takes the shields: r falls from 0.274064 to 0.199847, \(U_E\) from 275.43 V to 200.84 V, and \(Z_E\) from 0.8440 Ω to 0.5631 Ω. The EPR ratio stays at 0.384615 — with the same \(k\) on every branch it is \(|1-k|\) in any topology.

docs.title: Step 6 — Why dividing the current matters
docs.text:
Older versions of groundinsight gave every route the full source current. That mode is still available, so that old studies can be reproduced:

legacy = build_ring([50.0], {50.0: 1000.0}, phase_impedance_formula=Z_RED)
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore", gi.ModelAssumptionWarning)
    gi.run_fault(legacy, fault="fault_at_remote_bus", phase_current_mode="paths")
old = legacy.res_fault("fault_at_remote_bus").row(0, named=True)
print(f"paths mode: U_E = {old['U_E_V']:.2f} V, EPR ratio = {old['r_epr']:.6f}")

paths mode: U_E = 522.19 V, EPR ratio = 1.000000

With 1000 A on both routes the coupling is counted twice, and the earthing network sees \((1-2k)\,I\) instead of \((1-k)\,I\). For this cable \(|1-2k| = |0.625 - 1.5j| / |0.625 + 1.5j| = 1\): the EPR comes out as if the shields did not couple at all, 2.6 times too high. With other cables the same mistake can drive the result towards zero instead. The default, phase_current_mode="auto", divides the current and needs nothing from you (Phase currents in rings and meshes).

docs.title: Step 7 — Add a harmonic
docs.text:
A fault current is rarely a pure 50 Hz sine. Add the frequencies to the network and give the source an RMS value for each; the fault scales every frequency with 1.0 unless scalings says otherwise:

net = build_ring([50.0, 250.0], {50.0: 1000.0, 250.0: 200.0},
                 phase_impedance_formula=Z_RED)
gi.run_fault(net, fault="fault_at_remote_bus")
for row in net.res_fault("fault_at_remote_bus").iter_rows(named=True):
    label = "RMS" if row["is_rms"] else f"{row['frequency_Hz']:.0f} Hz"
    ratios = ("" if row["is_rms"] else
              f"   r = {row['r_current']:.6f}   EPR ratio = {row['r_epr']:.6f}")
    print(f"{label:>6}: I_F = {row['I_F_A']:7.2f} A   U_E = {row['U_E_V']:7.2f} V{ratios}")

 50 Hz: I_F = 1000.00 A   U_E =  200.84 V   r = 0.199847   EPR ratio = 0.384615
250 Hz: I_F =  200.00 A   U_E =   15.71 V   r = 0.070255   EPR ratio = 0.083045
   RMS: I_F = 1019.80 A   U_E =  201.46 V

Every frequency is an independent solve; the 50 Hz row is that of Step 3. At 250 Hz the shield reactance dominates its resistance, the shield takes nearly all of the return current, and the EPR ratio falls to \(0.25/\lvert 0.25 + 3j\rvert = 0.083045\). The RMS row combines the frequencies, \(\sqrt{200.84^2 + 15.71^2}\) = 201.46 V; it has no reduction factors, because a ratio of RMS values is not a property of the network.

docs.title: Step 8 — Which reduction factor to read
docs.text:
Column Field Meaning Use it for r_current (res_fault), reduction_factor_current (res_all_impedances) value_current share of the fault current that returns through the soil, \(\lvert I_E\rvert/\lvert 3I_0\rvert\) the reduction factor r of EN 50522; sensitivity to electrodes and soil r_epr (res_fault), reduction_factor (res_all_impedances) value EPR at the fault with coupling over EPR without comparing cables: for a homogeneous run it is the tabulated \(\lvert 1 - Z_m/Z_s\rvert\), and it does not respond to the electrodes

For a check against the limits of the standard, compare \(U_E\) itself with the permissible value — Compare results with EN 50522 limits describes the procedure.

docs.title: What next
docs.text:
• Tasks after the tutorials — sweeps, outages, imports, thermal checks, transients and more.
  • Phase currents in rings and meshes — when the split is exact, and what a mixed ring of cable and overhead line does.
  • The example notebooks in Examples — a 20-station MV ring, a fault sweep along a feeder, the analysis layer.

docs.title: Diagnostics, logging and warnings
docs.text:
A result can be correct and still need a remark: the phase current of a ring was split with a proxy, a frequency was scaled by default, a reactance had no meaning at 0 Hz. groundinsight delivers such remarks as diagnostics — warnings with a stable code, a severity and the elements they concern — so a script, a GUI or a server can act on them. This guide reads them from a result, checks a network before solving, collects them around other calls, makes them errors in a test run and switches on logging. The script is diagnostics.py; its output is at the end of the page. Every code is listed in Warnings and diagnostics.

Where the remark arises How you get it during a solve Result.diagnostics of the result before a solve gi.check_network around any other call collecting() from groundinsight.diagnostics as a Python warning the warning filters, e.g. to make it an error what the library does logging, switched on with set_log_level

docs.title: Read the diagnostics of a result
docs.text:
gi.run_fault and gi.solve collect every package warning raised during the run into Result.diagnostics, a list of gi.Diagnostic records:

Field Meaning code stable identifier such as PHASE_PROXY — branch on it, never on the message text severity info, warning or error category the warning class, e.g. ModelAssumptionWarning (a modelling assumption) or InputWarning (incomplete input) message the text a person reads elements the elements concerned, as (kind, name) pairs

The records are kept even when the warnings themselves are filtered or shown only once, so a result always carries its complete set; net.res_fault(fault) counts them in n_diagnostics. The records are pydantic models: model_dump() gives a JSON-ready dict.

In the example the cable type declares no phase_impedance_formula, so the phase current of the ring is split with proxy impedances, and the result says which branches that concerns (PHASE_PROXY):

station = gi.BusType(name="station", system_type="Station", voltage_level=20.0,
                     impedance_formula="2.0")
cable = gi.BranchType(name="cable without phase impedance", grounding_conductor=True,
                      self_impedance_formula="(0.2 + j*2*pi*f*1.2e-3)*l",
                      mutual_impedance_formula="(j*2*pi*f*1.0e-3)*l")
ring = gi.create_network(name="ring", frequencies=[50.0])
for name in ("S0", "S1", "S2", "S3"):
    gi.create_bus(name=name, type=station, network=ring)
for name, a, b in (("K1", "S0", "S1"), ("K2", "S1", "S2"), ("K3", "S2", "S3"), ("K4", "S3", "S0")):
    gi.create_branch(name=name, type=cable, from_bus=a, to_bus=b, length=1.0, network=ring)
gi.create_source(name="infeed", bus="S0", values={50.0: 1000.0}, network=ring)
gi.create_fault(name="F", bus="S2", network=ring)

result = gi.run_fault(ring, "F")
for record in result.diagnostics:  # code, severity, category, message, elements
    if record.code == "PHASE_PROXY":
        proxy_branches = sorted(name for kind, name in record.elements if kind == "branch")
payload = json.dumps([record.model_dump() for record in result.diagnostics])  # for a front end

docs.title: Check a network before solving
docs.text:
gi.check_network(net, fault=None) returns every problem of a network at once as gi.Diagnostic records and never raises: error where run_fault would raise or describe another network than the one you built (a branch or source on a bus that does not exist is otherwise dropped without a word), warning where the network solves but part of the input has no effect (ISOLATED_BUS, SOURCE_FREQUENCY_GAP, …). The check neither assembles nor solves, so it is cheap enough to run after every edit. Its topology checks — isolated buses, earthing islands, whether a source reaches the fault — run only on a network whose references are consistent: fix the reference errors first, then check again. In the example the first check finds the unconnected bus (ISOLATED_BUS); after a source on a bus that does not exist is added, the check reports that error (SOURCE_UNKNOWN_BUS, which would make the solver ignore the source) and holds back the topology checks until it is fixed.

gi.create_bus(name="X", type=station, network=ring)                 # no branch to it
first_check = gi.check_network(ring)

ring.sources["ghost"] = gi.Source(name="ghost", bus="nowhere",      # as a hand-edited
                                  values={50.0: 10.0})              # file could carry it
issues = gi.check_network(ring)
blocking = [d.code for d in issues if d.severity == "error"]

docs.title: Collect warnings outside a solve
docs.text:
Creating elements, importing, the thermal checks and the transient solvers raise their warnings directly. Collect them with groundinsight.diagnostics.collecting(): inside the with block every package warning is also recorded as a gi.Diagnostic. The collection belongs to the current thread or asyncio task, so two runs in parallel never mix their records.

with collecting() as records:  # warnings raised outside a solve
    gi.create_source(name="extra", bus="S1", values={50.0: 5.0, 150.0: 1.0}, network=ring)

docs.title: Filter warnings, or make them errors
docs.text:
Diagnostics are ordinary Python warnings of the classes gi.ModelAssumptionWarning, gi.InputWarning, gi.DCLimitWarning, gi.TransientModelWarning and gi.NetworkFrequencyOrderWarning, all subclasses of gi.GroundinsightWarning. The usual tools apply: warnings.simplefilter("ignore", gi.InputWarning) silences a category on the screen (the result still records it), warnings.simplefilter("error", ...) turns it into an exception that carries code and elements, and on the command line python -W error::groundinsight.ModelAssumptionWarning does the same — useful in a test suite that must not accept a heuristic result.

del ring.sources["ghost"]
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("error", gi.ModelAssumptionWarning)  # e.g. in a CI job
    try:
        gi.run_fault(ring, "F")
    except gi.ModelAssumptionWarning as raised:
        strict_code = raised.code

docs.title: Logging is opt-in
docs.text:
The library logs what it does — sessions, migrations, cache use, the summary of a study — to the logger groundinsight, which has a NullHandler, so nothing is printed unless you ask. Anything that qualifies a result is a diagnostic, not a log line. gi.set_log_level("INFO") attaches a console handler (repeated calls do not stack handlers); logging.captureWarnings(True) routes the warnings into logging as well, as text — code and elements stay with the records.

import groundinsight as gi

gi.set_log_level("INFO")      # console output of the "groundinsight" logger
gi.set_log_level("WARNING")   # quieter again

For a bug report, gi.show_versions() returns the versions of groundinsight, Python, the platform and the companion packages.

docs.title: In a GUI or a server
docs.text: The service layer groundinsight.api hands the records to a front end as DiagnosticDTO (code, severity, category, message and element references) in every result DTO and in the report of the pre-flight check, unchanged. A front end branches on code to choose an icon or a help text, highlights the elements in its views and shows message as it is. See Service layer and command line.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Output of diagnostics.py
result: PHASE_PROXY (warning, ModelAssumptionWarning)
proxy split on: ['K1', 'K2', 'K3', 'K4']
as JSON for a front end: 1 record(s)
check: warning ISOLATED_BUS [('bus', 'X')]
check again: error SOURCE_UNKNOWN_BUS [('source', 'ghost'), ('bus', 'nowhere')]
blocking: ['SOURCE_UNKNOWN_BUS']
collected: [('SOURCE_FREQUENCY_OUTSIDE_NETWORK', [('source', 'extra')])]
turned into an error: PHASE_PROXY

PHASE_PROXY names exactly the four branches of the ring; the test suite finds the ring branches from the topology and compares. SOURCE_FREQUENCY_OUTSIDE_NETWORK is raised when the source is created, not by a solve, which is why it has to be collected.

docs.title: Compare results with EN 50522 limits
docs.text:
EN 50522 requires that the touch voltages of an installation stay within permissible values that depend on the fault duration. This page shows which groundinsight result feeds which quantity of that verification, how the procedure runs, and which parts of it the model does not cover. It refers to the clauses of EN 50522:2022 by number and name and does not reproduce the permissible values: take them from the edition you apply.

Scope of the results

groundinsight is a research and engineering tool. Its results support, but do not replace, an assessment according to EN 50522 / IEC 61936-1 by a qualified person, including the measurements the standards require. The software is provided under the MIT License, without warranty of any kind.

docs.title: What the model gives you
docs.text:
Per fault and per frequency, groundinsight computes the fault current, the earth potential rise of every bus, the shield currents, the earth current and the earthing impedance at the fault location, and the reduction factor of EN 50522. It does not compute:

  • touch voltages, step voltages and surface potentials — there is no model of the soil surface;
  • additional resistances such as footwear or a surface layer, which the prospective touch voltage of the standard takes into account (Annex A);
  • the permissible touch voltage itself;
  • potentials transferred to other systems (Clause 6);
  • the dimensioning for corrosion and mechanical strength (5.2); the thermal check of earthing conductors is available separately (check_conductor_limits, check_node_limits, see Analysis).

docs.title: Which result is which symbol
docs.text:
EN 50522 Meaning groundinsight In the tables 3I_0 earth-fault current at the fault location ResultReductionFactor.i_fault — the source currents that reach the fault, times the fault scalings I_F_A of res_fault() r reduction factor ResultReductionFactor.value_current r_current of res_fault(); reduction_factor_current of res_all_impedances() I_E earth current, r·3I_0 ResultReductionFactor.i_earth I_E_A of res_fault() Z_E earthing impedance ResultReductionFactor.z_earthing, equal to ResultGroundingImpedance.value Z_E_Ohm, Z_E_degree of res_fault(); grounding_impedance_Ohm of res_all_impedances() U_E earth potential rise ResultReductionFactor.u_earthing, equal to the uepr_freq of the fault bus U_E_V of res_fault(); EPR_V of the fault bus in res_buses() U_T, U_vT touch voltage, prospective touch voltage not computed – U_Tp permissible touch voltage not part of the package EN 50522:2022, 5.4.1 and Annexes A, B t_F fault duration not used by the solve from the protection
  • value, the column reduction_factor, is not the r of EN 50522. It is the EPR ratio with and without the inductive coupling — a property of the line, blind to the electrodes (conventions).
  • Z_E is the driving-point impedance of the whole earthing network at the fault bus, the stations bonded through screens and earth wires included — what an earthing-impedance measurement at the station sees. It is not the electrode of the station, Z_B (glossary).
  • Complex values are in the package's sign frame (conventions); the verification uses magnitudes.
  • Fault.t_k_s is the short-circuit duration T_k of IEC 60909-0 for the thermal checks. The fault duration t_F of the touch-voltage verification comes from the same protection, but the solve does not use it.

docs.title: The procedure
docs.text:
1. Fault current and fault duration. Get 3I_0 at the fault location — from the network operator, or from a short-circuit calculation after IEC 60909-0 (a pandapower case can be imported, see I/O) — per frequency as RMS values, and the fault duration t_F from the protection settings.
  2. Model. Build the network with branch types from data sheets (how-to) and the electrode impedances Z_B of the stations. Put the fault current at the infeed as Source.values, the fault at the station under study.
  3. Solve and read U_E, Z_E, I_E and r per frequency, and U_E as the total RMS over the frequencies (see Harmonics and DC): net.res_fault(fault) reports all of them in one frame (below).
  4. Permissible touch voltage. Read U_Tp(t_F) from EN 50522:2022, 5.4.1; Annexes A and B derive it and the prospective permissible touch voltage.
  5. Design procedure. Apply the procedure of 5.4.3 (the flow chart of the earthing-system design, Figure 9): it compares U_E with U_Tp, taking the recognised measures M of Annex E into account, and tells you when the touch voltages themselves have to be determined — by measurement (Annex H), or by a calculation of surface potentials, which groundinsight does not do. An installation that is part of a global earthing system follows its own branch of the procedure (Annex N).
  6. Measure. Clause 8 and Annex L describe the measurements of the earthing impedance (L.2), the earth potential rise (L.3) and touch voltages (L.4). Compare them with the model; the model does not replace them.
  7. Document the assessment (Clause 10).

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
A 20 kV feeder: substation UW (0.5 Ω) and five stations with ring electrodes, bonded through the screens of the three-phase cable system of the data-sheet how-to in sections of 1.2 km, ρ = 100 Ω·m. Fault at station S3, with 1000 A at 50 Hz and 50 A at 250 Hz from the infeed (illustrative values).

cable_system = gi.BranchType(
    name="3x NA2XS(F)2Y 1x300RM/25 12/20 kV, trefoil, screens bonded both ends",
    grounding_conductor=True,
    self_impedance_formula=(
        "(0.727/3 + pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.03151272))*l"
    ),
    mutual_impedance_formula=(
        "(pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.03151272))*l"
    ),
    phase_impedance_formula=(
        "((0.1 + pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.00806059))"
        " - (pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.03151272))**2"
        "/(0.727/3 + pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.03151272)))*l"
    ),
)
substation = gi.BusType(
    name="substation", system_type="Substation", voltage_level=20.0,
    impedance_formula="0.5",
)
station = gi.BusType(  # ring earth electrode around 10 m x 10 m
    name="station", system_type="Station", voltage_level=20.0,
    impedance_formula="2*rho/(3*1.13*sqrt(100.0))",
)

FREQUENCIES = [50.0, 250.0]
SOURCE_VALUES = {50.0: 1000.0, 250.0: 50.0}  # A RMS, 3I_0 per frequency
FAULT_BUS = "S3"

net = gi.create_network(name="feeder", frequencies=FREQUENCIES)
names = ["UW", "S1", "S2", "S3", "S4", "S5"]
gi.create_bus(name="UW", type=substation, specific_earth_resistance=100.0, network=net)
for name in names[1:]:
    gi.create_bus(name=name, type=station, specific_earth_resistance=100.0, network=net)
for i, (a, b) in enumerate(zip(names[:-1], names[1:], strict=True), start=1):
    gi.create_branch(
        name=f"K{i}", type=cable_system, from_bus=a, to_bus=b, length=1.2,
        specific_earth_resistance=100.0, network=net,
    )
gi.create_source(name="infeed", bus="UW", values=SOURCE_VALUES, network=net)
gi.create_fault(name="F", bus=FAULT_BUS, scalings={50.0: 1.0, 250.0: 1.0}, network=net)

result = gi.run_fault(net, "F")  # the fault by name (positional)
rf = result.reduction_factor

ROWS = []
for f in FREQUENCIES:
    i_f = abs(complex(rf.i_fault[f].real, rf.i_fault[f].imag))  # 3I_0
    r = rf.value_current[f]  # EN 50522 reduction factor
    i_e = abs(complex(rf.i_earth[f].real, rf.i_earth[f].imag))  # I_E = r * 3I_0
    z_e = abs(complex(rf.z_earthing[f].real, rf.z_earthing[f].imag))  # Z_E
    u_e = abs(complex(rf.u_earthing[f].real, rf.u_earthing[f].imag))  # U_E
    ROWS.append({"f": f, "I_F": i_f, "r": r, "I_E": i_e, "Z_E": z_e, "U_E": u_e,
                 "chain": r * i_f * z_e})

U_E_RMS = math.sqrt(sum(row["U_E"] ** 2 for row in ROWS))  # total RMS over frequencies

U_TP_V = None  # U_Tp(t_F) from EN 50522:2022, 5.4.1 / Annex B, for your fault duration

if U_TP_V is None:
    verdict = "U_Tp not set: read it from EN 50522:2022 for the fault duration t_F"
else:
    verdict = "U_E <= U_Tp" if U_E_RMS <= U_TP_V else "U_E > U_Tp: follow the design procedure"

Output of en50522_check.py:

f 3I0 r IE |ZE| |UE| r·3I0·|ZE| 50 Hz 1000.0 A 0.2165 216.5 A 1.189 Ω 384.4 V 257.3 V 250 Hz 50.0 A 0.0766 3.8 A 2.232 Ω 9.10 V 8.56 V

U_E as total RMS: 384.6 V — the value to compare with U_Tp(t_F).

|U_E| is the earth potential rise of S3 in res_buses(), and |Z_E| is the driving-point impedance an independent nodal solve of the same electrodes and screens gives; the test suite checks both.

docs.title: The key figures in one frame
docs.text:
The script reads the quantities from the result objects to show where each one lives. net.res_fault(fault) puts them side by side in one frame — one row per frequency and an RMS row, read from the stored result without solving again: I_F_A is 3I_0, r_current is r, I_E_A is I_E, Z_E_Ohm (with Z_E_degree) is Z_E and U_E_V is U_E. The column r_epr of the same frame is the EPR-based factor, not the r of EN 50522 (Result tables).

KEY_FIGURES = net.res_fault("F").select(  # one row per frequency and an RMS row
    "frequency_Hz", "is_rms", "I_F_A", "r_current", "I_E_A", "Z_E_Ohm", "U_E_V"
)
Output of en50522_check.py, last lines
res_fault    I_F_A r_current   I_E_A  Z_E_Ohm    U_E_V
    50 Hz   1000.0    0.2165   216.5    1.189   384.45
   250 Hz     50.0    0.0766     3.8    2.232     9.10
      RMS   1001.2         -   216.5        -   384.56

On the RMS row the ratio and the impedance are empty (null); U_E_V there is the total RMS of U_E over the frequencies, the value to compare with U_Tp(t_F). The test suite recomputes every figure of the frame with an independent nodal solver.

The chain \(U_E = r \cdot 3I_0 \cdot Z_E\) of the standard is a hand formula. It holds where the standard's lumped picture holds — a long, homogeneous cable run with the fault far from the infeed — and there the model reproduces it. On this short feeder, with the fault two stations from either end, it gives 257 V at 50 Hz instead of the 384 V the model computes, 33 % low. Compare U_E itself with the permissible value; the difference to the chain shows how far the installation is from the lumped picture.

docs.title: Harmonics and DC
docs.text:
The permissible touch voltages of EN 50522 are given for the power frequency; the standard applies to installations with nominal frequencies up to 60 Hz. For a fault current with harmonics or a DC component, compare the total RMS of U_E over all frequencies — 384.6 V above — with the curve U_Tp(t_F). For the body current this is a conservative choice: IEC 60479-2:2019 describes the effect of a current at a higher frequency by a frequency factor, the ratio of the threshold current at that frequency to the threshold at 50/60 Hz, and the thresholds of perception, let-go and ventricular fibrillation rise with frequency. Counting every component with its full RMS value against the 50/60 Hz curve therefore overstates the effect of the harmonics on the body current. The impedance of the skin, however, falls with frequency (DIN IEC/TS 60479-1 (VDE V 0140-479-1):2007-05, 4.2), which works the other way; whether the total RMS is conservative in terms of the touch voltage as well is not shown here.

A DC component enters the total RMS with its full magnitude. IEC 60479-1:2018 treats the effects of direct current in a clause of its own; for the fault durations of interest its thresholds lie above the 50/60 Hz thresholds, so counting a DC component against the 50/60 Hz curve overstates its effect on the body current as well.

docs.title: EPR is an upper bound of the touch voltage
docs.text: The touch voltage is the part of U_E that a person bridges between a touched part and the point where the feet stand. For a person standing in the potential funnel of the same earthing system, the surface potential there lies between remote earth and U_E, so the touch voltage cannot exceed U_E. A result U_E ≤ U_Tp therefore covers the touch voltage; U_E > U_Tp does not mean that the touch voltage is too high, only that it has to be determined. Potentials transferred from other installations (Clause 6) are outside this bound.

docs.text:
1. EN 50522:2022, Earthing of power installations exceeding 1 kV a.c., with amendment EN 50522:2022/A1:2024 — clause names as listed in the national edition STN EN 50522:2022, https://normy.normoff.gov.sk/norma/134904/nahlad.
  2. IEC 61936-1:2021, Power installations exceeding 1 kV AC and 1,5 kV DC — Part 1: AC, edition 3.0, Clause 10 "Earthing systems".
  3. IEC 60909-0:2016, Short-circuit currents in three-phase a.c. systems — Part 0: Calculation of currents.
  4. IEC 60479-1:2018, Effects of current on human beings and livestock — Part 1: General aspects.
  5. IEC 60479-2:2019, Effects of current on human beings and livestock — Part 2: Special aspects, Clause 3.1 (frequency factor) and Clause 4 (alternating currents above 100 Hz); preview: https://cdn.standards.iteh.ai/samples/102313/18ea5a5451cf4f3bad4023ded332d0be/IEC-60479-2-2019.pdf.
  6. DIN IEC/TS 60479-1 (VDE V 0140-479-1):2007-05, Effects of current on human beings and livestock — Part 1: General aspects (IEC/TS 60479-1:2005
  7. Corrigendum October 2006), 4.2 (impedance of the skin).

docs.title: Harmonics, fault scalings and DC
docs.text: This guide sets up a fault study with several frequencies — the fundamental, harmonics, direct current — and shows what the solver does when the input covers only part of them. It uses one script, harmonics.py; its output is at the end of the page.

docs.title: Frequencies and source values
docs.text:
Network.frequencies lists the frequencies the network is solved at, in Hz, as floats; 0.0 is DC. Every bus and branch evaluates its impedance formulas at each of them, and each frequency is an independent solve of the same nodal system. Keep the list strictly increasing — a shuffled list is kept but announced (FREQUENCY_ORDER), because the FFT transient solver maps bins by position.

Source.values holds the RMS phasor of the source current per frequency, in A: the fundamental and the harmonic content of the earth-fault current at the infeed, from a measurement or a harmonic study. A peak value from a waveform record has to be divided by √2 first (Conventions).

The example: a substation UW (0.5 Ω) feeds an earth fault at station S (ring electrode, 5.90 Ω at ρ = 100 Ω·m) over 3 km of the cable system of the data-sheet how-to, with 1000 A at 50 Hz, 60 A at 250 Hz and 40 A at 350 Hz (illustrative values):

cable_system = gi.BranchType(
    name="3x NA2XS(F)2Y 1x300RM/25 12/20 kV, trefoil",
    grounding_conductor=True,
    self_impedance_formula=(
        "(0.727/3 + pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.03151272))*l"
    ),
    mutual_impedance_formula=(
        "(pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.03151272))*l"
    ),
)
substation = gi.BusType(name="substation", system_type="Substation", voltage_level=20.0,
                        impedance_formula="0.5")
station = gi.BusType(name="station", system_type="Station", voltage_level=20.0,
                     impedance_formula="2*rho/(3*1.13*sqrt(100.0))")  # ring electrode

FREQUENCIES = [50.0, 250.0, 350.0]
SOURCE_VALUES = {50.0: 1000.0, 250.0: 60.0, 350.0: 40.0}  # A, RMS per frequency
LENGTH_KM = 3.0

net = gi.create_network(name="harmonics", frequencies=FREQUENCIES)
gi.create_bus(name="UW", type=substation, specific_earth_resistance=100.0, network=net)
gi.create_bus(name="S", type=station, specific_earth_resistance=100.0, network=net)
gi.create_branch(name="K", type=cable_system, from_bus="UW", to_bus="S", length=LENGTH_KM,
                 specific_earth_resistance=100.0, network=net)
gi.create_source(name="infeed", bus="UW", values=SOURCE_VALUES, network=net)
gi.create_fault(name="F", bus="S", scalings={50.0: 1.0, 250.0: 1.0, 350.0: 1.0}, network=net)

docs.title: Fault scalings
docs.text:
Fault.scalings multiplies the current of every source that reaches the fault, per frequency. The source values describe the infeed; the scalings describe the fault — which share of each frequency this fault draws. The rules:

  • scalings left out, None or {} means 1.0 at every frequency, without a warning.
  • A frequency missing from a non-empty mapping is scaled with 1.0 (full contribution), and the run announces it once (SCALINGS_INCOMPLETE). Write every frequency to make the choice explicit.
  • 0.0 excludes a frequency from this fault: {50.0: 1.0, 250.0: 0.0} solves the fault at 50 Hz alone, whatever the source carries at 250 Hz.
  • Fault.scaling_at(frequency) returns the factor the solve uses.
gi.run_fault(net, "F")
figures = net.res_fault("F")  # one row per frequency and one RMS row

net.faults["F"].scalings = {50.0: 1.0, 250.0: 0.0, 350.0: 0.0}  # this fault: 50 Hz only
gi.run_fault(net, "F")
u_e_rms_fundamental_only = net.res_fault("F").filter("is_rms")["U_E_V"][0]

docs.title: Per-frequency and RMS results
docs.text:
res_fault, res_buses and res_branches have one row per frequency and one RMS row per element, which combines the frequencies as \(\sqrt{\sum_f |X(f)|^2}\) — the 0 Hz term with its full magnitude. The RMS row has is_rms true and frequency_Hz null, and its ratios, impedances and angles are null: a reduction factor has no RMS. Select a frequency with pl.col("frequency_Hz") == 250.0 and the RMS row with pl.col("is_rms"). res_all_impedances has no RMS row; the comparison frames of an outage study write frequency_Hz as text. All columns: Result tables.

For the comparison with the permissible touch voltage of EN 50522, use the total RMS of U_E against the 50 Hz curve. That is conservative for the body current, not shown for the touch voltage; see Compare results with EN 50522 limits.

Check it by hand. For one line between two stations the earth current has a closed form: with the source at UW and the fault at S, \(I_E = I\,(Z_s - Z_m)/(Z_{UW} + Z_S + Z_s)\) and \(U_E = Z_S\,I_E\). At 50 Hz the cable gives \(Z_s - Z_m = 3 \cdot 0.727/3 = 0.727\ \Omega\) (the screens' resistance; the earth-return terms cancel) and \(Z_{UW} + Z_S + Z_s = 7.275 + 1.940j\ \Omega\), so \(I_E = 1000 \cdot 0.727 / 7.529 = 96.56\) A, \(r = 0.0966\) and \(U_E = 5.900 \cdot 96.56 = 569.67\) V — the first row of the output. The test suite recomputes every row this way.

docs.title: When the input does not cover every frequency
docs.text:
Input What the solve does Announced as a non-empty scalings without some network frequencies scales those with 1.0 SCALINGS_INCOMPLETE (InputWarning), once per run a source that reaches the fault, without a value at some network frequencies the source contributes 0 A there SOURCE_FREQUENCY_GAP (InputWarning), once per source and run a source that reaches the fault, without a value at any network frequency refuses: it would contribute 0 A everywhere ValueError naming the source, its keys and the network frequencies a source value at a frequency the network does not solve ignores the value SOURCE_FREQUENCY_OUTSIDE_NETWORK (InputWarning), when the source is created

The first two arrive in Result.diagnostics; the last one is raised by create_source before any solve, so collect it with groundinsight.diagnostics.collecting(). gi.check_network(net) reports all three before a solve. Every code: Warnings and diagnostics.

net.faults["F"].scalings = {50.0: 1.0, 250.0: 1.0}  # 350 Hz missing: scaled with 1.0
missing_scaling = gi.run_fault(net, "F")

net.faults["F"].scalings = None  # 1.0 at every frequency, no warning
net.sources["infeed"].values = {50.0: 1000.0, 250.0: 60.0}  # 350 Hz missing: 0 A there
missing_value = gi.run_fault(net, "F")

net.sources["infeed"].values = {16.7: 1000.0}  # no network frequency at all
try:
    gi.run_fault(net, "F")
except ValueError as refused:
    no_value = str(refused).split(". ")[0]

with collecting() as outside:  # announced when the source is created
    gi.create_source(name="extra", bus="UW", values={50.0: 10.0, 150.0: 5.0}, network=net)

docs.title: Direct current (f = 0)
docs.text:
A DC study is an ordinary solve at f = 0; only the input needs care.

  • Network: frequencies=[0.0], or a mixed list such as [0.0, 50.0] — the 0 Hz bin is independent, and a study with both returns the same 50 Hz answer as one with 50 Hz alone.
  • Current source: a real value at 0.0, e.g. values={0.0: 1000.0}.
  • Voltage source: voltage and source_impedance with a 0.0 entry; the source impedance needs a real part, a purely inductive one is zero at DC.
  • Fault: no 0.0 key needed (1.0 by default); 0.0: 0.0 keeps DC out of a fault. The IEC 60909 characteristics (i_k_a, r_to_x, kappa) describe an alternating current and have no meaning in a DC study.

How a formula is read at 0 Hz. The value is the limit for \(f \to 0\), found by approaching on 1e-6, 1e-7, 1e-8 Hz:

  • a reactance written as j*2*pi*f*L vanishes, and the Carson earth-return terms of a cable tend to their limit (zero for the mutual impedance) — nothing to announce;
  • a constant reactance such as + j*0.2 has no reading at DC: the 0 Hz bin keeps the real part and drops the reactance, with a DC_LIMIT warning (DCLimitWarning) when the element is created;
  • a pole — a series capacitance \(1/(j\omega C)\) — is an open circuit;
  • an exact zero — a purely inductive bond — is an ideal short circuit, which the nodal system cannot invert. The element gets a stand-in of \(\sqrt{\varepsilon_\text{mach}}\,Z_\text{min} = 1.49\cdot10^{-8}\,Z_\text{min}\), where \(Z_\text{min}\) is the smallest other impedance of the network at 0 Hz, and the run says so (DC_LIMIT in Result.diagnostics). Only the 0 Hz bin is affected.
dc = gi.create_network(name="dc_chain", frequencies=[0.0])
for name, z in (("A", "0.8"), ("B", "12.0"), ("C", "3.5")):
    gi.create_bus(name=name, network=dc, type=gi.BusType(
        name=f"electrode {name}", system_type="Station", voltage_level=20.0, impedance_formula=z))
bond = gi.BranchType(name="bond", grounding_conductor=True,  # purely inductive: 0 at DC
                     self_impedance_formula="j*2*pi*f*1e-6*l", mutual_impedance_formula="0")
conductor = gi.BranchType(name="conductor", grounding_conductor=True,
                          self_impedance_formula="0.35*l", mutual_impedance_formula="0")
gi.create_branch(name="AB", type=bond, from_bus="A", to_bus="B", length=1.0, network=dc)
gi.create_branch(name="BC", type=conductor, from_bus="B", to_bus="C", length=1.0, network=dc)
gi.create_source(name="injection", bus="A", values={0.0: 1000.0}, network=dc)  # DC, real
gi.create_fault(name="F", bus="C", network=dc)
dc_result = gi.run_fault(dc, "F")
dc_potentials = {bus.name: bus.uepr_freq[0.0].real for bus in dc_result.buses}
stand_in = next(d for d in dc_result.diagnostics if d.code == "DC_LIMIT")
dc_substitute_ohm = float(stand_in.message.split("modelled with ")[1].split(" Ohm")[0])

Check it by hand. In the chain above (electrodes 0.8 Ω, 12 Ω and 3.5 Ω, bond A–B purely inductive, 0.35 Ω from B to C, 1000 A injected at A, fault at C) the stand-in is \(1.49\cdot10^{-8} \cdot 0.35\ \Omega = 5.2\cdot10^{-9}\ \Omega\). The exact answer merges A and B into one node with \(0.8 \parallel 12 = 0.75\ \Omega\): \(u_{AB}\,(1/0.75 + 1/0.35) - u_C/0.35 = 1000\) and \(u_C\,(1/3.5 + 1/0.35) - u_{AB}/0.35 = -1000\) (the package's earth-side frame) give \(u_A = u_B = 57.07\) V and \(u_C = -266.30\) V — what the solve reports. Prefer the merge when the potential difference across an ideal bond is part of what you report, or give the bond a small honest resistance, which also removes the warning.

What is refused. An impedance that is inverted — an electrode, a conductor with grounding_conductor=True, a source impedance — may not have a negative real part, nor a real part of \(-\infty\) at 0 Hz (a log(f) term without a factor f), nor be NaN; above 0 Hz it may not be zero either. Each raises a ValueError that names the element, the frequency and the formula. +inf (the formula "nan") stays legal everywhere: it is the open end.

with collecting() as constant_reactance:  # '+ j*0.2' does not vanish at DC
    gi.create_branch(name="CA", network=dc, from_bus="C", to_bus="A", length=1.0,
                     type=gi.BranchType(name="fixed X", grounding_conductor=True,
                                        self_impedance_formula="0.35*l + j*0.2",
                                        mutual_impedance_formula="0"))
try:  # log(f) runs to minus infinity at DC: refused for an electrode
    gi.create_bus(name="D", network=dc, type=gi.BusType(
        name="log", system_type="Station", voltage_level=20.0, impedance_formula="1 + log(f)"))
except ValueError as refused:
    log_refused = str(refused).split(". ")[1]

The reasoning behind these rules — the three kinds of singularity at 0 Hz, the measured accuracy of the stand-in — is in the explanation of direct current; the formula side is summarised in Formula syntax. Every transient study contains a 0 Hz bin as well: Transient simulation.
