docs.title: Admissible soil resistivity (inverse rho / rho-f)
docs.text:
The forward question is "what earth potential rise does this soil give?". The inverse one is "how poor may the soil become before the earth potential rise exceeds the limit?" — the margin of an installation against seasonal or uncertain soil resistivity. This guide answers it with gi.find_max_rho_scaling and, for a fitted rho-f characteristic, with gi.find_max_rho_f_scaling. The script is inverse_rho.py; its output is at the end of the page.

The example is the 20 kV feeder of the EN 50522 how-to: earth fault at S3, 1000 A at 50 Hz and 50 A at 250 Hz, station electrodes of 5.90 Ω at ρ = 100 Ω·m.

cable_system = gi.BranchType(
    name="3x NA2XS(F)2Y 1x300RM/25 12/20 kV, trefoil",
    grounding_conductor=True,
    self_impedance_formula=(
        "(0.727/3 + pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.03151272))*l"
    ),
    mutual_impedance_formula=(
        "(pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.03151272))*l"
    ),
)
substation = gi.BusType(name="substation", system_type="Substation", voltage_level=20.0,
                        impedance_formula="0.5")
station = gi.BusType(name="station", system_type="Station", voltage_level=20.0,
                     impedance_formula="2*rho/(3*1.13*sqrt(100.0))")

STATIONS = ["S1", "S2", "S3", "S4", "S5"]
FAULT_BUS = "S3"
net = gi.create_network(name="feeder", frequencies=[50.0, 250.0])
gi.create_bus(name="UW", type=substation, specific_earth_resistance=100.0, network=net)
for name in STATIONS:
    gi.create_bus(name=name, type=station, specific_earth_resistance=100.0, network=net)
names = ["UW"] + STATIONS
for i, (a, b) in enumerate(zip(names[:-1], names[1:], strict=True), start=1):
    gi.create_branch(name=f"K{i}", type=cable_system, from_bus=a, to_bus=b, length=1.2,
                     specific_earth_resistance=100.0, network=net)
gi.create_source(name="infeed", bus="UW", values={50.0: 1000.0, 250.0: 50.0}, network=net)
gi.create_fault(name="F", bus=FAULT_BUS, scalings={50.0: 1.0, 250.0: 1.0}, network=net)

docs.title: Choose the limit
docs.text: u_limit is a limit on the earth potential rise at the fault bus, RMS over all frequencies — not the touch voltage. The earth potential rise U_E is an upper bound of the touch voltage; EN 50522 compares it with the permissible touch voltage U_Tp(t_F) of the fault duration in its design procedure, and that procedure (with the recognised measures M of the standard) says which value U_E may reach for your installation. Take u_limit from there: the procedure, the clauses and the treatment of harmonics are in Compare results with EN 50522 limits. The package contains no permissible values; the 500 V of the example are illustrative.

docs.title: The largest admissible scaling of rho
docs.text:
gi.find_max_rho_scaling(network, fault, bus_names, u_limit) multiplies the specific_earth_resistance of every bus in bus_names by one factor c, evaluates the bus-type formulas again and finds by log-bisection over c_bounds (default (1e-3, 1e3)) the largest c whose RMS earth potential rise at the fault bus stays at or below u_limit.

  • Only the buses are scaled. The specific_earth_resistance of the branches — the soil in the earth-return terms of a Carson-type cable formula — stays as it is.
  • Before the bisection a scan of monotonicity_grid points (default 9) over c_bounds checks that the earth potential rise grows with c, which a bisection assumes; a formula whose reactance does not scale with ρ can turn, and the search then says so instead of returning a wrong maximum.
  • The network is left as it was, also when the search fails or is cancelled (should_cancel=); progress= reports every solve.
  • Every trial after the first one per fault location re-solves only the matrix values, bit for bit like a full run_fault, so a search costs little more than its first solve (see Large and meshed networks).
U_LIMIT_V = 500.0  # illustrative: the EPR limit your EN 50522 assessment sets

result = gi.find_max_rho_scaling(net, "F", bus_names=STATIONS, u_limit=U_LIMIT_V)
if not result["converged"]:
    raise RuntimeError(f"no maximum: {result['status']}, bracket {result['c_bracket']}")

docs.title: Read the result
docs.text:
c_max is always a factor whose earth potential rise was computed and found admissible. Whether it is also the largest one depends on how the search ended — read converged (or status) before using it:

status converged What c_max means "converged" True The bracket closed to within tol_rel; the threshold lies in c_bracket. "bracket_within_tol_on_entry" True The bracket was narrower than tol_rel from the start; same guarantee. "bracket_fully_admissible" False Every factor up to c_bounds[1] was admissible: c_max is that bound, a lower bound of the true maximum, and c_bracket is (c_hi, inf). Widen c_bounds. "max_iter_reached" False The step cap ended the search; c_max is admissible but possibly far below the threshold. Raise max_iter. "non_monotone" False The earth potential rise turns inside c_bounds; c_max is the largest admissible factor the scan measured, refined inside its interval — a lower bound.

c_bracket is the interval that provably contains the threshold, bracket_rel_width its relative width (compare it with tol_rel), rho_max the scaled resistivity per bus and u_epr_rms_at_c_max the earth potential rise at c_max. Do not branch on iterations: two different statuses can both end with zero steps.

docs.title: A rho-f characteristic
docs.text:
When the electrodes are described by a fitted rho-f vector \(Z = k_1\rho + (k_2 + jk_3)f + (k_4 + jk_5)\rho f\) (the form groundfield exports), gi.find_max_rho_f_scaling(network, bus_names, u_limit, k_ref) scales the whole vector, \(k = c \cdot k_\text{ref}\), gives it to every bus of bus_names (evaluated with each bus's own ρ) and sweeps each of those buses as the fault location: an existing fault at the bus is used, otherwise a temporary one with fault_scalings (default 1.0) is created and removed again. It finds the largest c for which no swept bus exceeds u_limit, and returns k_max, max_epr_rms_at_c_max, epr_rms_per_bus_at_c_max and the same status, converged and c_bracket as above. gi.evaluate_max_epr_under_k evaluates one vector without a search, and gi.select_rho_f_from_catalog ranks a whole catalogue against the limit.

K_REF = (0.059, 0.0, 2e-4, 0.0, 1e-6)  # fitted rho-f vector of the station electrodes

rho_f = gi.find_max_rho_f_scaling(net, bus_names=STATIONS, u_limit=U_LIMIT_V, k_ref=K_REF)

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Output of inverse_rho.py
rho search: status = converged, converged = True
c_max = 1.6939, bracket = (1.6939, 1.6953), EPR at c_max = 500.0 V
rho_max at S3 = 169.4 Ohm*m
rho-f search: status = converged, c_max = 0.6127, k1_max = 0.03615 Ohm/(Ohm*m)
largest EPR at c_max: 499.8 V, fault at S5

The station electrodes may see 1.69 times the assumed resistivity before the earth potential rise at S3 reaches 500 V. The rho-f search is stricter because it also faults the other stations: with the fitted characteristic the station at the end of the feeder, S5, exceeds the limit first, so the characteristic may only be 0.61 times the fit. The test suite recomputes the earth potential rise at both ends of the bracket with the independent reference solver of the tests.

docs.title: Outage and what-if studies
docs.text:
What happens to the earth potential rise when a cable is out of service, a ring is opened or a station is cut off? This guide takes elements out of service with gi.Outage, compares the scenarios with gi.run_outage_study and reads the comparison frames. The script is outage.py; its output is at the end of the page.

The example is a 20 kV ring: substation UW and three stations, bonded through the screens of the cable system of the data-sheet how-to (with its phase impedance, so the phase current divides over both halves of the ring), earth fault at S2.

cable_system = gi.BranchType(
    name="3x NA2XS(F)2Y 1x300RM/25 12/20 kV, trefoil",
    grounding_conductor=True,
    self_impedance_formula=(
        "(0.727/3 + pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.03151272))*l"
    ),
    mutual_impedance_formula=(
        "(pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.03151272))*l"
    ),
    phase_impedance_formula=(
        "((0.1 + pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.00806059))"
        " - (pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.03151272))**2"
        "/(0.727/3 + pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.03151272)))*l"
    ),
)
substation = gi.BusType(name="substation", system_type="Substation", voltage_level=20.0,
                        impedance_formula="0.5")
station = gi.BusType(name="station", system_type="Station", voltage_level=20.0,
                     impedance_formula="2*rho/(3*1.13*sqrt(100.0))")

FAULT_BUS = "S2"
net = gi.create_network(name="ring", frequencies=[50.0])
gi.create_bus(name="UW", type=substation, specific_earth_resistance=100.0, network=net)
for name in ("S1", "S2", "S3"):
    gi.create_bus(name=name, type=station, specific_earth_resistance=100.0, network=net)
for name, a, b in (("K1", "UW", "S1"), ("K2", "S1", "S2"), ("K3", "S2", "S3"), ("K4", "S3", "UW")):
    gi.create_branch(name=name, type=cable_system, from_bus=a, to_bus=b, length=1.2,
                     specific_earth_resistance=100.0, network=net)
gi.create_source(name="infeed", bus="UW", values={50.0: 1000.0}, network=net)
gi.create_fault(name="F", bus=FAULT_BUS, network=net)

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
A gi.Outage names the buses and branches to take out of service. While a scenario is solved their active flag is False: an inactive bus leaves the nodal system, an inactive branch carries no current — neither screen nor phase current — and induces no coupling. Nothing else changes, so scenarios need no copy of the network.

gi.run_outage_study(network, fault=..., scenarios=[...]) solves the base case (include_base=True, labelled base) and every scenario, and puts the elements back in service afterwards.

  • With on_error="raise" (the default) a scenario whose solve fails ends the study. With on_error="record" it is noted in OutageStudyResult.failures and the study goes on — the scenarios that disconnect something are often the interesting ones. The base case always raises, because every comparison needs it.
  • A scenario that islands the faulted station gives 0 V everywhere: no source reaches the fault any more, so no current flows. That is the answer, not an error (gi.check_network calls it FAULT_NOT_REACHED). Taking the faulted bus itself out leaves nothing to solve and fails.
  • progress= and should_cancel= report and stop a long study; a cancelled study restores the network to the state it had before.
SCENARIOS = [
    gi.Outage(name="K2 out", disabled_branches=["K2"]),
    gi.Outage(name="K4 out", disabled_branches=["K4"]),
    gi.Outage(name="S2 islanded", disabled_branches=["K2", "K3"]),
]
study = gi.run_outage_study(
    net, fault="F",
    scenarios=SCENARIOS + [gi.Outage(name="fault bus out", disabled_buses=[FAULT_BUS])],
    on_error="record",
)
compared = study.compare_buses()
at_fault_bus = compared.filter(
    (pl.col("bus_name") == FAULT_BUS) & (pl.col("frequency_Hz") == "RMS")
)

docs.title: Reading the comparison
docs.text:
OutageStudyResult.compare_buses() and .compare_branches() return one row per element, frequency, scenario and metric (EPR_V and I_branch_A unless columns= names others), with value, the difference delta_vs_base to the reference scenario and the relative difference delta_pct_vs_base in per cent. Two things differ from the frames of a single solve:

  • frequency_Hz is text here — "50.0" for a frequency and "RMS" for the RMS row — because it is the key the scenarios are joined on. Filter with pl.col("frequency_Hz") == "RMS", not with is_rms, which these frames do not have.
  • delta_pct_vs_base is null where the reference value is 0 — a frequency the fault does not excite, a bus islanded in the reference scenario, an element without current. "Ten per cent of nothing" has no answer, and because the marker is null rather than NaN, Polars aggregations skip it. Rank by the absolute difference when a zero reference is possible.

against= compares with another scenario than the base case; the column suffix follows its label:

against_islanded = study.compare_buses(against="S2 islanded").filter(
    (pl.col("bus_name") == FAULT_BUS) & (pl.col("frequency_Hz") == "RMS")
    & (pl.col("scenario") == "K2 out")
).row(0, named=True)

Columns: Result tables.

docs.title: One scenario by hand
docs.text:
outage_context — gi.outage_context(network, outage) — takes the elements out for the duration of a with block and restores them — and the network's path memo — on exit, also after an exception. Inside it, gi.solve returns the result without storing it, or gi.run_fault stores it as usual.

with gi.outage_context(net, gi.Outage(name="K2 out", disabled_branches=["K2"])):
    one_off = gi.solve(net, "F")  # the network itself stays untouched by solve
k2_out_epr = next(b.uepr for b in one_off.buses if b.name == FAULT_BUS)

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Output of outage.py
    scenario EPR S2 / V  delta / V delta / %
        base      231.9        0.0       0.0
      K2 out      447.7      215.7      93.0
      K4 out      369.4      137.5      59.3
 S2 islanded        0.0     -231.9    -100.0
K2 out against S2 islanded: delta = 447.7 V, delta / % = None
recorded failures: {'fault bus out': "Fault bus 'S2' is inactive or missing; cannot solve."}
outage_context, K2 out: EPR S2 = 447.7 V
out of service after the study: []

Opening the ring next to the fault (K2 out) almost doubles the earth potential rise at S2: the screens of only one side of the ring carry the current back. None is the null of the percentage column, because the islanded reference is 0 V. The test suite recomputes every scenario with the independent reference solver of the tests, with the same elements inactive.

docs.title: Import from pandapower (topology and short circuit)
docs.text:
A distribution network that already exists in pandapower does not have to be typed again. This guide imports its topology, reads a short-circuit case solved by pandapower and writes the IEC 60909 characteristics of the earth fault onto the grounding model. Two scripts, pandapower_topology.py and pandapower_shortcircuit.py; their outputs follow each part.

The importer needs the optional extra:

pip install "groundinsight[pandapower]"

docs.title: What pandapower provides — and what it does not
docs.text: pandapower describes the electrical network: buses, lines with their positive- and zero-sequence data, transformers, switches. It does not describe the earthing network: the electrodes of the stations, the screens of the cables and their coupling to the phase conductor. The import therefore takes the topology from pandapower — which buses exist, which lines join them, how long they are, what is in service — and the earthing side from the types you pass in gi.ImportDefaults: default_bus_type for every bus, default_branch_type for every line. Write those types from data sheets (how-to); the ones below are illustrative.

docs.title: Import the topology
docs.text:
net_pp = pn.example_simple()

station = gi.BusType(name="MV station", system_type="Station", voltage_level=20.0,
                     impedance_formula="2*rho/(3*1.13*sqrt(100.0))")
cable_system = gi.BranchType(
    name="3x NA2XS(F)2Y 1x300RM/25 12/20 kV, trefoil",
    grounding_conductor=True,
    self_impedance_formula=(
        "(0.727/3 + pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.03151272))*l"
    ),
    mutual_impedance_formula=(
        "(pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.03151272))*l"
    ),
)
bond = gi.BranchType(name="busbar bond", grounding_conductor=True,
                     self_impedance_formula="(0.05 + j*2*pi*f*1e-3)*l",
                     mutual_impedance_formula="0")
defaults = gi.ImportDefaults(
    rho=100.0,
    frequencies=[50.0],
    default_bus_type=station,
    default_branch_type=cable_system,
    switch_branch_type=bond,          # closed bus-to-bus switches become 1 m branches
    derive_phase_impedance=True,      # phase_impedance_formula from r/x of each line
)

gi.preview_pandapower_import(net_pp, voltage_level_kV=..., defaults=...) lists every element with keep or skip and the reason, before anything is built; gi.from_pandapower(...) builds the network. Pass the same defaults to both, so the preview shows the switches the way they will be imported.

preview = gi.preview_pandapower_import(net_pp, voltage_level_kV=20.0, defaults=defaults)
counts = preview.group_by("status", "kind").len().sort("status", "kind")

with collecting() as records:
    net = gi.from_pandapower(net_pp, defaults=defaults, voltage_level_kV=20.0,
                             network_name="example_simple, 20 kV")

What decides the result:

  • Voltage level. A bus is imported when its vn_kv equals voltage_level_kV within a relative tolerance of 1e-9 — math.isclose(vn_kv, voltage_level_kV, rel_tol=1e-9) — so rounding noise from a CSV export does not drop the whole level. A line is imported when both ends are. A bus without a usable vn_kv is skipped (IMPORT_BUS_SKIPPED); if nothing is left, IMPORT_EMPTY says so — usually a wrong voltage_level_kV. A default bus type written for another level is announced (IMPORT_VOLTAGE_LEVEL_MISMATCH).
  • Closed bus-to-bus switches bond earthing systems. A closed switch between two buses (et="b") is imported as a short branch of ImportDefaults.switch_branch_type (length switch_length_km, 1 m by default). Without switch_branch_type it is left out — and a bus reached only through it is isolated and reads 0 V, the answer a grounding study must never get by accident. The import says so (IMPORT_SWITCH_NOT_IMPORTED); the preview calls it no_switch_branch_type. An open bus-to-bus switch is no connection (switch_open).
  • An open line switch opens the phase conductor, not the screen. A switch at a line end (et="l") is the switching state of that line. Open, it interrupts the phase conductor at that end; the screen is bonded to the station earth independently of the switch and stays connected at both stations — pandapower carries nothing that would say otherwise. The import gives such a line default_branch_type with phase_impedance_formula = "nan" (type <name>_phase_open): it carries no fault current, and its screen stays in the earthing network. It names line and switch (IMPORT_LINE_SWITCH_OPEN, severity info); the preview marks the switch and its line line_switch_open, a closed line switch line_switch_closed (it changes nothing). A ring operated open at a line switch therefore arrives open — see below. If the screen is interrupted as well, set the branch inactive. The legacy phase_current_mode="paths" enumerates routes over every active branch and does not see an open phase conductor; the default mode does.
  • Transformers and impedance elements are not modelled; they are listed in the preview and announced (IMPORT_ELEMENT_NOT_IMPORTED). A switch at a transformer terminal changes nothing (switch_not_bus_to_bus).
  • in_service becomes active, so an element out of service is out of the solve as well.
  • Lengths come from length_km; a line without a usable length gets 1 km (IMPORT_LENGTH_DEFAULT), a self-loop or a length that cannot be a branch is skipped (IMPORT_LINE_SKIPPED).

The whole skip vocabulary is on the I/O page.

with collecting() as records_without:
    isolated = gi.from_pandapower(
        net_pp, voltage_level_kV=20.0,
        defaults=defaults.model_copy(update={"switch_branch_type": None}))

docs.title: The phase-conductor impedance
docs.text:
The default phase-current mode solves the phase-conductor network of rings and meshes, and needs a phase_impedance_formula on every branch of a mesh (otherwise the split uses a proxy, PHASE_PROXY). derive_phase_impedance — ImportDefaults(derive_phase_impedance=True) — writes one per line from pandapower's r_ohm_per_km and x_ohm_per_km: (r + I*x)*l. Two approximations come with it:

  • It is the positive-sequence impedance R₁ + jX₁ of the line. The phase network wants the reduced impedance Z_red \(= Z_{pp} - Z_m^2/Z_s\) of the phase conductor with the screen's return (data-sheet how-to). The split of the current over parallel routes depends only on the ratios of their impedances, so the approximation is exact only when all routes are of the same construction — the same ratio \(Z_\text{red}/(R_1 + jX_1)\) on every line. Mixed cable and overhead-line rings need their phase formulas written by hand.
  • The reactance is pandapower's value at the network frequency, used at every frequency. For harmonic studies write the formula with j*2*pi*f*L instead; at 0 Hz the constant reactance is dropped with a DC_LIMIT warning.

The earth-return formulas are never derived: they depend on the soil and the cable geometry, which pandapower does not carry.

docs.title: A ring operated open
docs.text:
example_simple has a ring MV Main Bus – MV Bus 1 – MV Bus 2 whose Line 3 is open at its switch at MV Bus 2. The import opens the phase conductor of Line 3, so a fault at MV Bus 2 is fed over Line 4 alone; the same net with every switch closed shows the ring that is not operated:

gi.create_source(name="infeed", bus="MV Transformer Bus", values={50.0: 1000.0}, network=net)
gi.create_fault(name="F", bus="MV Bus 2", network=net)
gi.run_fault(net, "F")
phase_currents_open = dict(net.electrical_network.phase_currents[50.0])

# For comparison: the same pandapower net with every switch closed.
net_pp_closed = copy.deepcopy(net_pp)
net_pp_closed.switch["closed"] = True
ring = gi.from_pandapower(net_pp_closed, defaults=defaults, voltage_level_kV=20.0)
gi.create_source(name="infeed", bus="MV Transformer Bus", values={50.0: 1000.0}, network=ring)
gi.create_fault(name="F", bus="MV Bus 2", network=ring)
gi.run_fault(ring, "F")
phase_currents_closed = dict(ring.electrical_network.phase_currents[50.0])
line_3 = ring.branches["Line 3"].type
Output of pandapower_topology.py
preview keep: 4 bus
preview keep: 3 line
preview keep: 2 switch
preview skip: 3 bus
preview skip: 1 line
preview skip: 6 switch
preview skip: 1 trafo
imported: 4 buses, branches ['Line 2', 'Line 3', 'Line 4', 'switch_bus_1']
import diagnostics: ['IMPORT_LINE_SWITCH_OPEN', 'IMPORT_ELEMENT_NOT_IMPORTED']
Line 3 imported as: 3x NA2XS(F)2Y 1x300RM/25 12/20 kV, trefoil_phase_open [('branch', 'Line 3'), ('switch', 'switch_bus_5')]
derived phase impedance of Line 3, switch closed: (0.5939 + I * 0.372) * l
without switch_branch_type: 3 branches, ['IMPORT_LINE_SWITCH_OPEN', 'IMPORT_SWITCH_NOT_IMPORTED', 'IMPORT_ELEMENT_NOT_IMPORTED']
phase current, as imported (Line 3 open): Line 2 0.0 A, Line 3 0.0 A, Line 4 1000.0 A
phase current, every switch closed: Line 2 129.9 A, Line 3 129.9 A, Line 4 871.6 A

With one cable type on every line the switch state moves the phase and screen currents — what the thermal check reads — but not the EPR: every coupling EMF is \(k\,I_p\) with the same \(k = Z_m/Z_s\), which amounts to injecting \((1-k)\,I_F\) however the phase current divides. In a ring of mixed construction the EPR moves as well.

The 110 kV buses, the 110 kV line and the transformer are skipped; the 20 kV level is imported with all four buses connected. Without switch_branch_type the MV Transformer Bus would stand alone.

docs.title: Read a short-circuit case
docs.text:
A limit check needs more of the fault current than its RMS value: the peak \(i_p\) and the thermal equivalent current \(I_{th}\) depend on the R/X of the fault loop and on the clearing time — quantities of the phase-side short-circuit calculation, which pandapower does. For an earth fault (fault="1ph") pandapower.shortcircuit.calc_sc needs, at minimum:

Element Columns external grid s_sc_max_mva, rx_max, x0x_max, r0x0_max (the _min ones for case="min") lines r_ohm_per_km, x_ohm_per_km, c_nf_per_km and the zero sequence r0_ohm_per_km, x0_ohm_per_km, c0_nf_per_km (endtemp_degree for case="min") transformers, if any the zero-sequence data vk0_percent, vkr0_percent, mag0_percent, mag0_rx, si0_hv_partial and vector_group 
net_pp = pp.create_empty_network(f_hz=50.0)
names = ["UW", "S1", "S2", "S3"]
index = {name: pp.create_bus(net_pp, vn_kv=20.0, name=name) for name in names}
pp.create_ext_grid(net_pp, index["UW"],
                   s_sc_max_mva=300.0,   # short-circuit power of the infeed
                   rx_max=0.1,           # R/X, positive sequence
                   x0x_max=1.0,          # X0/X1
                   r0x0_max=11.0)        # R0/X0 -- low-resistance earthing
for i, (a, b) in enumerate(zip(names[:-1], names[1:], strict=True), start=1):
    pp.create_line_from_parameters(
        net_pp, index[a], index[b], length_km=1.2, name=f"K{i}",
        r_ohm_per_km=0.100, x_ohm_per_km=0.110, c_nf_per_km=400.0, max_i_ka=0.5,
        r0_ohm_per_km=0.400, x0_ohm_per_km=0.350, c0_nf_per_km=400.0)
sc.calc_sc(net_pp, fault="1ph", case="max", ip=True, ith=True, tk_s=0.5)

gi.read_shortcircuit_results(net_pp) turns net_pp.res_bus_sc into a frame in amperes with one row per bus; the fault type, case and clearing time come from the solved net. Two deliberate deviations from pandapower:

  • For fault="1ph" pandapower leaves ip_ka and ith_ka empty. The import computes \(\kappa = 1.02 + 0.98\,e^{-3R/X}\) on the earth-fault loop, \(R/X = (2R_1 + R_0)/(2X_1 + X_0)\), and from it \(i_p = \kappa\sqrt{2}\,I_k''\) and \(I_{th} = I_k''\sqrt{m + n}\); kappa_origin says iec_closed_form. Where pandapower does publish ip_ka, its value is used (pandapower).
  • \(I_{th}\) is always recomputed: pandapower sets the DC heat factor \(m\) to zero for \(\kappa > 1.99\), where its limit is 2 — too small an \(I_{th}\), in the unsafe direction.

A bus without the data for κ is announced (SC_KAPPA_MISSING), a κ outside (1, 2] implied by pandapower's own numbers as well (SC_KAPPA_OUT_OF_RANGE).

sc_results = gi.read_shortcircuit_results(net_pp)  # amperes, one row per bus

docs.title: Write the characteristics onto the model
docs.text:
gi.apply_shortcircuit_characteristics(network, net_pp, fault) takes the row of the fault bus — matched by bus name, so the groundinsight network may be imported or built by hand — and writes R/X, κ and the share of \(I_k''\) onto every source that feeds the fault, and the clearing time t_k_s and the AC heat factor n_factor onto the fault. set_source_values=True also replaces the source currents by those shares; it is off by default, so a hand-tuned excitation is not replaced silently. The returned frame is the audit trail: i_k_previous_a next to i_k_a. A replaced t_k_s or n_factor of the fault is announced (SC_VALUE_REPLACED), an equal split between sources that inject nothing (SC_SPLIT_EQUAL), several matching rows (SC_ROW_AMBIGUOUS) and a voltage source that keeps its values (SC_VOLTAGE_SOURCE_SKIPPED). The thermal check then uses these characteristics (Thermal limits of earthing conductors).

cable_system = gi.BranchType(
    name="3x NA2XS(F)2Y 1x300RM/25 12/20 kV, trefoil",
    grounding_conductor=True,
    self_impedance_formula=(
        "(0.727/3 + pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.03151272))*l"
    ),
    mutual_impedance_formula=(
        "(pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.03151272))*l"
    ),
    conductor_material="Cu", cross_section_mm2=69.7,  # three 25 mm2 screens, see the data-sheet how-to
    theta_final_C=gi.final_temperature("Cu", "XLPE"),
)
station = gi.BusType(name="station", system_type="Station", voltage_level=20.0,
                     impedance_formula="2*rho/(3*1.13*sqrt(100.0))")
defaults = gi.ImportDefaults(rho=100.0, frequencies=[50.0], default_bus_type=station,
                             default_branch_type=cable_system)
net = gi.from_pandapower(net_pp, defaults=defaults, voltage_level_kV=20.0)
gi.create_source(name="infeed", bus="UW", values={50.0: 1000.0}, network=net)
gi.create_fault(name="F", bus="S2", network=net)

with collecting() as records:
    report = gi.apply_shortcircuit_characteristics(net, net_pp, "F", set_source_values=True)
gi.run_fault(net, "F")
limits = gi.check_conductor_limits(net, "F")
Output of pandapower_shortcircuit.py
S2: I_k'' = 2039.8 A, R/X = 3.169, kappa = 1.0201 (iec_closed_form)
S2: i_p = 2942.6 A, m = 0.00512, I_th = 2045.0 A, t_k = 0.5 s
source 'infeed': 1000.0 A -> 2039.8 A (share 1), kappa 1.0201
fault 'F': t_k_s = 0.5 s, n_factor = 1
apply diagnostics: []
K1: I_th = 1933.2 A, I_adm = 17874.6 A, utilization = 0.108
K2: I_th = 1912.9 A, I_adm = 17874.6 A, utilization = 0.107
K3: I_th = 65.4 A, I_adm = 17874.6 A, utilization = 0.004

Check it by hand. pandapower reports for S2 \(R_1 = 0.386\ \Omega\), \(X_1 = 1.723\ \Omega\), \(R_0 = 17.043\ \Omega\) and \(X_0 = 2.175\ \Omega\), so \(R/X = (2 \cdot 0.386 + 17.043)/(2 \cdot 1.723 + 2.175) = 3.169\) and \(\kappa = 1.02 + 0.98\,e^{-9.51} = 1.0201\) — the low-resistance earthing makes the loop almost resistive. \(i_p = 1.0201 \cdot \sqrt 2 \cdot 2039.8 = 2942.6\) A. The test suite recomputes every row from pandapower's raw results this way.

docs.title: Large and meshed networks
docs.text: How large can a network get, what costs the time, and what to avoid in meshed grids. This guide summarises the measurements of the current release and shows the one setting that turns a fast solve into an endless one. The script is performance.py; its output is at the end of the page.

docs.title: What a solve costs
docs.text:
run_fault assembles the nodal admittance matrix of the earthing network and the reduced matrix of the phase-conductor network straight into sparse form and factorises each once per frequency; the factorisation is reused for every source and for the second solve without coupling that the EPR-based reduction factor needs. The cost grows almost linearly with the number of buses (exponent 1.12 from 1000 to 8000 buses), and so does the memory. Measured on the development container (CPU time, median of three interleaved runs, seven frequencies; from the change log):

Network Before → after ring, 1000 buses 1.06 → 0.12 s run_fault ring, 2000 buses 4.04 → 0.22 s run_fault ring, 2500 buses 7.8 → 0.30 s run_fault radial, 2000 buses, three sources 18.1 → 0.27 s run_fault 40 × 40 mesh, four sources 7.0 → 0.35 s run_fault radial, 2000 buses, three sources 17.3 s → 0.017 s phase-conductor stage alone ring, 2000 buses 5.6 → 0.032 s bus_response ring, 2000 buses 2.8 → 0.031 s analyze_cuts ring, 1000 buses, every bus scaled 5.47 s → 0.59 s find_max_rho_scaling 40 × 40 mesh 11.3 s → 1.86 s find_max_rho_scaling ring, 1000 buses, ten fault locations 23.9 s → 1.42 s find_max_rho_f_scaling ring, 4000 buses 0.21 s → 0.035 s res_buses ring, 5000 buses 2.02 s → 1.51 s building the network

At 4000 buses a ring solves in 0.53 s, a radial feeder with three sources in 0.57 s and a 50 × 50 mesh in 0.59 s; the dense kernel of earlier releases did not fit into 2 GB there. Peak memory of a 1000-bus ring went from 146 to 25 MB. The times are for this machine; yours scale with it.

docs.title: What still costs time
docs.text:
• Building a large network. Every element evaluates its formulas at every frequency when it is created (with SymPy, cached per formula) and checks the values: a 5000-bus ring takes 1.5 s to build, a 50 000-bus ring 16.7 s. Build once, then edit (net.update_bus, net.update_branch) instead of rebuilding.
  • The result objects. On the largest networks the per-element result objects are the largest remaining share of a run: 0.2–0.3 s of the 0.53 s of the 4000-bus ring. The frames res_buses and res_branches are built column-wise.
  • The FFT transient solver solves a dense matrix per frequency bin; its memory is bounded by fft_block_bytes (Transient studies).
  • Path enumeration — see below.

docs.title: Studies reuse their first solve
docs.text: find_max_rho_scaling and find_max_rho_f_scaling evaluate the same fault for twenty or more trial values of the electrode impedances. Only the first trial per fault location is a full solve; every later one assembles the matrix values again with the same code, factorises them and solves the injection of the first solve — bit for bit what a full run_fault would give, so the searches take the same steps and return the same answer (Admissible soil resistivity). run_sweep and run_outage_study solve each point in full. Different networks can be solved in parallel threads, one network per thread; threads share one interpreter, so for CPU-bound studies in parallel use processes — for example the process backend of the service layer's job runner.

docs.title: Do not enumerate paths in meshed networks
docs.text:
The default phase_current_mode="auto" solves the phase-conductor network as a sparse system: it only needs to know which sources reach the fault, a breadth-first search, and net.paths stays empty after a solve. The legacy mode phase_current_mode="paths", the transient state-space solver and an explicit gi.create_paths(net) instead enumerate every simple path from each source to the fault — and their number grows exponentially with the number of meshes, not with the number of buses: 2, 12, 184 and 8512 paths between the opposite corners of a 2 × 2 to 5 × 5 grid, 1 262 816 for 6 × 6, which took about a minute. Before the default mode stopped enumerating, a 6 × 6 grid spent 55–68 s on the paths and milliseconds on the solve; now it solves in 0.09 s.

Use create_paths only for radial or lightly meshed networks, when you want the paths as data. The search refuses to produce more than max_paths paths (100 000 by default) and names the bus pair instead of running for hours; set the limit per network with PathfinderSettings: net.pathfinder_settings = gi.PathfinderSettings(max_paths=...) (Pathfinder).

station = gi.BusType(name="station", system_type="Station", voltage_level=20.0,
                     impedance_formula="2.0")
cable = gi.BranchType(name="cable", grounding_conductor=True,
                      self_impedance_formula="(0.2 + j*2*pi*f*1.2e-3)*l",
                      mutual_impedance_formula="(j*2*pi*f*1.0e-3)*l",
                      phase_impedance_formula="(0.1 + j*2*pi*f*0.4e-3)*l")

ring = gi.create_network(name="ring 500", frequencies=[50.0])
names = [f"S{i}" for i in range(500)]
for name in names:
    gi.create_bus(name=name, type=station, network=ring)
for i, name in enumerate(names):
    gi.create_branch(name=f"K{i}", type=cable, from_bus=name, to_bus=names[(i + 1) % 500],
                     length=0.5, network=ring)
gi.create_source(name="infeed", bus="S0", values={50.0: 1000.0}, network=ring)
gi.create_fault(name="F", bus="S250", network=ring)
ring_result = gi.run_fault(ring, "F")  # sparse solve, no path enumeration
ring_epr = next(b.uepr for b in ring_result.buses if b.name == "S250")

def grid(k):
    """A k x k mesh of stations, source and fault at opposite corners."""
    net = gi.create_network(name=f"grid {k}x{k}", frequencies=[50.0])
    for r in range(k):
        for c in range(k):
            gi.create_bus(name=f"B{r}_{c}", type=station, network=net)
    for r in range(k):
        for c in range(k):
            if c + 1 < k:
                gi.create_branch(name=f"H{r}_{c}", type=cable, from_bus=f"B{r}_{c}",
                                 to_bus=f"B{r}_{c + 1}", length=0.5, network=net)
            if r + 1 < k:
                gi.create_branch(name=f"V{r}_{c}", type=cable, from_bus=f"B{r}_{c}",
                                 to_bus=f"B{r + 1}_{c}", length=0.5, network=net)
    gi.create_source(name="infeed", bus="B0_0", values={50.0: 1000.0}, network=net)
    gi.create_fault(name="F", bus=f"B{k - 1}_{k - 1}", network=net)
    return net

path_counts = {}
for k in (2, 3, 4, 5):
    mesh = grid(k)
    gi.run_fault(mesh, "F")                    # default mode: nothing enumerated
    assert not mesh.paths
    gi.create_paths(mesh)                      # paths as data: the exhaustive search
    path_counts[k] = len(mesh.paths)

capped = grid(5)
capped.pathfinder_settings = gi.PathfinderSettings(max_paths=1000)  # this network only
try:
    gi.run_fault(capped, "F", phase_current_mode="paths")
except ValueError as refused:
    cap_message = str(refused).split(". ")[0]

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Output of performance.py
ring: 500 buses, EPR at S250 = 159.44 V, paths enumerated: 0
ring diagnostics: ['EARTH_GROUP_SPREAD']
2x2 grid: 2 simple paths from corner to corner
3x3 grid: 12 simple paths from corner to corner
4x4 grid: 184 simple paths from corner to corner
5x5 grid: 8512 simple paths from corner to corner
capped at 1000 paths: Enumerating the simple paths from bus 'B0_0' to bus 'B4_4' exceeded the limit of 1000 paths

The path counts are the known numbers of self-avoiding corner-to-corner paths in a square grid (OEIS A007764); the test suite compares them. Along a ring of 250 km the electrode currents turn in phase, so the split into the stations that feed the soil and those that return the current is less sharp than usual — the solve says so with EARTH_GROUP_SPREAD, and I_E and the current-based reduction factor describe the dominant direction (Warnings and diagnostics).

docs.title: Save, load and migrate
docs.text:
A network can be kept in two ways: as a project file — one network in one JSON file, to mail, to version or to open in the GUI — or in a SQLite database that holds a catalogue of bus and branch types and many networks. This guide uses both, migrates a database written by an earlier release and shows what happens to files from an untrusted source. The script is persistence.py; its output is at the end of the page.

station = gi.BusType(name="station", system_type="Station", voltage_level=20.0,
                     impedance_formula="2*rho/(3*1.13*sqrt(100.0))")
substation = gi.BusType(name="substation", system_type="Substation", voltage_level=20.0,
                        impedance_formula="0.5")
cable = gi.BranchType(name="cable", grounding_conductor=True,
                      self_impedance_formula="(0.2 + j*2*pi*f*1.2e-3)*l",
                      mutual_impedance_formula="(j*2*pi*f*1.0e-3)*l")
net = gi.create_network(name="Umspannwerk Süd", frequencies=[50.0, 250.0])
gi.create_bus(name="UW", type=substation, specific_earth_resistance=100.0, network=net)
gi.create_bus(name="S", type=station, specific_earth_resistance=100.0, network=net)
gi.create_branch(name="K", type=cable, from_bus="UW", to_bus="S", length=3.0, network=net)
gi.create_source(name="infeed", bus="UW", values={50.0: 1000.0, 250.0: 50.0}, network=net)
gi.create_fault(name="F", bus="S", scalings={50.0: 1.0, 250.0: 1.0}, network=net)
gi.run_fault(net, "F")

docs.title: The project file
docs.text:
gi.save_network_to_json(network, path) writes the network — elements, types, frequencies and the stored results — as JSON, and gi.load_network_from_json(path) reads it back.

  • UTF-8 on every platform. Names with Ω, ρ or ü are stored the same on Windows, macOS and Linux. A file that is not UTF-8 — only 0.6.0 and earlier on a non-UTF-8 system wrote such files — is read with the platform encoding and announced (PROJECT_FILE_LEGACY_ENCODING); saving it again writes UTF-8.
  • Atomic. The file is written to a temporary file next to the target and then moved over it, so a failure leaves an existing project file intact.
  • Versioned. The file starts with schema_version (the version of the file layout) and groundinsight_version (the release that wrote it).
gi.save_network_to_json(net, "project.json")       # UTF-8, atomic, with schema_version
header = list(json.loads(Path("project.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8")))[:2]
from_json = gi.load_network_from_json("project.json")

Network.model_dump_json() and gi.Network.model_validate_json(text) remain available for a network embedded in your own file format; the project-file functions add the header, the encoding rules and the atomic write.

docs.title: What is promised for old and new files
docs.text:
• Files of every earlier release load. A project file without schema_version (0.6.0 and earlier) is read unchanged. A database is migrated to the current schema when it is opened, after a copy of the original is kept as <name>.db.bak. Results stored before the earthing voltage and impedance were redefined at the fault bus load with those quantities empty and an info record LEGACY_EARTHING_DEFINITION in Result.diagnostics; solve the fault again.
  • Files of a newer schema are refused with a ValueError that names both schema versions, instead of being read with whatever the newer release added silently dropped. Update groundinsight to open them.
newer = json.loads(Path("project.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
newer["schema_version"] = 99                          # as if a later release wrote it
Path("from_the_future.json").write_text(json.dumps(newer), encoding="utf-8")
try:
    gi.load_network_from_json("from_the_future.json")
except ValueError as refused:
    newer_refused = str(refused).split(" (written")[0]

docs.title: The database
docs.text:
gi.Database — gi.Database(path) — opens (or creates) a SQLite file and offers the operations as methods: save_bustype, load_bustypes, save_branchtype, load_branchtypes, save_network (with its types and stored results), load_network, list_networks, delete_network, and their counterparts for types. It is a context manager; every operation runs in a short-lived session of its own, and two Database objects on the same file share a lock, so a GUI or a server may use them from several threads. gi.Database(":memory:") gives a private in-memory database. The module-level helpers (gi.start_dbsession, gi.save_network_to_db, gi.load_network_from_db, …) work as before on a default Database; the old globals gi.session and gi.db_session still resolve but are deprecated. Details: Database API.

for old_file in ("library.db", "library.db.bak"):     # start from a fresh file
    Path(old_file).unlink(missing_ok=True)
with gi.Database("library.db") as db:
    db.save_bustype(station)                          # a reusable type catalogue
    db.save_branchtype(cable)
    db.save_network(net)                              # with its types and stored results
with gi.Database("library.db") as db:
    stored = db.list_networks()
    from_database = db.load_network("Umspannwerk Süd")

docs.title: Migrate a database
docs.text:
needs_migration — gi.needs_migration(path) — classifies a file: "none" (current), "add_columns" (columns of a later release missing), "legacy_scoped" (elements keyed by name alone, up to 0.4.0) or "pickle_frequencies" (frequency lists stored with pickle, up to 0.6.0). migrate_database — gi.migrate_database(path, backup=True) — converts the file in place after copying it to .bak, and returns a gi.MigrationReport — migrated, kind, backup_path, the rows written, the columns added, and in needs_attention whether anything was filled in or left out that you should look at. gi.Database(path) does the same on opening (migrate=True, the default); with migrate=False the file stays untouched and its first use raises an error that names migrate().

connection = sqlite3.connect("library.db")            # simulate a file of an earlier release:
connection.execute("ALTER TABLE bus_types DROP COLUMN electrode_current_split")
connection.commit()
connection.close()

kind_before = gi.needs_migration("library.db")       # "add_columns"
report = gi.migrate_database("library.db")            # copies library.db to library.db.bak first
kind_after = gi.needs_migration("library.db")         # "none"
with gi.Database("library.db") as db:                 # Database(...) migrates on opening by default
    after_migration = db.load_network("Umspannwerk Süd")

The script simulates a file of an earlier release by removing a column that a later release added; a real file from 0.5.0 lacks exactly such columns.

docs.title: Files from an untrusted source
docs.text:
A .db or .json file is shared like a document — mailed, checked into a repository, downloaded. Two properties keep opening one from running code:

  • The formula guard. Impedance formulas are parsed with SymPy, which evaluates Python. Every formula — typed, imported or loaded — passes the formula guard first: arithmetic over names and numbers, a fixed list of functions, and bounds on the size of numbers, exponents and terms; string literals, attribute access, other calls and dunder names are refused (Formula syntax).
  • No pickle. Databases store frequency lists as JSON. Files of 0.6.0 and earlier stored them with pickle; the migration converts them with an unpickler that resolves nothing but list, float and int, and aborts on anything else.

The guard bounds the work per formula, not the size of a file: a file with many types and elements still takes time to load. A server that opens files from strangers should do so in a worker process with a time limit; a session of the service layer also refuses files above its max_buses and max_branches on opening.

untrusted = json.loads(Path("project.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
untrusted["buses"]["S"]["type"]["impedance_formula"] = "__import__('os').getcwd()"
Path("untrusted.json").write_text(json.dumps(untrusted), encoding="utf-8")
try:
    gi.load_network_from_json("untrusted.json")
except ValueError as refused:  # a pydantic ValidationError is a ValueError
    untrusted_refused = re.search(r"Impedance formula [^(]*", str(refused)).group(0).strip()

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Output of persistence.py
project file header: ['schema_version', 'groundinsight_version']
JSON round trip identical: True
newer schema: ValueError: 'from_the_future.json' uses project-file schema version 99
database holds: ['Umspannwerk Süd']
database round trip identical: True
migration: add_columns -> none, backup library.db.bak, added {'bus_types': ['electrode_current_split']}
after migration identical: True

"Identical" compares the complete JSON serialisation of the network — every element, type, frequency and stored result — before saving and after loading.

docs.title: Service layer and command line
docs.text: A notebook works with a Network directly. A front end — a GUI, a server, a batch tool — needs more: a project it can open and save, edits it can undo, long calculations off its event loop, and data it can send as JSON. The service layer groundinsight.api provides exactly that, without any physics of its own, and the command line groundinsight is built on it. This guide walks through a session, its commands and jobs, the JSON shapes and the command line. The script is service_layer.py; its output is at the end of the page. The design rules of the layer and its full API are on the service page.

docs.title: A session holds one project
docs.text:
ProjectSession is one open project: ProjectSession.from_example(name) (the documented networks quickstart, minimal, mv_ring), ProjectSession.from_file(path) for a project file, or ProjectSession.from_store(store, key) for a server that keeps projects in a MemoryStore or a DatabaseStore. The constructor takes the resource limits a server sets per user — max_buses, max_branches (a larger file is refused on opening), max_job_runtime_s, max_undo and max_paths.

A front end reads the project only through data-transfer objects (DTOs): summary() (NetworkSummaryDTO), tables() (the element tables of Network.to_tables), check() (the pre-flight check) and solve(fault) / result(fault) (FaultResultDTO: the key figures of Network.res_fault, the rows of res_buses and res_branches, the diagnostics as DiagnosticDTO, the revision it was computed from and whether it is stale).

session = ProjectSession.from_example("quickstart")   # or ProjectSession.from_file("projekt.json")
summary = session.summary()                            # NetworkSummaryDTO
result = session.solve("fault_at_remote_bus")          # FaultResultDTO
rms = result.key_figures.rms()                         # the RMS row of Network.res_fault

docs.title: Every edit is a command
docs.text:
A front end changes the project only through session.apply(command). The commands — AddBus, UpdateBus, RemoveBus and their counterparts for branches, sources, faults and the two type catalogues, plus SetFrequencies — call the library's editing API, so the library validates the input and derives the impedances. A command is atomic: a rejected one raises CommandError and changes nothing, not even the revision. session.undo() and session.redo() restore the network exactly; revision identifies an input state, and a result knows whether it is stale for the current one — the library's verdict (Network.is_result_stale), so undoing an edit makes the result current again. parse_command({"op": "update_bus", ...}) builds a command from JSON.

report = session.apply(UpdateBus(name="bus_fault", fields={"specific_earth_resistance": 250.0}))
stale_after_edit = session.is_stale("fault_at_remote_bus")
session.undo()
stale_after_undo = session.is_stale("fault_at_remote_bus")

docs.title: Jobs
docs.text:
Anything that can take longer than a moment runs as a job: session.submit_solve(fault) or session.submit(request) with a SolveRequestDTO, SolveAllRequestDTO, SweepRequestDTO, OutageStudyRequestDTO or MaxRhoRequestDTO returns a handle at once. The job runs on a snapshot of the network taken at submission, so editing can go on. handle.status() reports state and progress, handle.cancel() stops the job at the next unit of work, and handle.result(timeout=...) returns the DTO or raises JobCancelled, JobTimeout or JobFailed. The JobRunner of a session runs jobs in a thread by default; JobRunner(backend="process") runs them in a separate process, which costs the interpreter start but can stop a job hard and runs truly in parallel.

handle = session.submit_solve("fault_at_remote_bus")  # returns at once
job_result = handle.result(timeout=60)                # FaultResultDTO, or raises
job_state = handle.status().state

docs.title: JSON in, JSON out
docs.text:
Every DTO is a pydantic model with dto_schema_version; model_dump_json() is its wire format and never contains NaN or Infinity (a non-finite number is null). json_schemas() returns the JSON schema of every DTO, of all commands and of all job requests — the request and response schemas of a REST API. session.save(path) writes the library's project file (UTF-8, atomic, with schema_version) without stored results, so a file saved by a front end opens in a notebook and the other way round.

wire = result.model_dump_json()                       # never NaN or Infinity
schemas = json_schemas()                              # JSON schema of every DTO
session.save("projekt.json")                          # library project file, without results
session.close()

docs.title: The command line
docs.text:
Installing groundinsight installs the console script groundinsight (python -m groundinsight is the same):

groundinsight run projekt.json                           # the only fault of the project
groundinsight run projekt.json --fault F1 --format json  # the FaultResultDTO
groundinsight run projekt.json --format csv              # the rows of res_fault
groundinsight check projekt.json                         # the pre-flight check

groundinsight run opens the file in a session, runs the pre-flight check for the fault, solves it and prints the key figures per frequency and as RMS with the diagnostics (--format table, the default), the FaultResultDTO (json) or the key-figure rows with the columns of RES_FAULT_SCHEMA (csv). --phase-current-mode paths selects the legacy phase-current mode. groundinsight check prints every finding of check_network. The exit code is 0 on success, 1 when the check or the result reports an error, and 2 for a usage error (an unknown fault, a file that is not a project, run without --fault on a project with several faults).

For the project saved by the script, groundinsight run projekt.json prints after a two-line header (version, network, fault and input digest):

Output of groundinsight run projekt.json

   550       25          1.314        1.314  bus_fault  0.03785    0.03536    0.884    1.314      1.437
   RMS     1026          276.1        276.1  bus_fault        -          -    274.6    276.1          -

followed by the diagnostic SCALINGS_INCOMPLETE: the quickstart example gives its fault a scaling at 50 Hz only, so the harmonics are scaled with 1.0 (Harmonics, fault scalings and DC). r_epr is the EPR-based reduction factor, r_current the reduction factor of EN 50522 (Result tables).

docs.title: The GUI
docs.text:
The separate distribution groundinsight-gui is a desktop and browser front end built with NiceGUI on this service layer; it is released together with the library and carries the same version. Its source is in the gui/ directory of the repository.

pip install groundinsight-gui        # browser mode
python -m groundinsight_gui          # opens http://127.0.0.1:8080

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Output of service_layer.py
project 'QuickstartNet': 2 buses, 1 branch, faults ['fault_at_remote_bus'], frequencies [50.0, 250.0, 350.0, 450.0, 550.0]
RMS: I_F = 1026.2 A, EPR at the fault = 276.1 V, I_E = 274.6 A, U_E = 276.1 V
diagnostics: ['SCALINGS_INCOMPLETE']
after the edit: revision 1, stale True; after undo: revision 0, stale False

The test suite compares the key figures of the session with res_fault of a plain run_fault on the same example network, and runs the command line on the saved file.

docs.title: Parameter sweeps and statistics
docs.text:
A single solve answers one question; a study asks it over a range — the soil resistivity, the characteristic of an electrode, the harmonic content, the fault location. This guide runs one fault over such a grid with gi.run_sweep, stacks the results into one frame and reduces it with gi.summarize and gi.classify. The script is sweeps.py; its output is at the end of the page.

The example is the 20 kV feeder of the EN 50522 how-to: substation UW and five stations bonded through the screens of a cable system, earth fault at S3, 1000 A at 50 Hz and 50 A at 250 Hz.

cable_system = gi.BranchType(
    name="3x NA2XS(F)2Y 1x300RM/25 12/20 kV, trefoil",
    grounding_conductor=True,
    self_impedance_formula=(
        "(0.727/3 + pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.03151272))*l"
    ),
    mutual_impedance_formula=(
        "(pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.03151272))*l"
    ),
)
substation = gi.BusType(name="substation", system_type="Substation", voltage_level=20.0,
                        impedance_formula="0.5")
station = gi.BusType(name="station", system_type="Station", voltage_level=20.0,
                     impedance_formula="2*rho/(3*1.13*sqrt(100.0))")  # ring electrode

STATIONS = ["S1", "S2", "S3", "S4", "S5"]
FAULT_BUS = "S3"
net = gi.create_network(name="feeder", frequencies=[50.0, 250.0])
gi.create_bus(name="UW", type=substation, specific_earth_resistance=100.0, network=net)
for name in STATIONS:
    gi.create_bus(name=name, type=station, specific_earth_resistance=100.0, network=net)
names = ["UW"] + STATIONS
for i, (a, b) in enumerate(zip(names[:-1], names[1:], strict=True), start=1):
    gi.create_branch(name=f"K{i}", type=cable_system, from_bus=a, to_bus=b, length=1.2,
                     specific_earth_resistance=100.0, network=net)
gi.create_source(name="infeed", bus="UW", values={50.0: 1000.0, 250.0: 50.0}, network=net)
gi.create_fault(name="F", bus=FAULT_BUS, scalings={50.0: 1.0, 250.0: 1.0}, network=net)
before = net.model_dump_json()

docs.title: One point per parameter combination
docs.text:
A gi.SweepPoint is a label plus the changes that define it:

Field Changes Use it for bus_rho specific_earth_resistance of the named buses, with their bus-type formula evaluated again the soil around the electrodes bus_impedance the impedance table Bus.impedance of the named buses, written directly — the formula is bypassed a measured or fitted characteristic fault the fault solved at this point the fault location fault_scalings the scalings of the fault for this point the harmonic content parameters nothing — copied into every result row as columns plotting against the physical parameter

bus_rho changes the buses only: the specific_earth_resistance of the branches, which enters the earth-return terms of a Carson-type cable formula, stays as it is. To vary the soil along the cables as well, give the points a fault and network of their own, or build one network per soil value.

RHO_VALUES = [30.0, 100.0, 300.0, 1000.0]  # Ohm*m at the station electrodes
soil_points = [
    gi.SweepPoint(label=f"rho={rho:g}", bus_rho={name: rho for name in STATIONS},
                  parameters={"rho_Ohm_m": rho})
    for rho in RHO_VALUES
]
soil = gi.run_sweep(net, fault="F", points=soil_points)

gi.run_sweep(network, fault=..., points=...) solves the fault once per point, undoes the point's changes after the solve, and when it ends — finished, failed or cancelled — the network is left as it was: same stored results, same active fault, same paths (the script checks it with model_dump_json()). on_error decides what a failing point does: with "record" (the default) it is noted in SweepResult.failures with its message and the sweep goes on; with "raise" the first failure ends it. progress= and should_cancel= report and stop a long sweep.

docs.title: A catalogue of rho-f characteristics
docs.text:
gi.rho_f_points turns a catalogue of five-parameter rho-f vectors — the form \(Z = k_1\rho + (k_2 + jk_3)f + (k_4 + jk_5)\rho f\) that groundfield exports — into points that set the impedance table of one bus. It refuses a vector whose real part is not positive at some frequency, naming the label and the frequency, because the solver would reject it anyway.

K_VECTORS = {  # Z = k1*rho + (k2 + j*k3)*f + (k4 + j*k5)*rho*f, illustrative fits
    "small electrode": (0.10, 0.0, 2e-4, 0.0, 1e-6),
    "ring electrode": (0.059, 0.0, 2e-4, 0.0, 1e-6),
    "meshed grid": (0.02, 0.0, 2e-4, 0.0, 1e-6),
}
characteristic = gi.run_sweep(net, fault="F", points=gi.rho_f_points(
    bus=FAULT_BUS, k_vectors=K_VECTORS, frequencies=net.frequencies, rho=100.0))

docs.title: Reading the results
docs.text: SweepResult.buses(), .branches() (only with collect_branches=True), .impedances() and .cuts() (only with cuts=) stack the frames of the points: the columns of res_buses, res_branches, res_all_impedances or CutAnalysis.to_polars, preceded by point (the label) and one column per key of parameters; rho_f_points adds bus, rho_Ohm_m and k1 … k5. The RMS rows have is_rms true, as in a single solve. Columns: Result tables.

docs.title: Summarise and classify
docs.text:
summarize — gi.summarize(frame, value, by=...) — reduces one column to n, n_null, n_nan, mean, std, min, quantiles (p05, p50, p95 by default) and max, per group of by=. Read n_nan first: a failed point recorded as NaN propagates into the mean and the quantiles. classify — gi.classify(frame, value, edges, labels=...) — adds a column with the band of each row; a null or NaN value gets no band rather than the highest one.

Neither function knows a limit. The permissible values of EN 50522 depend on the fault duration, the edition and the measures taken, so the edges come from your study — Compare results with EN 50522 limits shows where they come from. The bands below are illustrative.

stacked = pl.concat([soil.buses(), characteristic.buses()], how="diagonal")
fault_bus_rms = stacked.filter((pl.col("bus_name") == FAULT_BUS) & pl.col("is_rms"))
summary = gi.summarize(fault_bus_rms, "EPR_V")
EDGES_V = [300.0, 600.0]  # bands of your study -- not limits of a standard
LABELS = ["up to 300 V", "300 V to 600 V", "above 600 V"]
classes = gi.classify(fault_bus_rms, "EPR_V", EDGES_V, labels=LABELS)

docs.text:
Output of sweeps.py
           point  U_E RMS / V  class
          rho=30        200.7  up to 300 V
         rho=100        384.6  300 V to 600 V
         rho=300        622.8  above 600 V
        rho=1000        788.8  above 600 V
