  ring electrode        384.5  300 V to 600 V
     meshed grid        283.1  up to 300 V
n = 7, min = 200.7 V, median = 384.6 V, max = 788.8 V
network unchanged: True

U_E RMS is the total RMS of the earth potential rise of S3 over 50 Hz and 250 Hz. The point rho=100 reproduces the worked example of the EN 50522 how-to (384.6 V); ring electrode describes the same electrode by its rho-f fit and differs only by the small reactance the fit carries. The test suite recomputes every point with the independent reference solver of the tests, with the station impedances evaluated from the formulas.

docs.title: Thermal limits of earthing conductors
docs.text: Does an earthing conductor survive the fault current it carries? This guide checks the screens and earth wires between the stations with gi.check_conductor_limits and the earthing conductor and the electrode at each station with gi.check_node_limits, by the adiabatic short-time rating of IEC 60949 with the thermal equivalent current of IEC 60909-0. The script is thermal.py; its output is at the end of the page.

docs.title: The check
docs.text:
For each conductor the check compares the thermal equivalent short-time current

\[ I_{th} = I_\text{RMS}\,\sqrt{m + n} \]

with the adiabatic limit

\[ I_\text{adm} = \frac{k\,S}{\sqrt{t_k}}, \qquad k = K\,\sqrt{\ln\frac{\theta_f + \beta}{\theta_i + \beta}} , \]

where \(S\) is the cross-section, \(t_k\) the short-circuit duration (t_k_s), \(m\) the DC heat factor from the peak factor \(\kappa\) (IEC 60909-0), \(n\) the AC heat factor (1 far from generators), and \(K\), \(\beta\) the material constants. utilization is \(I_{th}/I_\text{adm}\), within_limit is utilization <= 1. Every column: Result tables.

docs.title: What the check needs
docs.text:
• On the types. A BranchType is checked when it declares conductor_material and cross_section_mm2 (optionally theta_initial_C, default 20 °C, and theta_final_C). A BusType declares its two elements separately: earthing_conductor_* for the conductor that carries the full injected current I_inj into the station, and electrode_* for the electrode that carries the share into the soil, I_bus. Mixing the two currents up is the classic sizing error — at the faulted station the earthing conductor carries the whole fault current, the electrode often a small part of it.
  • current_split (earthing_conductor_current_split, electrode_current_split, between 0 and 1, default 1) is the share one physical conductor carries when the model lumps several: 0.5 for a ring electrode reached from two sides, 1/N for N parallel legs. It is never derived — the geometry is not in the model.
  • The excitation. t_k_s and n_factor come from the fault, kappa or r_to_x from the sources that feed it (set by hand, or imported from a pandapower case — see Import from pandapower). Keyword arguments of the checks (t_k_s=, kappa=, r_to_x=, n_factor=, frequency=) override the model for a sensitivity study. Several infeeds with different R/X are combined into one current-weighted κ (SC_KAPPA_MIXED); sources without data are announced (SC_DATA_INCOMPLETE).
  • An element with half of its thermal data (a material without a cross-section) is announced (THERMAL_DATA_INCOMPLETE); one with none is reported with its currents and within_limit null — enough to size it by hand, but not a pass.
cable_system = gi.BranchType(
    name="3x NA2XS(F)2Y 1x300RM/25 12/20 kV, trefoil",
    grounding_conductor=True,
    self_impedance_formula=(
        "(0.727/3 + pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.03151272))*l"
    ),
    mutual_impedance_formula=(
        "(pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.03151272))*l"
    ),
    conductor_material="Cu",
    cross_section_mm2=69.7,  # three 25 mm2 screens, see the data-sheet how-to
    theta_final_C=gi.final_temperature("Cu", "XLPE"),  # 250 degC, insulation limit
)
substation = gi.BusType(name="substation", system_type="Substation", voltage_level=20.0,
                        impedance_formula="0.5")
station = gi.BusType(
    name="station", system_type="Station", voltage_level=20.0,
    impedance_formula="2*rho/(3*1.13*sqrt(100.0))",
    earthing_conductor_material="Cu",               # carries the full injected current
    earthing_conductor_cross_section_mm2=50.0,
    earthing_conductor_theta_final_C=gi.final_temperature("Cu", "bare"),
    electrode_material="Steel",                     # carries the share into the soil
    electrode_cross_section_mm2=90.0,
    electrode_theta_final_C=gi.final_temperature("Steel", "galvanized"),
    electrode_current_split=0.5,                    # ring electrode, reached from two sides
)

STATIONS = ["S1", "S2", "S3", "S4", "S5"]
FAULT_BUS = "S3"
T_K_S = 0.5
R_TO_X = 0.1
net = gi.create_network(name="feeder", frequencies=[50.0])
gi.create_bus(name="UW", type=substation, specific_earth_resistance=100.0, network=net)
for name in STATIONS:
    gi.create_bus(name=name, type=station, specific_earth_resistance=100.0, network=net)
names = ["UW"] + STATIONS
for i, (a, b) in enumerate(zip(names[:-1], names[1:], strict=True), start=1):
    gi.create_branch(name=f"K{i}", type=cable_system, from_bus=a, to_bus=b, length=1.2,
                     specific_earth_resistance=100.0, network=net)
gi.create_source(name="infeed", bus="UW", values={50.0: 1000.0}, r_to_x=R_TO_X, network=net)
gi.create_fault(name="F", bus=FAULT_BUS, t_k_s=T_K_S, network=net)
gi.run_fault(net, "F")

conductors = gi.check_conductor_limits(net, "F")  # t_k_s, kappa, n_factor from the model
nodes = gi.check_node_limits(net, "F")

docs.title: Materials and final temperatures
docs.text:
The tables are top-level names of the package (gi.<name>).

IEC60949_MATERIALS holds \(K\) and \(\beta\) of IEC 60949 and a default final temperature for copper, aluminium and steel — 300 °C for all three, the value for bare buried conductors. FINAL_TEMPERATURES lists final temperatures by material and covering (bare, PVC, XLPE, EPR, and tinned copper or galvanized steel), with the source named in the module; final_temperature(material, covering) reads it and raises for a combination the table does not have instead of guessing. CABLE_INSULATION_LIMITS holds the short-circuit limits of the insulation materials (PVC 160 °C, XLPE and EPR 250 °C): the screen of an XLPE cable may not get hotter than its insulation, whatever the copper could take.

Covering Cu Al Steel bare 300 °C 300 °C 300 °C PVC 160 °C 160 °C 160 °C XLPE, EPR 250 °C 250 °C 250 °C

Check the values against the edition of EN 50522 you apply before a design decision; the tables are deliberately incomplete rather than filled with plausible numbers.

docs.title: A direct-current component
docs.text:
The check excludes the 0 Hz component of a current: \(I_{th}\) is built from the alternating components, because \(m\) already describes the decaying DC offset of an alternating fault current. A genuine direct current that flows during \(t_k\) — a DC railway, a rectifier — adds about \(I_{dc}^2\) to \(I_{th}^2\), which the check would then miss. It reports the 0 Hz part in I_dc_A and announces it (THERMAL_DC_EXCLUDED, ModelAssumptionWarning) with the increase of \(I_{th}\) that \(I_{th}^2 = I_{ac}^2\,(m + n) + I_{dc}^2\) gives.

dc_net = net.model_copy(deep=True)
dc_net.frequencies = [0.0, 50.0]  # re-derives every element at 0 Hz as well
dc_net.sources["infeed"].values = {0.0: 150.0, 50.0: 1000.0}
gi.run_fault(dc_net, "F")
with gi.diagnostics.collecting() as dc_records:
    with_dc = gi.check_conductor_limits(dc_net, "F")

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Output of thermal.py
K1: I_th = 864.1 A of I_adm = 17874.6 A, utilization 0.048
K2: I_th = 870.9 A of I_adm = 17874.6 A, utilization 0.049
K3: I_th = 899.3 A of I_adm = 17874.6 A, utilization 0.050
K4: I_th = 112.6 A of I_adm = 17874.6 A, utilization 0.006
K5: I_th = 54.6 A of I_adm = 17874.6 A, utilization 0.003
kappa = 1.7460, m = 0.06825, k = 181.3 A*s^0.5/mm2
S3 earthing_conductor: I = 1000.0 A (split 1), I_adm = 13765.9 A, within limit: True
S3 electrode: I = 32.6 A (split 0.5), I_adm = 8967.6 A, within limit: True
not assessed (no thermal data): ['UW']
with 150 A DC, K1: I_dc = 106.6 A, I_ac = 836.1 A, I_th = 864.1 A; ['THERMAL_DC_EXCLUDED']

Check it by hand. With R/X = 0.1, \(\kappa = 1.02 + 0.98\,e^{-0.3} = 1.7460\); at 50 Hz and \(t_k = 0.5\) s, \(m = \frac{1}{2 f t_k \ln(\kappa - 1)}\left(e^{4 f t_k \ln(\kappa - 1)} - 1\right) = 0.06825\). Copper from 20 °C to 250 °C gives \(k = 226\,\sqrt{\ln\frac{250 + 234.5}{20 + 234.5}} = 181.3\ \text{A}\sqrt{\text{s}}/\text{mm}^2\), so the screens of 69.7 mm² admit \(181.3 \cdot 69.7/\sqrt{0.5} = 17\,875\) A. The earthing conductor at the faulted station S3 carries the full 1000 A, its electrode \(2 \cdot 32.6 = 65.2\) A, of which one side of the ring takes half. The test suite recomputes \(k\), \(I_\text{adm}\), \(I_{th}\) and the node currents this way.

docs.title: Transient studies
docs.text: A real earth-fault current switches on, may carry a decaying DC offset and switches off again. This guide computes the earth potential rise and the screen currents over time with gi.TransientStudy, chooses between its two solvers and reads the warnings that come with them. The script is transient.py; its output is at the end of the page. The derivations of both solvers are in Transient simulation.

docs.title: Choose the solver
docs.text:
solver="fft" solver="state_space" model the stationary nodal system at every FFT bin, from the impedance formulas a state-space model from the lumped R/L/C fields, evaluated at one frequency f_eval needs the impedance formulas only R_formula (and optionally L_formula, C_formula) on the bus types, R_self_formula, L_self_formula (C_self_formula, R_mutual_formula, M_mutual_formula) on the branch types sources current sources with a galvanic connection to the fault bus current and voltage (Thévenin) sources mutual coupling not modelled — the earth potential rise comes out higher (conservative), and the solve says so modelled for current sources frequency dependence exact per bin fixed at f_eval (the smallest positive network frequency, or solve(..., f_eval=...)) watch for the window: the response must have decayed before t_end branches without R_self/L_self are left out

Use the FFT solver for a fast answer on a network without coupling, or as a conservative bound; use the state-space solver when the coupling between phase conductor and screens matters — in a cable network it usually does. On a network without coupling, with a window long enough, the two agree to numerical precision: that is the cheapest cross-check the package offers.

docs.title: Describe the network for both solvers
docs.text:
The impedance formulas serve the stationary solve and the FFT solver; the lumped fields serve the state-space solver. Declare both when you want to compare:

L_SELF_H_PER_KM = 1.2e-3     # screen-earth loop inductance (illustrative)
L_MUTUAL_H_PER_KM = 1.0e-3   # screen-phase mutual inductance
LENGTH_KM = 3.0

substation = gi.BusType(name="substation", system_type="Substation", voltage_level=20.0,
                        impedance_formula="0.5", R_formula="0.5")
station = gi.BusType(name="station", system_type="Station", voltage_level=20.0,
                     impedance_formula="2.0", R_formula="2.0")
cable = gi.BranchType(
    name="cable", grounding_conductor=True,
    self_impedance_formula=f"(0.2 + j*2*pi*f*{L_SELF_H_PER_KM})*l",   # stationary, FFT
    mutual_impedance_formula=f"(j*2*pi*f*{L_MUTUAL_H_PER_KM})*l",
    R_self_formula="0.2*l", L_self_formula=f"{L_SELF_H_PER_KM}*l",    # state space
    R_mutual_formula="0", M_mutual_formula=f"{L_MUTUAL_H_PER_KM}*l",
)
net = gi.create_network(name="transient", frequencies=[50.0])
gi.create_bus(name="UW", type=substation, network=net)
gi.create_bus(name="S", type=station, network=net)
gi.create_branch(name="K", type=cable, from_bus="UW", to_bus="S", length=LENGTH_KM, network=net)
gi.create_source(name="infeed", bus="UW", values={50.0: 1000.0}, network=net)  # RMS
gi.create_fault(name="F", bus="S", network=net)
stationary = gi.run_fault(net, "F")
stationary_epr = next(b.uepr for b in stationary.buses if b.name == "S")

docs.title: The source waveform
docs.text:
The waveform factories of gi.waveforms take peak values of the instantaneous current, whereas Source.values holds RMS phasors: a fault current of 1000 A RMS has the amplitude \(\sqrt 2 \cdot 1000\) A. step, sinusoidal_with_dc_offset (switched sinusoid with a decaying DC offset, dc_amplitude, dc_decay_tau) and damped_oscillation are provided; any vectorised callable f(t) works. Both solvers use the waveform as the literal injection and ignore Fault.scalings — scale the waveform itself; a fault with scalings other than 1 is announced (TRANSIENT_MODEL).

fault_current = gi.waveforms.sinusoidal_with_dc_offset(
    amplitude=math.sqrt(2) * 1000.0,  # peak of 1000 A RMS
    frequency_hz=50.0, t_on=0.02, t_off=0.12, dc_amplitude=0.0,
)

docs.title: Solve and read the result
docs.text:
study.set_observation(buses=..., branches=...) names what is recorded; study.solve(t_end=..., dt=..., solver=...) returns a ResultTransient with time_s, epr_t[bus] and i_branch_t[branch] (instantaneous values, in the earth-side sign frame of the stationary results) and to_polars() for a long frame. progress= and should_cancel= report and stop a long solve.

results, diagnostics = {}, {}
for solver in ("fft", "state_space"):
    study = gi.TransientStudy(net, "F")
    study.set_source_waveform("infeed", fault_current)
    study.set_observation(buses=["S"], branches=["K"])
    with collecting() as records:
        results[solver] = study.solve(t_end=0.3, dt=1e-4, solver=solver)
    diagnostics[solver] = records

def steady_rms(result, bus, start=0.08, stop=0.10):
    """RMS of an EPR trace over one full period of the steady state."""
    t = np.asarray(result.time_s)
    u = np.asarray(result.epr_t[bus])
    window = (t >= start - 1e-9) & (t < stop - 1e-9)
    return float(np.sqrt(np.mean(u[window] ** 2)))

rms_fft = steady_rms(results["fft"], "S")
rms_state_space = steady_rms(results["state_space"], "S")

docs.title: The warnings of a transient study
docs.text:
Code Solver Meaning TRANSIENT_MODEL FFT the network has mutual coupling, which the FFT solver ignores (the coupled branches are named); also: the window ends while the response still rings — lengthen t_end or pass zero_pad=True —, the fault carries scalings, or M_mutual exceeds L_self (a unit slip) TRANSIENT_SOURCE_NOT_CONNECTED FFT a source with a waveform has no galvanic connection to the fault bus and injects nothing TRANSIENT_PHASE_SPLIT state space meshed network: the phase current is split as at f_eval, and the split depends on frequency, so a DC offset and harmonics are split as at f_eval (below 1 % of the peak on a mixed cable/line ring) TRANSIENT_BRANCH_SKIPPED state space branches without R_self/L_self are left out TRANSIENT_COUPLING_SKIPPED state space the coupling is modelled for current sources only TRANSIENT_RESISTIVE_COUPLING_IGNORED state space mutual data on branches without inductance is ignored DC_LIMIT FFT every FFT grid contains a 0 Hz bin, so every formula is evaluated at DC; see Harmonics, fault scalings and DC

They arrive as warnings; collect them with groundinsight.diagnostics.collecting() around solve. Details: Warnings and diagnostics.

docs.title: Memory and time
docs.text: The FFT solver assembles a dense \(n \times n\) admittance matrix per frequency bin — \(16\,n^2\) bytes for \(n\) active buses — in batches of at most 512 bins that stay within the byte budget fft_block_bytes of solve, 256 MiB by default. The budget binds from about 180 buses on; a 400-bus solve over 1001 bins peaks at about 0.3 GB. A smaller budget saves memory and costs time on mid-size networks (150 buses, 1001 bins: 0.7 s at the default, 4.5 s at 1 MiB); the result does not change. The state-space solver's cost grows linearly with the number of samples.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Output of transient.py
stationary EPR at S: 381.2 V (RMS)
        fft: steady-state RMS 776.0 V, peak 1097.3 V, codes ['TRANSIENT_MODEL']
state_space: steady-state RMS 381.2 V, peak 539.3 V, codes []

The state-space solver reproduces the stationary result in the steady state; its peak is √2 times the RMS value plus a small switching transient. The FFT solver ignores the coupling and reports twice the earth potential rise — and says so.

Check it by hand. For the two-bus line the earth current is \(I_E = I\,(Z_s - Z_m)/(Z_{UW} + Z_S + Z_s)\) with \(Z_s = (0.2 + j\,2\pi\,50 \cdot 1.2\cdot10^{-3}) \cdot 3 = 0.6 + 1.131j\ \Omega\) and \(Z_m = j\,2\pi\,50 \cdot 10^{-3} \cdot 3 = 0.942j\ \Omega\): \(U_E = 2 \cdot 1000 \cdot |0.6 + 0.188j| / |3.1 + 1.131j| = 381.2\) V. Without the coupling (\(Z_m = 0\)): \(2 \cdot 1000 \cdot |0.6 + 1.131j| / |3.1 + 1.131j| = 776.0\) V — the FFT value. The test suite checks both steady states against these closed forms.

docs.title: Bus and branch types from data sheets
docs.text:
A BranchType and a BusType carry their impedances as formula strings in f, rho and l (formula syntax). This page shows how to turn a cable data sheet, an overhead-line conductor table and an earth-electrode geometry into those strings, with a worked example for the single-core cable NA2XS(F)2Y 1×300 RM/25 12/20 kV.

Every number on this page is computed by types_from_datasheets.py, which evaluates each cable quantity three ways — the closed form, Pollaczek's integral and a groundinsight network — and the test suite checks the agreement stated below.

Check the inputs before you use the types

The data-sheet values are quoted with their source. Values that a data sheet does not give — the build-up between insulation and screen wires, the stranding factor of the conductor, the geometry of the overhead line — are estimates and are marked as such. Replace them by the values of your cable and line.

docs.title: What a branch type needs
docs.text:
Field Quantity Symbol self_impedance_formula loop of the earthing conductor (cable screen, earth wire) with earth return Z_s mutual_impedance_formula coupling between the loop of the faulted phase conductor and that loop, both with earth return Z_m phase_impedance_formula loop of the faulted phase conductor with earth return, the screen bonded at both ends Z_red = Z_pp − Z_m²/Z_s grounding_conductor=True the branch has a screen or earth wire bonded to the buses –

Each formula is the impedance of the whole branch: a per-km expression times l. The types below also set conductor_material and cross_section_mm2 of the screen, which the thermal check of the earthing conductors reads.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Input Symbol Where it comes from DC resistance of the screen per km R<sub>s</sub>′ data sheet or test certificate of the cable; else the EN 60228 value of the screen cross-section mean radius of the screen r<sub>s</sub> diameter over insulation plus the build-up to the middle of the screen wires DC resistance of the conductor per km R<sub>c</sub>′ data sheet (EN 60228) geometric mean radius of the conductor GMR<sub>c</sub> conductor radius × e<sup>−1/4</sup> for a solid round conductor outer diameter D data sheet; the axis distance of touching cables soil resistivity ρ measurement (EN 50522:2022, Annex L.1) frequencies f the study: 50 Hz and the harmonics of interest

docs.title: Screen–earth loop and coupling
docs.text:
Carson's formula [3] with the equivalent earth-return depth \(D_E = 658\,\sqrt{\rho/f}\) m gives, per km,

\[ Z_s' = R_s' + \pi^2\,10^{-4}\,f + j\,4\pi\,10^{-4}\,f\,\ln\frac{D_E}{r_s}, \qquad Z_m' = \pi^2\,10^{-4}\,f + j\,4\pi\,10^{-4}\,f\,\ln\frac{D_E}{r_s} \qquad [\Omega/\text{km}]. \]
  • \(\pi^2 10^{-4} f = \omega\mu_0/8\) is the resistance of the earth return, 0.0493 Ω/km at 50 Hz; \(4\pi 10^{-4} f = \omega\mu_0/(2\pi)\) is the reactance per unit of the logarithm, 0.0628 Ω/km at 50 Hz.
  • The core and its concentric screen link the same flux outside \(r_s\), so the mutual impedance has the same logarithm as the screen loop and \(Z_s' - Z_m' = R_s'\). The screen is treated as thin: its internal reactance is neglected and its transfer impedance is its DC resistance, which holds while the wire diameter is small against the skin depth (1.3 mm in copper at 2.5 kHz, against 0.75 mm wires here).
  • 658 is the rounded constant; the exact low-frequency limit of the earth-return integral is \(2e^{1/2-\gamma}/\sqrt{\omega\mu_0/\rho} = 658.87\sqrt{\rho/f}\) m (\(\gamma\) Euler's constant). The closed form assumes homogeneous soil, neglects displacement currents and holds while the conductor depth and radius are small against \(1/\lvert m\rvert\), \(m = \sqrt{j\omega\mu_0/\rho}\).

For one line between ideally bonded stations the reduction factor is

\[ r = \left\lvert 1 - \frac{Z_m}{Z_s} \right\rvert = \frac{R_s'}{\lvert Z_s' \rvert}, \]

which is what ResultReductionFactor.value reproduces for a single branch. The reduction factor of EN 50522 in a network, value_current, depends on the electrodes as well; see Compare results with EN 50522 limits.

docs.title: Phase impedance for rings and meshes
docs.text:
In a ring or mesh the source current divides over several routes, and phase_current_mode="auto" computes that split on a network of phase conductors. The impedance it needs is the loop of the faulted phase conductor with the screen bonded at both ends:

\[ Z_{pp}' = R_c' + \pi^2\,10^{-4}\,f + j\,4\pi\,10^{-4}\,f\,\ln\frac{D_E}{\mathrm{GMR}_c}, \qquad Z_\text{red}' = Z_{pp}' - \frac{Z_m'^2}{Z_s'}. \]

Eliminating the screen current of a branch from its two loop equations leaves exactly \(Z_\text{red}\) in front of the phase current. It is neither the positive-sequence impedance \(R_1 + jX_1\) nor the conductor resistance; for a branch without an earthing conductor it is \(Z_{pp}\). The pandapower importer can derive the formula from a line's r_ohm_per_km/x_ohm_per_km (ImportDefaults.derive_phase_impedance): that is the positive-sequence impedance, a proxy that splits a ring exactly only when all its routes have the same construction. In a radial network the split is fixed by the topology and the formula does not change the result; declare it anyway, so the type stays correct when the network gets a second infeed. How the split and the coupling are modelled is explained in Phase currents in rings and meshes.

docs.title: Worked example: NA2XS(F)2Y 1×300 RM/25 12/20 kV
docs.text:
Data of the cable, ρ = 100 Ω·m, 50 Hz and the 5th harmonic (250 Hz):

Quantity Value Source conductor Al, 300 mm², Rc′ = 0.100 Ω/km at 20 °C Prysmian data sheet [1], EN 60228 [2] screen Cu wires 25 mm², Rs′ = 0.727 Ω/km at 20 °C EN 60228 value for 25 mm² [2] insulation 5.5 mm, diameter over insulation 32.9 mm Prysmian data sheet [1], row 1x300RM/25 outer diameter 41.9 mm Prysmian data sheet [1] semiconductive layers, swelling tape, wire diameter 0.6 mm, 0.4 mm, 0.75 mm estimates mean screen radius rs 32.9/2 + 0.6 + 0.4 + 0.75/2 = 17.825 mm from the rows above conductor radius, GMR 32.9/2 − 5.5 − 0.6 = 10.35 mm; GMR = 8.06 mm estimate, solid-conductor factor e−1/4 laying depth h 0.7 m rating conditions of the data sheet [1]; only used for method (b)

The screen radius enters only through a logarithm: ±5 % in rs moves r at 50 Hz by ±0.2 %. The screen resistance enters directly; at 20 °C it is the lower bound, and a warm screen gives a higher r (see the three-phase system).

The data and the closed form, as the snippet writes them:

# NA2XS(F)2Y 1x300 RM/25 12/20 kV. Sources: Prysmian data sheet
# "NA2XS(F)2Y 12/20KV CPR F" (row 1x300RM/25) and EN 60228 (DC resistance
# of a class-2 conductor of the nominal cross-section, at 20 °C).
R_CORE = 0.100  # Ohm/km, Al conductor 300 mm², data sheet
R_SCREEN = 0.727  # Ohm/km, Cu wire screen 25 mm², EN 60228 value for 25 mm²
D_OVER_INSULATION = 32.9e-3  # m, nominal diameter over insulation, data sheet
T_INSULATION = 5.5e-3  # m, nominal insulation thickness, data sheet
D_OUTER = 41.9e-3  # m, nominal outer diameter, data sheet
DEPTH = 0.7  # m, laying depth of the data sheet's current ratings

# Build-up between the insulation and the screen wires: estimates.
T_SEMICON = 0.6e-3  # m, inner and outer semiconductive layer, each
T_BEDDING = 0.4e-3  # m, semiconductive swelling tape under the wires
D_WIRE = 0.75e-3  # m, diameter of one screen wire

R_SCREEN_MEAN = round(D_OVER_INSULATION / 2 + T_SEMICON + T_BEDDING + D_WIRE / 2, 8)
R_CONDUCTOR = round(D_OVER_INSULATION / 2 - T_INSULATION - T_SEMICON, 8)
GMR_CONDUCTOR = round(math.exp(-0.25) * R_CONDUCTOR, 8)  # solid round conductor

RHO = 100.0  # Ohm*m
FREQUENCIES = [50.0, 250.0]  # Hz

def earth_return_depth(rho, f):
    """Equivalent earth-return depth ``D_E = 658*sqrt(rho/f)`` in m."""
    return 658.0 * math.sqrt(rho / f)


def loop_impedance(r_dc, radius, rho, f):
    """
    Conductor-earth loop impedance per km after Carson, in Ohm/km.

    ``r_dc + pi²·1e-4·f + j·4·pi·1e-4·f·ln(D_E/radius)``. With ``r_dc = 0``
    and the screen radius it is the mutual impedance of a conductor and its
    concentric screen, both with earth return.
    """
    return complex(
        r_dc + math.pi**2 * 1e-4 * f,
        4 * math.pi * 1e-4 * f * math.log(earth_return_depth(rho, f) / radius),
    )


def loop_expression(r_dc, radius, parallel=1):
    """
    The same loop impedance as a formula expression in ``f`` and ``rho``.

    ``parallel`` conductors of resistance ``r_dc`` each are written as
    ``r_dc/parallel``; ``radius`` is then their geometric mean radius.
    """
    if not r_dc:
        resistance = ""
    elif parallel == 1:
        resistance = f"{r_dc!r} + "
    else:
        resistance = f"{r_dc!r}/{parallel} + "
    return (
        f"({resistance}pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/{radius!r}))"
    )


def reduced_phase_expression(z_pp, z_m, z_s):
    """``Z_red = Z_pp - Z_m²/Z_s`` as a formula expression."""
    return f"({z_pp} - {z_m}**2/{z_s})"

z_s_expr = loop_expression(R_SCREEN, R_SCREEN_MEAN)
z_m_expr = loop_expression(0.0, R_SCREEN_MEAN)
z_pp_expr = loop_expression(R_CORE, GMR_CONDUCTOR)

cable = gi.BranchType(
    name="NA2XS(F)2Y 1x300RM/25 12/20 kV, own screen",
    grounding_conductor=True,
    self_impedance_formula=f"{z_s_expr}*l",
    mutual_impedance_formula=f"{z_m_expr}*l",
    phase_impedance_formula=f"{reduced_phase_expression(z_pp_expr, z_m_expr, z_s_expr)}*l",
    conductor_material="Cu",
    cross_section_mm2=25.0,
)

The type this builds, written out:

import groundinsight as gi

cable = gi.BranchType(
    name="NA2XS(F)2Y 1x300RM/25 12/20 kV, own screen",
    grounding_conductor=True,
    self_impedance_formula=(
        "(0.727 + pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.017825))*l"
    ),
    mutual_impedance_formula=(
        "(pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.017825))*l"
    ),
    phase_impedance_formula=(
        "((0.1 + pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.00806059))"
        " - (pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.017825))**2"
        "/(0.727 + pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.017825)))*l"
    ),
    conductor_material="Cu",
    cross_section_mm2=25.0,
)

docs.title: Three ways to the same numbers
docs.text:
(a) Closed form — the formulas above, evaluated in plain Python.

(b) Pollaczek's integral [5] for a conductor buried at depth \(h\) in homogeneous soil, evaluated with scipy.integrate.quad:

\[ Z_E' = \frac{j\omega\mu_0}{2\pi}\left[K_0(m r) - K_0(2mh) + 2\int_0^\infty \frac{e^{-2h\sqrt{\lambda^2+m^2}}}{\lambda + \sqrt{\lambda^2+m^2}}\,d\lambda\right], \qquad Z_m' = Z_E'(r_s),\quad Z_s' = R_s' + Z_E'(r_s). \] 
MU0 = 4e-7 * math.pi  # H/m


def pollaczek_earth_impedance(radius, depth, rho, f):
    """
    Earth-return part of a conductor-earth loop, conductor buried at ``depth``.

    Pollaczek's integral for homogeneous soil, displacement currents
    neglected, in Ohm/km:
    ``jωμ0/(2π)·[K0(m·r) − K0(m·2h) + 2∫ exp(−2h·√(λ²+m²))/(λ+√(λ²+m²)) dλ]``
    with ``m = √(jωμ0/ρ)``.
    """
    omega = 2 * math.pi * f
    m = cmath.sqrt(1j * omega * MU0 / rho)

    def integrand(lam):
        s = cmath.sqrt(lam * lam + m * m)
        return cmath.exp(-2 * depth * s) / (lam + s)

    upper = 40.0 / depth  # the integrand is below exp(-80) beyond
    points = sorted({abs(m), 10 * abs(m), 1 / (2 * depth)})
    parts = [
        integrate.quad(
            lambda lam, part=part: getattr(integrand(lam), part),
            0.0, upper, points=points, limit=400, epsabs=0.0, epsrel=1e-11,
        )[0]
        for part in ("real", "imag")
    ]
    bracket = (
        special.kv(0, m * radius) - special.kv(0, m * 2 * depth) + 2 * complex(*parts)
    )
    return 1j * omega * MU0 / (2 * math.pi) * bracket * 1e3


def internal_reactance(f):
    """Internal reactance of a solid round conductor, ``ωμ0/(8π)``, Ohm/km."""
    return 1j * 2 * math.pi * f * MU0 / (8 * math.pi) * 1e3

(c) A one-branch network — the type above between two stations, solved with run_fault; ResultReductionFactor.value of a single branch is \(\lvert 1 - Z_m/Z_s\rvert\):

station = gi.BusType(
    name="station", system_type="Substation", voltage_level=20.0,
    impedance_formula="2.0",
)
net = gi.create_network(name="one_branch", frequencies=FREQUENCIES)
gi.create_bus(name="A", type=station, specific_earth_resistance=RHO, network=net)
gi.create_bus(name="B", type=station, specific_earth_resistance=RHO, network=net)
gi.create_branch(
    name="K", type=cable, from_bus="A", to_bus="B", length=1.0,
    specific_earth_resistance=RHO, network=net,
)
gi.create_source(name="infeed", bus="A", values={50.0: 1000.0, 250.0: 100.0}, network=net)
gi.create_fault(name="F", bus="B", scalings={50.0: 1.0, 250.0: 1.0}, network=net)
result = gi.run_fault(net, "F")
r_model = result.reduction_factor.value  # {50.0: ..., 250.0: ...}

Result, impedances in Ω/km:

f method Zs′ Zm′ Zred′ r 50 Hz (a) closed form 0.77635 + 0.68254j 0.04935 + 0.68254j 0.44301 + 0.38746j 0.703286 50 Hz (b) Pollaczek, h = 0.7 m 0.77643 + 0.68254j 0.04943 + 0.68254j 0.44302 + 0.38742j 0.703244 50 Hz (c) groundinsight 0.77635 + 0.68254j 0.04935 + 0.68254j 0.44301 + 0.38746j 0.703286 250 Hz (a) closed form 0.97374 + 3.15988j 0.24674 + 3.15988j 0.77993 + 0.40208j 0.219869 250 Hz (b) Pollaczek, h = 0.7 m 0.97465 + 3.15938j 0.24765 + 3.15938j 0.77988 + 0.40207j 0.219883 250 Hz (c) groundinsight 0.97374 + 3.15988j 0.24674 + 3.15988j 0.77993 + 0.40208j 0.219869
  • (a) and (c) agree to rounding (about 1e-16): the model evaluates the same formula and reproduces the closed form of the reduction factor.
  • (a) against (b) shows how good the \(D_E\) approximation is. At 50 Hz the earth-return resistance differs by 0.17 %, the reactance by about 1e-6, and r by 4.2·10⁻⁵ (1.4·10⁻⁵ at 250 Hz). At 50 Hz most of that is the rounded constant: with 658.87 instead of 658 the difference in r drops to 4.8·10⁻⁶. The rest is the burial depth; it shrinks in proportion to \(h\).
  • Over 16.7 Hz … 2.5 kHz and 10 … 10 000 Ω·m (depth 0.7 m) the closed form stays within 1.5·10⁻⁴ of the integral in r and within 0.5 % in \(\lvert Z_s'\rvert\) and \(\lvert Z_m'\rvert\); the largest deviation in r on a 40 × 40 grid of that range is 1.3·10⁻⁴, near 400 Hz and 10 Ω·m. The integral itself is checked against an independent quadrature (mpmath) to 1e-9 and against its analytic low-frequency limit.

docs.title: Three-phase system: the other two screens
docs.text:
A three-phase cable system of single-core cables has three screens. With all of them bonded at both ends, the faulted core drives current into all three, and the three screens return it in parallel. groundinsight has no coupling between the screens of one branch, so the system is one branch whose type describes the screen bundle: the screens in parallel, seen from the faulted core. Eliminating the individual screen currents gives

\[ Z_{s,\text{eq}} = \frac{1}{\mathbf 1^T Z_{ss}^{-1}\mathbf 1},\qquad Z_{m,\text{eq}} = Z_{s,\text{eq}}\;\mathbf 1^T Z_{ss}^{-1} z_c , \]

with \(Z_{ss}\) the 3×3 matrix of screen loop and screen–screen impedances and \(z_c\) the couplings of the faulted core to each screen. In trefoil every row of \(Z_{ss}\) has the same sum, and the result is exactly the bundle formula: resistance \(R_s'/3\), and \(\mathrm{GMR} = (r_s s^2)^{1/3}\) in both logarithms (\(s\) = axis distance = outer diameter for touching cables), so again \(Z_{s,\text{eq}} - Z_{m,\text{eq}} = R_s'/3\).

def bundle_equivalent(positions, faulted, r_screen, r_dc, rho, f):
    """
    Equivalent screen-bundle impedances seen by one faulted core, Ohm/km.

    ``positions`` are the cable axes (x, y) in m; the screens are bonded at
    both ends, so they share one voltage drop. Eliminating their individual
    currents from ``Z_ss·I = U·1 − z_c·I_core`` gives
    ``Z_s,eq = 1/(1ᵀ Z_ss⁻¹ 1)`` and ``Z_m,eq = Z_s,eq · 1ᵀ Z_ss⁻¹ z_c``.
    """
    n = len(positions)
    z_ss = np.empty((n, n), dtype=complex)
    z_c = np.empty(n, dtype=complex)
    for i in range(n):
        for k in range(n):
            d = r_screen if i == k else math.dist(positions[i], positions[k])
            z_ss[i, k] = loop_impedance(r_dc if i == k else 0.0, d, rho, f)
        d = r_screen if i == faulted else math.dist(positions[i], positions[faulted])
        z_c[i] = loop_impedance(0.0, d, rho, f)
    ones = np.ones(n)
    z_s_eq = 1 / (ones @ np.linalg.solve(z_ss, ones))
    z_m_eq = z_s_eq * (ones @ np.linalg.solve(z_ss, z_c))
    return complex(z_s_eq), complex(z_m_eq)


def screen_current_shares(positions, faulted, r_screen, r_dc, rho, f):
    """
    Share of each screen in the bundle current, screens ideally bonded.

    With no voltage drop along the screens the coupling alone drives them:
    ``I = −Z_ss⁻¹ z_c`` per ampere in the faulted core. Returns
    ``|I_k| / |Σ I|`` for every screen.
    """
    n = len(positions)
    z_ss = np.empty((n, n), dtype=complex)
    z_c = np.empty(n, dtype=complex)
    for i in range(n):
        for k in range(n):
            d = r_screen if i == k else math.dist(positions[i], positions[k])
            z_ss[i, k] = loop_impedance(r_dc if i == k else 0.0, d, rho, f)
        d = r_screen if i == faulted else math.dist(positions[i], positions[faulted])
        z_c[i] = loop_impedance(0.0, d, rho, f)
    currents = -np.linalg.solve(z_ss, z_c)
    return np.abs(currents) / abs(currents.sum())


TREFOIL = [(0.0, 0.0), (D_OUTER, 0.0), (D_OUTER / 2, D_OUTER * math.sqrt(3) / 2)]
GMR_TREFOIL = round((R_SCREEN_MEAN * D_OUTER**2) ** (1 / 3), 8)  # bundle GMR = core-bundle GMD
# The thermal check compares the bundle current with cross_section_mm2: give the
# cross-section that covers the screen of the faulted core at 50 Hz.
SHARE_FAULTED_SCREEN = screen_current_shares(TREFOIL, 0, R_SCREEN_MEAN, R_SCREEN, RHO, 50.0)[0]
S_BUNDLE_MM2 = round(25.0 / SHARE_FAULTED_SCREEN, 1)

z_s3_expr = loop_expression(R_SCREEN, GMR_TREFOIL, parallel=3)
z_m3_expr = loop_expression(0.0, GMR_TREFOIL)
cable_system = gi.BranchType(
    name="3x NA2XS(F)2Y 1x300RM/25 12/20 kV, trefoil, screens bonded both ends",
    grounding_conductor=True,
    self_impedance_formula=f"{z_s3_expr}*l",
    mutual_impedance_formula=f"{z_m3_expr}*l",
    phase_impedance_formula=f"{reduced_phase_expression(z_pp_expr, z_m3_expr, z_s3_expr)}*l",
    conductor_material="Cu",
    cross_section_mm2=S_BUNDLE_MM2,
)

cable_system = gi.BranchType(
    name="3x NA2XS(F)2Y 1x300RM/25 12/20 kV, trefoil, screens bonded both ends",
    grounding_conductor=True,
    self_impedance_formula=(
        "(0.727/3 + pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.03151272))*l"
    ),
    mutual_impedance_formula=(
        "(pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.03151272))*l"
    ),
    phase_impedance_formula=(
        "((0.1 + pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.00806059))"
        " - (pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.03151272))**2"
        "/(0.727/3 + pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.03151272)))*l"
    ),
    conductor_material="Cu",
    cross_section_mm2=69.7,
)
f r, own screen only r, three screens in trefoil (bundle formula = matrix reduction = groundinsight) 50 Hz 0.703286 0.341570 250 Hz 0.219869 0.080223

The other two screens halve the reduction factor at 50 Hz. Which type is right depends on how the screens are bonded: all three at both ends — the usual case — is the bundle; a cable system whose screens are bonded at one end only, or cross-bonded, needs its own derivation.

  • Flat formation. The rows of \(Z_{ss}\) differ, and the bundle formula with geometric mean distances is an approximation: for touching cables it is off by 0.1 … 0.2 % in r at 50 Hz and by 2 … 5 % at 250 Hz (outer and middle phase faulted). Compute the bundle with the matrix reduction (bundle_equivalent in the snippet) at the study frequencies and check the formula against it.
  • Thermal check of the screens. check_conductor_limits compares the current of the branch — here the bundle — with cross_section_mm2. The three screens do not share it equally: with the screens ideally bonded, the coupling drives 35.9 % of the bundle current through the screen of the faulted core at 50 Hz, and 48.1 % at 250 Hz (a voltage drop along the bundle adds an equal part to every screen). The type therefore carries 25 mm²/0.359 = 69.7 mm² instead of 75 mm², which covers the faulted core's screen at 50 Hz; with a large harmonic content use the larger share.
  • Screen temperature. r grows with the screen resistance. With the screens at 70 °C instead of 20 °C (factor 304.5/254.5 for copper) r of the trefoil system at 50 Hz rises from 0.342 to 0.397. The 20 °C value is the lower bound and gives the lower earth potential rise.

docs.title: Overhead line with earth wire
docs.text:
For a line whose earth wire is bonded to the towers and the stations, the earth wire takes the place of the screen. With the earth wire's resistance \(R_{ew}'\) and geometric mean radius, and the distance \(d\) between the faulted phase conductor and the earth wire:

\[ Z_s' = R_{ew}' + \pi^2 10^{-4} f + j\,4\pi 10^{-4} f \ln\frac{D_E}{\mathrm{GMR}_{ew}}, \qquad Z_m' = \pi^2 10^{-4} f + j\,4\pi 10^{-4} f \ln\frac{D_E}{d}. \]

When the faulted phase is not known, or the line is transposed, use for \(d\) the geometric mean of the distances of the three phases to the earth wire; two earth wires form a bundle like the screens above. Model each span as a branch and each tower as a bus whose electrode is the tower footing.

Example: phase conductor 94-AL1/15-ST1A (Al/St 95/15, 0.3060 Ω/km, Ø 13.60 mm), earth wire 47-AL1/8-ST1A (0.6129 Ω/km, Ø 9.45 mm) [4], earth wire 2 m above the faulted phase at 10 m.

# 20 kV overhead line: phase conductor 94-AL1/15-ST1A (Al/St 95/15), earth wire
# 47-AL1/8-ST1A (Al/St 50/8), EN 50182 values; geometry: estimate.
R_EARTH_WIRE = 0.6129  # Ohm/km at 20 °C
GMR_EARTH_WIRE = round(math.exp(-0.25) * 9.45e-3 / 2, 8)  # m, solid-conductor approximation
R_PHASE_OHL = 0.3060  # Ohm/km at 20 °C
GMR_PHASE_OHL = round(math.exp(-0.25) * 13.6e-3 / 2, 8)  # m, solid-conductor approximation
H_PHASE, H_EARTH_WIRE = 10.0, 12.0  # m above ground, earth wire above the faulted phase
D_PHASE_EARTH_WIRE = H_EARTH_WIRE - H_PHASE  # m

z_ew_expr = loop_expression(R_EARTH_WIRE, GMR_EARTH_WIRE)
z_pe_expr = loop_expression(0.0, D_PHASE_EARTH_WIRE)
overhead_line = gi.BranchType(
    name="20 kV OHL 94-AL1/15-ST1A with earth wire 47-AL1/8-ST1A",
    grounding_conductor=True,
    self_impedance_formula=f"{z_ew_expr}*l",
    mutual_impedance_formula=f"{z_pe_expr}*l",
    phase_impedance_formula=(
        f"{reduced_phase_expression(loop_expression(R_PHASE_OHL, GMR_PHASE_OHL), z_pe_expr, z_ew_expr)}*l"
    ),
)


def carson_earth_impedance(h_i, h_j, x, d, rho, f):
    """
    Carson's loop or mutual impedance of overhead conductors, in Ohm/km.

    With earth return, without the internal impedance:
    ``jωμ0/(2π)·ln(D/d) + jωμ0/π·∫ exp(−(h_i+h_j)λ)·cos(xλ)/(λ+√(λ²+m²)) dλ``,
    ``D`` the distance to the image conductor.
    """
    omega = 2 * math.pi * f
    m = cmath.sqrt(1j * omega * MU0 / rho)
    height = h_i + h_j

    def integrand(lam):
        return cmath.exp(-height * lam) * math.cos(x * lam) / (lam + cmath.sqrt(lam * lam + m * m))

    upper = 80.0 / height
    points = sorted({abs(m), 10 * abs(m), 1 / height})
    parts = [
        integrate.quad(
            lambda lam, part=part: getattr(integrand(lam), part),
            0.0, upper, points=points, limit=400, epsabs=0.0, epsrel=1e-11,
        )[0]
        for part in ("real", "imag")
    ]
    image = math.hypot(x, height)
    z = 1j * omega * MU0 / (2 * math.pi) * math.log(image / d)
    return (z + 1j * omega * MU0 / math.pi * complex(*parts)) * 1e3

overhead_line = gi.BranchType(
    name="20 kV OHL 94-AL1/15-ST1A with earth wire 47-AL1/8-ST1A",
    grounding_conductor=True,
    self_impedance_formula=(
        "(0.6129 + pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.00367983))*l"
    ),
    mutual_impedance_formula=(
        "(pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/2.0))*l"
    ),
    phase_impedance_formula=(
        "((0.306 + pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.00529585))"
        " - (pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/2.0))**2"
        "/(0.6129 + pi**2*1e-4*f + j*4*pi*1e-4*f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/0.00367983)))*l"
    ),
)
f r (a) closed form r (b) Carson's integral r (c) groundinsight 50 Hz 0.712107 0.711893 0.712107 250 Hz 0.551584 0.550026 0.551584

Method (b) is Carson's integral for conductors above ground. Overhead conductors sit much higher than a buried cable, so the closed form loses accuracy sooner: 2·10⁻⁴ in r at 50 Hz, 1.6·10⁻³ at 250 Hz, and up to 2·10⁻² at 2.5 kHz in 10 Ω·m soil.

docs.title: Electrode impedance of a station
docs.text:
A BusType needs the impedance of the station's electrode to remote earth, Z_B — not the earthing impedance of the network at that station (see the glossary). Two sources:

  • A measurement. An earthing-impedance measurement at a station whose cable screens are connected measures the network's driving-point impedance, not Z_B. Measure with the screens and earth wires disconnected, or derive Z_B from the measured value and the network. groundmeas manages and evaluates such measurements, including impedance against frequency and soil resistivity.
  • A standard formula for the electrode geometry. The common ones and two published variants each, at ρ = 100 Ω·m:
Electrode Formula in the BusType (source) Value Second formula (source) Value rod, L = 3 m, Ø 20 mm ρ/(2πL)·(ln(4L/a) − 1), a = radius (Dwight [6]) 32.31 Ω ρ/L (rough rule [7]) 33.33 Ω ring around 10 m × 10 m, D = 1.13·√A 2ρ/(3D) (rough rule [7], [8]) 5.90 Ω ρ/(2π²D)·(ln(8D/d) + ln(4D/s)), d = 10 mm, s = 2·0.5 m (Dwight [6]) 5.79 Ω mesh 40 m × 40 m, 400 m conductor, 0.8 m deep ρ·(1/LT + (1 + 1/(1 + h·√(20/A)))/√(20A)) (Sverak, IEEE 80 [9]) 1.32 Ω ρ/4·√(π/A) + ρ/LT (Laurent–Niemann, IEEE 80 [9]) 1.36 Ω 
# Earth electrodes as BusType formulas in rho (Ohm*m); dimensions in m.
rod = gi.BusType(  # one rod, L = 3 m, diameter 20 mm (Dwight 1936)
    name="rod 3 m", system_type="Station", voltage_level=20.0,
    impedance_formula="rho/(2*pi*3.0)*(log(4*3.0/0.01) - 1)",
)
ring = gi.BusType(  # ring around 10 m x 10 m, D = 1.13*sqrt(A)
    name="ring 10 m x 10 m", system_type="Station", voltage_level=20.0,
    impedance_formula="2*rho/(3*1.13*sqrt(100.0))",
)
mesh = gi.BusType(  # mesh 40 m x 40 m, 400 m of conductor at 0.8 m (IEEE 80, Sverak)
    name="mesh 40 m x 40 m", system_type="Substation", voltage_level=110.0,
    impedance_formula=(
        "rho*(1/400.0 + 1/sqrt(20*1600.0)*(1 + 1/(1 + 0.8*sqrt(20/1600.0))))"
    ),
)
measured = gi.BusType(  # a measured 50 Hz impedance, inductive part scaled with f
    name="station, measured", system_type="Station", voltage_level=20.0,
    impedance_formula="0.42 + j*0.08*f/50",
)

The two variants agree within 4 %; the soil model behind them — homogeneous ρ — is the larger uncertainty. Frequency dependence is a modelling choice. The formulas give a resistance, the same at every frequency. A measured impedance with an inductive part is written so that the reactance scales with frequency (0.42 + j*0.08*f/50 above); that form also tends to the resistance at 0 Hz by itself.

docs.title: At 0 Hz
docs.text:
DC studies and every FFT transient study evaluate the formulas at 0 Hz, where f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/r) is 0·∞. The evaluator approaches 0 Hz numerically (formula syntax); for the types on this page it returns:

Formula Value at 0 Hz Message self_impedance_formula Rs′·l, the DC resistance of the screen none phase_impedance_formula Rc′·l, the DC resistance of the conductor none mutual_impedance_formula about π²·10⁻¹²·l Ω — zero for every practical purpose, r = 1 none

The mutual impedance tends to zero: its real part \(\pi^2 10^{-4} f\) has no constant term, so what the approach ends on, the value at 10⁻⁸ Hz, is all that is left of it. A test relative to the value cannot judge such a limit — the real part changes by 90 % of itself per decade however small it is — but the step shrinks ten-fold per decade, as for anything linear in f, and the evaluator accepts that as converged at every length. A formula that behaves like \(\sqrt{f}\) or \(\log f\) near 0 Hz still gets a DCLimitWarning "converges only slowly". The electrode formulas contain no f and are unchanged at 0 Hz.

docs.title: Check a new type
docs.text:
• Run a one-branch network and compare value with \(\lvert 1 - Z_m/Z_s\rvert\) of the closed form, as method (c) does.
  • Compare r at 50 Hz with the typical values that EN 50522:2022 lists for cables and lines (Annex I).
  • Evaluate the formulas at the lowest ρ, the lowest frequency and the shortest length of the model: a negative real part or a NaN is refused (formula syntax), and so is a real part that runs to −∞ at 0 Hz, which a log(f) term without a factor f produces.

docs.title: Citing groundinsight
docs.text: If you use groundinsight in scientific work, please cite it, and cite the version you used — gi.__version__ tells you which one that is. The entries below are generated from CITATION.cff in the repository, the file GitHub shows under Cite this repository.

docs.title: BibTeX
docs.text:
@software{ehlert_groundinsight,
  author  = {Ehlert, Christian},
  title   = {groundinsight: Simulation of grounding systems in electrical power grids},
  version = {0.6.0},
  url     = {https://github.com/Ce1ectric/groundinsight}

docs.text: Ehlert, C. (n.d.). groundinsight: Simulation of grounding systems in electrical power grids (Version 0.6.0) [Computer software]. https://github.com/Ce1ectric/groundinsight

docs.title: Citing the method
docs.text: groundinsight implements the methods described on the pages under Understanding the model. When your work relies on a particular part of the model — the reduction factor on a current basis, the phase-current split, the location response — name that part as well, so a reader can find its definition and its assumptions.

docs.title: Contributing to groundinsight
docs.text: Contributions are welcome: bug reports, documentation, tests and code. For anything beyond a small fix, please open an issue first so the approach can be agreed before you invest the time. This page describes how to set up a working copy, how to run the tests and build the documentation, and the conventions the code base follows — a pull request is reviewed against them.

docs.title: Setting up a working copy
docs.text:
groundinsight needs Python 3.12 or newer and uses Poetry for its environments.

git clone https://github.com/Ce1ectric/groundinsight.git
cd groundinsight
poetry install --with dev,docs --extras pandapower

The dev group holds the test tools, the docs group the documentation toolchain, and the pandapower extra the optional importer, which the test suite and the example notebooks exercise.

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text:
poetry run pytest                          # the suite and the doctests
GROUNDINSIGHT_CI=1 poetry run pytest       # as in CI
poetry run pytest -m "not slow"            # without the size and timing checks
poetry run pytest --cov=groundinsight      # with coverage

Locally, a test that needs an optional package or tool that is not installed skips. With GROUNDINSIGHT_CI=1, as in the CI jobs, such a skip fails instead, because there it means the environment is incomplete.

docs.title: Building the documentation
docs.text:
poetry run mkdocs serve                    # live preview
poetry run mkdocs build --strict           # what CI runs

--strict turns every broken link or anchor into an error. The build executes the example notebooks in docs/examples/, which takes about a minute the first time and is cached afterwards. Three rules keep the pages honest, and the test suite checks all of them:

  • Example code of the pages lives in docs/snippets/*.py and is included with --8<-- "docs/snippets/<file>.py:<section>"; the tests run the snippets and compare what they print with what the page shows.
  • Every python block on a page runs, or starts with # fragment (or # fragment: <what it assumes>) to mark it as an excerpt.
  • Notebooks are committed without outputs. The build runs them, so a page always shows the output of the code next to it.

docs.title: Language
docs.text: Code, comments, docstrings, documentation, commit messages and changelog entries are written in English.

docs.title: Code conventions
docs.text:
Module header. The first line of a module names its path, followed by a module docstring that says what the module is for and why it is built the way it is. Inside the package the path is relative to src/groundinsight/ (# analysis/response.py), elsewhere relative to the repository root (# tests/test_audit_pass19_docs_structure.py).

Docstrings. Every public module, class, function and method has a docstring in NumPy style — Parameters, Returns, Raises, Warns, Notes, Examples as they apply. A docstring states the contract and the reasons for it. The history of a change belongs in CHANGELOG.md, not in the docstring.

Type hints. Use the typing forms the code base uses throughout: Optional[float], List[str], Dict[str, complex], Tuple[int, ...].

Logging, not print. Library code reports progress through logging.getLogger(__name__). The package attaches a NullHandler, so it stays quiet until the user opts in with gi.set_log_level(...). A library function never prints.

Errors. Input the package cannot use raises the built-in exception that fits — ValueError for a value, TypeError for a type, RuntimeError for a computation that failed — with a message that names the element, the value and what to do about it. Where a caller needs to tell errors apart, the package defines a subclass of the built-in it specialises, so an existing except ValueError keeps working: ProjectError and CommandError of the service layer are ValueErrors, JobFailed and StudyCancelled are RuntimeErrors. A result that only looks plausible is worse than an error: an input that cannot be computed raises, it does not return zeros.

Diagnostics. A condition that does not stop the calculation but changes how a result must be read — a heuristic phase split, a frequency the fault scalings do not cover — is a warning with a stable code. Emit it with groundinsight.diagnostics.emit:

# fragment: inside the package, `branch` is the branch concerned
from groundinsight.diagnostics import ModelAssumptionWarning, emit

emit(
    ModelAssumptionWarning,
    f"Branch '{branch.name}' declares no phase impedance; ...",
    code="PHASE_PROXY",
    elements=[("branch", branch.name)],
)

The category is a subclass of GroundinsightWarning (ModelAssumptionWarning, InputWarning, ...). run_fault keeps every warning of a run in Result.diagnostics, where a program reads the code and the elements instead of parsing the text. A new code is documented on the reference page Warnings and diagnostics (docs/reference/warnings.md); a test checks that every code of the package is listed there.

Public and internal API. The public API is what groundinsight and groundinsight.api export in __all__; every exported name is rendered in the API reference, which CI checks. Functions that other modules of the package share but application code should not use carry no leading underscore and start the second paragraph of their docstring with "Internal API" — see Internal API. Underscore names stay inside the module that defines them; a test fails when one module uses an underscore name of another.

docs.title: Tests first, and two methods for every number
docs.text:
• Write the test first. A bug fix starts with a test that fails on the current code and passes with the fix; say in the pull request that it failed before.
  • Every numerical claim is checked by at least two independent methods: a closed form, an independent formulation of the same model, a second solver, or a measurement. tests/_reference_mna.py, for example, solves the documented model by modified nodal analysis in the physical sign frame, independently of the package's nodal solver. A test that compares the code with a number it produced last month checks nothing.
  • What the documentation states, the tests reproduce: a page that shows a number gets a snippet or a notebook that computes it, and a test that computes it a second way.

docs.title: Changelog, breaking changes and deprecation
docs.text:
Every user-visible change gets an entry under [Unreleased] in CHANGELOG.md, in its category: Breaking, Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, Security, Docs or Internal. An entry starts with a bold sentence that says what changed, then why, with the measured numbers where there are any.

  • A change that can break working user code is listed under Breaking as well, with a migration note that says what to change.
  • A deprecated feature keeps working and emits a DeprecationWarning for at least two releases and six months before it is removed. A renamed parameter keeps its old name as an alias with a warning for that period.

docs.title: Versions and releases
docs.text:
groundinsight uses calendar versioning, YYYY.M.MICRO: the year, the month without a leading zero, and a counter that restarts at 0 every month (2026.11.0, 2026.11.1, 2026.12.0). The maintainer cuts a release with

poetry run python scripts/release.py --dry-run     # show what would happen
poetry run python scripts/release.py               # next calendar version

The script sets the version in every place that records it (the library, CITATION.cff and the GUI distribution), moves the [Unreleased] block of the changelog into a dated section, commits, tags the commit and pushes it. The release workflow then runs the tests on the tagged commit and publishes to PyPI.

docs.title: Formatting and linting
docs.text:
Lint, do not reformat. Do not run a formatter over files your change does not otherwise touch, and keep formatting changes out of functional pull requests: a mass reformat hides the real change from review and from git blame. Match the style of the code around your change.

The two linters are pinned in the dev group, and the CI job lint runs the same two commands; a finding fails the build:

poetry run ruff check src tests scripts gui docs/snippets
poetry run numpydoc lint $(git ls-files 'src/groundinsight/*.py')

Fix a finding by a deliberate edit, not with ruff --fix over code your change does not otherwise touch. A # noqa: <code> carries a one-line reason and stands only where the rule is wrong for that line. tests/test_audit_pass19_standards.py checks what the linters cannot: module headers, docstrings that state the contract and its reason rather than the history, examples for every public object, warnings with a package category, the canonical parameter names, and a complexity ratchet -- no function may become more complex than tests/data/complexity_ratchet.toml records, and an entry goes once its function is back at the limit.

Every warning is an error in the test suite. A test that provokes a package warning asserts it with pytest.warns; where the warning comes with the test's network and the test is about something else, it acknowledges the warning by name with acknowledge(...) from tests/_warning_policy.py, with a one-line reason next to it.

docs.title: Commits and pull requests
docs.text:
• Commit subjects follow Conventional Commits: fix(solver): ..., docs: ..., test: ..., perf(results): .... The body says why.
  • One topic per pull request; the tests and the documentation of a change belong to the same pull request as the change.
  • Run the test suite and the strict documentation build before you ask for a review.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: The package builds on NumPy, SciPy, SymPy, Polars, Pydantic, SQLAlchemy, Matplotlib and further open-source libraries, each under its own license; the metadata of an installed package name it (pip show <package>).

docs.title: Conventions and units
docs.text: The rules on this page change numbers when they are missed: a length in metres instead of kilometres, a peak value where an RMS value belongs, a phase angle read in the wrong frame, a missing fault scaling. Each rule is stated with an example that the test suite recomputes.

docs.title: Units
docs.text: Quantity Unit Where branch length l, Branch.length km formulas, create_branch(length=...) specific earth resistance rho Ω·m specific_earth_resistance of buses and branches, formulas frequency f Hz, as float keys Network.frequencies, Source.values, Fault.scalings, result dictionaries; 0.0 is DC currents A, RMS Source.values, result columns ending in _A voltages, earth potential rise V, RMS uepr, EPR_V, u_earthing impedances Ω per element (per-km value × l for a branch) formulas, grounding_impedance_Ohm, z_earthing phase angles degrees, relative to the phasor reference of the sources result columns ending in _degree time s ResultTransient.time_s, Fault.t_k_s cross-sections, temperatures mm², °C thermal fields of the types

docs.title: Phasors are RMS, waveforms are instantaneous
docs.text:
Every phasor in the stationary model is an RMS phasor: Source.values, the Thévenin voltage, and every phasor in the results. The RMS row of a result frame (is_rms true, frequency_Hz null) combines the frequencies as \(X_\text{RMS} = \sqrt{\sum_f |X(f)|^2}\), with the 0 Hz term entering with its full magnitude.

The transient solvers work with instantaneous values. The waveform factories in gi.waveforms take peak amplitudes: amplitude of sinusoidal_with_dc_offset and of damped_oscillation is the peak of the alternating part, dc_amplitude the initial value of the decaying offset, and step holds its amplitude as an instantaneous level. ResultTransient.epr_t and i_branch_t are instantaneous volts and amperes. To reproduce a stationary run with values={50.0: I}, drive the transient with amplitude=math.sqrt(2) * I:

import math
import groundinsight as gi

station = gi.BusType(name="station", system_type="Station", voltage_level=20.0,
                     impedance_formula="2.0")
line = gi.BranchType(name="line", grounding_conductor=True,
                     self_impedance_formula="(0.2 + j*2*pi*f*1.2e-3)*l",
                     mutual_impedance_formula="0")
net = gi.create_network(name="rms", frequencies=[50.0])
gi.create_bus(name="S", type=station, network=net)
gi.create_bus(name="F", type=station, network=net)
gi.create_branch(name="K", type=line, from_bus="S", to_bus="F", length=2.0, network=net)
gi.create_source(name="Q", bus="S", values={50.0: 1000.0}, network=net)  # 1000 A RMS
gi.create_fault(name="F1", bus="F", scalings={50.0: 1.0}, network=net)
stationary = gi.run_fault(net, "F1")

study = gi.TransientStudy(net, "F1")
study.set_source_waveform("Q", gi.waveforms.sinusoidal_with_dc_offset(
    amplitude=math.sqrt(2) * 1000.0, frequency_hz=50.0))  # peak of 1000 A RMS
study.set_observation(buses=["F"])
transient = study.solve(t_end=0.2, dt=1e-5, solver="fft")

The stationary EPR at F is 382.39 V (RMS). The RMS of the transient EPR over its last period is the same 382.39 V, and its peak is 540.8 V = √2 × 382.39 V. (The FFT solver reminds you with a TransientModelWarning that the window ends while the source is still on; for a steady-state comparison that is intended.) If a data source gives peak amplitudes, divide the alternating components by √2 before filling values; a DC component stays as it is.

docs.title: Signs and phase angles
docs.text:
Magnitudes, RMS values, the reduction factors and the impedances do not depend on a sign convention. Phase angles and the signs of complex results do, and groundinsight uses two frames:

  • Phase and shield currents are reported for the physical fault: the phase current flows from the source to the fault, and ResultBranch.i_s_freq (I_branch_A, I_branch_degree) is the shield current counted positive from from_bus to to_bus.
  • Earth-side quantities — the potentials uepr_freq (EPR_V, EPR_degree, u_earthing), the electrode currents ia_freq (I_bus_A, I_bus_degree) and the injections i_inj_freq (I_inj_A, I_inj_degree) — are reported for a current that enters the earthing network at the source bus and leaves it at the fault bus. That is the reverse of the physical direction, so each of these phasors is the negative of its physical value: add 180° to read the physical phase angle.

Two buses show it. S (electrode 0.5 Ω) feeds 1000 A at 50 Hz to a fault at F (electrode 2 Ω) over a 5 km line with Z_s = (0.2 + 0.4j) Ω/km and Z_m = (0.05 + 0.35j) Ω/km:

import groundinsight as gi

s_type = gi.BusType(name="S", system_type="Substation", voltage_level=20.0,
                    impedance_formula="0.5")
f_type = gi.BusType(name="F", system_type="Station", voltage_level=20.0,
                    impedance_formula="2.0")
line = gi.BranchType(name="line", grounding_conductor=True,
                     self_impedance_formula="(0.2 + 0.4*j)*l",
                     mutual_impedance_formula="(0.05 + 0.35*j)*l")
net = gi.create_network(name="signs", frequencies=[50.0])
gi.create_bus(name="S", type=s_type, network=net)
gi.create_bus(name="F", type=f_type, network=net)
gi.create_branch(name="L", type=line, from_bus="S", to_bus="F", length=5.0, network=net)
gi.create_source(name="Q", bus="S", values={50.0: 1000.0}, network=net)
gi.create_fault(name="F1", bus="F", scalings={50.0: 1.0}, network=net)
result = gi.run_fault(net, "F1")

By hand, with the phase current I = 1000 A from S to F: the shield returns Is = I·(ZS + ZF + Zm)/(ZS + ZF + Zs) = 807.7 + 38.5j A from F to S, the soil carries IE = I − Is = 192.3 − 38.5j A, and the electrodes rise to uF = ZF·IE and uS = −ZS·IE.

Quantity Reported Physical (by hand) Relation EPR at the fault bus F −384.6 + 76.9j V (168.7°) +384.6 − 76.9j V (−11.3°) negated EPR at the source bus S 96.2 − 19.2j V −96.2 + 19.2j V negated electrode current at F −192.3 + 38.5j A +192.3 − 38.5j A negated injection at S / F +1000 A / −1000 A the fault current enters the earthing system at F negated shield current of L (S → F) −807.7 − 38.5j A 807.7 + 38.5j A flowing from F to S same, counted from_bus → to_bus phase current of L +1000 A 1000 A from S to F same

The EPR at the fault bus is therefore reported at about 180° from the source phasor when the earthing is mostly resistive. Model and assumptions describes the shield current in the earth-side frame — positive from to_bus to from_bus — which is the same physical current. The transient time series follow the earth-side frame of the stationary result: with a source waveform √2·I·sin(ωt) and mostly resistive earthing, the EPR at F is negative when the source current peaks.

docs.title: Frequencies, source values and fault scalings
docs.text:
• Network frequencies are floats; integer keys are converted. 0.0 is DC.
  • Source values are given per frequency. An active source that reaches the fault but has no value at any network frequency makes run_fault raise a ValueError that names the source, its keys and the network frequencies — it would contribute 0 A everywhere. A source that misses some network frequencies contributes 0 A at those and is announced once per source and run (InputWarning, code SOURCE_FREQUENCY_GAP). Keys outside the network frequencies are announced when the source is created (SOURCE_FREQUENCY_OUTSIDE_NETWORK) and ignored by the solve.
  • Fault scalings multiply every source current that feeds the fault, per frequency. scalings is optional: left out, None or {} means 1.0 at every frequency. A frequency missing from a non-empty mapping is also scaled with 1.0, and the run announces the gap once (InputWarning, code SCALINGS_INCOMPLETE). Give 0.0: 0.0 to keep a frequency, for example DC, out of a fault. Fault.scaling_at(frequency) returns the factor used.

docs.title: Which reduction factor is which
docs.text:
Field Column of res_all_impedances() Definition Use ResultReductionFactor.value reduction_factor EPR at the fault bus with coupling over EPR without coupling a property of the line: \(\lvert 1 - Z_m/Z_s \rvert\) for one line, independent of the fault-bus electrode ResultReductionFactor.value_current reduction_factor_current \(\lvert I_E \rvert / \lvert 3I_0 \rvert\), earth current over fault current the reduction factor r of EN 50522

The two coincide only for ideally bonded stations. See Compare results with EN 50522 limits and Reduction factors and earthing impedance.

docs.title: Formula syntax
docs.text:
Bus and branch types describe their impedances with formula strings. A formula is evaluated once per network frequency and per element, with the element's own soil resistivity and, for a branch, its length. This page lists what a formula may contain, the limits the formula guard enforces, why that guard exists, and the messages you get when a formula is refused.

How to derive a formula from a cable or electrode data sheet is the subject of the how-to Bus and branch types from data sheets.

docs.title: Where formulas appear
docs.text:
Type Field Unit of the result Used by BusType impedance_formula Ω the frequency-domain solve BusType R_formula, L_formula, C_formula Ω, H, F the transient solvers only BranchType self_impedance_formula Ω per branch the solve (shield–earth loop Z_s) BranchType mutual_impedance_formula Ω per branch the solve (phase–shield coupling Z_m) BranchType phase_impedance_formula Ω per branch the phase-current split in rings and meshes (Z_red) BranchType R_self_formula, L_self_formula, C_self_formula, R_mutual_formula, M_mutual_formula Ω, H, F the transient solvers only

A branch formula gives the impedance of the whole branch: write a per-km expression and multiply it by l.

docs.title: Symbols
docs.text:
Symbol Meaning Unit Available in f frequency Hz bus and branch formulas rho specific earth resistance ρ of the element (specific_earth_resistance of the bus or branch) Ω·m bus and branch formulas l branch length (Branch.length) km only in branch formulas j, I imaginary unit – bus and branch formulas pi π – bus and branch formulas E Euler's number e – bus and branch formulas

Any other name is rejected when the type is created. Names are case-sensitive, and the message suggests the case-insensitive match when there is one (L → l, Rho → rho). A bus has no length, so l in a bus formula is rejected as well, with the hint that it is defined only in branch formulas. Constants such as a screen radius are therefore written as numbers into the formula; the how-to on data sheets builds those strings with a few lines of Python.

docs.title: Numbers and operators
docs.text:
• Numbers are decimal, with an optional exponent: 0.25, 658, 1.5e-3. Hexadecimal, octal and binary literals are refused. Write very small or very large factors with an exponent part, 1e-15 rather than 10**-15.
  • The operators are +, -, *, /, ** and parentheses, plus the comma between the arguments of a call. Nothing else is accepted: no attribute access (.), indexing ([]), comparison, assignment, ;, @, lambda or string literal.
  • Precedence is Python's: ** binds tighter than a leading minus, so -f**2 is −(f²).

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
A name followed by ( must be one of these 28 functions. Every one of them is a SymPy function that is translated to NumPy for the evaluation.

Group Functions roots, exponential, logarithm sqrt, exp, log, ln — log(x) is the natural logarithm, log(x, b) the logarithm to base b, ln is the same as log complex numbers Abs, abs (magnitude), re, im, arg, conjugate, sign trigonometric sin, cos, tan, asin, acos, atan, atan2 hyperbolic sinh, cosh, tanh, asinh, acosh, atanh piecewise Min, Max (at most three arguments each), floor, ceiling

A formula is parsed by SymPy (sympify), compiled with lambdify and evaluated for all network frequencies at once. A result may be complex. Where the evaluation on the real axis returns NaN — the square root or logarithm of a negative number — it is repeated on the complex plane, so sqrt(1 - (f/40)**2) at 50 Hz is 0.75j, as SymPy defines it.

import groundinsight as gi

rod = gi.BusType(
    name="rod 3 m", system_type="Station", voltage_level=20.0,
    impedance_formula="rho/(2*pi*3.0)*(log(4*3.0/0.01) - 1)",
)
cable = gi.BranchType(
    name="illustrative cable", grounding_conductor=True,
    self_impedance_formula="(0.25 + j*2*pi*f*0.4e-3)*l",
    mutual_impedance_formula="(j*2*pi*f*0.35e-3)*l",
)
net = gi.create_network(name="syntax", frequencies=[50.0, 250.0])
bus = gi.create_bus(name="A", type=rod, specific_earth_resistance=100.0, network=net)
print(bus.impedance[50.0])  # 32.31 Ohm, the same at 250 Hz: the formula has no f

docs.title: The open end: "nan"
docs.text: A formula string that is exactly nan — any case, surrounding whitespace allowed — is not evaluated: it stands for an infinite impedance at every frequency. Use it for an open end, for example the self impedance of a broken shield. A formula that merely contains the three letters (resonance) is an ordinary formula.

docs.title: Direct current (f = 0)
docs.text:
0.0 is an ordinary network frequency. Several common formulas cannot be evaluated at 0 Hz as written — Carson's f*log(658*sqrt(rho/f)/r) is 0·∞ there — and the evaluator decides by approaching 0 Hz on 1e-6, 1e-7, 1e-8 Hz:

  • a finite limit (a removable singularity) is used as the value; a conductor then tends to its DC resistance;
  • a growing sequence (a pole, 1/(j*2*pi*f*C)) is an open circuit;
  • a finite reactance that survives at 0 Hz (0.25 + j*0.6) has no physical reading; the real part is used and a DCLimitWarning names the formula;
  • a limit that is still moving over the last decade is used and announced by a DCLimitWarning ("converges only slowly") — unless the step shrinks at least five-fold per decade, which counts as converged however small the value is: anything linear in f shrinks it ten-fold, Carson's pi**2*1e-4*f included, while sqrt(f) (3.2-fold) and log(f) (not at all) are reported;
  • a real part of −∞ — log(f) with no factor f in front — is refused for a bus, a grounding conductor and a source impedance: it is the limit of a negative resistance, not an open circuit. A study that does not list 0 Hz never evaluates it there; a transient study always does.

The how-to on data sheets shows what this means for the Carson formulas (At 0 Hz); the full treatment is in Direct current (f = 0).

docs.title: Why the guard exists
docs.text: Formula strings reach sympy.sympify and sympy.lambdify, and both evaluate Python. Formulas also travel inside files: a JSON project file, a SQLite database, the import defaults of a colleague. Without a check, opening such a file could run arbitrary code, or stall the machine with a short string such as 9**9999999, which SymPy would expand into millions of digits while it parses. The guard therefore checks every formula before SymPy sees it, with Python's own tokenizer: names, calls and operators against the whitelists above, and the size of every number the formula can build against the limits below. A string the tokenizer cannot split is refused rather than passed on. Types are validated wherever they are created, so the same check runs when a network is loaded from JSON or from a database.

docs.title: Resource limits
docs.text:
Limit Value Why characters in a formula string 4096 an impedance formula is a handful of terms digits of a number literal 100 (decimal notation only) SymPy computes with such a number exactly exponent of a power 12 (written out or computed; a power in the exponent is refused) the exponent multiplies the size of an exact result digits of an exact intermediate number 10 000 bounds nested powers and products of exact numbers digits of the integer built by floor/ceiling 100 SymPy evaluates the argument to every digit first argument of exp, sinh, cosh 10100 in magnitude the evaluation cost grows with the argument terms (numbers, names, operations and calls) 512 SymPy simplifies the whole expression while parsing function calls 8 SymPy simplifies every call while parsing arguments of one call 3 Max and Min compare their arguments pairwise

The longest formula in this documentation, the phase impedance of a three-phase cable system in the how-to on data sheets, has 213 characters, 99 terms, 6 calls and exponent 2.

docs.title: Common errors
docs.text:
Mistakes caught when the type is created (the message excerpt is what BranchType(..., self_impedance_formula=<formula>) reports):

Formula Message (excerpt) Remedy rho*L uses the unknown symbol 'L' (did you mean 'l'?) names are case-sensitive x*l uses the unknown symbol 'x' write the value of x as a number 10**-15*f uses the exponent -15 -- above the limit of 12 write 1e-15*f f**f**2 contains a nested exponentiation no power in an exponent eval(rho) calls 'eval', which is not an allowed function only the 28 functions above rho.real contains a disallowed operator '.' write re(rho) f == 50 contains a disallowed operator '==' use Min/Max/sign for case distinctions '1'*l must not contain string literals write the number without quotes 0x10*l hexadecimal, octal or binary literal write 16*l Max(f, rho, l, 1)*l calls Max() with 4 arguments, above the limit of 3 nest: Max(Max(f, rho), Max(l, 1)) exp(1e101)*l evaluates exp() at an argument of up to about 1e101 rescale the argument sqrt(rho*l could not be tokenized close the parenthesis lambda: 1 contains a disallowed name 'lambda' formulas are expressions

Values that are refused when an element is evaluated, here as the impedance_formula of a bus in a 50 Hz network with ρ = 100 Ω·m:

Bus formula Message (excerpt) Remedy 0 It is exactly zero at 50 Hz an ideal earth is a small finite value, e.g. 1e-6 0.05*rho - 10 Its real part is negative the fit is used outside its range; check the lowest ρ

A formula that evaluates to NaN at some frequency — 0/0, 0*log(0) away from 0 Hz, a NaN parameter — is refused with a message that names the formula, the frequency and the parameters. log(0) itself is −∞, and a real part of −∞ is refused as well (at 0 Hz). Check a new formula at the lowest ρ, the lowest frequency and the shortest length of the model.

docs.title: Glossary and symbols
docs.text:
One line per symbol or term, with the field or column where groundinsight reports it. The symbols follow EN 50522 where the standard has one.

Z_B and Z_E are two different impedances

The impedance of a single bus electrode to remote earth is Z_B, never Z_E. Z_E is the earthing impedance of EN 50522: the driving-point impedance of the whole earthing network at the fault location, the electrodes bonded through cable screens and earth wires included. In a cable network it is well below the electrode of the faulted station.

docs.title: Quantities at the fault
docs.text: Symbol or term Meaning In groundinsight EPR earth potential rise: the potential of an earthing system against remote earth ResultBus.uepr, uepr_freq; column EPR_V of res_buses() U_E earth potential rise of the earthing system at the fault location (EN 50522) ResultReductionFactor.u_earthing, equal to the uepr_freq of the fault bus Z_E earthing impedance of EN 50522: the driving-point impedance of the earthing network at the fault bus (electrodes and shields, without coupling and without Thévenin loops) ResultReductionFactor.z_earthing, ResultGroundingImpedance.value Z_G the name of Z_E in the result tables (grounding impedance) columns grounding_impedance_Ohm, grounding_impedance_deg of res_all_impedances() Z_dp driving-point impedance: the voltage at a bus per ampere injected there against remote earth Z_E is Z_dp at the fault bus; gi.bus_response, gi.analyze_cuts I_F, 3I_0 fault current, the earth-fault current 3I_0 of EN 50522: the scaled source currents that reach the fault ResultReductionFactor.i_fault I_E earth current: the part of the fault current that returns through the soil, summed over the electrodes of the earth group ResultReductionFactor.i_earth earth group the buses whose electrodes feed the soil, from the fault outwards up to where the potential profile turns ResultReductionFactor.earth_buses r reduction factor of EN 50522, the earth current over the fault current ResultReductionFactor.value_current; column reduction_factor_current value EPR ratio at the fault bus with and without the inductive coupling; for a single line the magnitude of 1 − k, whatever the electrodes ResultReductionFactor.value; column reduction_factor U_T, U_vT touch voltage and prospective touch voltage not computed; U_E is their upper bound U_Tp permissible touch voltage of EN 50522, a function of the fault duration not part of the package t_F fault duration, set by the protection; the argument of U_Tp not used by the stationary solve T_k short-circuit duration of IEC 60909-0, used by the thermal checks Fault.t_k_s

docs.title: Impedances of the model
docs.text: Symbol or term Meaning In groundinsight Z_B impedance of the electrode of one bus (Erder) to remote earth BusType.impedance_formula, Bus.impedance Z_s self impedance of the shield–earth loop of a branch: cable screen or earth wire with earth return BranchType.self_impedance_formula, Branch.self_impedance Z_m mutual impedance between the loop of the faulted phase and the shield–earth loop, both with earth return BranchType.mutual_impedance_formula, Branch.mutual_impedance k coupling ratio Z_m/Z_s; the shield carries k times the phase current when both ends are ideally bonded – Z_pp self impedance of the phase–earth loop – Z_red phase–earth loop impedance with the shield bonded at both ends, Z_pp − Z_m²/Z_s; what the phase-current split needs BranchType.phase_impedance_formula, Branch.phase_impedance D_E equivalent earth-return depth of Carson's formula, 658·√(ρ/f) m the Carson formulas of the how-to on data sheets GMR geometric mean radius of a conductor or bundle the radius in a Carson formula ρ (rho) specific earth resistance of the soil specific_earth_resistance of buses and branches; formula symbol rho

docs.title: Conductors and terms
docs.text: Symbol or term Meaning In groundinsight earthing conductor the lumped connection (Erdungsleiter) that carries the current between the installation and the earthing system ResultBus.i_inj; columns I_inj_A, I_inj_degree earth electrode the part in the soil (Erder); carries the current that leaves into the soil at this bus ResultBus.ia; columns I_bus_A, I_bus_degree shield, screen metallic screen of a cable, the earthing conductor of a cable branch a branch with grounding_conductor=True earth wire conductor of an overhead line that bonds the towers to the stations a branch with grounding_conductor=True RMS root mean square; every phasor of the stationary model is an RMS phasor, and the RMS rows combine the frequencies as the root of the summed squares column is_rms grounding, earthing the same thing; result names use "grounding", the EN 50522 terms "earthing" –
